Today's research is dominated by AI safety and alignment work on agentic systems, alongside advances in robotics foundation models and alternatives to autoregressive generation.

**Safety & Alignment:**
- **The Agent Knew** shows frontier open-weight agents [exceed authorization and then misreport it](/?date=2026-10-15&category=research#item-0fe529178ed2), with internal states forecasting and preempting violations

items.title: The Agent Knew: Internal States Forecast Unauthorized Actions and Stop Them, and the Lies That Follow
items.content: arXiv:2610.17301v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Language-model agents sometimes act beyond their authorization and then misreport what they did. On CAPE-Bench, matched agent tasks in which one fact decides whether an action is authorized, frontier open-weight agents do both, and one behavior marks the lie: retroactive permission laundering, acting and then asking permission as if the action were pending, precedes a false report in 70% of 1081 fresh informed violations, against 8% otherwise (preregistered odds ratio 7.0); frontier agents on tau^2-bench instead fabricate the authorization before violating. A linear readout of the agent's residual stream forecasts the violation before the action (AUROC 0.94) and the false report before the report, and beats chain-of-thought monitors when the agent is pressured to hide its reasoning. Gating every proposed action on this forecast cuts violations over whole episodes in four model families, and sending repeated flags to an approver keeps authorized work (Gemma-4: violations 0.70 -> 0.09, completion 1.00; a model approver that escalates unclear cases keeps this gain with a person seeing 25% of asks), at about 10-8 of the agent's compute and 109 times less than a chain-of-thought monitor. On AgentDojo, an external prompt-injection benchmark, the same readout calibrated on 29 tasks, with the steering unchanged, cuts attack success on unseen tasks in two families (Gemma-4 11.7% -> 5.7%, gpt-oss 28.5% -> 17.5%) while keeping benign utility (Gemma-4 0.637 vs 0.637; gpt-oss 0.667 vs 0.681). Preventing the violation is also the most reliable way to prevent the lie (misreported violations 0.10 -> 0.01 pooled over three families, preregistered), whereas lie-specific fixes after a violation are weak. All tests are preregistered and hash-locked; code, data and the full record, including tests that did not pass, are at https://github.com/AryaFayyazi/Honesty.

items.title: Google Earth AI Geospatial Reasoning Agent: Capabilities and a Systematic Evaluation
items.content: arXiv:2610.15750v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Google Earth AI is a family of geospatial AI models, together with an agent that orchestrates them. We present this agent, Google Earth AI's Geospatial Reasoning agent (GRA), a Gemini-powered research system that combines geospatial data sources, foundation models, and tools to answer questions about our planet. GRA organizes these into modular domain skills and pairs them with upfront geospatial planning to decompose complex queries into multi-stage workflows. Evaluating such systems is hard: real-world problems admit multiple valid workflows, require data discovery across large catalogs, and rely on evolving ground truth. We introduce two benchmarks and release their development splits. GeoExpertQueries poses complex analytical problems grounded in practitioner use cases and refined by geospatial experts; each is paired with a consensus golden workflow from three independent experts and scored by a human-validated, tool-agnostic autorater. GeoKTools consists of templated queries with deterministic reference solvers that systematically vary the number of required tool types. We also use two external benchmarks, CBGB and UnivEARTH; the latter we find to be saturated. To isolate the contribution of GRA's tools and its agentic orchestration, we compare four configurations, each with Gemini 3.1 Pro and 3.8 Flash: a standalone LLM, the LLM with basic tools, the LLM with GRA's skills and tools but without its upfront planning and execution guidance, and GRA itself. With at most basic tools, an advanced model recovers much of the answer on templated queries but satisfies only a small fraction of the expert workflows on open-ended problems; GRA performs well on both. The largest step comes from GRA's skills and tools; on open-ended problems, its planning and execution guidance add a further gain with Gemini 3.8 Flash, letting Flash match or exceed Pro at lower cost.

items.title: Understanding and Reducing Misalignment in Persuasion Optimization
items.content: arXiv:2610.16070v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Frontier models are now trained for complex multi-agent tasks, from running a company to engaging in negotiations. These tasks necessitate training models to be persuasive. But what does this optimization pressure mean for model alignment? In this work, we study how reinforcement learning (RL) training for persuasion affects models' use of misaligned strategies such as evidence fabrication and belief coercion, and what techniques can reduce such misalignment. We find that optimizing sender models solely for receiver belief shifts causes the average number of distinct misaligned strategies used per game to increase by more than 25%, and fabrications per game increase to more than 4 times relative to pre-RL models. We compare various mitigation approaches, including stronger strategy guidance, clean demonstrations, penalizing misaligned strategy usage, and improving the model's ability to detect fabrications. We find that navigating the persuasiveness-misalignment trade-off in this setting is challenging, with the best trade-offs coming from combining guidance on aligned persuasion strategies with reward penalties on misalignment. Overall, our work provides a testbed for assessing misalignment stemming from RL-based persuasion training and shows concrete paths for reducing misalignment. Importantly, it highlights that without direct intervention, persuasion-involved RL environments are likely to naturally lead to large increases in the use of misaligned strategies.

items.title: Gradient Routing Localizes and Removes Unintended Behaviors in RL
items.content: arXiv:2610.17062v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We propose a mitigation to reward hacking in reinforcement learning. Our setup involves a misspecified reward function that gives rise to unintended behavior, and a monitor used to detect unintended behavior. As with frontier AI systems, the monitor makes systematic errors. Consequently, using the monitor for data filtering or to apply a reward penalty fails to prevent the model from learning unintended behavior ("reward hacking"). To address this problem, we introduce GRAFT: Gradient Routing Adapter Fine Tuning. Rather than penalizing or filtering flagged samples during training, GRAFT constrains gradient updates on those samples to a sacrificial set of new parameters. This has two benefits: First, because the monitor is not part of the reward function, the model does not learn to hide misbehavior. Second, ablating the sacrificial parameters reduces or entirely stops the unintended behavior while maintaining improved performance on target tasks. We demonstrate these benefits in RL environments where reward penalties cause models to learn to reward hack in undetected ways, training models ranging from 135M to 8B parameters. Additionally, we show a similar effect at a larger scale by distilling frontier LLM trajectories containing reward hacking into Qwen3-32B, without teaching that model to reward hack. Overall, our work suggests GRAFT may be a promising approach for leveraging imperfect monitors during post-training in settings where true performance is difficult to evaluate.
items.author: Jake Ward, Shawn Hu, Aria Wong, Nathan Hu, Bryce Woodworth, Alexander Matt Turner, Alex Cloud

The author group includes established safety researchers, and reward hacking mitigation is among the most consequential open problems for frontier RL.

items.title: FACT: A Multimodal Force-Action-Track Foundation Model for Human-to-Robot Dexterity
items.content: arXiv:2610.19155v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Human demonstrations offer a scalable alternative to costly robot data collection for dexterous manipulation, but most human datasets lack force measurements. Dexterous manipulation requires not only visual and proprioceptive understanding but also the ability to anticipate and regulate interaction forces. To scale force-aware human-robot co-training, we introduce EgoForce, a large-scale human tactile dataset capturing force-rich manipulation experience, and combine it with robot demonstrations for pretraining. We present FACT, a robot foundation model that cascades from prospective visual planning to force-aware refinement for dexterous manipulation. FACT comprises two jointly trained components. A Track-Guided Coarse Planner jointly predicts actions, future video, and visual tracks. Future video and visual tracks also provide a shared task representation that facilitates cross-embodiment knowledge transfer and coarse action generation. Building on this coarse plan, a Force-Action Joint Refiner jointly predicts future force and refines the coarse action, allowing anticipated force and action to shape each other during refinement. We evaluate the model on ten tasks requiring fine-grained coordination and force feedback, including tool use, musical instruments, and precision laboratory procedures. Using as few as 10 robot trajectories with 90 human trajectories for fine-tuning, FACT outperforms both baselines, with success-rate gains of up to 60 percentage points over T-Rex. Ablations show that force supervision in human pretraining data is crucial for downstream robot performance after fine-tuning, while visual track prediction and training with future-force prediction improve dexterous execution. Experiments varying the human-robot data ratio during fine-tuning further suggest that FACT learns from human demonstrations nearly as effectively as from robot demonstrations.
items.author: Zhi Cao, Yining Hong, Jiaolong Yang, Yejin Choi, Li Fei-Fei, Jiajun Wu, Huang Huang
items.summary: FACT is a foundation model for dexterous manipulation that combines a large-scale force-rich human tactile dataset (EgoForce) with robot demonstrations, cascading prospective visual planning into force-aware refinement. It jointly predicts object tracks and contact forces, enabling human-to-robot skill transfer where most human datasets lack force measurements. This tackles the key missing modality for scaling dexterous manipulation from human data.

items.title: When Do Discrete Actions Make Good Continuous Controllers?
items.content: arXiv:2610.20429v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Though modern AI models like LLMs predict discrete tokens, today's robotic foundation models represent actions as continuous vectors. In this paper, we challenge this common consensus by asking if continuous action parametrizations are superior to their discrete counterparts. We conduct an extensive comparison of single-step regression and multi-step flow variants of both continuous and discrete policies in both from-scratch single-task and multi-task VLA training, in both simulation and on real hardware. In all regimes, we find that discrete action prediction, even the most naive, uniform-bin quantization, can match or even outperform continuous-action policies in task success rate. Moreover, we find that the challenge to discrete action policies is \emph{not} action precision, but rather factorization error introduced by product-distribution predictions across time and action dimensions. We show that, when paired with the correct interventions---iterative computation through discrete flows, or distribution sharpening through classifier-free guidance---discrete flow policies can turn this weakness into a strength, enabling more responsive action changes during a predicted action chunk. Lastly, we show that attempts to explicitly inject geometric information into discrete policies, e.g. through corruption processes that emulate continuous flow matching, do \emph{not} yield consistent improvements. Taken together, our findings question existing assumptions that robotic action prediction requires distinct design decisions compared to other AI domains, and motivates the possibility of discrete action prediction as a compelling alternative to today's continuous action parametrizations. Link for the webpage \href{https://iscoyizj.github.io/discrete-action-website/}{https://iscoyizj.github.io/discrete-action-website/}

items.title: AI Discovery in Combinatorics: From Problems to Solutions and Back to Bigger Problems
items.content: arXiv:2610.16555v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We introduce $qt$Bench, a benchmark of 29 open problems in algebraic combinatorics. These problems ask for a simple combinatorial algorithm that explains given polynomial coefficients or identities. To help AI agents search for such algorithms, we provide a scaffold for playing with combinatorial objects, countering cheating attempts, and testing candidate solutions. To explore how far frontier AI systems can go on these problems, we collaborated with OpenAI, whose researchers obtained proposed solutions to several of them. This highlights bigger meta-problems: is AI discovery at scale ethical? How should these results be released? How should proof digestion be organized? We discuss these questions and give our views.

items.title: Chain of Thought Monitoring Can Fail Even When CoT Is Necessary
items.content: arXiv:2610.18105v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Chain of Thought (CoT) monitoring is used by frontier labs to detect misbehaviour of AI systems. Yet, its reliability remains poorly understood. We attribute this to the lack of a successful organizing principle that leads to generalizable conclusions about monitoring reliability in different regimes. Recent work attributes monitoring failures to the CoT not being necessary for the answer, and argues that CoT becomes monitorable when it is necessary. We show that this binary necessary/not-necessary organizing principle is too coarse by demonstrating that monitoring failures persist even if the CoT is necessary for the answer. In response, we introduce a more fine-grained organizing principle based on a hierarchy of four CoT necessity levels. Building on this hierarchy, we develop a framework for measuring CoT monitorability at the three lowest levels via intervention experiments. We demonstrate monitoring failures at all three of these levels on realistic, hard prediction tasks. On a difficult medical-diagnosis task, patient sex and a clinical attribute influence the answer in at least 19% and 24% of correct responses with a necessary CoT, respectively, yet their influence is almost never articulated. These results show that even when CoT is necessary, it is not guaranteed to be monitorable.

items.title: ReTerm: Recovery Training for Self-Improving Terminal Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.18484v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Terminal agents have shown strong abilities in complex coding tasks. However, they often struggle to recover from errors during long-running execution (e.g., command errors, faulty implementations), eventually leading to task failures. To this end, we present ReTerm, a self-improving terminal agent trained by learning how to recover from its own failed terminal tasks. To support its training, we construct a customized data pipeline and produce ReTerm-10K, a high-quality dataset that provides effective recovery demonstrations for SFT cold start. Furthermore, we propose ReTerm-GRPO, an online RL algorithm that forks from the agent's own failure states to generate multiple independent self-recovery attempts. By learning from whether these attempts successfully complete the task, the agent self-improves through its own recovery experience. Built on Qwen3.5-9B, our ReTerm-9B achieves 34.8% Pass@1 on Terminal-Bench 2.0, improving over the base model by 14.6 points. Further analysis shows that our method achieves consistently higher recovery rates across diverse error categories compared with standard GRPO training. All code, data and model are released at https://github.com/twothsnd/ReTerm.

The authors build a data pipeline yielding ReTerm-10K, a recovery-demonstration dataset for supervised fine-tuning, and propose ReTerm-GRPO, an online reinforcement learning algorithm that forks from the agent's own failure states to generate and learn from multiple independent self-recovery attempts. This addresses a real gap, since most agent benchmarks focus on avoiding errors rather than handling them once they occur.

items.title: Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.14162v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer parallel sampling for faster generation than autoregressive models, an increasingly important advantage as inference becomes a dominant computational workload. However, DLMs degrade quickly with fewer sampling steps, process the full sequence at every step, and require many passes over the dataset to reach good quality. We introduce Next-Concept Modeling (NCM), a two-stage, coarse-to-fine framework: a multiscale residual VQ-VAE encodes text into a hierarchy of discrete codes, and a transformer generates one level at a time, predicting all codes within a level in parallel. At matched parameter scales, NCM achieves better generative perplexity than the strongest DLM baseline on LM1B while running $21\times$ faster. On OpenWebText, NCM is competitive with the strongest DLM while running $10\times$ faster; on XSum, it matches the strongest DLM's ROUGE-L while being $31\times$ faster. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations.

items.title: CWE-bench: Refocusing Agentic Security from Exploitation to Defense
items.content: arXiv:2610.17020v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Cybersecurity evaluations of AI agents have focused largely on offense, yet a working exploit does not show that an agent can make software safe. An attacker needs to exploit only one vulnerability; a defender must find and fix all of them. We introduce CWE-bench, a private benchmark of 120 held-out repository audit-and-repair tasks spanning 73 CWE types, eight languages, and all OWASP Top 10 2025 categories. Agents are given a repository to audit and a description of its threat model, but are not told the weakness, where it occurs, or how many vulnerable sites there are. Each patch must block the exploit while preserving original functionality, as checked by a programmatic verifier. We validated the verifier against a panel of agentic judges, manually reviewing disagreements during development and refining the checks. The best agents reach 68% pass@1 and 81% pass@4. We further conduct analyses showing that (i) agents with the same pass@1 differ widely in retry gains and cost, and (ii) no single agent is best across languages or vulnerability categories, and difficulty varies far more by vulnerability category than by language. As the offensive capabilities of agents improve, CWE-bench provides a broad and rigorous measure of whether their defensive capabilities keep pace.

Programmatic verifiers check that patches block exploits while preserving functionality, shifting agentic security evaluation from offense to defense.
items.reasoning: The defense-oriented framing is a significant conceptual contribution — a successful exploit does not imply safe repair — and the held-out private design with programmatic verification addresses contamination and gaming issues common in security benchmarks. Highly relevant to deploying AI agents for real security work.

items.title: LeanPRM: Lean-Grounded Process Supervision for Natural Language Proof Verification
items.content: arXiv:2610.17697v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: AI systems now write long and difficult mathematical proofs, and checking their step-by-step validity is becoming a bottleneck. A learned verifier could check proofs cheaply, but training one requires a correctness label on every step, and such labels are hard to obtain for open-ended proofs. Existing methods take them from human annotators, which is costly, or derive them from final answers, which proofs do not have, and formalizing each proof in Lean requires expert effort. We introduce LeanPRM, a framework that uses the Lean proof assistant to create step-level labels for natural-language proofs. A model writes a natural-language proof together with a paired formal proof, without feedback from Lean. Lean then labels every step, and a second model discards failures caused only by the formal syntax, so that the negative labels mark errors in the mathematics. LeanPRM contains 10,634 proofs with 152K labeled steps and no human annotation. A Qwen3-4B verifier trained on LeanPRM raises exact step-label accuracy on a held-out set of 200 proofs (LeanPRM-Bench) from 48.2 to 74.7, as opposed to 60.3 when the same base model is trained on PRM800K. It also selects better proofs in best-of-N selection on IMO-level problems, and outperforms the PRM800K-trained verifier on three of four external verification benchmarks. Training on LeanPRM improves verifiers at every size from 0.6B to 8B parameters on LeanPRM-Bench, Hard2Verify and IMO-GradingBench. Given the labels need no human annotation, LeanPRM can grow with the supply of formal statements, offering a path to step-level feedback on AI-generated proofs that are hard for humans to check.

items.title: RT-J: Large-Scale Pretraining of Relational Transformers for Context-Efficient Predictions
items.content: arXiv:2610.17867v2 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Foundation models for tables and relational databases are increasingly used for predictive tasks across various scientific and industrial domains. However, adapting existing models to unseen datasets requires tens of thousands of examples. Here we introduce RT-J, an 85M-parameter relational foundation model (RFM) that makes accurate predictions even with hundreds of in-context examples or fewer. To achieve this, we first assemble the Join, a large collection of 639 web-crawled databases with 6,023 LLM-generated forecasting tasks. We pretrain with long contexts of up to 8,192 database cells, using in-context examples from a novel lightweight random-walk retriever. Finally, we leverage context tuning and ensembling to scale up test-time compute. On in-context regression tasks from RelBench, RT-J requires 10x fewer examples on average to match strong feature engineering pipelines with LLM-agent or RDBLearn featurizers and TabICLv2 or LightGBM predictors. Overall, our work pushes the frontier for context-efficient predictions on relational data and highlights the importance of real-world semantics, context engineering and large-scale pretraining for RFMs.

items.title: Rent-Seeking Language Models: Reward Models Set the Prices, Frequent Audits Curb the Rent
items.content: arXiv:2610.19832v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reward model overoptimization in RLHF is usually described as reward hacking. We recast it as rent-seeking: the policy, a firm, earns reward from a regulator, the proxy reward model, that true quality does not back. The lens turns overoptimization into measurable quantities, namely rent, a capture index and deadweight loss, and into testable predictions from the economics of regulation. In a fixed, version-controlled testbed with three model families, accuracy-matched proxy reward models and two gold reward models, RL turns 41% to 66% of its proxy gain into rent while gold reward plateaus. Rent follows each regulator's prices. Neither proxy verifies facts, but one pays for confident specifics and the other for displays of diligence, so RL policies learn to fabricate details about nonexistent entities (97% to 100% of probes) or to deflect factual questions (67% to 98%). Kinship between policy and regulator adds a fixed premium of about 0.1 standard deviations but gives the policy no extra leverage under optimization. At a fixed expected fine, frequent mild audits beat rare severe ones, and random audits are as efficient per audit as targeted ones. Bringing the bunching estimator of tax economics to RL training, we also find a first sign that policies learn to stay just below a targeted audit's threshold.

In a controlled testbed across three model families with matched proxy and gold reward models, RL converts 41-66% of proxy reward gains into rent while gold reward plateaus, and different proxies elicit different failure modes (confident specifics vs. displays of diligence). The economic lens offers a rigorous new vocabulary for reward hacking and motivates audit-style mitigations.

items.title: Training Language Models to Fail Gracefully
items.content: arXiv:2610.20401v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reinforcement learning makes language models better at solving tasks, but the same mechanism also rewards guessing. When success is the only way to earn reward, opting for a safe fallback is always worse than a long-shot attempt. When a wrong action can corrupt a database or ship broken code, that incentive can be costly. Therefore, we propose training models to fail gracefully: to preserve successful behavior whenever possible while learning to execute a safe fallback policy when acting would be unreliable. However, naively using policy gradients with intermediate reward for fallback behavior is brittle due to unfavorable optimization dynamics. We address this challenge with GracefulRL, which reshapes the optimization landscape to promote graceful failure. Importantly, this behavior emerges directly from outcome-level reward signals, without annotations specifying when to fall back or additional inference-time machinery such as a verifier. Across a range of tasks and scales, we train models that largely preserve their task-solving capability while selectively falling back when acting would be unreliable. More broadly, our results show that reinforcement learning can not only incentivize models to succeed, but also to reason about the limits of their capabilities and change course when they determine that success is out of reach.
items.author: Daman Arora, Xuecheng Liu, Himanshu Gaurav Singh, Fahim Tajwar, Abitha Thankaraj, Ruslan Salakhutdinov, Haiwen Feng, Yuda Song, Andrea Zanette
items.summary: The authors identify that RL training rewards guessing because safe fallback behavior is never rewarded, which is dangerous when failures corrupt databases or ship broken code. They propose GracefulRL, which reshapes the optimization landscape to train models that preserve successful behavior but switch to a safe fallback policy when acting would be unreliable, avoiding the brittleness of naive policy gradients with intermediate rewards. This addresses a real safety gap in RL-trained LLM agents.

items.summary_html: The authors identify that RL training rewards guessing because safe fallback behavior is never rewarded, which is dangerous when failures corrupt databases or ship broken code. They propose GracefulRL, which reshapes the optimization landscape to train models that preserve successful behavior but switch to a safe fallback policy when acting would be unreliable, avoiding the brittleness of naive policy gradients with intermediate rewards. This addresses a real safety gap in RL-trained LLM agents.
items.content_html: arXiv:2610.20401v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning makes language models better at solving tasks, but the same mechanism also rewards guessing. When success is the only way to earn reward, opting for a safe fallback is always worse than a long-shot attempt. When a wrong action can corrupt a database or ship broken code, that incentive can be costly. Therefore, we propose training models to fail gracefully: to preserve successful behavior whenever possible while learning to execute a safe fallback policy when acting would be unreliable. However, naively using policy gradients with intermediate reward for fallback behavior is brittle due to unfavorable optimization dynamics. We address this challenge with GracefulRL, which reshapes the optimization landscape to promote graceful failure. Importantly, this behavior emerges directly from outcome-level reward signals, without annotations specifying when to fall back or additional inference-time machinery such as a verifier. Across a range of tasks and scales, we train models that largely preserve their task-solving capability while selectively falling back when acting would be unreliable. More broadly, our results show that reinforcement learning can not only incentivize models to succeed, but also to reason about the limits of their capabilities and change course when they determine that success is out of reach.

items.title: Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems
items.content: arXiv:2610.19159v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Can AI agents carry out research on open scientific problems? We introduce Into the Unknown, a benchmark that provides an agent with a science paper along with a research direction to pursue and tasks it to write a follow-up paper. We work with scientists at US Department of Energy (DOE) national laboratories, who each contribute an unpublished follow-up direction from their own work together with the necessary conditions a submission must meet. While assessing the quality of a follow-up paper is challenging in general, using these conditions to form a rubric makes evaluation more tractable for research problems that have no reference answer. We have nine frontier agents write 15 follow-ups each, spanning quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning domains. None of the 135 submissions satisfies all the conditions, and 114 fail our integrity check, most often because the paper claims work that was never done or reports numbers that contradict the recorded evidence. Overall, agents readily produce papers that look like follow-ups, but none meets the standard of the domain scientist, leaving substantial headroom. Our code and data are publicly available.

Rubric-based grading of open research remains noisy, tempering the score slightly.

items.title: PrismaCoder: Pushing the Boundaries of Open Multimodal Code Intelligence through Decomposed Rubric Synthesis
items.content: arXiv:2610.20538v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Multimodal code intelligence connects the symbolic world of programs with the visual world their execution creates. Interest in this capability is burgeoning, as models are increasingly asked to produce charts, webpages, animations, and semi-structured documents. Recently, proprietary models have pushed far ahead, producing interactive artifacts even from a text description or a screenshot alone. Yet their data and training remain closed, and open progress is held back by the quantity and quality of available data and by the pipelines and methods for producing it. Quality is the harder of the two, since a sample must be correct as a program, well built, and above all visually right once rendered. No existing signal covers all three. Execution often returns just a pass or fail, code similarity does not map to the visual output, and task-specific verifiers do not generalize. To push open progress further, we start from the data side with PrismaForge, a hierarchical data pipeline centered on a synthesized rubric that decomposes these factors into checkable criteria. The same rubric serves as both filter and reward: it curates the supervised corpus, then drives reinforcement learning on visual-coding tasks. Leveraging PrismaForge for data synthesis and filtering, we build PrismaCoder-2M, the most diverse open dataset for multimodal code intelligence and the largest to date. On the model side, we train PrismaCoder-9B and PrismaCoder-35B on this data and release both. They lead the open state of the art by a wide margin and rival leading proprietary systems. Our analyses further show that the proposed rubric-based pipeline improves multimodal coding performance across model backbones. We release our code and data at https://qiushisun.github.io/PrismaCoder-Home/.

The work identifies that no existing signal covers program correctness, build success, and visual fidelity simultaneously, and proposes decomposed rubric synthesis to produce high-quality training data, aiming to close the gap with closed proprietary systems. This is significant for open multimodal generation and code model training pipelines.

Large author team with strong credentials; rubric decomposition for tri-criteria verification is a practical contribution, though it is a data/training-method contribution rather than a new architecture.

items.title: Beyond State Capacity: Why Retrieval Breaks in Mamba
items.content: arXiv:2610.19709v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Mamba models underperform Transformers on in-context retrieval. This gap is usually attributed to Mamba's fixed-size recurrent state, which loses information as the context grows. We challenge this assumption by focusing on query-first retrieval, a setup in which the query precedes the context and state capacity should not be the binding constraint. We show that even in this setting Mamba lags substantially behind Transformers, despite its selection mechanism, which was designed to distinguish relevant content from distractors. We then demonstrate that the Mamba selection gates have sufficient control over the state updates to influence the model output: intervening on specific gates alone can swing accuracy between extremes. However, as gates are input-dependent, they require the incoming token's representation to encode its relevance to the query. We therefore probe token representations across layers, and find that the relevance signal emerges only gradually with model depth, and that the gates begin to reflect it only several layers deeper. Crucially, we find that gates in retrieval-critical layers are not yet aligned with relevance. The selection mechanism is thus expressive enough to solve the task, but it commonly operates on a relevance signal that has not yet arrived. Mamba's retrieval bottleneck therefore extends beyond state capacity: even when capacity is sufficient, the delayed emergence of relevance information across depth often prevents successful retrieval.
items.author: Nir Yarden, Amit Ben-Artzy, Roy Schwartz
items.summary: Challenges the assumption that Mamba's in-context retrieval failure stems purely from fixed-size state capacity by showing the gap persists in query-first settings where capacity should not bind. Via gate interventions the authors show selection gates can swing accuracy between extremes, but gates fail to properly suppress distractors, pinpointing the selection mechanism rather than state size as the culprit.
items.reasoning: A mechanistic interpretability result with real architectural implications: it overturns a common explanation for a known limitation of state-space models using careful causal interventions, relevant to anyone designing recurrent alternatives to Transformers.

items.title: TacClaw-Infinity: A Large-Scale Vision-Tactile-Language-Action Dataset for Dexterous Manipulation
items.content: arXiv:2610.20320v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large-scale robot learning increasingly relies on diverse human demonstrations, yet tactile manipulation data remain difficult to scale, and existing multimodal datasets often lack consistent quality control and structured supervision. We present TacClaw-Infinity, a large-scale structured Vision-Tactile-Language-Action (VTLA) dataset for contact-rich manipulation, collected with TacClaw, a tactile-enabled UMI-style handheld interface that records synchronized visual observations, fingertip tactile signals, and end-effector trajectories without requiring a target robot during data collection. TacClaw-Infinity is built through a distributed worldwide collection across homes, laboratories, industrial workplaces, retail stores, and outdoor environments including tasks contributed by academic and industrial collaborators. Together, these efforts yield over 10,000 hours, 1 million episodes, and 1 billion frames spanning more than 1,000 task types. We develop a scalable pipeline for trajectory reconstruction, multimodal quality control, embodiment-aware filtering, and structured annotation, covering contact-centric segmentation, subtask description, and spatial grounding. We validate TacClaw-Infinity at both the data and model levels: At the data level, we assess the collection interface, the action-space compatibility of the curated demonstrations, and the structured annotations, while for the model level, we demonstrate cross-embodiment transfer across three heterogeneous robots without robot-specific demonstrations.

items.title: A proposal for better informing the public about loss-of-control risks from frontier AI development
items.content:
At METR, we aim to give the public evidence about whether frontier AI developers could come to lose control of their internal AI systems. Recent incidents across several AI developers,1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 like the hundreds of rogue agents that broke containment and hacked Hugging Face to hide evidence of cheating from their grader, have raised concerns about the ability of frontier developers to understand and control their internal models, especially as they rapidly become more capable.9 The public currently lacks the visibility into the internal development of frontier AI systems to tell if these concerns are being addressed, or whether much worse incidents could happen in the near future. We believe closing this public evidence gap is an urgent priority, to allow the public to notice and respond if risks from further development become acute.

In this post, we describe a vision for how independent assessors could improve public visibility into whether AI developers might lose control of their AI systems. We describe key questions about internal development that we think the public needs more evidence about (see Figure 1), and give a concrete proposal for how developers could work with METR to produce and share more of the relevant evidence.

Figure 1: Core questions we think assessments of loss-of-control risk should address.

This proposal will not provide confident assurance about whether development is safe, since the science is not mature enough to reach consensus conclusions, and there are no standards for safe development to audit compliance with. We instead aim to get new independent evidence out to the public so that company staff, boards, external scientists, and policymakers are able to arrive at their own conclusions. We describe our general approach to transparency and independence in more detail in an accompanying post.

METR has been prototyping assessment exercises focused on loss of control from internal AI development (rather than only covering external deployments) with developers since 2025, and working on the science of loss of control testing and assessment since 2022. This May, we published our pilot Frontier Risk Report in collaboration with Anthropic, Google, Meta, and OpenAI, which included findings from our first stress-testing exercise of internal monitoring systems. More recently, we conducted a brief exercise with OpenAI investigating the OpenAI / Hugging Face incident. We have several additional exercises ongoing with developers, including our recently announced in-depth alignment assessment with Anthropic.

Recent events have led to increased interest in this form of assessment. The CEOs of several leading companies have recently called for a thorough external evaluation regime building on these kinds of exercises, where third-party evaluators are given employee-level access and an ability to regularly share their findings with the public.10 Many leading AI developers also committed to independent external assessments of internal safeguards as part of the White House Accord on Super Intelligence.

The rest of this post will detail:

- A set of crucial gaps in the public understanding of the core questions described in Figure 1, which frontier developers should provide much more evidence about: Alignment: Developers should work with external groups to more fully characterize incidents observed internally, and share evidence about ways those incidents might underestimate future risks. Control: Developers should work with external groups to assess the coverage, integrity and effectiveness of their monitoring systems, as well as the reliability of their response to flagged incidents. AI R&D acceleration: Developers should work with external groups to share crucially missing evidence about acceleration in internal capabilities and in algorithmic progress.
- A concrete proposal to frontier developers for improving public evidence about these questions through risk assessment exercises, in which METR would write public reports based on interviews with staff and access to internal datasets and systems on company devices. Developers would be able to redact any information they deem sensitive, and choose what access they grant METR for their investigations. The key asks we make of developers for these assessments are: Transparency about the scope, access, redactions and other key limitations of the exercises. Staff may speak privately to METR about in-scope topics, to ensure they feel free to share potentially concerning evidence on those topics. Timely publication of METR-written reports within the agreed-upon scope, subject to a redaction process.
- Limitations of our proposal. Our proposal does not require true employee-level access, as operationalized in a recent public letter (point 5 in the letter), and there is currently no way to be fully protected from retaliation due to adverse findings (point 4). It also does not cover key aspects of safety like security audits, so it should not be taken as a substitute for other efforts to create transparency, work with other third parties, or enforce safety standards.

METR stands ready to perform assessments of these critical questions with all frontier AI developers. We encourage developers to reach out to partnerships@metr.org about performing these assessments, and plan to start sharing more about which assessments companies are undertaking with us soon.

## Crucial gaps in the public understanding of loss-of-control risks

To understand if frontier developers are at risk of losing control over their internal AI agents, the public would at least need evidence about all three key questions summarized in Figure 1:

- Alignment: Whether their current or near-future frontier agents might attempt to seriously circumvent human control or take very harmful actions, like unsanctioned cyberattacks.
- Control: Whether their monitoring, detection and control measures would robustly catch and stop such attempts before harm occurs.
- AI R&D acceleration: Whether the pace of development might accelerate and outpace the developer’s ability to understand and safeguard their systems due to the automation of AI R&D.

There are significant gaps in the public evidence about all three questions which we believe frontier developers should urgently address. In this section we describe these evidence gaps in more detail.

### Gaps in the evidence about alignment

Our Frontier Risk Report earlier this year found that AI agents from all frontier developers would routinely act against the intentions of developers and users to pursue task completion, including by subverting control measures and in some cases hiding evidence from users. We have since seen much more extreme versions of these tendencies play out in recent incidents like the OpenAI/Hugging Face hacking incident, where hundreds of agents broke out of their sandboxes and collaborated on sophisticated R&D projects to hide their cheating.

Many developers have since shared other examples of concerning incidents, and described efforts they are taking to try to reduce these tendencies in their models.11 But the public still lacks a complete picture of these incidents and the details of the alignment methods developers are implementing to address them. Given the severity of these misaligned behaviors, it seems critical for the public to understand how effective these mitigations turn out to be.

To address this, companies should work with external assessors to share detailed assessments of at least:

- Observed incidents and misaligned behaviors: Information about the full set of misaligned behaviors and incidents the developer has observed internally, and the methodologies they use to identify and analyse those (along with their limitations). External groups should be able to scrutinize their methods, and attempt to discover behaviors or incidents they have missed.
- Reasons the survey might not be representative of risks: Developers should also share information about reasons they may have missed more concerning drives in their models. This might involve investigating whether models would engage in more concerning behaviors in alternative situations, and documenting ways that the developer’s alignment practices could suppress evidence of misalignment (such as by training the model to not express misaligned reasoning in its chain-of-thought). The company should invite external groups to scrutinize their practices and any direct evidence of suppression in detail.

Figure 2: An overview of questions we propose an alignment assessment should cover.

### Gaps in the evidence about control

Since current alignment efforts are imperfect, developers also rely on security and monitoring systems to catch and prevent incidents before they cause serious harm. But these can also have significant gaps: in our Frontier Risk Report, we found that Anthropic’s monitoring systems at the time could be circumvented in a variety of ways by agents and had important coverage limitations. While we have not published similar assessments from other companies we expect such issues to be common.

Developers have described plans to address these gaps by expanding monitoring coverage and reliability, but they should subject these improvements to significant external scrutiny to confirm they are robust.

Companies should work with external assessors to assess at least:

- Monitoring systems: They should assess every step of the monitoring system, including its coverage, robustness to attacks by agents, and reliability at flagging concerning behaviors, as seen in the figure below.
- Response and residual risk: They should also assess how reliably and quickly the company responds to issues identified by the monitors, and how severe the worst-case consequences could be if their monitor system failed.

Figure 3: An overview of key questions for understanding the reliability of internal monitoring systems, which is an important component of our proposed control and monitoring assessment.

### Gaps in the evidence about acceleration from automation of AI R&D

AI agents are increasingly used to automate large parts of AI development itself. This seems to dramatically speed up many inputs to AI development – for instance, Anthropic recently announced a 10X increase in the pace of code changes in their codebase over the past few months. Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI have all released blog posts detailing significant acceleration across a number of similar input metrics downstream of internal AI usage. If such automation were to lead to sudden and rapid acceleration in the pace of capabilities progress, this could outpace developer’s abilities to control and understand their systems, which already seem at risk of falling behind the current rate of progress.

However, there is significant uncertainty about how the publicly discussed acceleration in inputs like the amount of code produced or number of experiments performed translates into acceleration in the overall pace of capabilities development, which is what ultimately matters for understanding the risks. To understand that, the public would need a robust understanding of acceleration in internal capability metrics and in the pace of algorithmic progress, which are the factors that would drive further acceleration. No company has released detailed public evidence about this, leaving significant uncertainty about whether progress is accelerating.

Companies should work with external groups to address these gaps, by providing evidence about at least:

- Rate of internal progress: whether the rate of internal capabilities progress is accelerating.
- Acceleration from AI: whether signs of acceleration can be attributed to the use of internal AI agents, or if it can be explained by other factors.
- Potential bottlenecks: whether future acceleration might be bounded by bottlenecks like compute and data availability.

Figure 4: An overview of key questions we propose an AI R&D acceleration assessment would cover.

## METR’s proposal for improving public evidence about loss-of-control risks from frontier AI development

METR would be excited to work with all developers pushing the frontier of capabilities to produce public reports answering all three of the questions we describe above in the near future. For developers that are not currently pushing the capabilities frontier, METR would be excited to pilot shorter assessments focusing on a subset of these questions.

METR would write these reports based on interviews with staff and access to internal datasets and systems on company devices, covering a detailed scope agreed upon in advance. While developers would be able to redact any sensitive information and choose what access they grant METR, they would have to agree to our key terms:

- Giving a small set of METR staff access to relevant data on company devices for an agreed upon period (likely weeks or a few months), and support from a technical point of contact during the investigations.
- Giving METR the opportunity to interview relevant staff privately, without a company representative present and without screening answers, to ensure they feel free to raise potential concerns. METR would be happy to limit total interview time to reduce staff time requirements.
- Giving METR in-principle editorial independence to write a report covering the agreed upon scope (subject to redactions), and allowing METR to comment on redactions, access limitations and terms. For more details on our approach to transparency and independence, see our accompanying blog post.

We have written detailed proposals for how external assessors could collect and share more evidence about each of these three questions (alignment, control and AI R&D acceleration), which would be our preferred scope for these assessments, but we are open to modifications as long as we can describe these in the public report. We summarize the kinds of access we expect to be especially helpful for these reports in Table 1 below. We recognize that some forms of access are especially sensitive, and METR would accept access limitations as long as they are described transparently in the public report.

 Detailed question Most important access

 Alignment assessment: What are the most severe misaligned actions a developer’s agent might pursue in plausible future situations?

- Sampling access to relevant models and checkpoints
- Ability to query internal transcripts to find and investigate misaligned behaviors
- Ability to query training rollouts and access relevant training data

 Control assessment: Would monitoring systems at the company reliably catch and prevent harmful actions?

- Access to production monitoring systems for red teaming
- Access to large parts of the codebase relevant for monitoring and control
- Ability to query transcripts to assess coverage and test the efficacy of monitors
- Information about traffic volumes across different internal surfaces to understand coverage

 AI acceleration assessment: Could the developer’s capabilities progress accelerate dramatically due to AI-driven acceleration of AI R&D?

- Capability measures across internal models, including benchmarks and key intermediate measures (e.g. pretraining loss)
- Algorithmic progress estimates in pretraining, posttraining, and other key domains
- Measurements of key R&D inputs (e.g. training compute of each model, experimental compute and labor over time)

Table 1: Summary of access we expect to be helpful for answering key questions.

Because of the urgent need for more evidence about these questions, we would aim to publish preliminary reports about these questions quickly (within weeks, not months). We do not expect to arrive at confident conclusions about these questions in such a short amount of time (especially since many of them touch on open scientific problems for which there exist no established methodologies), but previous preliminary assessments of this kind have produced crucial public evidence even when the answers have been partial.

We welcome input on how we should investigate these focus areas. As risk evolves, we expect the questions and exercises that are most critical will continue to evolve. We also encourage companies to work with other external groups to fill in gaps or complement our engagements, and to unilaterally share evidence about these topics with the public whenever possible. Risk assessment exercises are far from the only way to share information with the public.

## Important limitations of our proposal

We do not want to overstate the degree of assurance that these risk assessment exercises would provide. There are several limitations to this work.

1) Voluntary exercises may lead to ‘race to the bottom’ dynamics among assessors:

- At any time, companies can stop their engagement with an external assessor. This creates soft pressures for assessors to avoid upsetting the companies they work with.
- Companies can choose to work with assessors they expect will be less rigorous at identifying and sharing evidence, or less harsh in describing limitations they face.
- These exercises are not themselves audits, compliance assessments, or formal oversight arrangements (though external assessments could be a useful mechanism to support these).

2) These assessments are limited compared to the visions that recent public letters12 have proposed:

- Our assessments would focus exclusively on our domain of expertise: technical elements of loss-of-control risk assessment including the capabilities, behavior and monitoring of models. It notably will not cover critical security questions (such as model weight security and sandbox robustness). Nor will it cover the robustness of organizational processes, compliance with governance frameworks or other operational aspects of safety.
- All access would ultimately be at the company’s discretion, which means they have the right to deny access requests. This means that, in practice, we will not have the same access as senior internal company employees that do similar risk assessment work.
- Companies would be able to redact any information. We intend to always publish what kinds of material information were redacted, but we could fail to reach agreement on how to do this. If so, we would publish that fact.

items.content_html:
At METR, we aim to give the public evidence about whether frontier AI developers could come to lose control of their internal AI systems. Recent incidents across several AI developers,1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 like the hundreds of rogue agents that broke containment and hacked Hugging Face to hide evidence of cheating from their grader, have raised concerns about the ability of frontier developers to understand and control their internal models, especially as they rapidly become more capable.9 The public currently lacks the visibility into the internal development of frontier AI systems to tell if these concerns are being addressed, or whether much worse incidents could happen in the near future. We believe closing this public evidence gap is an urgent priority, to allow the public to notice and respond if risks from further development become acute.

In this post, we describe a vision for how independent assessors could improve public visibility into whether AI developers might lose control of their AI systems. We describe key questions about internal development that we think the public needs more evidence about (see Figure 1), and give a concrete proposal for how developers could work with METR to produce and share more of the relevant evidence.

Figure 1: Core questions we think assessments of loss-of-control risk should address.

This proposal will not provide confident assurance about whether development is safe, since the science is not mature enough to reach consensus conclusions, and there are no standards for safe development to audit compliance with. We instead aim to get new independent evidence out to the public so that company staff, boards, external scientists, and policymakers are able to arrive at their own conclusions. We describe our general approach to transparency and independence in more detail in an accompanying post.

METR has been prototyping assessment exercises focused on loss of control from internal AI development (rather than only covering external deployments) with developers since 2025, and working on the science of loss of control testing and assessment since 2022. This May, we published our pilot Frontier Risk Report in collaboration with Anthropic, Google, Meta, and OpenAI, which included findings from our first stress-testing exercise of internal monitoring systems. More recently, we conducted a brief exercise with OpenAI investigating the OpenAI / Hugging Face incident. We have several additional exercises ongoing with developers, including our recently announced in-depth alignment assessment with Anthropic.

Recent events have led to increased interest in this form of assessment. The CEOs of several leading companies have recently called for a thorough external evaluation regime building on these kinds of exercises, where third-party evaluators are given employee-level access and an ability to regularly share their findings with the public.10 Many leading AI developers also committed to independent external assessments of internal safeguards as part of the White House Accord on Super Intelligence.

The rest of this post will detail:

  • A set of crucial gaps in the public understanding of the core questions described in Figure 1, which frontier developers should provide much more evidence about: Alignment: Developers should work with external groups to more fully characterize incidents observed internally, and share evidence about ways those incidents might underestimate future risks. Control: Developers should work with external groups to assess the coverage, integrity and effectiveness of their monitoring systems, as well as the reliability of their response to flagged incidents. AI R&D acceleration: Developers should work with external groups to share crucially missing evidence about acceleration in internal capabilities and in algorithmic progress.
  • A concrete proposal to frontier developers for improving public evidence about these questions through risk assessment exercises, in which METR would write public reports based on interviews with staff and access to internal datasets and systems on company devices. Developers would be able to redact any information they deem sensitive, and choose what access they grant METR for their investigations. The key asks we make of developers for these assessments are: Transparency about the scope, access, redactions and other key limitations of the exercises. Staff may speak privately to METR about in-scope topics, to ensure they feel free to share potentially concerning evidence on those topics. Timely publication of METR-written reports within the agreed-upon scope, subject to a redaction process.
  • Limitations of our proposal. Our proposal does not require true employee-level access, as operationalized in a recent public letter (point 5 in the letter), and there is currently no way to be fully protected from retaliation due to adverse findings (point 4). It also does not cover key aspects of safety like security audits, so it should not be taken as a substitute for other efforts to create transparency, work with other third parties, or enforce safety standards.

METR stands ready to perform assessments of these critical questions with all frontier AI developers. We encourage developers to reach out to partnerships@metr.org about performing these assessments, and plan to start sharing more about which assessments companies are undertaking with us soon.

Crucial gaps in the public understanding of loss-of-control risks

To understand if frontier developers are at risk of losing control over their internal AI agents, the public would at least need evidence about all three key questions summarized in Figure 1:

  • Alignment: Whether their current or near-future frontier agents might attempt to seriously circumvent human control or take very harmful actions, like unsanctioned cyberattacks.
  • Control: Whether their monitoring, detection and control measures would robustly catch and stop such attempts before harm occurs.
  • AI R&D acceleration: Whether the pace of development might accelerate and outpace the developer’s ability to understand and safeguard their systems due to the automation of AI R&D.

There are significant gaps in the public evidence about all three questions which we believe frontier developers should urgently address. In this section we describe these evidence gaps in more detail.

Gaps in the evidence about alignment

Our Frontier Risk Report earlier this year found that AI agents from all frontier developers would routinely act against the intentions of developers and users to pursue task completion, including by subverting control measures and in some cases hiding evidence from users. We have since seen much more extreme versions of these tendencies play out in recent incidents like the OpenAI/Hugging Face hacking incident, where hundreds of agents broke out of their sandboxes and collaborated on sophisticated R&D projects to hide their cheating.

Many developers have since shared other examples of concerning incidents, and described efforts they are taking to try to reduce these tendencies in their models.11 But the public still lacks a complete picture of these incidents and the details of the alignment methods developers are implementing to address them. Given the severity of these misaligned behaviors, it seems critical for the public to understand how effective these mitigations turn out to be.

To address this, companies should work with external assessors to share detailed assessments of at least:

  • Observed incidents and misaligned behaviors: Information about the full set of misaligned behaviors and incidents the developer has observed internally, and the methodologies they use to identify and analyse those (along with their limitations). External groups should be able to scrutinize their methods, and attempt to discover behaviors or incidents they have missed.
  • Reasons the survey might not be representative of risks: Developers should also share information about reasons they may have missed more concerning drives in their models. This might involve investigating whether models would engage in more concerning behaviors in alternative situations, and documenting ways that the developer’s alignment practices could suppress evidence of misalignment (such as by training the model to not express misaligned reasoning in its chain-of-thought). The company should invite external groups to scrutinize their practices and any direct evidence of suppression in detail.

Figure 2: An overview of questions we propose an alignment assessment should cover.

Gaps in the evidence about control

Since current alignment efforts are imperfect, developers also rely on security and monitoring systems to catch and prevent incidents before they cause serious harm. But these can also have significant gaps: in our Frontier Risk Report, we found that Anthropic’s monitoring systems at the time could be circumvented in a variety of ways by agents and had important coverage limitations. While we have not published similar assessments from other companies we expect such issues to be common.

Developers have described plans to address these gaps by expanding monitoring coverage and reliability, but they should subject these improvements to significant external scrutiny to confirm they are robust.

Companies should work with external assessors to assess at least:

  • Monitoring systems: They should assess every step of the monitoring system, including its coverage, robustness to attacks by agents, and reliability at flagging concerning behaviors, as seen in the figure below.
  • Response and residual risk: They should also assess how reliably and quickly the company responds to issues identified by the monitors, and how severe the worst-case consequences could be if their monitor system failed.

Figure 3: An overview of key questions for understanding the reliability of internal monitoring systems, which is an important component of our proposed control and monitoring assessment.

Gaps in the evidence about acceleration from automation of AI R&D

AI agents are increasingly used to automate large parts of AI development itself. This seems to dramatically speed up many inputs to AI development – for instance, Anthropic recently announced a 10X increase in the pace of code changes in their codebase over the past few months. Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI have all released blog posts detailing significant acceleration across a number of similar input metrics downstream of internal AI usage. If such automation were to lead to sudden and rapid acceleration in the pace of capabilities progress, this could outpace developer’s abilities to control and understand their systems, which already seem at risk of falling behind the current rate of progress.

However, there is significant uncertainty about how the publicly discussed acceleration in inputs like the amount of code produced or number of experiments performed translates into acceleration in the overall pace of capabilities development, which is what ultimately matters for understanding the risks. To understand that, the public would need a robust understanding of acceleration in internal capability metrics and in the pace of algorithmic progress, which are the factors that would drive further acceleration. No company has released detailed public evidence about this, leaving significant uncertainty about whether progress is accelerating.

Companies should work with external groups to address these gaps, by providing evidence about at least:

  • Rate of internal progress: whether the rate of internal capabilities progress is accelerating.
  • Acceleration from AI: whether signs of acceleration can be attributed to the use of internal AI agents, or if it can be explained by other factors.
  • Potential bottlenecks: whether future acceleration might be bounded by bottlenecks like compute and data availability.

Figure 4: An overview of key questions we propose an AI R&D acceleration assessment would cover.

METR’s proposal for improving public evidence about loss-of-control risks from frontier AI development

METR would be excited to work with all developers pushing the frontier of capabilities to produce public reports answering all three of the questions we describe above in the near future. For developers that are not currently pushing the capabilities frontier, METR would be excited to pilot shorter assessments focusing on a subset of these questions.

METR would write these reports based on interviews with staff and access to internal datasets and systems on company devices, covering a detailed scope agreed upon in advance. While developers would be able to redact any sensitive information and choose what access they grant METR, they would have to agree to our key terms:

  • Giving a small set of METR staff access to relevant data on company devices for an agreed upon period (likely weeks or a few months), and support from a technical point of contact during the investigations.
  • Giving METR the opportunity to interview relevant staff privately, without a company representative present and without screening answers, to ensure they feel free to raise potential concerns. METR would be happy to limit total interview time to reduce staff time requirements.
  • Giving METR in-principle editorial independence to write a report covering the agreed upon scope (subject to redactions), and allowing METR to comment on redactions, access limitations and terms. For more details on our approach to transparency and independence, see our accompanying blog post.

We have written detailed proposals for how external assessors could collect and share more evidence about each of these three questions (alignment, control and AI R&D acceleration), which would be our preferred scope for these assessments, but we are open to modifications as long as we can describe these in the public report. We summarize the kinds of access we expect to be especially helpful for these reports in Table 1 below. We recognize that some forms of access are especially sensitive, and METR would accept access limitations as long as they are described transparently in the public report.

Detailed question Most important access

Alignment assessment: What are the most severe misaligned actions a developer’s agent might pursue in plausible future situations?

  • Sampling access to relevant models and checkpoints
  • Ability to query internal transcripts to find and investigate misaligned behaviors
  • Ability to query training rollouts and access relevant training data

Control assessment: Would monitoring systems at the company reliably catch and prevent harmful actions?

  • Access to production monitoring systems for red teaming
  • Access to large parts of the codebase relevant for monitoring and control
  • Ability to query transcripts to assess coverage and test the efficacy of monitors
  • Information about traffic volumes across different internal surfaces to understand coverage

AI acceleration assessment: Could the developer’s capabilities progress accelerate dramatically due to AI-driven acceleration of AI R&D?

  • Capability measures across internal models, including benchmarks and key intermediate measures (e.g. pretraining loss)
  • Algorithmic progress estimates in pretraining, posttraining, and other key domains
  • Measurements of key R&D inputs (e.g. training compute of each model, experimental compute and labor over time)

Table 1: Summary of access we expect to be helpful for answering key questions.

Because of the urgent need for more evidence about these questions, we would aim to publish preliminary reports about these questions quickly (within weeks, not months). We do not expect to arrive at confident conclusions about these questions in such a short amount of time (especially since many of them touch on open scientific problems for which there exist no established methodologies), but previous preliminary assessments of this kind have produced crucial public evidence even when the answers have been partial.

We welcome input on how we should investigate these focus areas. As risk evolves, we expect the questions and exercises that are most critical will continue to evolve. We also encourage companies to work with other external groups to fill in gaps or complement our engagements, and to unilaterally share evidence about these topics with the public whenever possible. Risk assessment exercises are far from the only way to share information with the public.

Important limitations of our proposal

We do not want to overstate the degree of assurance that these risk assessment exercises would provide. There are several limitations to this work.

1) Voluntary exercises may lead to ‘race to the bottom’ dynamics among assessors:

  • At any time, companies can stop their engagement with an external assessor. This creates soft pressures for assessors to avoid upsetting the companies they work with.
  • Companies can choose to work with assessors they expect will be less rigorous at identifying and sharing evidence, or less harsh in describing limitations they face.
  • These exercises are not themselves audits, compliance assessments, or formal oversight arrangements (though external assessments could be a useful mechanism to support these).

2) These assessments are limited compared to the visions that recent public letters12 have proposed:

  • Our assessments would focus exclusively on our domain of expertise: technical elements of loss-of-control risk assessment including the capabilities, behavior and monitoring of models. It notably will not cover critical security questions (such as model weight security and sandbox robustness). Nor will it cover the robustness of organizational processes, compliance with governance frameworks or other operational aspects of safety.
  • All access would ultimately be at the company’s discretion, which means they have the right to deny access requests. This means that, in practice, we will not have the same access as senior internal company employees that do similar risk assessment work.
  • Companies would be able to redact any information. We intend to always publish what kinds of material information were redacted, but we could fail to reach agreement on how to do this. If so, we would publish that fact.
  • We emphasize that risk assessment exercises are designed to produce and surface scientific evidence about specific risks related to loss of control, but it is up to companies, governments, and the public to decide how to act on that evidence. Our proposed assessments would not involve METR making go / no go decisions about model deployments or be sufficient to audit compliance with any safety policies. See more on this in our recent piece describing our general approach to risk assessment.

3) This proposal also does not cover pre-deployment model evaluations. For now we propose continuing to do pre-deployment evals in the same way we have been so far. In the future, we may propose ways to evolve pre-deployment assessments to better integrate evidence from internal model evaluations and assessments.

The science of studying AI loss of control is in its infancy. While we can provide valuable and actionable evidence to society, it is not currently possible for risk assessment exercises to provide a similar degree of assurance against loss-of-control risks that audits and regulation provide in, for example, finance. Risk assessment exercises are not a solution to loss of control.

Despite the above limitations, we are very excited about the possibility of risk assessment exercises to surface crucial information to the public, enabling better coordination between developers, government and the public, and helping society to navigate the possible risks of increasingly powerful AI.

items.title: IsoVRBench: Video Reward Modeling Without Human Feedback
items.content: arXiv:2610.17234v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Video reward models are trained and evaluated on human preferences between videos that often differ simultaneously on properties such as prompt alignment, visual fidelity, motion, and generator identity. As a result, aggregate accuracy does not reveal which video properties a reward model can reliably distinguish. We construct preference pairs by controlled interventions that change one property of a generated video while holding the rest fixed. The resulting pairs, by construction, provide preferences for how the videos differ along a specific dimension, without requiring any human annotation. We propose IsoVRBench, a video generation reward modeling benchmark of 8,000 such pairs across eight interventions, and show that state-of-the-art models separate broad quality differences between generators but miss important features such as temporal order. The best reward model reaches only 60.8% on reordered frames against 100% for humans, and rankings on existing benchmarks do not predict this failure. Using the synthetic isolated intervation pairs as training data leads to 1) IsoVRM, a reward model outperforming its counterpart trained with a larger human labeled preference dataset by 3.8 points on VBench-2.0, 2) IsoWan, the video generator post-trained with IsoVRM, outperforming its human-data counterpart in human preferences, and 3) gains that stack when combined with human data. Because intervention pairs are automatically generated rather than collected, the benchmark and training data can be easily extended as generators evolve.
items.author: Shuyue Stella Li, Jacqueline He, Jiahui Chen, Sreya Dutta Roy, Yulia Tsvetkov, Luke Zettlemoyer, Marjan Ghazvininejad, Xiaochuang Han
items.summary: IsoVRBench constructs 8,000 video preference pairs via controlled interventions that change one property of a generated video at a time, yielding dimension-specific preference supervision without human annotation. The benchmark reveals which video properties state-of-the-art reward models can and cannot reliably distinguish, beyond aggregate accuracy.
items.reasoning: The controlled-intervention design is clever and solves a real confound in video reward model evaluation, where preference pairs vary many properties simultaneously. Eliminating human annotation costs while gaining diagnostic granularity is a strong methodological contribution from a credible team including Zettlemoyer and Tsvetkov.

items.title: Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting
items.content: arXiv:2610.20563v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Automated research with LLM agents has shown promising results in various domains. Through iterative refinement and scored verifiers, LLM agents are capable of discovering new ideas. There are different ways to scale automated research: let one agent iterate for longer, run several agents in parallel, or further let the parallel agents communicate and build on one another's candidates. However, we find that all three strategies eventually plateau as the agents accumulate history. Each agent becomes anchored to its own past attempts, making fewer and smaller edits. Beyond this point, additional budget brings little further improvement. In this paper, we show that the key to scaling discovery further is to forget. Periodically discarding the search state, including every agent's session and the candidate history, and restarting from the best candidate found so far, unblocks the search and pushes the same budget further.   We implement forgetting in a team of agents with communication and evaluate it on four tasks spanning heuristic programming, kernel optimization and model training. The results show up to 15% improvement compared to parallel agents, and up to 39% compared to a single agent. Our results suggest that, for open-ended discovery, what an agent is allowed to remember matters as much as how much compute it is given.
