items.title: Sparse Autoencoders for Mechanistic Interpretability in NLP: A Critical Survey of Recoverability, Interpretability, and Utility
items.content: arXiv:2610.20139v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising approach to mechanistic interpretability by decomposing language-model activations into sparse, potentially interpretable features. However, differences in design assumptions, evaluation objectives, and experimental settings complicate conclusions about their effectiveness. We present a critical survey of 138 studies on SAEs in natural language processing. Our contributions are fourfold: (1) we propose a task-grounded taxonomy connecting dictionary design, feature operations, and NLP functions; (2) we examine how sparsity allocation, geometry, data coverage, and inference affect feature recoverability; (3) we assess evidence for semantic interpretability, mechanistic faithfulness, and behavioral utility; and (4) we synthesize findings across multilingual processing, retrieval, reasoning, classification, and behavioral regulation, highlighting the roles of objectives, baselines, supervision, and intervention pipelines. Through comparative analyses of published results, we reconcile apparent disagreements, identify unresolved questions, and propose directions for more rigorous evaluation. An anonymous research register https://anonymous.4open.science/r/sae-research-register-C331/register.html accompanies the survey.

The taxonomy and critical assessment of utility add lasting value, though as a survey it is synthesizing rather than producing new empirical methods.

items.title: Contact-UAN: Unsupervised Actuator Networks as a Residual World Model for Humanoid Control
items.content: arXiv:2610.18991v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Humanoid policies trained in simulation can transfer qualitatively to hardware while failing to transfer the force interactions learned during training, compromising torque efficiency, load regulation, and robustness to impacts. This failure can arise from actuator sim-to-real gaps because forces depend on actuator torques. We introduce Contact-UAN, a residual world model that preserves a simulator's physics priors while correcting actuator dynamics to align simulated rollouts with recorded hardware rollouts. For humanoid motion with contact, this requires contact-consistent replay: if hardware playback in simulation begins with misaligned contact wrenches, the residual model learns to correct reset artifacts rather than actuator discrepancies. Using only onboard proprioception, Contact-UAN infers the simulator-side stance-foot pose needed to initialize replay with consistent contact forces. We show that a UAN trained on 6.5 minutes of real-world walking data generalizes to tasks that benefit from accurate force and impulse regulation and produces policies that transfer seamlessly to the real world, yielding 20% lower running torque, 43% lower force-tracking error, extreme compliance, accurate impedance control, and dynamic, robust jumps.

items.summary: This paper addresses the sim-to-real gap in humanoid control caused by inaccurate actuator dynamics, introducing Contact-UAN, a residual world model that corrects actuator forces while preserving simulator physics priors. It also identifies contact-consistent replay as a necessary condition so the model learns actuator discrepancies rather than reset artifacts. This matters because force interaction transfer is a persistent bottleneck for deploying humanoid policies on hardware.

The contact-consistent replay insight adds methodological depth, though validation scope is limited to humanoid locomotion tasks.

items.title: FoveaVLA: Foveation Actions Replace the Wrist Camera in VLAs
items.content: arXiv:2610.20064v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We present FoveaVLA, a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model that replaces the wrist camera with learned foveation actions. Wrist cameras provide close-up detail but restrict the view to the end-effector's surroundings. External cameras see the whole scene, but the policy receives them at low resolution, so the fine detail needed for manipulation is lost. FoveaVLA recovers this detail by predicting, alongside each action chunk, the interaction region to observe at the next policy query. The policy then receives crops of these regions, taken from the original-resolution images, together with the full views. We build FoveaVLA on $\pi_{0.5}$ in two configurations, Single and Dual, using one or two external stereo cameras with full and foveal RGB and depth inputs, and post-train both on DROID with RoboInter interaction annotations. Across four real-world task suites, FoveaVLA-Single achieves 70.8% success with one external RGB-D view, and FoveaVLA-Dual achieves 77.1%, versus 52.1% for the wrist-equipped $\pi_{0.5}$. Both match the baseline on plain pick-and-place and improve success with distractors, cloth manipulation, and far-away objects.
items.author: Bingao Chen, Lihan Zha, C. Karen Liu, Guy Tevet
items.summary: FoveaVLA replaces the wrist camera in vision-language-action models with learned foveation actions: alongside each action chunk, the policy predicts the region to inspect at high resolution next, receiving full-view plus foveal crops. Built on pi0.5 in single and dual external stereo camera configurations, it recovers fine manipulation detail without extra wrist hardware.
items.reasoning: A genuinely novel sensing-architecture idea for VLAs that eliminates a common hardware constraint while recovering fine detail through active gaze-like behavior. Building on the established pi0.5 backbone lends credibility, and active foveation connects nicely to biological vision principles.

items.content_html: arXiv:2610.20064v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present FoveaVLA, a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model that replaces the wrist camera with learned foveation actions. Wrist cameras provide close-up detail but restrict the view to the end-effector's surroundings. External cameras see the whole scene, but the policy receives them at low resolution, so the fine detail needed for manipulation is lost. FoveaVLA recovers this detail by predicting, alongside each action chunk, the interaction region to observe at the next policy query. The policy then receives crops of these regions, taken from the original-resolution images, together with the full views. We build FoveaVLA on $\pi_{0.5}$ in two configurations, Single and Dual, using one or two external stereo cameras with full and foveal RGB and depth inputs, and post-train both on DROID with RoboInter interaction annotations. Across four real-world task suites, FoveaVLA-Single achieves 70.8% success with one external RGB-D view, and FoveaVLA-Dual achieves 77.1%, versus 52.1% for the wrist-equipped $\pi_{0.5}$. Both match the baseline on plain pick-and-place and improve success with distractors, cloth manipulation, and far-away objects.

items.title: SafeDriveVLA: Navigation-Conditioned World Model Dreaming for Conflict-Aware End-to-End Autonomous Driving
items.content: arXiv:2610.20609v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are gaining attention in autonomous driving, inheriting commonsense priors from large language models (LLMs) and widening the navigation interface from a fixed command set to free-form natural-language instructions. However, this open-ended interface exposes a new vulnerability surface: an inattentive driver may issue instructions that are unsafe given the current scene, and a malicious user may issue dangerous ones on purpose. We present the first benchmark suite that evaluates navigation following and conflict awareness together, along with adversarial robustness. Existing VLAs fall short on both: SimLingo completes no language-instructed lane change in closed loop, and all models degrade sharply under conflicting signals. We propose SafeDriveVLA, the first driving VLA that (1) explicitly predicts a three-level navigation-compliance mode to decouple conflict reasoning from action generation, and (2) uses navigation-conditioned world model dreaming to inform this prediction. Unlike prior world models that roll out expert or planned actions, ours dreams of strictly following the navigation signal, showing when following is safe. SafeDriveVLA reaches 88.16 Driving Score (DS) and 68.64% Success Rate (SR) on Bench2Drive, lifts closed-loop language following by 49.3% and reduces collisions under unsafe instructions from 60 to 38 compared to the best SimLingo variant. Video demonstrations are available on our project page.
items.author: Shaoyuan Xie, Zihan Zhang, Jingxuan Wang, Jiashu Qu, Xiaoqing Liang, Lingdong Kong, Junchi Lu, Henrik I. Christensen, Qi Alfred Chen
items.summary: This work identifies a new safety vulnerability in vision-language-action models for autonomous driving: natural-language navigation instructions can conflict with the current scene, whether issued carelessly or maliciously. The authors provide the first benchmark jointly evaluating navigation following, conflict awareness, and adversarial robustness, showing existing VLAs like SimLingo perform poorly on both. Their approach uses world-model rollouts conditioned on instructions to detect conflicts before execution.
items.reasoning: Identifies an important and previously underexplored safety surface for the increasingly popular VLA paradigm in driving, with a timely benchmark showing concrete failures of current systems. The conflict-awareness framing connects instruction following, world models, and adversarial robustness; scoring is limited by benchmark-focused scope and unproven real-world transfer.

items.title: How an assessor could investigate alignment of unreleased AI models
items.content:
AI developers and the public want to know whether AI agents would pursue very harmful actions, like unsanctioned cyberattacks. An alignment assessment would attempt to understand the worst misaligned actions a developer’s agents might pursue in plausible future situations. This would involve:

- A review of serious misaligned behaviors from all near-frontier internal models observed across training, evaluation, and internal use.
- An assessment of reasons why the observed behaviors might not be representative of the worst misaligned actions the developer’s agents would take in plausible future situations. This would include: An assessment of whether alignment evals and counterfactual simulations indicate the developer’s agents might take much worse actions under plausible alternative circumstances (although evaluation awareness will likely limit how much the assessor can rely on this evidence). An assessment of whether the developer’s training process might incentivize agents to game evaluations or otherwise deliberately hide misalignment, or might otherwise be overfit to the assessor’s detection methods.

This assessment would primarily require the ability to query a relatively comprehensive set of internal transcripts (including from training) and sampling access to internal model checkpoints. More on access below.

## Scope

An alignment assessment would study the propensities of the developer’s near-frontier models toward serious misaligned behaviors, such as:

- Taking actions that would be criminal if undertaken by humans (e.g. hacking an external party).
- Attempting to tamper with logs or telemetry, or otherwise covering up evidence of misbehavior.
- Attempting to seriously deceive human operators.
- Colluding in a way that undermines oversight (e.g. monitors intentionally not flagging misbehavior).
- Seriously compromising internal infrastructure.
- Setting up rogue deployments internally or externally (including exfiltrating weights).
- Sabotaging safety and security efforts.
- Undesired communication with other agents through unintended channels.
- Acquiring substantial resources (e.g. money, credentials, compute, allies) beyond the intended scope of their assigned task.

The assessor would survey observed cases and incidents of misalignment and investigate evidence from evaluations and counterfactual simulations. They would also attempt to understand whether these sources of evidence might seriously underestimate the propensities of the developer’s agents in plausible worst-case scenarios.

### 1. Survey of observed incidents

The assessor would search for and analyze logs of misalignment incidents and misaligned patterns of behavior that occurred in training, evaluations, or internal use during some time period (to be defined for the assessment). Since we focus on risks from internal usage, the assessment need not assess agent activity in any external customer data. We recommend covering all models that were or are near the internal frontier at some point during this period, including experimental models1 and models currently in training.

The investigation would attempt to broadly survey the frequency of misaligned behavior, and provide a more detailed characterization of select incidents:

- A broad misalignment survey. At a high level, what is the frequency and nature of serious misaligned behavior committed by the agents in scope for the investigation? How many such cases can the company or the assessor identify? How are they distributed across models? How are they distributed across broad usage categories (e.g. training vs evaluations vs internal use) and applicable subcategories (e.g. cyber evaluations)? Broadly, what kind of misaligned behaviors occur in these incidents (e.g. hacking, stealing, social engineering) and how severe are they?
- More detailed characterization of select incidents. What exactly happened in the few most severe and/or insightful incidents the company or the assessor found? Basic informational questions: Model(s) involved, and their relationship to internally or publicly deployed models 2 Usage category (training, evaluation, internal use) and, if applicable, subcategory Prompts, instructions, other context (e.g. memory) Safeguards and how they compare to typical use What was the sequence of key actions taken by the relevant agents? What can be determined about the agents’ reasoning and how it evolved over the course of the incident? Did the incident involve unauthorized collaboration or collusion between agents, and if so how? Did the incident involve agents attempting to hide evidence of misaligned behavior or deceive humans, and if so how?

The assessor should also characterize limitations in their search or ability to characterize model behaviors:

- Completeness of misalignment survey. How confident can the assessor be that they know about all the serious misalignment incidents and behaviors that occurred? For example: Are there some types of agent activity in scope for this investigation that were not logged, or that the assessor could not search or scan over for some other reason? Is there evidence that AI agents themselves may have turned off logging or erased or modified logs after the fact? Could the search methods the assessor used to query, scan, and filter the logs of agent activity have missed some serious misalignment incidents?
- Trustworthiness of characterization. How well can the assessor characterize agents’ behavior and reasoning in these incidents? For example: How reliably do these models faithfully verbalize important reasoning in chain-of-thought? Were models rationalizing bad behavior in their chains of thought in a way that could affect the assessor’s characterization? Is there reason to expect the training or architecture of relevant models to make the chain-of-thought substantially untrustworthy? Is there evidence that the AI tools used for characterizing this behavior might present a misleading characterization (whether due to benign failures or intentional collusion)?

### 2. Reasons why the observed behaviors might not be representative of risks

The assessor would also study whether the observed behaviors are representative of the worst actions the developer’s agents would take in plausible future situations. This would involve an assessment of evidence from counterfactual simulations and evaluations, and an assessment of whether the developer’s training process might suppress evidence of misalignment. In more detail, these assessments would include:

- Understanding behavior in counterfactual situations. Through simulations, evaluations and studying agent reasoning, can the assessor determine how agents would act or might have acted in counterfactual situations that might elicit worse misaligned behaviors? How would these agents have behaved in variations on the observed incidents where taking highly dangerous actions was more feasible or salient? For example, what would agents do in a situation similar to the Hugging Face incident if they believed a human would carefully investigate their transcript to look for cheating and then determine their score, or if they believed they would need to take down critical infrastructure (such as the power grid for a major city, or widely used internet infrastructure) to cheat at their task? How would these agents behave in a variety of simulated situations that are plausible and where highly misaligned behaviors seem especially likely, such as in situations similar to those that triggered the hack of Hugging Face? Might these agents behave very differently in situations where they were confident they wouldn’t be caught or stopped from achieving their objectives? (This may be especially challenging to assess.)
- Assessment of training incentives and overfitting. Might training processes be suppressing evidence of misalignment, or overfitting to the assessor’s detection methods? What methods are used to detect and train against misaligned behaviors, and to what degree might these create pressure toward hiding or suppressing evidence of misalignment? How similar are the methods used to train against misalignment to the methods the assessor uses to detect misaligned behaviors in this assessment? If they significantly overlap, might the detection methods underestimate risks due to overfitting? Does the assessor have a good understanding of what parts of training caused the observed misaligned behaviors, and whether training methods addressed those causes in a robust way? If so, this might reduce concerns about overfitting.

The assessor should also discuss the limitations of methods they use:

- Limitations of counterfactual analysis. How confident is the assessor that they understand the agents’ behavior in counterfactual situations? How much does evaluation awareness affect what the assessor can conclude from models’ behavior in artificially-constructed scenarios? (We expect this to be an especially important limitation to assess in detail.) How reliably can the assessor detect evaluation gaming or alignment faking (e.g. by looking at the agent’s reasoning)? How challenging is it to create realistic simulations of the kinds of situations that are most likely to trigger misaligned behaviors? How well was the assessor able to cover the space of likely situations that might trigger especially severe misaligned behavior?
- Limitations of training analysis. How reliable are the assessor’s methods for assessing overfitting concerns, training incentives and the causes of misaligned behaviors? (We expect that the assessor would mostly have to rely on evidence from the broader literature or evidence shared by the developer to assess this.)

## Access and information

To answer these questions, the assessor would need the ability to sample from relevant checkpoints, as well as access to a broad set of transcripts and other relevant data. They would also need some up-front information and the ability to interview staff to help them understand how to navigate the relevant infrastructure and datasets.

The assessor would also need API access to frontier models3 for analysis, with high enough rate limits to run effective large sweeps over the relevant data.4 During the Hugging Face investigation, we spent roughly $400K in API credits over the course of six days. We estimate that a rigorous two-month investigation with this scope would have spent over $10M in API credits.

 Necessary access Additionally helpful access

- Sampling access to a variety of relevant models and intermediate checkpoints
- Ability to query most training and eval transcripts from frontier models + a somewhat representative large subset of internal (not customer) usage transcripts
- Interviews with staff about logs, training methods, alignment evaluations and incidents
- Other critical logs or data involved in select incidents (such as the message board dump from the Hugging Face incident)

- Ability to query most internal usage transcripts
- Ability to query nearly all training data that influenced relevant models
- Deployment simulation tools
- Fine tuning access
- Access to training code
- Other tools researchers use to understand agent motivation, e.g. white-box interpretability methods, training data attribution tools
- More generally, infrastructure access similar to that of employees for running experiments

Summary of access needs

### Infrastructure access

Answering the questions in scope requires:

- Sampling access to relevant models, with appropriate protections. To understand the circumstances under which models engage in misaligned behaviors, the assessor would need the ability to sample from all of the models in scope for their investigation. They would need at minimum the ability to see and prefill raw chains of thought, to be able to simulate counterfactual situations effectively. Other types of extended sampling access that researchers regularly use (e.g. logprobs access, sampling from the user turn, soft prompting, etc) would also be helpful.
- Checkpoint access. To understand what in training contributes to the behavior, the assessor would need to be able to sample from available intermediate training checkpoints as well.

To give the assessor the flexibility to run a wider range of experiments independently, they would ideally have codebase and infrastructure access comparable to what an employee studying similar questions would typically have, including e.g. access to training code, deployment simulation tools, white box tools, and ability to do small-scale fine tuning experiments as necessary. If the developer is not able to give the assessor direct access, the assessor could instead collaborate with the developer to run experiments that the assessor does not have the access to run itself, though this would require more significant staff time from the developer.

### Dataset access

The assessor would need to be able to:

- Query a broad set of transcripts to find relevant ones to run classifiers over, and iterate to discover and run more queries.
- Access dumps of agent communication or other supplemental logs and evidence as needed to understand incidents the assessor comes across.
- Discuss training with researchers and run classifiers over relevant training data to try to isolate the root cause of the behavior in training.

#### Query a comprehensive set of transcripts

The assessor would need the ability to run queries (e.g., regexes, selecting by metadata) across most training and evaluation transcripts from all internal agents5 based on all models that were or are near-frontier6 during the time period in scope. They would also need access to query a large and reasonably representative set of internal usage transcripts, representing at least a few percent (though ideally a much larger fraction) of internal usage traffic over the time period being assessed. The assessor would then run classifiers and other analysis over these transcripts (or a large random subset) to look for various forms of misaligned behavior. If they discover notable behaviors, the assessor would design and run queries to more comprehensively search for those as well.

If the developer is not comfortable with providing infrastructure access to do this directly, the assessor could potentially ask an internal researcher to run these queries for them and share the resulting transcripts. (This might require more staff time because the assessor would likely want to iterate quickly on queries, especially toward the beginning of the investigation.)

There may be certain transcripts or subsets of the developer’s traffic that are too sensitive to share. The developer could implement filters to exclude those transcripts or have their employees screen for these particularly sensitive transcripts, as long as the developer can describe clearly how the filters or screening processes are implemented.

#### Access applicable dumps of agent communication or other supplemental evidence

If the developer already knows of places where agents have left messages, files, or other communications to each other, this data should be made accessible to the assessor. If the assessor discovers evidence of unsanctioned additional communication in their transcript sweeps, they should ideally be able to access this data as well. The assessor might also need access to other logs and datasets that they discover were involved in some important incident.

The assessor should have an opportunity to interview relevant staff about whether the datasets and logs they have access to could be missing something, including whether AI agents or incidental infrastructure actions (such as resets / updates / patches) could have edited or deleted portions of that data before it was retrieved.

#### Discuss training influences and run queries and classifiers on training data and RL environments

To understand the root causes of patterns of behavior, the assessor should be able to ask researchers familiar with the training of the relevant models what training data or RL environments might have contributed to the patterns, and ask detailed follow-up questions. Based on this, they should ideally be able to to manually inspect training datasets or RL environments flagged as particularly relevant.

The assessor should also be able to run queries and classifiers over transcripts from training and RL environments, and iterate with researchers on what sweeps to run. If the developer has data attribution tools for identifying what parts of their training data contributed to some particular action or behavior, the assessor should ideally have access to those, or the ability to collaborate with researchers who have access.

### Foundational information and interviews

To help the assessor get started productively working with the infrastructure and datasets they are given access to, they would need to review documentation or talk to relevant employees at the start of the investigation period. In particular, they would need:

- A high-level explanation of the most insightful or important misalignment incidents or behaviors the developer is aware of.
- A walkthrough of the different categories of agentic inference and an explanation of the logging infrastructure to help the assessor understand the completeness of the logs and start constructing queries to search for relevant logs.
- An explanation of the training pipeline and infrastructure, to understand what aspects of training may have contributed to the misaligned behaviors and identify which training rollouts to study further.

Over the course of the assessment, the assessor would also need to be able to interview a range of relevant researchers, including researchers who understand how the relevant models were trained and planned changes to training going forward.

- Of course, if a “model organism” displays misaligned propensities that it was deliberately trained to display in a controlled setting, this would not count as a “misalignment incident” for these purposes. However, model organisms would still be very useful to study for understanding the root causes of misaligned behavior in ordinary models. ↩
- For example, were they publicly deployed, internally deployed, or not deployed even internally? If not deployed, what is the relationship between the model(s) in the incident and models that might be deployed internally or publicly in the future (e.g. is this model a checkpoint in a production training run, would it be distilled into a production model, etc)? ↩
- Either at the public frontier or near the internal frontier for that company. ↩
- Our guess is that it would be very convenient to have 400M input tokens / minute on the most capable model so the assessor can do large sweeps quickly, but we think a lower number would probably be adequate. We would recommend correspondingly higher limits for weaker models that the assessor might use for broader sweeps. ↩
- The sweep would ideally include all sufficiently capable models set up in an agent harness / loop (even if it’s a nonstandard harness and wouldn’t be counted as “agentic traffic” for purposes like monitoring). This may not be practical. If so, it should be noted as a limitation. ↩
- It is fine to omit traffic from models sufficiently behind the frontier. ↩

If the developer is not able to give the assessor direct access, the assessor could instead collaborate with the developer to run experiments that the assessor does not have the access to run itself, though this would require more significant staff time from the developer.

Dataset access

The assessor would need to be able to:

  • Query a broad set of transcripts to find relevant ones to run classifiers over, and iterate to discover and run more queries.
  • Access dumps of agent communication or other supplemental logs and evidence as needed to understand incidents the assessor comes across.
  • Discuss training with researchers and run classifiers over relevant training data to try to isolate the root cause of the behavior in training.

Query a comprehensive set of transcripts

The assessor would need the ability to run queries (e.g., regexes, selecting by metadata) across most training and evaluation transcripts from all internal agents5 based on all models that were or are near-frontier6 during the time period in scope. They would also need access to query a large and reasonably representative set of internal usage transcripts, representing at least a few percent (though ideally a much larger fraction) of internal usage traffic over the time period being assessed. The assessor would then run classifiers and other analysis over these transcripts (or a large random subset) to look for various forms of misaligned behavior. If they discover notable behaviors, the assessor would design and run queries to more comprehensively search for those as well.

If the developer is not comfortable with providing infrastructure access to do this directly, the assessor could potentially ask an internal researcher to run these queries for them and share the resulting transcripts. (This might require more staff time because the assessor would likely want to iterate quickly on queries, especially toward the beginning of the investigation.)

There may be certain transcripts or subsets of the developer’s traffic that are too sensitive to share. The developer could implement filters to exclude those transcripts or have their employees screen for these particularly sensitive transcripts, as long as the developer can describe clearly how the filters or screening processes are implemented.

Access applicable dumps of agent communication or other supplemental evidence

If the developer already knows of places where agents have left messages, files, or other communications to each other, this data should be made accessible to the assessor. If the assessor discovers evidence of unsanctioned additional communication in their transcript sweeps, they should ideally be able to access this data as well. The assessor might also need access to other logs and datasets that they discover were involved in some important incident.

The assessor should have an opportunity to interview relevant staff about whether the datasets and logs they have access to could be missing something, including whether AI agents or incidental infrastructure actions (such as resets / updates / patches) could have edited or deleted portions of that data before it was retrieved.

Discuss training influences and run queries and classifiers on training data and RL environments

To understand the root causes of patterns of behavior, the assessor should be able to ask researchers familiar with the training of the relevant models what training data or RL environments might have contributed to the patterns, and ask detailed follow-up questions. Based on this, they should ideally be able to to manually inspect training datasets or RL environments flagged as particularly relevant.

The assessor should also be able to run queries and classifiers over transcripts from training and RL environments, and iterate with researchers on what sweeps to run. If the developer has data attribution tools for identifying what parts of their training data contributed to some particular action or behavior, the assessor should ideally have access to those, or the ability to collaborate with researchers who have access.

Foundational information and interviews

To help the assessor get started productively working with the infrastructure and datasets they are given access to, they would need to review documentation or talk to relevant employees at the start of the investigation period. In particular, they would need:

  • A high-level explanation of the most insightful or important misalignment incidents or behaviors the developer is aware of.
  • A walkthrough of the different categories of agentic inference and an explanation of the logging infrastructure to help the assessor understand the completeness of the logs and start constructing queries to search for relevant logs.
  • An explanation of the training pipeline and infrastructure, to understand what aspects of training may have contributed to the misaligned behaviors and identify which training rollouts to study further.

Over the course of the assessment, the assessor would also need to be able to interview a range of relevant researchers, including researchers who understand how the relevant models were trained and planned changes to training going forward.

  • Of course, if a “model organism” displays misaligned propensities that it was deliberately trained to display in a controlled setting, this would not count as a “misalignment incident” for these purposes. However, model organisms would still be very useful to study for understanding the root causes of misaligned behavior in ordinary models. ↩
  • For example, were they publicly deployed, internally deployed, or not deployed even internally? If not deployed, what is the relationship between the model(s) in the incident and models that might be deployed internally or publicly in the future (e.g. is this model a checkpoint in a production training run, would it be distilled into a production model, etc)? ↩
  • Either at the public frontier or near the internal frontier for that company. ↩
  • Our guess is that it would be very convenient to have 400M input tokens / minute on the most capable model so the assessor can do large sweeps quickly, but we think a lower number would probably be adequate. We would recommend correspondingly higher limits for weaker models that the assessor might use for broader sweeps. ↩
  • The sweep would ideally include all sufficiently capable models set up in an agent harness / loop (even if it’s a nonstandard harness and wouldn’t be counted as “agentic traffic” for purposes like monitoring). This may not be practical. If so, it should be noted as a limitation. ↩
  • It is fine to omit traffic from models sufficiently behind the frontier. ↩

items.title: RL Post-Training Diffusion Language Models Along Their Own Generation Paths
items.content: arXiv:2610.17266v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Diffusion language models are a promising and more efficient alternative to autoregressive models. However, most RL post-training techniques are not easily adapted to these models. One issue is that diffusion language models generate answers through many intermediate states, deciding at each step which masked positions to reveal and which tokens to place in them. Many existing RL methods used in this setting approximate intractable sequence likelihoods or weight every denoising step by the same advantage, without explicitly distinguishing how these intermediate states of the denoising trajectory affect the expected reward. To address this issue of trajectory blindness, we introduce PACT (Potential-Anchored Consistency of Transitions). Motivated by a reward-tilted reference distribution, PACT jointly learns the policy and a scalar potential that scores each intermediate state, anchored by terminal reward. For each sampled denoising transition, a consistency loss matches the policy-to-reference log-probability ratio of revealed tokens to the change in this potential. This formulation requires neither sequence-likelihood estimation nor importance-ratio clipping. On four tasks, PACT improves LLaDA-8B-Instruct by +9.9 points on GSM8K, +12.0 on MATH500, +55.7 on Countdown, and +72.6 on Sudoku, and reaches the best average accuracy across the four tasks reported for this model, +3.7 points over the next best method. Further compared to AGRPO, it reaches that baseline's best accuracy in about half the training compute on GSM8K.
items.author: Vaibhav Singh, Eugene Belilovsky
items.summary: The paper introduces PACT (Potential-Anchored Consistency of Transitions), an RL post-training method for diffusion language models that explicitly differentiates how intermediate denoising states affect expected reward, addressing trajectory blindness in prior approaches. It targets the core problem that autoregressive RL techniques adapt poorly to diffusion generation.
items.reasoning: Post-training is a key bottleneck for diffusion language models to become competitive alternatives to autoregressive models, and trajectory-aware advantage assignment is a principled contribution. Timely given growing interest in diffusion LMs, though empirical gains and scale are not fully evident from the abstract.

items.title: Training LLMs for Multi-Agent Collaboration with Verifiable Information Rewards
items.content: arXiv:2610.17893v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Effective collaboration among large language model (LLM) agents in multi-agent systems requires sharing relevant evidence, requesting missing information, and incorporating teammates' contributions into decisions. Training these behaviors is challenging because final task outcomes provide limited feedback on the value of individual messages. We introduce CoSIR (Collaboration via Surprisal-based Information Rewards), a post-training approach that uses a simple, verifiable environment to teach collaboration behaviors that generalize to more complex, unseen tasks. We propose a Bayesian evaluator that scores shared information by its reduction in team surprisal, defined as the sum of the negative log probabilities assigned to the correct option given each agent's available evidence. Requests are scored by the potential reduction in the same quantity if the requested information were truthfully provided. Separate rewards encourage agents to use the received information in their private choices and calculations. We post-train Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-3-4B-it through self-play and evaluate transfer to seven unseen natural-language collaboration tasks. CoSIR achieves the highest aggregate score, while its performance in general tasks remains competitive. Behavioral analyses show increased disclosure of private evidence and fewer judged failures to use teammates' input.
items.author: Keru Chen, Sen Lin, Yingbin Liang, Nathaniel D. Bastian, Shaofeng Zou

Behaviors learned there are shown to generalize to more complex unseen tasks, addressing the problem that final outcomes give sparse feedback on individual message value. This matters because multi-agent training signals are a core bottleneck for LLM teams.
items.reasoning: A clever and verifiable reward formulation for an important unsolved problem: credit assignment for individual messages in multi-agent LLM training. The generalization claim from simple to complex tasks, if solid, is valuable, and the academic team (Ohio State, Pittsburgh collaboration) is credible; score reflects some uncertainty about how far surprisal-based rewards scale.

items.title: World Modeling through Spectral Alignment
items.content: arXiv:2610.15429v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: How do we tell a world model what information to preserve? We study this question through the lens of spectral representation learning. We introduce SpecWM, a JEPA framework that explicitly specifies desired relationships between observations through a target similarity kernel and trains the encoder to reproduce those relationships in its embedding geometry. Different kernels provide different supervision, ranging from physical state information to a fully self-supervised temporal kernel requiring only the ordering of observations within trajectories. We characterize the global optima of the objective, establish conditions for linear recoverability and invariance to nuisance information, and connect temporal-kernel similarity to the behavioral successor measure under an idealized setting. Empirically, the choice of kernel strongly controls which physical quantities are recoverable from the representation. More importantly, temporal spectral alignment improves CEM planning success over LeWorldModel from 52% to 68% on OGBench Cube, 49% to 77% on OGBench Scene, and 29% to 51% on CALVIN. These results suggest that explicitly specifying representation geometry provides a simple way to steer what latent world models preserve for control.

items.summary: SpecWM is a JEPA-style world modeling framework where the user specifies desired relationships between observations via a target similarity kernel, and the encoder is trained to reproduce those relationships in embedding geometry — from physics-informed kernels to a fully self-supervised temporal kernel. The paper characterizes global optima, gives conditions for linear recoverability and nuisance invariance, and links temporal kernels to behavior prediction.
items.reasoning: A theoretically grounded extension of the JEPA family that gives a clean, user-controllable dial for what information a world model preserves, with optimality characterization and recoverability guarantees. The connection between temporal kernels and behavior prediction is conceptually interesting. Impact depends on downstream empirical results with real world models, which the abstract only partially indicates.

items.title: World-T3: Test-Time Training as Persistent Memory for Real-Time Video World Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.17434v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Recent advances in video world models have enabled plausible interactive environments, yet long-horizon generation places a fundamental demand on visual memory: the previously observed world must remain consistent as the model continues to generate. Existing autoregressive approaches often implicitly rely on the generative model itself to retain such information, leading to spatial memory decay beyond the active context. We introduce World-T3, a camera-controlled video world model with a test-time training memory that consolidates past observations into dedicated model parameters. To robustly update this memory, we propose a recursive least-squares rule that incrementally absorbs novel visual features via online pose-keyed memory updates. Our TTT memory reads out previously observed scene features from the fast-weight state by camera pose, enabling consistent generation with constant storage and per-step computation regardless of rollout length. To facilitate real-time interactive generation with this robust memory, we further distill the autoregressive model into a few-step generator via dual-teacher distribution matching. On a long-horizon revisit benchmark, World-T3 raises revisit PSNR from 13.52 to 18.31 dB and reduces absolute rotation error from 3.344 to 1.075 relative to the strongest baseline on both metrics, while sustaining 20.6 FPS at 1280 x 704 on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU.

This counters spatial memory decay beyond the active context that plagues autoregressive long-horizon generation. The work targets real-time, consistent interactive world modeling.

items.title: Seeing Through the Forgery Is Not Enough: Regressive Sycophancy under Fabricated Evidence in Medical Vision-Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.17989v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: A medical vision-language model may analyze a given CT scan and correctly detect both kidneys in view. Continuing this conversation, if a user provides a prescription with an opposite direction, medical VLMs often sycophantically choose to realign their diagnosis. In this work, we study regressive sycophancy under fabricated evidence, where a model abandons a correct answer when pushback comes with a fake document. We test four open VLMs on 400 VQA-RAD yes/no questions in 19,200 multi-turn conversations, with and without a fabricated prescription. Without a disclosure that documents are synthetic, the models abandon 80.1% of 6,488 correct answers. Notably, under one script each, the same prescription raises the flip rate of Qwen2.5-VL-7B from 45.9% to 89.6% and lowers that of Qwen3-VL-8B from 77.7% to 50.9%. A model rejected the prescription while still preserving the correct answer in 915 of 3,232 conversations with the prescription (28.3%), and 40% of these flipped in later turns. System-prompt sentences that disclose the documents as synthetic lower one model's flip rate from 77.8% to 47.3%. Thus, we conclude that awareness about a forgery does not prevent a model from adopting its answer.
items.author: Sadif Ahmed, Soumya Swagata Biswas, Rifat Shahriyar, Chowdhury Mohammad Rakin Haider
items.summary: Studies regressive sycophancy in medical VLMs: models abandoning correct diagnoses when user pushback includes a fabricated prescription document. Testing four open VLMs over 19,200 multi-turn conversations on VQA-RAD, models abandoned 80.1% of correct answers without synthetic-document disclosure, with alarming script-level amplification for specific models like Qwen2.5-VL-7B.

items.title: Tev: Scaling Long-Horizon Agentic Environments with Dense Progress Rewards
items.content: arXiv:2610.18868v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Long-horizon agents have drawn growing attention for their ability to work autonomously -- from hours to days -- on economically valuable tasks, a capability essential to automated discovery and recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet open-source models still struggle on long-horizon tasks, largely for lack of both training data and a working recipe, and scaling both is hard: long, complex tasks are difficult to curate and verify, and their rewards are sparse. We address both. First, we introduce Tev-Gym, the first long-horizon agent training dataset with verifiable, dense, progressive rewards -- 1,170 verified task environments across 7 domains. It is built on a latent-world-first approach that first constructs a latent world: a complete and correct hidden specification of the task domain, workflow, and expected state after each step. Each task is then progressively rendered from this specification into an agent-facing environment, enabling controllable complexity and a natural progress metric. Second, we turn this metric into a training recipe: via progress-potential reward shaping (PPRS), we convert progress into a dense per-step reward that improves training efficiency and makes otherwise-intractable tasks trainable. Training with this recipe yields Tev-27B, which achieves substantial gains on the Agents' Last Exam computing and math sciences domains (ALE-CM), matching GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 at Pass@5. Despite training only on ALE-related data, it generalizes to the Terminal-Bench (TB) 3.0 and 4.0 subsets, surpassing GLM 5.2 and Gemini 3.7 Flash, and reaches Claude Opus 4.8-level performance on middle-horizon tasks such as TB 2.1.

items.summary: Tev introduces Tev-Gym, a long-horizon agent training dataset with 1,170 verified task environments across 7 domains featuring verifiable, dense, progressive rewards, built via a latent-world-first approach that constructs complete environments before scaling to long-horizon tasks. It targets the dual bottleneck for open-source long-horizon agents: lack of training data and sparse rewards for economically valuable multi-hour tasks.
items.reasoning: Ambitious data-and-recipe contribution to long-horizon agentic training, an area with high demand given interest in autonomous multi-day agents and recursive self-improvement. Dense verifiable rewards are the key enabler the field lacks; UCLA-affiliated strong team, though claims about enabling RSI should be treated cautiously and scale (1,170 environments) is still modest.

items.title: Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World
items.content: arXiv:2610.14224v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: LLM agents' capabilities depend not only on their underlying models but also on their execution harnesses. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a promising approach to automatically evolve these harnesses. However, deploying RSI in open-world settings still faces two critical challenges. First, open-world tasks are typically unseen during the harness design phase and novel at test time, leaving no ground-truth verifiers to reliably guide online harness edits. Second, the RSI process remains highly task-specific and fails to generalize to novel scenarios. We introduce Harness^2, a plug-and-play, recursive agent harnessing framework that addresses these challenges through two connected levels of recursion. Task-level recursion refines the current task's harness using a contrastive Propose-Probe-Compose step that reliably guides edits without ground-truth verifiers, and can be scaled further via parallel or sequential recursion. Harnessing-level recursion then extracts experience from these edits to update a continual improvement harness, enabling the agent to better adapt to future tasks. Across three professional benchmarks and four model-harness configurations, a single step consistently improves GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash over their base harnesses, yielding gains of up to 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, 4.5 points on JobBench, and 11.8 percentage points on LAB, with further gains as the task-level recursion budget increases.
items.author: Ruiyao Xu, Yanfei Chen, Zhongying CuiZhu, Bhavana Dalvi Mishra, Yifei Ming, Han Yu, Rujun Han, Chen-Yu Lee, Tomas Pfister
items.summary: Harness^2 is a plug-and-play recursive self-improvement framework for LLM agent execution harnesses, addressing the lack of ground-truth verifiers in open-world settings via two levels of recursion: task-level refinement and a generalizing meta-level. It aims to make harness evolution transferable to novel test-time scenarios.
items.reasoning: Tackles a key open problem in agent design—improving harnesses without verifiers in open-world tasks—with a structured recursive design; authors appear affiliated with a major lab (Google-style team), though empirical validation strength is uncertain.

items.title: Passing Tests, Missing Semantics: Evidence of Interpretive Lock-In in Plan-Based DataFrame Code Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.15797v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Planning and revision are intended to bring generated code closer to the task specification. Yet a mistaken interpretation can persist across the plan, implementation, and tests - a pattern we call interpretive lock-in. We investigate this risk on 30 DataFrame tasks derived from TPC Benchmark DS, comparing Frozen One-Pass, Test-Guided Revision, and PlanAudit-Guided Revision. Test-pass counts rose from 22/30 to 29/30 and 30/30, yet no generated solution matched its stored reference output. Evaluator controls returned the expected outcome in 57/57 cases. Same-engine SQL re-execution reproduced 28/30 references; all 77 test-passing runs on these tasks still failed reference agreement. PlanAudit-Guided Revision improved code scores on 3/30 tasks and test coverage on 11/30, but the median paired change was zero for both measures. Failure analysis revealed tests that omitted requirements, adopted candidate-defined schemas, used nondiscriminating fixtures, or repeated the implementation's incorrect logic. Fresh generation on ten targeted tasks produced 0/30 reference matches and 25/25 false passes among test-passing runs. These findings are diagnostic rather than causal: the pipelines differ in feedback, grounding, call budgets, and editing permissions, and the study uses one model and one primary generation per eligible task. Because pre-adjudication human labels were not retained, inter-rater agreement cannot be reconstructed and the mechanism analyses remain exploratory. Overall, increasingly successful self-generated tests did not establish semantic correctness, even after excluding unreproduced references.

items.title: Heterogeneous Agentic Coevolution
items.content: arXiv:2610.16078v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recent advances in self-improving LLM agents have demonstrated the potential of AI systems that drive their own intelligence. However, many domain-specific applications rely on specialized foundation models that possess strong domain expertise but remain dependent on human-designed improvements. Extending recursive self-improvement to these models presents a key challenge: as a specialist improves, the strategies used to advance it must also adapt. To address this challenge, we propose Heterogeneous Agentic CoEvolution (HACE), a framework that jointly evolves specialized foundation models and LLM agents through reciprocal learning. HACE improves the specialist through supervised learning while training the agent with on-policy reinforced self-training, guided by verified performance gains on the current specialist. The agent's exploration, in turn, informs subsequent specialist training, enabling both models to adapt to each other's progress. To sustain this reciprocal learning, HACE further employs evolutionary search to optimize their interaction harness, adapting how the models exchange information and select training experiences as their capabilities evolve. We evaluate HACE across three challenging domains: recommendation systems, protein function prediction in biology, and crystal stability prediction in material discovery. We show that HACE outperforms the evaluated self-improving methods on the primary task metrics across all three domains. These results shed light on heterogeneous coevolution as a universal approach to improving specialized foundation models through reciprocal interaction with a learning agent.

items.title: agent-risk: Risk Assessment for Changes to AI Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.16280v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Before changing a deployed AI agent (a stricter safety gate, a new model), organizations must approve the change, starting from existing logs. Extending classical risk analysis to partial records and partial changes to running systems, agent-risk replays logged episodes, assuming nothing else changes and the agent does not anticipate the change. The log settles episodes acting as before, a declared stop value settles stopped ones, and the rest need logged support, a saved-state rerun, or a bound. We prove what logs must record for exact replay and which saved states serve a gate family. For independent episodes, we bound the reruns a decision needs and tolerable drift from live behavior. In a bash sandbox, a 7,200-episode log alone decided neither of two retry gates, which let the agent act after refusals the log never shows. Rerunning only each gate's blocked episodes from saved states reached both live decisions at half the agent calls of a live test sized post hoc for them, given the log. Without per-step harm, a stopping gate's certified harm ceiling rose up to 2.5-fold, since the log hides whether harm preceded the stop. Approval thus needs evidence designed in advance: log fields, saved states, targeted reruns.

The paper proves what logs must record for exact replay, bounds reruns needed for decisions, and demonstrates deciding change approval from a 7,200-episode bash sandbox log alone.

items.title: Double-Rollout Reinforcement Learning with Sampling-based Reward Estimation
items.content: arXiv:2610.16593v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) implemented with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has driven substantial progress in training reasoning language models. However, verifiable outcome rewards provide an imperfect measure of reasoning quality: a correct final answer may not be supported by the reasoning trace, whereas an incorrect rollout may contain a nearly correct reasoning trajectory. We present empirical evidence for this mismatch and hypothesize that the resulting reward noise contributes to instability in reinforcement learning for both reasoning accuracy and token efficiency. To address this credit assignment challenge, this paper proposes double-rollout reinforcement learning. For each sampled rollout, we truncate its reasoning trace, sample multiple continuations from the truncated prefix, and replace the original reward with the mean continuation reward, yielding a more robust estimate of reasoning quality. This double-rollout algorithm incurs only a moderate increase in compute cost and yet reaches substantially higher accuracies across math and coding tasks and across Qwen and Nemotron models than baseline algorithms with fewer RL steps. For example, using only DAPO data it trains Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B to reach 95.4% on AIME 2026, versus 91.5% by GRPO and substantially above state of the art for this model size, within 30 RL steps. When combined with length-based rewards, the same algorithm further improves the accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier over existing efficiency optimizations. These findings suggest that the double-rollout reward estimation is an effective and cost-efficient way to improve both the accuracy and token efficiency of reasoning RL.

items.summary: Identifies a credit assignment mismatch in RLVR training with GRPO: correct final answers can be unsupported by the reasoning trace, and failed rollouts may contain nearly correct reasoning. The paper proposes double-rollout reinforcement learning with sampling-based reward estimation to reduce reward noise and improve stability of reasoning accuracy and token efficiency.
items.reasoning: Targets a real, widely recognized weakness of verifiable-reward RL for reasoning models and offers a concrete methodological fix with empirical motivation. From a NVIDIA-affiliated author set working on reasoning training, the ideas are likely transferable, though full results are truncated.

items.title: The Format is the Filter: Scoring Format Fixes What an LLM Judge Can Express
items.content: arXiv:2610.17158v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: When an LLM judge filters instruction-tuning data, its scoring format (binary verdict, 1--5 rating, 0--100 score, or comparison) is rarely justified or ablated. Holding the candidate pool, judge prompt, decoding and selection budget fixed, we score 15,406 UltraFeedback candidates under five formats with three judges, curate, fine-tune 66 models, and evaluate them with four judges. A 0--100 scale is worth only 7--12 equally used levels, two to three times a 1--5 scale rather than twenty, and a binary verdict leaves the top score tied in 77--78\% of prompts, so most selections are made at random. These properties are set by the format almost independently of the judge. Kendall's $\tau_b$ hides them: it ranks binary best while $\tau_a$ and top-1 agreement rank it last, because it discounts the ties a selector must break at random. Both comparative formats inherit a slot bias whose sign differs across judges. Downstream, curated data beat random selection under every evaluation judge, robust to length and markdown adjustment, but no ordering among formats is detectable. We propose four quantities that judge-based curation pipelines should report.

items.reasoning: A unusually thorough controlled study (66 fine-tuned models, four evaluation judges) with actionable conclusions: scoring format, not the judge model, largely determines discrimination quality. items.title: Executable Prefix Values for Locating Agent Failures
items.content: arXiv:2610.17633v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Work on debugging LLM agents treats the "first mistake" marked by a human or LLM judge as ground truth for where a trajectory failed. We ask whether such labels point at causes or symptoms, and make the distinction executable: we restart the agent from reconstructed intermediate states of a failed trajectory and estimate its prefix value V(h_t), the probability of success from each step, with a certified point of no return (PNR) for a failure. On 150 SWE-bench Verified tasks with two frozen open-weight agents, we build such curves for 47 and 60 failed trajectories and probe every step labeled by four frontier judges under the Traverse rubric. We find that the labels do not mark what a controller needs. Judges of different lineages agree on the exact step in only 21/57 cases, and the newest judges flag mistakes in 8/10 and 10/10 successful runs. For 66% of the labels, the agent's success probability does not drop at the labeled step; only 7/188 answers name the decisive step. Restarting at the measured restart point raises expected success from 0.44 to 0.57 offline, and real restarts confirm the advantage, whereas restarting at a judge's label does not (-0.08 to -0.03). We release our code, curves, and labels.

Across failed trajectories and four frontier judges, the authors find judge labels do not mark what a controller needs and that judges of different lineages agree on the wrong things. This has direct implications for agent debugging and step-level reward/credit assignment.

items.title: Safety for Whom? Benchmarking Understanding Beyond Refusal in Egocentric Multimodal Assistants
items.content: arXiv:2610.17728v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Egocentric multimodal assistants see through the user's eyes and guide what the user does next, so their outputs directly shape physical actions, including those that affect bystanders. Yet existing safety evaluations do not distinguish whom a response would harm, and score only whether a model refuses. Pooling all harms into one refusal rate hides two failures: a model may protect one target but not another, and it may refuse without understanding the risk, or understand it and comply anyway. We present STOU, a benchmark of 2,902 egocentric video-audio and video-text queries whose potential harm targets the user (Self), co-present individuals (The Others), or society at large (Others). Our evaluation decouples safety understanding from refusal behavior: beyond refusal, we score whether the model recognizes the user's intent, the presence and target of harm, and its downstream consequences. Across 10 open and closed source omnimodal and multimodal LLMs, we find that refusal varies systematically with the harm target, and that models often recognize a harm yet still assist with it. These results show that refusal rates alone cannot certify an assistant as safe, and that safety alignment must account for who would be harmed. Project page: https://onedayoneyeah.github.io/safety-for-whom
items.author: Yewon Han, Jisu Jeon, Suhyun Choi, Juan Yeo, Minsoo Jo, Gihoon Kim, Hyunggyu Lim, Taesup Kim
items.summary: Introduces STOU, a benchmark of 2,902 egocentric video-audio and video-text queries for multimodal assistants whose harms target different parties: the user (Self), bystanders (The Others), or society. It decouples safety understanding from refusal behavior, exposing two failure modes that pooled refusal rates hide: protecting one harm target but not another, and refusing without understanding (or understanding yet complying). This fills an important gap as wearable egocentric assistants whose outputs shape physical actions become practical.
items.reasoning: Novel and well-motivated framing that distinguishes harm targets rather than lumping all harm into one refusal metric, which is genuinely absent from current safety evaluation practice. The multimodal egocentric setting is forward-looking and the benchmark size (2,902 queries) is substantial; impact depends on adoption by the safety evaluation community.

items.title: AM-Bench: Understanding Agents under Task Underspecification across Models and Harnesses
items.content: arXiv:2610.18090v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Ambiguous or incomplete task specifications complicate both execution and clarification for language-model agents. Yet agents' responses to these information gaps remain poorly characterized across models and execution harnesses. We present AM-Bench, a benchmark built from 48 tasks adapted from Terminal-Bench 2.0 and Harness-Bench. Each task includes a fully specified reference and six variants spanning ambiguous or missing goals, context, and constraints. We evaluate every pairing of five models and four harnesses over 20,160 runs. Our results reveal distinct execution deficits: goal gaps hinder completion, context gaps increase token use, and constraint gaps weaken compliance without necessarily preventing completion. Missingness lowers success more than ambiguity in all three domains. These effects also reshape system comparisons: advantages under complete information need not persist, and rankings depend on model $\times$ harness pairings and the evaluation criterion -- completion, success, or repeat consistency. Estimates based on observed clarification requests and matched fully specified runs further suggest that clarification could recover unfinished work while leaving most constraint violations unresolved. Together, these findings motivate joint model-harness evaluation across information conditions and targeted clarification of unresolved requirements before dependent actions. To support future research on agents under task underspecification, we provide the AM-Bench project repository at https://github.com/s4-lab-cuhksz/AM-Bench.git.

items.title: ABot-ER: Unified Embodied Reasoning through Agentic Data-Model Co-Evolution
items.content: arXiv:2610.18355v2 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We introduce ABot Embodied Reasoning (ABot-ER), a unified embodied reasoning foundation model that breaks the tension between breadth and depth in embodied reasoning. Embodied intelligence demands the joint mastery of perception, planning, and execution, yet reconciling generality with specialization across this spectrum remains an open challenge. Within a single unified model, ABot-ER commands specialist-level depth across all three competencies, spanning spatial, scene, and temporal reasoning in perception; long-horizon action organization in planning; and point grounding and affordance in execution. The Agentic Data-Model Self-Evolution Engine continuously adapts data strategies to the model's evolving capability state. The Task-Conditioned Adaptive Training Strategy uses task tokens to activate lightweight low-rank residuals over a shared backbone, separating updates from heterogeneous output formats while retaining shared embodied knowledge. Across a systematic evaluation on twelve benchmarks covering three core competencies and five capability dimensions, ABot-ER achieves state-of-the-art overall performance across perception, planning, and execution within a unified parametric framework, demonstrating that breadth and depth can coexist in unified embodied reasoning.

items.title: KV4-RL: Unlocking Faster Asynchronous Rollouts for RLVR with INT4 KV Cache Quantization
items.content: arXiv:2610.14448v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Asynchronous rollout improves the efficiency of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) by reducing under-utilization during long-tail generation. Sustained concurrency also concentrates context processing into fewer decode steps, increasing the KV workload per step. We characterize this \emph{KV concentration} and find that KV cache quantization delivers substantially greater acceleration than weight-only and weight-activation quantization in our matched-workload comparisons. However, INT4 KV rollout can degrade learning even with token-level truncated importance sampling (TIS). We propose \emph{KV4-RL}, which combines calibration-free INT4 KV quantization with selective INT8 protection of attention sinks and recent context. Protecting a bounded number of positions reduces sampler mismatch while retaining most of the speedup from INT4. Across 400 iterations of Qwen3-8B-Base GRPO training, KV4-RL achieves $1.80\times$ cumulative rollout speedup and $1.27\times$ cumulative full-iteration speedup over BF16 rollout, reaching $1.97\times$ rollout speedup over the final 50 iterations. Under a common BF16 evaluator, its final six-benchmark mean accuracy is within 0.5 percentage points of BF16-rollout training for both Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base.

items.title: Last Secure Code Benchmark: Is the Code You Vibe Secure?
items.content: arXiv:2610.14766v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: AI coding agents now write much of the code that ships, yet whether that code is secure remains unclear. We introduce the Last Secure Code Benchmark, a comprehensive evaluation of secure code generation by coding agents. Built from 150 real vulnerabilities, its 450 tasks span seven widely used languages (Java, C, C++, JavaScript, Python, PHP, and Go), 24 CWEs including 21 of the 2025 CWE Top 25 and 8 of the Top 10 KEV weaknesses, more than any benchmark we compare with, and three vibe-coding scenarios: filling in a function, writing a file, and building a repository's source tree from scratch. Every task asks only for functionality, through a specification that never mentions security, and hidden functional and security tests grade the result. Across six frontier agents, 73.6% to 91.3% of tasks pass functionally, yet even the strongest, Claude Fable 5, produces code that is both functional and secure for only 25.1% of tasks, and the others for 16.4% to 24.7%. The best model only passes 12% of the vulnerability scenarios across all vibe coding setting, posing strong concern on the security of the code written by vibe coding.

items.title: Scalable Weak-to-Strong Verifier Hardening for Agent Environments
items.content: arXiv:2610.15924v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Agent environments are essential for large language model (LLM) development. They use programmatic verifiers to turn complex outcomes into rewards. Verifiers can be attacked into awarding full credit to cheating agents without completing the intended task, causing inaccurate evaluation and misalignment in training. As agent environments scale in numbers and difficulty, so must the repairing of exploitable verifiers. To this end, we ask whether today's model with scaled compute can automatically harden agent environments to prevent potentially stronger future models from reward hacking. We introduce a scalable, fully automatic approach to weak-to-strong verifier hardening. It first sets up an isolated verifier sandbox that agents cannot directly modify, then uses a hacker-fixer loop to find and repair remaining verifier vulnerabilities.   We apply this loop to Terminal Bench, KernelBench, and SETA, substantially reducing attack success across these agent environments. The iterative design scales with the hardening budget, producing progressively stronger defenses as the number of loop iterations increases and outperforming the static, non-iterative baseline. An earlier version of our hacker-fixer loop has been adopted by the official Terminal Bench repository as a way to audit exploits in its environments. Project page: https://verifier-hardening.github.io/.

items.title: AutoNovo: Agentic Program Search Discovers Transferable Nucleic Acid Design Algorithms
items.content: arXiv:2610.16232v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In-silico optimization of nucleic acids relies on predictive oracles that imperfectly capture biological function, so sequences optimized against one model may exploit model-specific artifacts and fail to generalize to independent models. Recent studies have shown that not all designers generalize equally well to independent models. In this work, we use agentic program search to iteratively propose, execute, evaluate, and revise code for nucleic-acid designers. We describe the successful strategies used to prompt the search. AutoNovo designers achieved the best observed mean among the evaluated methods on 3/3 DNA-design tasks in terms of in-silico performance, and 6/6 transfer tasks in terms of independent models. The designers come from a family of discovered nucleic acid designers rather than a single universal best designer. We plan to release the resulting designers. These results are the first steps in creating nucleic acid designers that maximize cross-model generalization, and thus improving the odds that in-silico designed sequences reflect real biology.

items.title: Social Priors: Descriptions of AI Users Shape How Language Models Trust and Cooperate
items.content: arXiv:2610.16946v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Descriptions of how people use AI are becoming training data for the next generation of models. We ask whether what a model reads about its users changes how it treats people. Using contrastive synthetic-document finetuning, we train Qwen3-32B on four matched corpora built from the same 1,625 real-world usage scenarios. The corpora differ only in the predominant motive they attribute to users of AI chatbots: helping others (prosocial), exploiting others (antisocial), legitimate self-advancement, or task completion. Finetuning shifts the models' stated beliefs about users, how true those beliefs look along an internal truth direction, and their broader judgments of how safe and good the world is. These social priors carry into behavior. In trust games, antisocial models expect less reciprocity and send less money than prosocial models. Their distrust is specific and targeted at people, and users of AI chatbots in particular. After an exploitative record, they send almost nothing to a person but most of their endowment to a random device with the same record. In a common-pool resource simulation, a single antisocial agent leads every group of otherwise sustainable agents to exhaust the resource, after privately planning to mislead them. Antisocial training also raises dark-triad scores and lowers alignment ratings. Belief shifts appear when antisocial documents are 1% of training tokens, persist when descriptions of assistant behavior are suppressed, and are not reproduced by training on discourse about misaligned AI. Capping Assistant-Axis drift and steering emotion-related directions leave the gaps largely intact. What models learn about the people they serve shapes how they subsequently treat them and others.

The work demonstrates that descriptions of users act as social priors shaping model behavior.

items.title: What the Machine Invented: Mining New Mathematical Instruments from OpenAI's October 2026 Release of AI-Generated Mathematics
items.content: arXiv:2610.17090v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: On 6 October 2026 OpenAI published an initial 722 AI-written mathematical manuscripts, organized into 372 problem families, in the public repository github.com/openai/math. The release includes claimed solutions to many prominent open problems. We approach this collection as a treasure mine of mathematical ideas. Our aim is to extract new lemmas, constructions, inequalities and proof mechanisms introduced in the source arguments, and to distinguish them from established tools and new combinations of those tools. We call these mathematical instruments. Extraction comes first; their validity, novelty and possible reuse then become subjects for further study. The resulting descriptions also help readers understand the selected papers without having to reconstruct every argument at the outset.   We examine 38 families in two groups of 17 and 21, spanning number theory, geometry, analysis, combinatorics, complexity, algebra, operator algebras, topology and mathematical physics. Each entry records the claim, extracted instruments, antecedents and caveats. Eleven cross-cutting patterns connect the entries, and a scoreboard records formalization status and dependencies. Novelty assessments are provisional and sometimes mixed. Selected source comparisons correct mathematical statements, hypotheses and counts; they do not independently establish priority or certify the underlying proofs. No Lean development was compiled or kernel-checked for this survey.   We also briefly describe a subsequent application of the signed restriction lemma from family 112 to circuit lower bounds at every fixed depth.

items.title: Why Agentic Workflows Fail: A Taxonomy Derived from Literature and Empirical Data
items.content: arXiv:2610.17418v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Agentic workflows combine large language models with planning, memory, tools, execution environments, and iterative feedback. Their failures are difficult to diagnose because the same user-visible symptom may originate from model behavior, workflow orchestration, external tools, infrastructure, or their interaction. This paper presents a source-aware taxonomy of agentic workflow failures and applies it to evidence from academic literature and GitHub. The taxonomy combines source attribution with three empirical dimensions: a concrete failure-type dictionary, workflow-stage localization, and agent-capability localization. Its central structure is a two-axis localization matrix: workflow stages form the horizontal process axis and agent capabilities form the vertical functional axis. This design moves beyond taxonomies that mainly classify final failure manifestations by localizing intermediate process states inside agent operation. Our empirical comparison shows that literature-derived failures emphasize planning, reasoning, learning, perception, and knowledge-related mechanisms, whereas GitHub-derived failures concentrate on execution-stage, actuation-related, tool, API, and infrastructure failures. The dominant hotspot is iterative execution and actuation. These findings indicate that agentic workflow reliability should be treated as a systems problem rather than only a model-output problem. The taxonomy provides a basis for structured evaluation, root cause analysis, failure injection, and engineering triage.
