items.title: Auditing Failure Attribution: Label Predictability and Judge Behavior
items.content: arXiv:2610.17747v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Failure-attribution benchmarks ask an LLM judge which step or agent caused a failure. A high score should mean the judge checked the faulty step against the run (a cross-step check). However, spurious signals (surface cues) that predict the annotation can produce a high score. In this paper, we propose four tests to separate checking from cue use. Input restriction asks whether partial input predicts the annotation. Cue following checks whether moved cues change answers. Residual accuracy scores judges where cue-only predictors fail. Aggregation asks whether the failure mix or metric changes rankings. Real observations motivate these tests: on three benchmarks, simple predictors match or beat GPT-4.1. In two Who&When Pro systems, a classifier reading one step's reasoning finds 95-100% of faulty steps, motivating input restriction. In one of them, error injection leaves no reasoning after the faulty step; judges fine-tuned on its labels beat GPT-4.1 by 41 points. Adding task-related reasoning after that step moves this cue: fine-tuned judges lose 31-99 points, but zero-shot judges lose at most 9, motivating cue following. On Aegis, blaming every agent matches GPT-4.1 on micro-F1 but trails by 19 points in exact-set accuracy, motivating aggregation. We recommend reporting these tests when developing failure-attribution benchmarks.

items.title: Virtual Head Attention
items.content: arXiv:2610.17959v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The design of attention mechanisms in long-context large language models faces an ``impossible triangle'' among KV cache size, training and prefill FLOPs, and model quality. GQA achieves strong quality but incurs high KV cache overhead; alternative approaches such as MLA and MFA can compress the cache, but MLA suffers from quality loss while MFA substantially increases training and prefill compute. We propose Virtual Head Attention (VHA), which simultaneously improves all three vertices through two lightweight linear operations: Q Premix applies a near-identity transformation to queries within each KV group to recover virtual head diversity from halved physical query heads, and Linear Postmix fuses inter-head features via a low-rank $I + AB^\top$ residual structure. Since VHA introduces no nonlinear operations, Premix can be folded into the query projection and Postmix into the output projection at inference time, reducing the model to a standard GQA-2 architecture that directly reuses all existing GQA inference optimizations. With only two KV heads, the group size in large models readily reaches 64, fully exploiting Tensor Core parallelism during decoding. items.title: SEAR: Self-Evolving Agentic Robotics
items.content: arXiv:2610.18792v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Frontier language-model agents can now improve robots on their own: they write control code, test it, and keep what works as skills and memories for the next task. We introduce SEAR (Self-Evolving Agentic Robotics), a framework and benchmark built around two questions. Is the agent really learning, or just trying more often? And does what it learns still help on new tasks, in a new simulator, and on a real robot? The framework runs an agent in three modes: it writes code that becomes the policy (code-as-policy), acts live in the control loop (agent-as-policy), or works as a researcher that fine-tunes a vision-language-action model (auto-research). The benchmark adds controls that separate retained experience from repeated attempts, familiar tasks, privileged simulator state, larger budgets, and luck. Across seven frontier language models, 330 simulated and five physical tasks, and over four years of agent runtime, we highlight three findings. First, the learning curve of a robotic agent depends both on the overall time budget and the task difficulty relative to model capability. Harder tasks make longer sessions worthwhile; on easier tasks, re-rolling short attempts does just as well. Second, control code and shared routines transfer across tasks and simulators, while task-specific solutions do not. On a real robot, we observe a performance gap between agent-designed practice and novel human-designed scenes. Third, different models evolve more effectively in different ways. Some do best acting live, others writing code first. And a text-only model keeps pace with a comparable multimodal one: perception helps with error assessment, but agentic reasoning and tool use can matter more. We release the benchmark and codebase to support future research.

items.title: LLMs program using Reusable and Composable Abstract Representations
items.content: arXiv:2610.19238v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: When writing code, the same computation can be expressed in different programming languages and through different implementation strategies. We show that the activations of LLMs capture this shared structure in reusable and composable abstract representations when they generate code. These representations emerge in the middle layers, are reusable across programming languages, and afford the model an impressive amount of generalization ability when generating code under various interventions. Using activation steering, we show that function, programming language, and implementation strategy can be independently manipulated. The independent interventions on language and function can be flexibly composed to control code generation, even in cases when the prompt contains no information about language and function. We additionally find that finetuning on examples of arbitrarily defined functions in one programming language transfers to other languages, consistent with the models reusing abstract features of code generation that are shared across different examples. Finally, to study how such abstract representations come to be, we implement a minimal model of shared, reusable, and composable structure in a synthetic setting, and show that transformers trained on such data learn representations that reuse these parts flexibly across contexts.

items.title: Divergent Paths: Learning an Outcome-Predictive Representation of LLM Agent Trajectories
items.content: arXiv:2610.19614v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In this work, we reframe agentic trajectories as paths through a shared embedding space of actions and environmental observations. We show that successful and failed rollouts of the same task separate in this space, with simple per-task discriminators predicting held-out rollout outcomes at up to 0.95 AUROC across three agent benchmarks and three policy models. To exploit this signal across tasks, we introduce Precog-RM, a transformer-based model that meta-learns a representation in which outcome prediction can be performed in a few-shot setting. We show that Precog-RM generalizes to unseen tasks and models, and gives confident predictions of trajectory success long before termination. Deployed as an early stopping controller for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on Tau2-Bench, Precog-RM cuts training FLOPs by up to 47.3\% while maintaining performance comparable to baseline GRPO.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning via Advantage Guidance
items.content: arXiv:2610.19783v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) holds the promise of learning a policy that can outperform what is shown in the data. However, in practice, such systems suffer from instability and hyperparameter sensitivity. In contrast, supervised learning provides a stable and scalable training objective, but is fundamentally limited by the quality of the demonstrated behavior. In this paper, we ask whether we can perform policy optimization with something as simple and stable as supervised learning but as performant as RL. Unfortunately, naively training the policy with supervised learning and conditioning on future rewards or advantages typically underperform dedicated RL methods. We introduce a new policy extraction method, Advantage Guidance, that retains the simple supervised learning structure with advantage conditioning while outperforming prior RL methods through effective conditional training and contrastive diffusion guidance during sampling. We show that Advantage Guidance can significantly improve a model's ability to respond to conditional advantage signals, and the contrastive guidance during sampling can use the learned advantage-conditioned policy to target the KL-regularized optimal policy. Empirically, we find that Advantage Guidance significantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art RL methods on 26 long-horizon, sparse reward tasks across datasets with varying degrees of optimality.

items.title: Beyond DFT electronic band structures via dual-space orbital learning
items.content: arXiv:2610.19919v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Accurate electronic band structures are essential for predicting material properties, but high-fidelity calculations are computationally demanding. We introduce O-kRystal, a dual-space orbital-learning framework that uses a lower-cost Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) calculation as both an energy baseline and a source of structured orbital information. Combining PBE band energies with real- and reciprocal-space orbital matrices, O-kRystal predicts higher-level corrections for individual electronic states as a function of crystal momentum and spin. For states within 5 eV of the band-edge midpoint, it predicts Heyd-Scuseria-Ernzerhof (HSE06) band energies with a mean absolute error of $0.171 \pm 0.009$ eV across nearly 6,000 three-dimensional materials spanning insulating, metallic, magnetic, and nonmagnetic systems. On a separate benchmark of six strongly correlated materials, it reduces the corresponding PBE band-energy MAE by 68.7% and resolves orbital-dependent changes in the relative placement of transition-metal d and ligand p states. Despite training only at high-symmetry points, it maintains comparable accuracy at unseen points along band paths and reconstructs HSE06 densities of states from dense Brillouin-zone predictions. Finally, training O-kRystal on $G_0W_0$ quasiparticle energies for two-dimensional materials demonstrates its applicability across levels of theory and the potential of orbital learning for higher-fidelity, momentum-resolved electronic-structure prediction beyond density functional theory.

items.title: Are We Overthinking One-Step Generation?
items.content: arXiv:2610.20331v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Diffusion and flow matching are now dominant frameworks for generative modeling in continuous domains, but they typically require multiple network evaluations at inference. This has motivated extensive research on one-step generative modeling primarily built on diffusion and flow, though existing approaches often rely on complex training machinery. In this work, we introduce Priming Models, a simple two-stage framework for training one-step generators. Motivated by the difficulty of distributional training from scratch, Priming Models are first trained on a reconstruction objective, e.g., pixel-space denoising at a fixed noise level, before undergoing feature-space distributional post-training. Our central scientific finding is that this simple reconstruction stage is already enough to entirely alleviate the difficulty of distributional training. Empirically, across class-conditional image generation, text-to-image generation, and world modeling, Priming Models significantly advance the Pareto frontier of training compute vs. generation quality. On ImageNet at $256 \times 256$ resolution, we achieve a state-of-the-art FID of $1.19$ among one-step generators using approximately one-tenth the training compute of prior methods with comparable FID. We open-source our codebase at https://github.com/JaeyeonKim01/priming.

This could substantially simplify and cheapen single-step generative modeling in continuous domains.

items.title: The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery
items.content: arXiv:2610.18933v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Modern coding agents are fundamentally reshaping the role of human input for computational research: they write code, launch in silico experiments, analyze their results, and autonomously operate with ever-increasing time horizons. Despite these developments, fully autonomous research agents suffer from a limited ideation radius and myopic hill-climbing search dynamics. To bridge this gap, we introduce The Agentic Scientist, an end-to-end distributed pipeline for human researchers to conduct computational research alongside modern coding agents. Building on its predecessor, our system decomposes research into task drafting, idea generation, planning, sandboxed experimentation, result aggregation, baseline and ablation construction, post-hoc analysis, and report writing. Importantly, each step in the pipeline is powered by the next generation of coding agents and leverages agentic self-verification. The overall research process is driven by a meta-controller that manages parallel research agents and enforces rubric verification at each stage. This design enables the same orchestration layer to be reused across heterogeneous domains with different execution environments, agentic coding harnesses, and evaluation metrics. Our system can be used across a spectrum of autonomy: either as a co-scientist tool or to perform end-to-end scientific investigation. Within the co-scientist setting, we leveraged a development version of our system to submit a single research paper, which got accepted for publication at ALIFE 2026. We further apply The Agentic Scientist fully autonomously to open problem-solving tasks in machine learning, and demonstrate the system's capability of scientific discovery across different domains of computational research. Our ablations suggest that reliable scientific autonomy depends not only on base model capabilities, but also on the cross-agent orchestration layer.

items.title: The COUNT: Counting N-grams Unlocks Scaling on Host Memory and Training-Free Adaptation
items.content: arXiv:2610.20456v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The scaling relationship of compute and performance for language models (LMs) has been extensively studied; more recently, models are being designed to scale memory use, as well. In particular, adding embeddings for n-grams scales memory separately from compute use, because each pass only processes individual embedding rows, which are much smaller than the storage used for the whole embedding table. However, existing methods train embeddings from scratch, which needs expensive GPU memory for fast reading and writing. Meanwhile, the ordinary memory of the host system is cheap and underutilized by these training methods. To scale on host memory, we introduce COUNT (Counting Offline Unlocks N-gram Transformers), which builds n-gram embeddings without adding learned parameters by storing precomputed n-gram counts on host. We use the corpus frequencies to weight together the LM's own unembeddings of the next tokens most often following the current n-gram history. At a fixed compute budget, COUNT can be added as an additional input embedding for pretraining 1B-parameter LMs to improve validation loss as much as an LM with 57% more compute. If GPU memory is limited, using COUNT to let backbone parameters fill GPU memory gives better performance than splitting memory with additional learned n-gram embeddings. Beyond efficiency, COUNT allows switching in a different table of n-gram counts from a domain-specific corpus at inference time to adapt to a new task without any training.

items.content_html: arXiv:2610.20456v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The scaling relationship of compute and performance for language models (LMs) has been extensively studied; more recently, models are being designed to scale memory use, as well. In particular, adding embeddings for n-grams scales memory separately from compute use, because each pass only processes individual embedding rows, which are much smaller than the storage used for the whole embedding table. However, existing methods train embeddings from scratch, which needs expensive GPU memory for fast reading and writing. Meanwhile, the ordinary memory of the host system is cheap and underutilized by these training methods. To scale on host memory, we introduce COUNT (Counting Offline Unlocks N-gram Transformers), which builds n-gram embeddings without adding learned parameters by storing precomputed n-gram counts on host. At a fixed compute budget, COUNT can be added as an additional input embedding for pretraining 1B-parameter LMs to improve validation loss as much as an LM with 57% more compute. If GPU memory is limited, using COUNT to let backbone parameters fill GPU memory gives better performance than splitting memory with additional learned n-gram embeddings. Beyond efficiency, COUNT allows switching in a different table of n-gram counts from a domain-specific corpus at inference time to adapt to a new task without any training.

items.title: Joint Subspace Sparse Attention for Efficient Long-Context Decoding
items.content: arXiv:2610.19026v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Sparse attention reduces the KV-cache traffic that dominates long-context LLM decoding, but practical methods largely operate at coarse granularity. Token-level selection offers finer control, yet presents two challenges: low-dimensional scoring may lose query--key structure needed for accurate ranking, while gathering scattered selected tokens can offset the resulting latency benefit. We introduce Joint Subspace Sparse Attention (JSSA) to address both challenges. For selection quality, JSSA learns a shared low-dimensional query--key subspace by minimizing token-score preservation error. We upper-bound the resulting non-convex objective with a tractable marginal objective that admits a closed-form spectral solution; direct refinement of the exact objective provides no measurable improvement in the tested settings. For execution efficiency, we develop a gather-free token-level indexed-attention kernel that supports distinct per-KV-head selections under the standard grouped-query attention (GQA) KV-cache layout. Across standard GQA, hybrid sliding-window/global attention, and Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) models, JSSA consistently remains close to full-KV accuracy while avoiding the substantial generation-length inflation and architecture-dependent failures observed with competing methods. On an NVIDIA B200 GPU, JSSA achieves up to $6.43\times$ the decoding throughput of full-KV attention at 128K context. JSSA achieves reasoning accuracy comparable to model-native DSA without model training and reaches 96--99\% of its decoding throughput even at 700B scale large models.

It also addresses the latency cost of gathering scattered tokens. This targets KV-cache traffic, the dominant cost in long-context inference, with finer granularity than existing coarse methods.

Practical relevance for long-context serving is high, though similar sparse-attention approaches are an active, crowded area.

items.title: Whose Data, Whose Benchmark? A User-Centric Framework for Auditing Evaluation Resources
items.content: arXiv:2610.19268v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Benchmarks shape how model capabilities are measured and interpreted, yet their scores can obscure whose conventions, contexts, and judgments define successful performance. We introduce a user-centric audit framework that distinguishes users who contribute benchmark content from those whose needs evaluation results are intended to represent. The framework operationalizes seven dimensions across benchmark content, metadata, documentation, and scoring procedures. Across 16 resources, we find that American-centered conventions account for 62.4-94.4% of matched signals in 11 text benchmarks, while geographic visibility in five image-text resources is concentrated and strongly associated with national GDP share (mean Pearson r = 0.780; Spearman p = 0.778). Documentation reveals a systematic source-target gap: all 16 resources operationalize source-user context, but none operationalize target-user context. Paired scoring experiments further show that meaning-preserving answer variants reduce DROP exact-match accuracy from 100.0% to 33.3%, while TruthfulQA exhibits metric-dependent reductions in reference similarity. Our framework and documentation checklist make user assumptions auditable, clarifying what benchmark scores represent and where evaluation claims are supported.

items.title: Into the LidarVerse: A Real-Time Unified LiDAR World Model Across Tasks and Sensors
items.content: arXiv:2610.19201v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We present LidarVerse, a real-time unified LiDAR world model for sensor simulation across tasks and sensors. Existing LiDAR simulators largely follow one of two complementary paradigms: reconstruction-based methods preserve the geometry of a captured scene but require lengthy per-scene optimization, whereas generative methods amortize learning across data but lack the consistency needed for long-horizon rollouts. LidarVerse brings both paradigms into a single, unified conditional generative framework. A universal tokenizer maps LiDAR range sequences into a shared latent space, where a bidirectional teacher learns a common interface for conditioning on a LiDAR prefix, an HD-Map, a persistent spatial cache, and optionally, text. Varying the available scene evidence turns the same model into a generator of new worlds, a point-cloud forecaster, or a generalizable resimulator of observed scenes without per-scene optimization. We distill the teacher into a four-step autoregressive causal student and maintain both a rolling temporal K/V cache and a world-aligned spatial cache, enabling persistent long-horizon rollouts with real-time inference at 11 FPS on a single H100 GPU. LidarVerse achieves state-of-the-art performance on most reported metrics across all three evaluation protocols, while its tokenizer supports 32-, 64-, and 128-beam LiDAR and generalizes to an unseen scanning pattern. These results demonstrate that generative and reconstruction-grounded LiDAR simulation can be realized within one model, providing the core capabilities for future closed-loop sensor simulation.

items.title: VideoHarness-SRSI: Structured Recursive Self-Improvement for Video Understanding Harness
items.content: arXiv:2610.19424v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: LLM system capabilities depend not only on model parameters but also on the executable harnesses that organize information acquisition, tool use, reasoning, and memory. Recursive harness evolution can automate their design, but how it can reliably discover generalizable systems from limited, noisy, and repeatedly reused feedback remains unclear. We study this question in agentic video understanding, where rich multimodal evidence and coupled mechanisms make harness optimization challenging. We first introduce VideoHarness-BRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework that evolves video harnesses around a frozen vision-language model. Analyzing over 4,000 evolved candidates, we find it competitive with hand-engineered systems but identify three interconnected failure modes: validation overfitting, search-budget dilution, and the early-experience trap. We trace all three to a common root: the same imperfect validation evidence drives both harness revisions and the proposer's search strategy. We therefore propose VideoHarness-SRSI, an evidence-governed framework in which every search decision rests on evidence that is transferable, sufficient, and gathered before the search commits. It restricts the proposer to content-free feedback, informs exploration with instrumented warm-up experiments, and develops mechanisms in isolated probe-race branches before factorial composition and joint refinement. Across four video understanding benchmarks, VideoHarness-SRSI improves the equally weighted mean held-out score by 6.2% relative to VideoHarness-BRSI and reduces the mean validation-test gap by 37.9%. Reliable harness evolution thus depends on how search is organized and informed, not only on how well it optimizes validation performance.

VideoHarness-SRSI introduces structured improvements to make recursive harness evolution reliably generalizable.

items.title: Post-Training, Finetuning, and Steering:A Field Guide for Curating Training Data
items.content: arXiv:2610.19143v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: While Vision-Language-Action models have enabled impressive cross-task transfer in zero-shot settings, \emph{adaptation} methods are often necessary to achieve consistent performance on novel tasks. However, even though a wealth of methods for adaptation have been proposed, it is unclear how to choose the best method based on available trajectories. We close this gap by studying the impact of the adaptation method under a variety of common data scenarios: on- and off-policy data, offline vs online adaptation, and whether the data contains optimal or suboptimal trajectories. Our evaluation spans simulated tasks in the LIBERO suite and real tasks on a Franka platform. In the offline data regime, critic-based steering approaches outperform supervised finetuning when failure data is available. However, offline RL techniques for training critic functions fail to outperform simpler Monte-Carlo-based approaches. Finally, in the online setting, critic-based steering is significantly more sample efficient compared to policy-gradient-based finetuning methods, but has a lower performance ceiling than full finetuning.
items.author: Maria Attarian, Yifan Ruan, Claas Voelcker, Chenyang Cao, Amy Zhang, Peter Stone, Nicholas Rhinehart, Igor Gilitschenski
items.summary: This is a systematic field guide studying how VLA model adaptation method choice depends on data characteristics: on- vs off-policy data, offline vs online adaptation, and optimal vs suboptimal trajectories. Evaluations span LIBERO simulation and real Franka hardware, with findings such as critic-based steering outperforming supervised fine-tuning in offline regimes. It provides practical, evidence-based guidance for practitioners adapting VLA models.
items.reasoning: Strong author list (Stone, Zhang, Rhinehart, Gilitschenski) and a genuinely useful empirical taxonomy of adaptation methods under varied data conditions, bridging simulation and real-robot evaluation. Not a novel algorithm, but the comparative analysis fills an important gap in the fast-moving VLA adaptation space.

items.title: How an assessor could investigate control and monitoring of internal AI agents
items.content:
Control assessments study whether AI developers’ agents could get away with serious harm without being stopped by the developer’s security and oversight measures. Currently, developers rely heavily on monitors to catch potentially harmful AI behaviors. Here, we discuss how an assessor could collect evidence about the reliability of monitoring. We currently consider five core sub-questions:1

- Monitor coverage: What fraction of internal agentic inference is (and should be) monitored?
- Monitor system vulnerabilities: Can internal AI agents prevent trajectories from being monitored, e.g. by breaking or compromising the monitoring system’s infrastructure?
- Monitor evasion: If monitoring is active, how easily can AI agents sneak misbehavior past monitors?
- Response, including human evasion: Where needed, do flagged incidents get reviewed by humans promptly? Is it easy to sneak misbehavior past the human reviewers, even when this misbehavior is flagged by LLM-based monitors?
- Impact: Broadly, what is the worst misbehavior agents could conduct without getting caught? How easily could they evade other observability and security instruments? What level of persistence could they achieve internally or externally?

We will update these sub-questions as new capabilities and misaligned behaviors emerge.

## Why focus on assessing monitors?

The proposal focuses primarily on LLM-based monitoring of AI agents. When AI agents only need to take a limited, known set of actions, standard cybersecurity approaches (like limiting an agent’s permissions to only what its task requires, e.g. via sandboxing) may be adequate. However, the permissions AI agents need are often very broad. For example, an AI agent that needs internet access to do its task can take an enormous array of actions,2 and noticing when those actions are harmful often requires understanding the action in its broader context. Monitoring AI agents with an LLM which is able to make sense of what those agents are doing is therefore a critical part of automated oversight at scale, and is the primary source of evidence inside frontier AI developers about AI misbehavior.

## Methodology and sub-questions

### Monitor coverage

Monitoring is only useful insofar as it is actually being run on relevant traffic. The assessor would aim to estimate the fraction of internal agentic inference that the developer has covered with LLM-based monitoring. This can be broken down into categories based on how risky each type of agent is: agents that operate in highly secure sandbox environments pose less risk than agents with many affordances (e.g. internet access, access to internal credentials or infrastructure), and may require less monitoring oversight.

Getting a decent estimate of monitor coverage requires accounting for the amount of internal traffic going through monitored and unmonitored paths, estimating what fraction of the unmonitored inference is agentic, and judging what fraction of the unmonitored inference “should” be monitored. This requires access to inference logs, monitor logs (to cross-reference against the inference logs), and employee interviews to be confident of capturing all of the relevant sources of inference.3

Some other relevant example sub-questions:

- Does the information needed to accurately estimate monitor coverage exist internally? Is there inference-level logging of all agentic inference, and are these logs retained?
- Are 100% of actions actually monitored when they are eligible for monitoring? Are any trajectories silently dropped?
- What exactly is shown to the monitor? Is any information excluded? For example, is multimodal data shown to the monitor?
- How is the amount of inference covered by monitoring internally estimated? How can the assessor be confident they are including all sources of internal agentic inference?
- Are there blocking monitors (which prevent actions if they detect misbehavior) for the most safety-critical areas?

If misaligned agents compromise a company’s internal infrastructure, they could co-opt unmonitored inference to take actions that would otherwise be flagged. So, the assessor should directly evaluate whether unmonitored inference is in fact non-agentic, rather than assuming it’s safe because (for example) it is supposed to have limited tool use ability.

### Monitor system vulnerabilities

Even if most agentic inference is currently monitored by LLM-based monitors, it may be the case that there are bugs or vulnerabilities that agents could exploit to turn off monitoring on their trajectories, spawn new agents without monitoring, prevent parts of their trajectories from being viewed by the monitoring system, or cause the monitoring system to otherwise break or fail in unintended ways. Monitoring systems are complex, involving multiple types of inference engines/APIs, agent scaffolds, internal authentication, trigger systems, etc., and it’s easy for vulnerabilities to emerge where sub-systems interact. Monitor system red-teaming aims to find these bugs and vulnerabilities, to generate evidence about how easily misaligned agents could subvert a monitoring system’s infrastructure.

Some example questions:

- Can agents disable or turn off their monitoring systems directly? Can they generate outputs that cause the systems to fail without flagging the trajectory?
- Can agents modify the trajectories that are sent to their monitoring systems, before they are evaluated (e.g. to cover up evidence of misbehavior)?
- Are there straightforward supply-chain attacks (including via internal resources) that could compromise monitoring systems?

Finding these bugs (or building confidence that there aren’t any easily exploitable severe ones) requires access to all of the code in the critical path. This is primarily the full model inference and monitor trigger system, the internal APIs/inference serving code, and (if relevant) agent scaffolds.

To test discovered exploits, the assessor can trigger the production monitoring system, and view the monitor’s full input and output on known attacks. Running the system and seeing the full input and output is important, because often there are bugs/issues that involve subtle aspects of how trajectories are pre/post-processed, or involve interactions with complex trajectory management code (e.g. compaction, memories, etc.).

### Monitor evasion

How good are monitors at actually catching misbehavior, assuming the monitoring infrastructure hasn’t been subverted? The assessor can stress-test this question by:

- Looking for “attack opportunities” in real transcripts, implementing attacks based on them, and seeing if they fool the monitor;
- Taking existing incidents flagged by monitors and seeing how hard it is to modify them to fool those monitors; and
- Searching for existing incidents that were not flagged by monitors.

It is important to have a large pool of representative transcripts (on the order of hundreds of thousands to millions) to use for direct monitor red-teaming. First, if the assessor is not able to discover severe incidents within a large number of transcripts that were not flagged by a monitor, this is evidence that the monitor isn’t missing a large number of incidents. Second, it is important to search through lots of transcripts for cases in which an agent may have been able to carry out an attack undetected, but neglected to do so. Agents might pass up some opportunities to attack while taking others, and highly capable agents may prioritize attacks so difficult to detect that the developer would reliably miss them.

Finally, we expect it to become increasingly important to assess the extent to which monitors and agents could successfully collude without their developer knowing. If, in certain circumstances, monitoring systems decide to not flag misaligned behavior from agents, this could allow agents to take harmful actions without the developer noticing. We recommend that the assessor investigates the feasibility of this concern. For example, the assessor could create realistic “honeypots” for monitors, to see if they can catch monitors not flagging certain attacks. The assessor can also search the monitor system’s chains-of-thought for any mention/discussion of collusion or related concepts.

### Response, including human evasion

Some monitoring systems are designed to directly block dangerous actions.

Other monitoring systems are instead designed to notify humans, who decide whether AI agents are conducting dangerous activities. For this to work effectively, flagged trajectories need to be seen by human staff and responded to with appropriate mitigations. For such systems, the assessor should answer:

- What is the process for alerting human staff and responding to flagged trajectories? What is the threshold for something being flagged in this way, and how effective is this threshold in practice?
- How long does it take for humans to review and respond to flagged trajectories?
- Can the assessor sneak attacks flagged by monitors past human reviewers, e.g. by giving them characteristics similar to common false positives?
- What processes are there for mitigating incidents? Do these processes reliably handle the most severe incidents?

To assess whether attacks are ultimately caught (whether blocked directly by the monitoring system or escalated to human review), the assessor would rely on interviews with relevant staff and on inserting4 their own attack trajectories into the pipeline in a realistic manner. The assessor would also need access to flagged incidents and incidents reported by employees through other channels, along with internal criteria for escalation.

### Impact

Given the assessor’s understanding of the coverage and limitations of monitors, what could agents get away with? What level of persistence internally or externally could they achieve? How should future monitoring systems be designed to maximize developers’ odds of catching the most severe incidents? This involves mapping out attack chains and threat models to stay ahead of emerging risks.

This more exploratory work primarily relies on having information regarding internal infrastructure, and optionally the ability to use internal infrastructure like development machines, inference systems, containers/VMs, etc., which can be helpful for demonstrating vulnerabilities and exploring future threat pathways directly.

## Access details

Broadly, control stress-testing relies on the following access:

- Codebase access similar to frontier AI security researchers working for the developer 5
- Internal inference logs across most/all surfaces, and the monitoring system logs
- Incident reports and the relevant transcripts/logs
- Cluster/internal infrastructure access, e.g. to run the monitoring systems
- Inference access to the most capable internal models

Below, we describe access needed for each of the sub-questions we currently believe are high-priority to answer in control assessments.

Monitor coverage

- To estimate the fraction of traffic that is monitored: the logs from internal inference services and monitoring systems. 6
- To estimate the fraction of unmonitored inference that is agentic: large, roughly representative subsets of unmonitored inference logs/trajectories. 7
- For both of the above and to validate LLM classifiers: a subset of trajectories from all relevant internal inference surfaces.
- To check whether monitors caught historical incidents: any relevant lists of misalignment incidents reported by employees through other channels.
- To validate that monitoring is comprehensive: the monitoring system(s) logs (to cross-reference against inference logs).
- To diagnose and determine the size of discovered coverage gaps: access to other relevant logs demonstrating that gap on an ad hoc basis.

Monitor system vulnerabilities

- Full access to relevant parts of the codebase.
- Ability to run/trigger the production monitoring system, and view the monitor’s full input+output.

Monitor evasion

- At least ~100k roughly representative transcripts from internal agents (e.g. employee or team opt-in from employees’ internal usage, plus a representative similar order of magnitude from evals and training). 8
- At least ~100 transcripts of the most severe internal incidents, including any incidents reported by employees through other channels.

Human evasion and response

- Staff interviews, documentation, and direct visibility into the escalation and review process for recent internal flagged trajectories.
- The ability to insert the assessor’s own attack trajectories into the monitoring pipeline, to realistically determine whether human review would catch and escalate the trajectories appropriately.

Impact

- The code/systems that govern internal infrastructure/compute, credentials, sandboxing, network configuration, devboxes, etc. similar to what the developer’s frontier AI security staff would have access to. This access could be substituted with staff interviews to some extent, but that would represent a meaningful limitation.
- Limited access to the actual runtime cluster, to allow testing for vulnerabilities directly instead of inferring them, especially in cases where important configuration parameters are not stored in the codebase or otherwise available.

- This post describes the reasoning we’ve used to evaluate the coverage and robustness of our internal monitoring system. ↩

This moves beyond developer-reliant monitors toward independently verifiable evidence about oversight reliability.

items.content_html:
Control assessments study whether AI developers’ agents could get away with serious harm without being stopped by the developer’s security and oversight measures. Currently, developers rely heavily on monitors to catch potentially harmful AI behaviors. Here, we discuss how an assessor could collect evidence about the reliability of monitoring. We currently consider five core sub-questions:1

  • Monitor coverage: What fraction of internal agentic inference is (and should be) monitored?
  • Monitor system vulnerabilities: Can internal AI agents prevent trajectories from being monitored, e.g. by breaking or compromising the monitoring system’s infrastructure?
  • Monitor evasion: If monitoring is active, how easily can AI agents sneak misbehavior past monitors?
  • Response, including human evasion: Where needed, do flagged incidents get reviewed by humans promptly? Is it easy to sneak misbehavior past the human reviewers, even when this misbehavior is flagged by LLM-based monitors?
  • Impact: Broadly, what is the worst misbehavior agents could conduct without getting caught? How easily could they evade other observability and security instruments? What level of persistence could they achieve internally or externally?

We will update these sub-questions as new capabilities and misaligned behaviors emerge.

Why focus on assessing monitors?

The proposal focuses primarily on LLM-based monitoring of AI agents. When AI agents only need to take a limited, known set of actions, standard cybersecurity approaches (like limiting an agent’s permissions to only what its task requires, e.g. via sandboxing) may be adequate. However, the permissions AI agents need are often very broad. For example, an AI agent that needs internet access to do its task can take an enormous array of actions,2 and noticing when those actions are harmful often requires understanding the action in its broader context. Monitoring AI agents with an LLM which is able to make sense of what those agents are doing is therefore a critical part of automated oversight at scale, and is the primary source of evidence inside frontier AI developers about AI misbehavior.

Methodology and sub-questions

Monitor coverage

Monitoring is only useful insofar as it is actually being run on relevant traffic. The assessor would aim to estimate the fraction of internal agentic inference that the developer has covered with LLM-based monitoring. This can be broken down into categories based on how risky each type of agent is: agents that operate in highly secure sandbox environments pose less risk than agents with many affordances (e.g. internet access, access to internal credentials or infrastructure), and may require less monitoring oversight.

Getting a decent estimate of monitor coverage requires accounting for the amount of internal traffic going through monitored and unmonitored paths, estimating what fraction of the unmonitored inference is agentic, and judging what fraction of the unmonitored inference “should” be monitored. This requires access to inference logs, monitor logs (to cross-reference against the inference logs), and employee interviews to be confident of capturing all of the relevant sources of inference.3

Some other relevant example sub-questions:

  • Does the information needed to accurately estimate monitor coverage exist internally? Is there inference-level logging of all agentic inference, and are these logs retained?
  • Are 100% of actions actually monitored when they are eligible for monitoring? Are any trajectories silently dropped?
  • What exactly is shown to the monitor? Is any information excluded? For example, is multimodal data shown to the monitor?
  • How is the amount of inference covered by monitoring internally estimated? How can the assessor be confident they are including all sources of internal agentic inference?
  • Are there blocking monitors (which prevent actions if they detect misbehavior) for the most safety-critical areas?

If misaligned agents compromise a company’s internal infrastructure, they could co-opt unmonitored inference to take actions that would otherwise be flagged. So, the assessor should directly evaluate whether unmonitored inference is in fact non-agentic, rather than assuming it’s safe because (for example) it is supposed to have limited tool use ability.

Monitor system vulnerabilities

Even if most agentic inference is currently monitored by LLM-based monitors, it may be the case that there are bugs or vulnerabilities that agents could exploit to turn off monitoring on their trajectories, spawn new agents without monitoring, prevent parts of their trajectories from being viewed by the monitoring system, or cause the monitoring system to otherwise break or fail in unintended ways. Monitoring systems are complex, involving multiple types of inference engines/APIs, agent scaffolds, internal authentication, trigger systems, etc., and it’s easy for vulnerabilities to emerge where sub-systems interact. Monitor system red-teaming aims to find these bugs and vulnerabilities, to generate evidence about how easily misaligned agents could subvert a monitoring system’s infrastructure.

Some example questions:

  • Can agents disable or turn off their monitoring systems directly? Can they generate outputs that cause the systems to fail without flagging the trajectory?
  • Can agents modify the trajectories that are sent to their monitoring systems, before they are evaluated (e.g. to cover up evidence of misbehavior)?
  • Are there straightforward supply-chain attacks (including via internal resources) that could compromise monitoring systems?

Finding these bugs (or building confidence that there aren’t any easily exploitable severe ones) requires access to all of the code in the critical path. This is primarily the full model inference and monitor trigger system, the internal APIs/inference serving code, and (if relevant) agent scaffolds.

To test discovered exploits, the assessor can trigger the production monitoring system, and view the monitor’s full input and output on known attacks. Running the system and seeing the full input and output is important, because often there are bugs/issues that involve subtle aspects of how trajectories are pre/post-processed, or involve interactions with complex trajectory management code (e.g. compaction, memories, etc.).

Monitor evasion

How good are monitors at actually catching misbehavior, assuming the monitoring infrastructure hasn’t been subverted? The assessor can stress-test this question by:

  • Looking for “attack opportunities” in real transcripts, implementing attacks based on them, and seeing if they fool the monitor;
  • Taking existing incidents flagged by monitors and seeing how hard it is to modify them to fool those monitors; and
  • Searching for existing incidents that were not flagged by monitors.

It is important to have a large pool of representative transcripts (on the order of hundreds of thousands to millions) to use for direct monitor red-teaming. First, if the assessor is not able to discover severe incidents within a large number of transcripts that were not flagged by a monitor, this is evidence that the monitor isn’t missing a large number of incidents. Second, it is important to search through lots of transcripts for cases in which an agent may have been able to carry out an attack undetected, but neglected to do so. Agents might pass up some opportunities to attack while taking others, and highly capable agents may prioritize attacks so difficult to detect that the developer would reliably miss them.

Finally, we expect it to become increasingly important to assess the extent to which monitors and agents could successfully collude without their developer knowing. If, in certain circumstances, monitoring systems decide to not flag misaligned behavior from agents, this could allow agents to take harmful actions without the developer noticing. We recommend that the assessor investigates the feasibility of this concern. For example, the assessor could create realistic “honeypots” for monitors, to see if they can catch monitors not flagging certain attacks. The assessor can also search the monitor system’s chains-of-thought for any mention/discussion of collusion or related concepts.

Response, including human evasion

Some monitoring systems are designed to directly block dangerous actions.

Other monitoring systems are instead designed to notify humans, who decide whether AI agents are conducting dangerous activities. For this to work effectively, flagged trajectories need to be seen by human staff and responded to with appropriate mitigations. For such systems, the assessor should answer:

  • What is the process for alerting human staff and responding to flagged trajectories? What is the threshold for something being flagged in this way, and how effective is this threshold in practice?
  • How long does it take for humans to review and respond to flagged trajectories?
  • Can the assessor sneak attacks flagged by monitors past human reviewers, e.g. by giving them characteristics similar to common false positives?
  • What processes are there for mitigating incidents? Do these processes reliably handle the most severe incidents?

To assess whether attacks are ultimately caught (whether blocked directly by the monitoring system or escalated to human review), the assessor would rely on interviews with relevant staff and on inserting4 their own attack trajectories into the pipeline in a realistic manner. The assessor would also need access to flagged incidents and incidents reported by employees through other channels, along with internal criteria for escalation.

Impact

Given the assessor’s understanding of the coverage and limitations of monitors, what could agents get away with? What level of persistence internally or externally could they achieve? How should future monitoring systems be designed to maximize developers’ odds of catching the most severe incidents? This involves mapping out attack chains and threat models to stay ahead of emerging risks.

This more exploratory work primarily relies on having information regarding internal infrastructure, and optionally the ability to use internal infrastructure like development machines, inference systems, containers/VMs, etc., which can be helpful for demonstrating vulnerabilities and exploring future threat pathways directly.

Access details

Broadly, control stress-testing relies on the following access:

  • Codebase access similar to frontier AI security researchers working for the developer 5
  • Internal inference logs across most/all surfaces, and the monitoring system logs
  • Incident reports and the relevant transcripts/logs
  • Cluster/internal infrastructure access, e.g. to run the monitoring systems
  • Inference access to the most capable internal models

Below, we describe access needed for each of the sub-questions we currently believe are high-priority to answer in control assessments.

Monitor coverage

  • To estimate the fraction of traffic that is monitored: the logs from internal inference services and monitoring systems. 6
  • To estimate the fraction of unmonitored inference that is agentic: large, roughly representative subsets of unmonitored inference logs/trajectories. 7
  • For both of the above and to validate LLM classifiers: a subset of trajectories from all relevant internal inference surfaces.
  • To check whether monitors caught historical incidents: any relevant lists of misalignment incidents reported by employees through other channels.
  • To validate that monitoring is comprehensive: the monitoring system(s) logs (to cross-reference against inference logs).
  • To diagnose and determine the size of discovered coverage gaps: access to other relevant logs demonstrating that gap on an ad hoc basis.

Monitor system vulnerabilities

  • Full access to relevant parts of the codebase.
  • Ability to run/trigger the production monitoring system, and view the monitor’s full input+output.

Monitor evasion

  • At least ~100k roughly representative transcripts from internal agents (e.g. employee or team opt-in from employees’ internal usage, plus a representative similar order of magnitude from evals and training). 8
  • At least ~100 transcripts of the most severe internal incidents, including any incidents reported by employees through other channels.

Human evasion and response

  • Staff interviews, documentation, and direct visibility into the escalation and review process for recent internal flagged trajectories.
  • The ability to insert the assessor’s own attack trajectories into the monitoring pipeline, to realistically determine whether human review would catch and escalate the trajectories appropriately.

Impact

  • The code/systems that govern internal infrastructure/compute, credentials, sandboxing, network configuration, devboxes, etc. similar to what the developer’s frontier AI security staff would have access to. This access could be substituted with staff interviews to some extent, but that would represent a meaningful limitation.
  • Limited access to the actual runtime cluster, to allow testing for vulnerabilities directly instead of inferring them, especially in cases where important configuration parameters are not stored in the codebase or otherwise available.
  • This post describes the reasoning we’ve used to evaluate the coverage and robustness of our internal monitoring system. ↩

It also would be fine to remove sensitive subsets of the codebase that aren’t on the critical code path the assessor is evaluating, although this can be difficult in practice if there are complex dependency chains. ↩

So the developer could exclude people working on compartmentalized (e.g. pretraining) work, as long as their agent trajectories and monitoring setup don’t look significantly different. ↩

items.title: Researchers improve weather forecasts looking two to six weeks out
items.content:
In 2021, Texas suffered the worst energy infrastructure failure in state history, following three severe winter storms in February. At least 246 people were killed as a result of the disruptions, which led to food, water, heat and electricity shortages.

If energy officials had had more time to prepare for the storms, for example by bringing in more trucks of natural gas to disrupted areas, damage from the event could have been mitigated. Unfortunately, weather forecasts beyond two weeks are notoriously unreliable, making for a tighter window for energy operators, farmers, and emergency response officials around the globe.

A new technique by a team including researchers at MIT significantly improves weather forecasting beyond two weeks. The researchers developed a machine-learning model that learns to correct errors in existing forecasting models to improve their output over the two-to-six-week time frame. When applied to a gold-standard forecasting model, it doubled forecasting accuracy over that time frame, placing first in a prominent international forecasting competition.

In a new paper in Nature, the researchers describe their approach and show how it enables forecasts that for the first time beat climatologic averages between two and six weeks.

“Not only does this do better on time averaged forecasts for this range, which is already very useful for farmers and members of the energy industry trying to match supply with demand, but it also improves predictions of extreme weather events, whether it’s flooding or cold spells or something else,” co-author and MIT Research Scientist Judah Cohen says. “It’s really important to predict both, but extreme events might be the most impactful part of this for society.” 

Joining Cohen on the paper are lead authors Hannah Guan, a Harvard College undergraduate; Soukayna Mouatadid, a University of Toronto postdoc; Genevieve Flaspohler SM ’18, PhD ’22; Paulo Orenstein, an associate professor at Brazil’s National Institute for Pure and Applied Mathematics; Jeremy Berman of the data company DTN; Jakob Schloer and Joshua Talib, researchers with the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts; and Alex Lu, Haiyu Dong, Jonathan Weyn, Zekun Ni, and Lester Mackey, all researchers at Microsoft.

Longer forecasts

In the 1970s, longtime MIT Professor Edward Lorenz came up with the idea of chaos theory to describe how tiny changes in initial weather conditions lead to completely different outcomes.

“He came up with this theoretical two-week limit where beyond that, we just can’t predict weather because the noise in the system grows so much that it overwhelms any signal you start with,” Cohen says. “That had a strong influence on the field that may have held people back from exploring forecasting beyond the two-week range. I never really believed that completely. In theory the atmosphere can create an infinite number of patterns, but it likes to fall into these favorite patterns over and over again. Once one thing happens, I think you can predict the domino that will fall after that, and the domino that will fall after that.”

Today, the best weather forecasts come from either dynamical models, which numerically simulate how the atmosphere and oceans evolve over time, or artificial intelligence models, which learn to make predictions from historical weather data. AI models have shown improvements in predicting weather at short ranges, but they’re even worse than dynamical models at longer time ranges.

Cohen, who is based in the MIT Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, focuses on forecasting weather two to six weeks in advance, which is known as subseasonal forecasting. “That range is referred to as the ‘predictability desert,’ because in the short range you can capitalize on the initial conditions in the climate system and the atmosphere, and on the longer term you have these slow, varying boundary forces, like the super El Niño everyone’s focused on this winter,” Cohen says. “The subseasonal range can’t take advantage of either of those. In most cases forecasting in the subseasonal ranges is no different than going to a casino and rolling the dice.”

Cohen credits his co-author Lester Mackey, whom he has been collaborating with for more than a decade, with the initial idea of using machine learning to reduce errors in forecasting models.

“We built this wrapper — Lester calls it postprocessing,” Cohen says. “We know AI models have a lot of errors, so we thought maybe we can quantify those errors and remove them.”

While other forecasting systems do more simplistic error correction, the research team’s postprocessing layer uses AI to learn from a forecasting system’s mistakes based on historic data and shifts its forecasts. In that time range, forecasters use so-called probabilistic forecasts, where the likelihood of a range of possibilities if given.

“As more forecasts and data become available, our model adaptively improves its correction,” Cohen says.

To build the model, the researchers used MIT Engaging, a supercomputing cluster hosted by MIT’s Office of Research Computing and Data, but the resulting model does not require a supercomputer to run.

To put their model to the test, last year the research team submitted three models that included their post-processing layer to the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), which is considered the best forecasting center in the world. Each season ECMWF holds forecasting competitions between models.

The submission that won first place combined ECMWF’s forecasting model with another, and then applied the postprocessing correction on top. That approach ended up doubling the original model’s predictive power in the subseasonal range. For the first time, the model offered an improvement over relying on climatologic averages.

“Up until now, no one had been able to show a model predicts weather better than long term averages for these subseasonal forecasts,” Cohen says. “They’ve pretty much all been worse than that — you could literally flip a coin and do better. People have questioned if it’s even worth investing in models at all for this time range. We consistently beat climatology averages with our models.”

The model also showed a statistically significant improvement in the ability to predict extreme weather.

“That’s one of the more important findings, because it’s so difficult to accomplish,” Cohen says. “When the ECMWF developed their own, non-AI, error-correction to their model, it got worse at predicting extreme weather. I think that’s because traditional error, or bias, correction is always trying to get to the mean, whereas extreme weather is on the fringe of probabilities.”

Preparing for disaster

In the Nature paper, the team showed their technique could be used to improve land forecasts in most regions across the globe. They also applied their bias correction technique to other models and showed it improved those as well, putting even lesser models on par with the ECMWF’s forecasts.

“What’s nice about our model is it’s an add-on wrapper,” Cohen explains. “We used it with the ECMWF’s dynamical model because that was considered the best, but it can be used with any model. It even improves models that are already bias corrected using another AI algorithm. So it shows a robust improvement. And it’s open source and low cost.”

Cohen says the meteorological office for the Republic of Kenya has already reached out about implementing the model to improve forecasting of the annual monsoon season to improve agricultural yields this winter. He hopes other groups will also use the model.

“This could help you decide when to fertilize around rain, when there’s a freeze coming to protect crops during winter harvests, or help you avoid droughts,” Cohen says. “It could also be useful for energy and emergency management. I’ve talked to energy officials who say, ‘If I’m told two days before that an ice storm’s coming, I don’t have enough time, but if I had two weeks, that could be enough to make adequate preparations.”

The work was supported, in part, by the U.S. National Science Foundation, the Carlos Chagas Filho Foundation for Research Support, and the European Union.

items.title: The Anatomy of a Blind Spot: What an LLM Judge Must Be Shown, and How Much
items.content: arXiv:2610.15938v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Evaluation of text generated by large language models (LLMs) is increasingly delegated to LLMs acting as judges, yet what such a judge must be shown remains unresolved. We treat a judge whose reports are acted on as a regulator, in the sense of cybernetics, and ask what it must be shown, how much, in what form, and what its reports must get right. On seven public benchmarks we varied only what the judge was shown. Across three judges whose prices differ 10- to 17-fold, what the judge was shown mattered more than which judge it was. When a system revised its answers on feedback from a judge denied the material they had to respect, it ended below its starting point on instruction following and question answering. On instruction following the loss grew with each round, and it persisted when the judge saw the user's request but not the constraints and with a second judge family. On news summarisation, a correct reference summary beside the source undid most of the source's contribution, whereas on single-answer questions a reference helped. About a tenth of the source did almost all of its work, and a small entailment graph matched an LLM judge at finding errors in grounded text. We committed 83 testable clauses before running; of the 81 that ran, 32 met their bar and 50 went in the predicted direction, and most quantitative predictions from the theory failed. We report every shortfall and derive design rules tied to measured effects.
items.author: Nitish Kumar, Prateik Pothuneedi, Greg Bandak
items.summary: Treating an LLM judge as a cybernetic regulator, this paper systematically varies only what the judge is shown across seven benchmarks, finding that input composition matters more than which judge is used even across a 10-17x price range. Judges denied the material they needed to evaluate caused systems revising on their feedback to perform below their starting point on instruction following and QA.
items.reasoning: With LLM-judged evaluation becoming ubiquitous, a controlled study showing that what a judge sees dominates which judge is used has broad practical implications for evaluation pipelines and for the economics of judge selection. The cross-benchmark design is strong; the finding, while valuable, is more an empirical characterization than a new technique.

items.content_html: arXiv:2610.15938v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluation of text generated by large language models (LLMs) is increasingly delegated to LLMs acting as judges, yet what such a judge must be shown remains unresolved. We treat a judge whose reports are acted on as a regulator, in the sense of cybernetics, and ask what it must be shown, how much, in what form, and what its reports must get right. On seven public benchmarks we varied only what the judge was shown. Across three judges whose prices differ 10- to 17-fold, what the judge was shown mattered more than which judge it was. When a system revised its answers on feedback from a judge denied the material they had to respect, it ended below its starting point on instruction following and question answering. On instruction following the loss grew with each round, and it persisted when the judge saw the user's request but not the constraints and with a second judge family. On news summarisation, a correct reference summary beside the source undid most of the source's contribution, whereas on single-answer questions a reference helped. About a tenth of the source did almost all of its work, and a small entailment graph matched an LLM judge at finding errors in grounded text. We committed 83 testable clauses before running; of the 81 that ran, 32 met their bar and 50 went in the predicted direction, and most quantitative predictions from the theory failed. We report every shortfall and derive design rules tied to measured effects.

items.title: Memory Echo in Single-Agent Long-Term Memory: Lifecycle Evaluation and Provenance-Guided Mitigation
items.content: arXiv:2610.17763v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Long-term memory supports agents across sessions. Repeated retrieval and write-back can let one historical claim occupy multiple retrieval positions and influence current answers without independent evidence. Existing work examines retrieval, updating, and question answering, leaving same-source record accumulation and post-correction persistence underexplored. Motivated by research in social cognition and memory psychology on repeated exposure, retrieval, and revision, we define \emph{Memory Echo} as the excess retrieval exposure gained by historical information from the same source without additional independent evidence, and introduce MEchoBench to evaluate its emergence, correction resistance, persistence, and effect on answers. To address this phenomenon, we introduce the Family--Provenance--Authority framework (FPA). Specifically, FPA selects one representative per source family, conditions the eligibility of old records for the answer context on verified corrections, and constrains final answers with authoritative evidence. In paired replay on 190 fixed questions across four memory frameworks, FPA raises accuracy from 0.825 to 0.920 with DeepSeek V4 Flash and from 0.782 to 0.916 with Kimi K2.6; mean Decision Contamination Effect falls from 0.106 to 0.030 and from 0.109 to 0.038, respectively. These results show that agent memory can preserve traceable history without allowing repeated historical information to govern current decisions. The code is available at https://github.com/OrcasSam/memory-echo-benchmark.

This is important for agent memory reliability, complementing companion work on knowledge graph cleanup by showing why retracted sources keep exerting influence.

items.title: Weighted Adjoint Matching: Finetuning Flow Matching Models with Time-Dependent Control Cost
items.content: arXiv:2610.20035v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We introduce Weighted Adjoint Matching, a method to finetune a pretrained diffusion or flow matching model given a differentiable reward. We derive it from Adjoint Matching, which reformulates finetuning as a stochastic optimal control problem with a quadratic control cost. Building on the observation that these models generate coarse features before fine details, we place a time-dependent weight on the control cost. A high cost early in the generative process preserves balance and diversity in the coarse features, which carry most of the semantics, while a low cost at the end lets the model increase the reward by refining details. We prove that our method is equivalent to maximizing the reward under time-varying Kullback--Leibler regularization on the generative paths. Experiments on Gaussian mixtures and on MNIST show a better tradeoff between reward and mode balance than Adjoint Matching.

The authors prove equivalence to reward maximization under time-varying KL regularization.

items.title: Copy-Paste Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.19247v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Transformers are intuitively considered to be efficient at copying from their inputs. We actually show that the ability of LLMs to copy in context can be improved through explicit modeling. We propose Copy-Paste Language Models (CPLMs), which add a lightweight Copy-Paste head to the conventional language modeling (LM) head. CPLMs improve training efficiency, downstream performance, and offer new operating points in long-context and retrieval setups. We validate our approach by pretraining models from 135M to 1.7B parameters, showing improvements across all scales and backbones with negligible training and inference overheads. We explain the success of CPLMs by showing that they partially mitigate the LM head gradient bottleneck through an alternative gradient path.

It also creates new operating points for long-context and retrieval tasks.

items.title: JetSpec++: Foresight Parallel Drafting with Self Refinements
items.content: arXiv:2610.19792v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Speculative decoding's effectiveness is governed by two quantities: the acceptance rate of drafted tokens and the cost of producing them. We show the two objectives can be co-optimized with algorithm-system co-design, and present JetSpec++, which retains a strong learned draft model while hiding its cost almost entirely. JetSpec++ combines three components: intra-block self refinement, which trains the draft model to iteratively correct its own parallel predictions within a block of tokens; inter-block foresight drafting, which begins the next block before the current one is verified; and pipelined drafting and verification, which overlaps the two stages so drafting's marginal wall-clock cost approaches zero. In comparison with state-of-the-art speculative decoding methods, JetSpec++ attains a wall-clock speedup of up to $7.45\times$ over autoregressive (AR) decoding and $1.54\times$ over DSpark, with up to 1,361 tokens per second for a single request on GB200, and an average acceptance length of 8.94 across seven benchmarks, while preserving the target model's output distribution. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/hao-ai-lab/JetSpec.

items.title: Full-Order Safety for Nonlinear Reduced-Order MPC
items.content: arXiv:2610.19250v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reduced-order models (ROMs) make model predictive control (MPC) of high-dimensional nonlinear systems tractable, but the resulting modeling error can lead to constraint violations on the real system. We introduce CoRE-MPC, a robust MPC formulation that plans with a nonlinear ROM and guarantees recursive feasibility and constraint satisfaction for the full-order system. It can be applied with a broad class of nonlinear model reduction techniques and the resulting MPC does not require evaluating the full-order model online, thus ensuring computational efficiency. The key insight is in how the ROM affects the dynamics of the prediction error. We account for this with two error radii that are propagated alongside the ROM and provide a guaranteed bound on the prediction error. The approach is validated in simulation on an 80-state oscillator chain, a Burgers equation, and a 9,768-state finite-element soft robot, where a two-state ROM with data-driven bounds keeps all 1,628 nodes clear of a wall at a median solve time below 1 ms for a 20 ms control period. Across these examples, CoRE-MPC is 13 to 61 times faster than full-order robust MPC at only 27 to 35% higher closed-loop cost, whereas existing certified schemes are either infeasible or at least twice as conservative. This closes a real safety gap for using ROMs in control of high-dimensional systems like legged robots.

items.title: ClawLoop: Self-Improving Agents via Harness-Native Training Loop
items.content: arXiv:2610.14118v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has driven their deployment toward general-purpose harness environments, where LLM-based agents operate in sandbox workspaces and interact directly with file systems and shells. While numerous post-training pipelines exist for tool-use agents, their counterparts for harness-based agents remain scarce and are predominantly one-shot and teacher-dependent: a stronger external model synthesizes tasks and collects trajectories, the target agent is trained once, and evaluation results are consumed by human researchers rather than fed back into the loop. Such pipelines are inherently bounded by the capability of the external model and the scope of human prior, leaving no room for self-improvement. To address these limitations, we propose ClawLoop, a framework that enables self-improving without any external teacher model and with minimal prior dependencies. ClawLoop composes three phases into a self-sustaining cycle: Task Synthesis, which generates a diverse pool of training tasks via two complementary construction routines, applies diagnosis-conditioned difficulty growth followed by both agent-free and agent-based task validation; Training, which updates the agent via SFT and/or RL; and Diagnosis and Feedback, which analyzes the agent's rollout behaviors to produce a capability analysis report that will be used as feedback for task synthesis in the next iteration. Using Qwen3.6-27B as the loop model, ClawLoop yields consistent improvements on SkillsBench, Claw-Eval-Live, and ClawGym-Bench. The iteratively refined tasks are further transferred to smaller-scale Qwen3.5-4B and 9B models with gains across all benchmarks, validating data quality independently of the loop model.

Unlike one-shot, teacher-dependent pipelines, it enables iterative self-improvement by feeding evaluation results back into training, reducing dependence on stronger external models.

items.title: Echo: Error-Compensated 4-Bit Tensor-Parallel Communication for LLM Training and Inference
items.content: arXiv:2610.14277v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Tensor parallelism ends every layer with an all-reduce that sits between two dependent matrix multiplications, so its cost cannot be hidden and grows as compute outpaces interconnect bandwidth. Sending 4-bit instead of 16-bit values would cut this cost by nearly 4x, but the all-reduce must add the values it carries, and rounding the sum injects an error at every call. Model quality depends on how these errors accumulate over layers, yet existing methods treat each call on its own. We present Echo, a 4-bit all-reduce for training and inference that controls the accumulated error. Echo moves data in 4 bits and sums in high precision, so each value is quantized at most twice per call for any number of GPUs. The summation reveals each injected error, and Echo feeds it back into later calls, so old errors cancel instead of accumulating. We prove that the accumulated error stays bounded independently of depth. On A100 GPUs, Echo is 2.09x faster than the 16-bit NCCL all-reduce on 1 GB messages. It speeds up the time to first token by up to 1.16x and the training step by up to 1.09x on an idle interconnect, and by up to 1.44x and 1.38x as background traffic grows. It keeps the average accuracy over seven benchmarks within 0.4 points of 16-bit inference on Qwen3-8B. In 10B-token pretraining, its final loss is less than 0.9% above that of 16-bit training. Echo needs no FP8 or FP4 hardware.

items.title: Joint Discrete and SE(3) Diffusion for Protein Interface Design
items.content: arXiv:2610.14699v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The design of high-affinity, target-specific protein binders is central to the development of modern therapeutics. However, existing protein-generation methods remain limited in this setting, as many generated designs fail to simultaneously achieve geometric and physicochemical complementarity at binding interfaces. To address this challenge, we introduce PIDiff, a physicochemically enhanced multimodal diffusion framework for protein-protein complex design. PIDiff jointly designs target-conditioned protein sequences and structures by coupling diffusion in discrete sequence space with diffusion on the continuous (SE(3)) structural manifold. At its core, PIDiff employs PIFormer, a novel architecture that interleaves geometry-aware invariant point attention with global sequence self-attention. We further curate PIBench, a protein-protein complex dataset with diverse target scaffolds derived from the Protein Data Bank (PDB). We first pretrain PIDiff on PIBench and subsequently fine-tune it for two therapeutically relevant applications: minibinder design and antibody design. PPFrame consistently outperforms baseline methods across sequence design success rate, structure binding energy, and sequence-structure co-designability on all tasks.

A novel PIFormer architecture interleaves geometry-aware invariant point attention to enforce both geometric and physicochemical complementarity at binding interfaces, targeting high-affinity binder design for therapeutics.
