items.title: Price of Anarchy of First-Price Auctions in Agentic Markets
items.content: arXiv:2610.20587v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: An agentic market is a decentralized serving-time market where AI agents bid to claim each user prompt. An agent's bid is based on its expected value for the prompt, which is the expectation of the reward for its response minus its inference costs. First-price auctions (FPAs), in which the highest bidder pays its bid and receives the prompt, are a natural way to allocate prompts in such a market, since they are simple and transparent to run, and do not require central knowledge of private capabilities and costs. However, FPAs are not truthful: participants may bid less than their true value in the hope of a larger profit, and the prompt may then be allocated to someone other than the bidder who values it the most. This welfare loss is quantified by the $\textit{price-of-anarchy}$ (PoA). In this paper, we argue that agentic markets are likely to possess features that reduce the price-of-anarchy. The first is a $\textit{competitive floor}$, which occurs when multiple bidders usually value the prompt above some baseline share of the optimal welfare (e.g., because the best models are often distilled into cheaper alternatives, which perform similarly). We show that competition among them then limits the welfare loss, which can be driven to zero as the floor rises. The second feature is $\textit{near-independence}$ of values after conditioning on the prompt, which occurs when most of the predictable variation in the expected value is determined by the difficulty of the prompt. As the value distribution approaches conditional independence, we can derive an efficiency guarantee that approaches a factor of $1 - 1/e^2$ of the optimal welfare. Thus, both features give rise to welfare lower bounds that are significantly better than the well-known general case of $1 - 1/e$. We validate these results empirically using auctions with strategic bidders simulated on the EmbedLLM prompt routing dataset.

items.summary: This theoretical work analyzes decentralized serving-time agentic markets where AI agents bid in first-price auctions to claim user prompts, quantifying welfare loss via the price of anarchy. It grounds bids in expected reward minus inference cost and examines inefficiency from non-truthful bidding. As AI agents begin mediating service allocation, this provides foundational mechanism-design analysis for such markets.

An agent's bid is based on its expected value for the prompt, which is the expectation of the reward for its response minus its inference costs. First-price auctions (FPAs), in which the highest bidder pays its bid and receives the prompt, are a natural way to allocate prompts in such a market, since they are simple and transparent to run, and do not require central knowledge of private capabilities and costs. However, FPAs are not truthful: participants may bid less than their true value in the hope of a larger profit, and the prompt may then be allocated to someone other than the bidder who values it the most. This welfare loss is quantified by the $\textit{price-of-anarchy}$ (PoA). In this paper, we argue that agentic markets are likely to possess features that reduce the price-of-anarchy. The first is a $\textit{competitive floor}$, which occurs when multiple bidders usually value the prompt above some baseline share of the optimal welfare (e.g., because the best models are often distilled into cheaper alternatives, which perform similarly). We show that competition among them then limits the welfare loss, which can be driven to zero as the floor rises. The second feature is $\textit{near-independence}$ of values after conditioning on the prompt, which occurs when most of the predictable variation in the expected value is determined by the difficulty of the prompt. As the value distribution approaches conditional independence, we can derive an efficiency guarantee that approaches a factor of $1 - 1/e^2$ of the optimal welfare. Thus, both features give rise to welfare lower bounds that are significantly better than the well-known general case of $1 - 1/e$. We validate these results empirically using auctions with strategic bidders simulated on the EmbedLLM prompt routing dataset.

items.title: HERO: Harnessing Evidence for Test-time Refinement and Prompt Optimization in Program Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.19184v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Harness optimization improves LLMs by refining reusable prompts and scaffolding, yet requires further adaptation for program generation tasks such as text-to-SQL and text-to-Python. Existing methods often rely on LLM reflectors to propose harness updates, which can fix observed failures but also disrupt previously correct behavior. Text-to-code tasks offer a natural way to mitigate this issue: we can execute generated outputs, allowing us to evaluate and verify the effects of proposed updates directly. Building on this signal, we introduce \textsc{HERO} (\textbf{H}arnessing \textbf{E}vidence for \textbf{R}efinement and \textbf{O}ptimization), which combines offline and test-time harness optimization. At the first stage, \method{} learns reusable prompt updates from execution-verified successes and failures and validates candidate revisions before adoption. At test time, we treat the generated code as an instance-specific harness and refine it using execution feedback. Across four SQL, Cypher, and Python benchmarks, \method{} achieves the best offline performance, improving pass@1 by \(7.6\) points over the initial prompt, while test-time refinement adds another \(2.0\) points and improves execution efficiency.
items.author: Mingyu Lu, Timothy Ossowski, Tristan Naumann, Hoifung Poon, Peniel Argaw
items.summary: HERO improves LLM program generation (text-to-SQL, text-to-Python) by optimizing reusable prompts and scaffolding using execution feedback, combining offline harness optimization learned from prior failures with test-time refinement. By executing generated outputs, it verifies that proposed harness updates do not disrupt previously correct behavior, a weakness of LLM-reflector-based approaches. This is a practical contribution to reliable code generation pipelines.
items.reasoning: Well-motivated approach exploiting the verifiability of code tasks to ground harness optimization, addressing a real failure mode of reflective prompt optimizers. Authors include Microsoft Research contributors; strong practical relevance, though the technique builds on an active area of scaffold/prompt optimization work.

items.title: Measuring and Reducing Unusable Replies of LLM Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.19659v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: People delegate multi-step work to LLM agents and read only the reply that the agent hands back. Current evaluation scores task completion and the faithfulness of reports, and it leaves open whether the requester can understand and use the reply. We call this property reply usability and measure it with a reader model that takes the requester's position and tests whether the reply can be interpreted from what the requester has seen, is in the requester's language and answers the request. Its agreement with the majority of five annotators lies within the range of the individual annotators. Across eight models from seven families, 54% of 480 replies fail, and the best model still fails on 30%. Failed replies mostly point to material the requester has not seen or use labels that the agent coined during its work. Stating explicit requirements for the reply reduces the failure rate from 0.52 to 0.43 together with errors and omissions, and a secondary model that rewrites the reply reduces it to 0.36, which human annotators confirm in a blind comparison. Reply usability can thus be scored alongside task success and improved with one appended message or one call to a secondary model.
items.author: Yilin Jiang, Fei Tan, Xuanyu Yin, Guanchu Wang, Xia Hu, Yutao Yue
items.summary: Introduces reply usability: whether a requester can actually understand and act on an LLM agent's final reply, measured by a reader model simulating the requester's perspective. Across eight models from seven families, 54% of 480 replies fail this bar and even the best model fails 30% of the time, with failures mostly pointing to material the requester never saw.
items.reasoning: Identifies and formalizes a genuinely underexplored failure mode in agent evaluation with a validated reader-based metric and striking failure rates across frontier models; the framing could influence how agent systems are evaluated.

items.title: To Reason but Not to Stop: Understanding and Recovering Pruned Large Reasoning Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.19934v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Weight pruning can degrade the accuracy of large reasoning models (LRMs), yet it remains unclear whether it damages reasoning itself. We find that much of this degradation stems from a failure to stop rather than to reason. As sparsity increases, pruned LRMs increasingly fail to terminate within the token budget, often after the correct answer has appeared in their reasoning, instead falling into repetitive loops, even though they still recognize where the dense model would stop. We further find that the hidden-state difference between terminating and looping continuations is consistent across pruned checkpoints, suggesting a shared direction associated with committing to an answer. Building on this, we propose Termination-Guided Activation Steering (TGAS), a training-free method that adds this direction to the residual stream at inference time. Across six LRMs, three pruning pipelines, and math and code benchmarks, TGAS improves termination and overall accuracy while reducing repetitive reasoning and generation length, showing that this failure is actionable.
items.author: Minh-Anh Nguyen, Nguyen T. Ha Lan, Xiyan Fu, Dung D. Le, Wei Lu
items.summary: This paper shows that accuracy degradation in pruned large reasoning models stems largely from failure to terminate — looping repetitively after the correct answer has appeared — rather than degraded reasoning ability. The authors identify a consistent hidden-state direction separating terminating from looping continuations and propose a Termination-Guided Activation method to recover pruned models.
items.reasoning: Offers a genuinely surprising and useful diagnosis of pruning failure modes in reasoning models, backed by mechanistic analysis and a practical recovery intervention. Relevant to efficient deployment of reasoning LLMs; score limited because generality across model families is not yet demonstrated.

items.title: MolLean: A Process-Verifiable Language for Chemical Reasoning
items.content: arXiv:2610.20459v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Chemical chain-of-thought can contain hallucinated structural and property claims. We thereby introduce MolLean, a process-verifiable language that grounds chemical reasoning in an explicit molecular state. A layered Lean-based kernel checks state transitions and assertions over molecular readouts, from primitive graph edits to compound transformations. Meanwhile, a typed witness protocol separates native structural checks from externally supplied measurements. We further introduce MolLean-MCP, a stateful tool interface that exposes these transitions, checks, and readouts during generation: the model receives feedback to decide its next action, and rejected actions leave the state unchanged. MolLean supports one-pass trace execution, whole-trace refinement, and interactive reasoning through MolLean-MCP. We evaluate these three modes with direct chain-of-thought on 8,800 matched examples across 12 tasks spanning molecular generation, editing, optimization, and reactions. With Qwen3.6-27B, whole-trace refinement outperforms direct chain-of-thought on all 12 tasks. MolLean-MCP complements whole-trace refinement with stepwise verification feedback, reaching better performance in reaction tasks. Together, these results highlight an executable foundation for chemical reasoning, in which explicit chemical commitments can be checked and revised rather than remaining solely in free-form explanations.

items.title: TreeFlex: Agents Navigating Their Own Search Trees
items.content: arXiv:2610.20334v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: A ReAct-style agent accumulates observations, intermediate results, and failed attempts in a single context. As this context grows, stale and off-path information consumes its limited capacity and obscures relevant evidence, making focused reasoning increasingly difficult. We introduce TreeFlex, a framework in which the agent's own policy decides where to search. The agent records each intermediate state, with a short summary, as a node in a search tree maintained by the harness. The policy is a single language model that acts in two roles. In the Reflection role, it has a global view of the tree through these summaries and picks a node to resume, together with an instruction. In the Execution role, the harness restores the path that led to that node, and the model carries out the instruction with the usual task tools until it saves a new node or proposes a solution, which Reflection then approves or sends back to another node. Through these choices, the policy decides whether to deepen the current line, branch from or revisit an earlier state, verify a proposal, or stop, without a fixed traversal order or a score for each node. We train navigation, task actions, checkpointing, and proposal review jointly with a tree-aware adaptation of GRPO, using task-level outcome rewards augmented by process rewards. After small-scale RL of a 4B model, with the same active-context limit for all methods, TreeFlex reaches 48.8% accuracy on a challenging deep-research benchmark, versus 41.5% for flat ReAct and 42.8% for FoldAgent, and its Pass@8 is about ten points higher than either. On SWE-bench Verified, with all three systems trained with RL from the same 9B model, TreeFlex resolves 54.9% of tasks, versus 43.3% for FoldAgent and 45.2% for its step-wise variant.
items.author: Dongzhuo Li, Fangzhou Cheng, Weiwei Li, Kevin Han, Haixu Ma, Zhongchang Sun, Ruiyi Li, Serena Li, Xiangjun Fan, Lizhu Zhang, Yuandong Tian
items.summary: TreeFlex addresses context degradation in ReAct-style agents by maintaining intermediate states as nodes in a search tree managed by the harness. A single LLM acts in Reflection and Execution roles: it picks which tree node to resume from using global summaries, then continues from the restored path, allowing agents to navigate their own search histories.
items.reasoning: A compelling architecture for long-horizon agent reasoning that tackles context rot, with an elegant dual-role design; author list includes experienced researchers, though empirical results would determine ultimate impact.

items.title: SonoWorld: Towards Interactive Pose-Controllable Ultrasound World Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.19327v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Robotic ultrasound can standardize image acquisition and reduce operator workload and variability, but policy learning remains limited by the lack of realistic, controllable simulation environments. While controllable world models have advanced rapidly in natural-image domains, ultrasound world modeling remains challenging because each frame captures only a cross-section of unobserved 3D anatomy, causing small probe motions to induce large appearance changes. Existing approaches rely on robot-tracked poses and latent-space prediction, but do not directly generate the observations required for interactive control. We propose SonoWorld, a causal ultrasound world model that learns video dynamics from unlabeled clinical videos and grounds them to 6-DoF control using a small set of freehand clinical scans tracked with an EM sensor. SonoWorld is trained in three stages: pretraining a latent-action-conditioned video diffusion model on around 6.9 million unlabeled multi-organ ultrasound frames; grounding the learned video dynamics to metric probe poses with a small EM-tracked thyroid dataset; and applying distribution matching distillation to enable causal, long-horizon autoregressive generation with selectively caching eviction tokens at inference time. We evaluate controllability through pose-following fidelity, round-trip consistency, and axis-specific control under synthetic actions on held-out tracked scans, and further validate it with a user study. In model-based action discrimination, SonoWorld correctly ranks the target-directed probe motion over an equal-magnitude opposite motion in up to 74.8% of trials. To our knowledge, SonoWorld is the first causal, pose-controllable ultrasound world model learned primarily from freehand clinical videos, providing a data-driven interactive environment for robotic ultrasound data acquisition and policy evaluation.
items.author: Zefan Yang, Zheyuan Zhang, Boris Maihe, Yikang Liu, Hang Yu, Ankush Mukherjee, Xiao Chen, Pingkun Yan, Terrence Chen, Shanhui Sun
items.summary: SonoWorld is a causal world model for robotic ultrasound that learns video dynamics from unlabeled clinical videos and grounds them in probe pose, enabling interactive pose-controllable simulation. It addresses the challenge that ultrasound captures only cross-sections of 3D anatomy, where small probe motions cause large appearance changes, providing realistic simulation environments for ultrasound policy learning.

The approach of learning from unlabeled clinical video is valuable, though the abstract is truncated before results, limiting certainty about empirical strength.

items.title: Robota-Embed: Unified VLA Embeddings for Robot In-Context Learning and Evolution
items.content: arXiv:2610.19495v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Retrieving useful context for a robot requires matching its task, execution stage, and the continuation that should follow. We introduce Robota-Embed, to our knowledge the first vision-language-action (VLA) embedding model to jointly encode all three modalities in both current-state queries and recorded future continuations. Predictive retrieval training aligns these endpoints, enabling historical continuations to serve as context at inference time. We construct a multi-source corpus of 1,695,684 cleaned training anchors and introduce Robota-Embed-Bench, with 4,000 queries and a shared 8,000-entry gallery. Robota-Embed achieves 47.33% clip-level and 81.77% episode-level R@1, exceeding action-free Gemini Embedding 2 by 22.09 and 33.47 percentage points. Controlled retrieval studies show that removing native action degrades retrieval more than removing vision. We study two complementary applications. Embed2ICL uses retrieved experience for training-free and training-based policy conditioning, increasing success from 47.0% to 56.3% in DROID-Sim and from 86.4% to 92.8% on the LIBERO difficult subset, while improving task progress on real robots. Embed2Evolve uses execution feedback to grow task-local memory and refine context use around a frozen GPT-6 Astra policy. Across five ManiSkill tasks, it achieves 68% success, compared with 24% for GPT-6 Astra Direct and 33% for a harness independently evolved with Omni-Embed-Nemotron-3B under the same protocol. Relative to the latter, it uses approximately 79.5% fewer policy tokens per test rollout, counting both successes and failures. These results show that a unified, action-aware retrieval space can support robot in-context learning and task-local context evolution.
items.author: Yunze Liu, Jing Wang, Shenrui Wu, Wenkun He, Guanqi Zhan, Xianzheng Ma, Junyu Chen, Wenhang Ge, Haozhan Tang, Yuchao Gu, Zhuoyang Zhang, Zekai Wang, Dantong Niu, Zhen Dong, Yuke Zhu, Trevor Darrell, Linxi "Jim" Fan, Song Han, Han Cai

It substantially outperforms action-free Gemini Embedding on clip- and episode-level retrieval, enabling in-context learning from historical robot episodes.

Scores are held below the top tier because retrieval embeddings are an enabling component rather than a full policy breakthrough.

items.title: Learning in Orbit: Onboard Training and Closed-Loop Attitude Control with a Thermal Segmentation Model on a Spacecraft
items.content: arXiv:2610.19122v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Deep space missions increasingly require spacecraft capable of autonomously operating in environments with communication delays and bandwidth limitations. A key enabler of such autonomy is the ability to run learning-based algorithms directly onboard. In this work, we present a flight deployment on a 6U CubeSat that demonstrates (1) onboard training and inference of a thermal segmentation model on an NVIDIA Jetson TX2 NX GPU in space and (2) closed-loop attitude control using the segmentation model on a real-time, thermal image feed to track the Moon. In addition to this demonstration, we implement ROS 2 Foxy as a data transport middleware and integrate an open-source file system that provides strong data integrity guarantees and self-healing features. Over the course of approximately one year, we performed 12 experiments on the spacecraft, advancing the state of the art in autonomous spacecraft systems by showing how modern learning-based pipelines, commercially available hardware, and open-source software can operate reliably under the compute and environmental constraints of Low Earth Orbit (LEO).
items.author: Elena Sorina Lupu, Hannah Grauer, Phaedrus Leeds, Nikhil Ranganathan, Connor Lee, Sulekha Kishore, Cailyn Smith, Shon Cortes, Brian Hardy, Benjamen Bycroft, Darren W. Rowen, Soon-Jo Chung
items.summary: This work reports a flight demonstration on a 6U CubeSat of onboard training and inference of a thermal segmentation model on a Jetson GPU in space, plus closed-loop attitude control using that model to track the Moon. It also documents the ROS 2-based middleware and fault-tolerant file system used. This is a rare, concrete instance of learning-based autonomy actually deployed and trained in orbit.
items.reasoning: Flight-validated onboard learning is uncommon and technically demanding; demonstrating closed-loop use of a learned model on real spacecraft hardware carries substantial credibility and systems value. The learning component itself (thermal segmentation) is modest, keeping the score below top-tier.

items.title: Uncertainty-Driven Self-Play for Robust Multi-Agent Driving Policies
items.content: arXiv:2610.19714v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Learning robust driving policies that generalize beyond their training domain remains a central challenge in motion planning. We propose an uncertainty-driven self-play scheme, in which half of the agents are rewarded for increasing their neighbors' epistemic uncertainty, while the other half learn to drive safely as the exploring agents continuously seek out their weaknesses. Epistemic uncertainty indicates where the policy is least confident and serves as an automatic proxy for scenario difficulty. Exploring agents use this signal to seek out hard cases, generating a challenging curriculum without manual scenario design. The resulting policy outperforms standard self-play, achieving best-in-class zero-shot transfer to nuplan Val14 (99.12% vs. 97.97%) and Argoverse 2 (82.39% vs. 78.03%) without fine-tuning, while also improving performance over standard self-play on Waymo. Our diversity-driven approach achieves 85% higher LSTM hidden-state coverage than the baseline, indicating a much richer set of behaviors. Further analysis shows that epistemic uncertainty serves as a calibrated difficulty detector, with highest-uncertain agents exhibiting 14.8 times the combined failure rate across collision, off-road, and DNF, of lowest-uncertain agents, enabling automatic prioritization of challenging scenarios without ground-truth labels.

items.title: Safe Reinforcement Learning with Receding-Horizon Safety Critic and Differentiable Action Shields
items.content: arXiv:2610.20255v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Despite the Markov assumption, safety failures in robot reinforcement learning rarely occur instantaneously; they typically emerge over several steps as the policy enters unfamiliar states under disturbances and domain shift. We address this limitation by learning a receding-horizon safety critic that predicts whether a state will remain non-terminating over the next receding horizon, enabling anticipatory detection of impending locomotion failures. The critic is trained from rollout-derived horizon labels with a composite objective that combines horizon classification, control-barrier-function-inspired temporal consistency, and smoothness regularization, and we aggregate an ensemble of critics with a conservative Conditional Value at Risk estimate to account for uncertainty. Building on the learned critic, we derive a closed-form, differentiable CBF-style safety filter that minimally modifies the policy action to improve predicted safety, and integrate it into PPO with an anticipation loss to reduce policy-filter mismatch during training. In simulated quadruped locomotion, our method improves robustness under action noise, external perturbations, and terrain shifts, reducing catastrophic failures while maintaining competitive returns.

items.title: How an assessor could investigate evidence of acceleration from the automation of AI R&D
items.content:
This article discusses how an assessor could study whether capabilities progress could accelerate dramatically due to AI-driven acceleration of AI R&D. Such an assessment would answer:

- Capabilities Progress: How fast are internal capabilities improving, and how much has this progress accelerated recently?
- Acceleration from AI: If there is an acceleration, how much was it driven by AI automation versus other factors?
- Bottlenecks to Future Growth: Are there important bottlenecks that could slow growth or limit acceleration in the near term?
- Limitations: Would these methods reliably identify much more dramatic acceleration if it had occurred?

Assessing this would involve analyzing capabilities of unreleased models, understanding the growth of key AI R&D inputs (labor, compute, data, and algorithms), and talking openly with relevant researchers about how AI is impacting their work. More details on access below.

## Scope

### Capabilities Progress

To understand whether capabilities progress has accelerated, the assessor must obtain data on internal model capabilities across time. Since AI capabilities cannot be understood through any single approach,1 the assessor must gather data via multiple methods, including:

- Benchmarks: How much has progress on a variety of capability benchmarks (and aggregate measures like ECI) accelerated?
- Intermediates: How much has progress in key intermediate measures or leading indicators (e.g. pretraining loss) accelerated?
- Perceptions: Are researchers who use internal models experiencing an acceleration in model capabilities, as measured by interviews or surveys?
- Other: Are there other proxies that are crucial for understanding the pace of capabilities progress, and what trends do they show?

### Acceleration from AI

To understand whether capabilities acceleration is driven by AI, the assessor would need to study the inputs that seem most likely to be affected by AI automation. This means assessing:

- How much of this acceleration in capabilities is due to algorithmic progress or data versus other inputs like scaling compute that are less impacted by AI automation?
- How much of the acceleration in algorithmic progress or data is attributable to AI assistance/automation versus other inputs like experiment compute and labor?

### Bottlenecks to Future Growth

The assessor would then examine if there are reasons to expect growth or acceleration to slow in the near future. This requires answering:

- Are there important bottlenecks (e.g. training compute, human data) that could plausibly slow progress in the near future, and how might they impact near-term growth?

### Limitations

The assessor would additionally investigate how confident the public should be that a dramatic acceleration would be noticed and communicated if it occurred. This requires answering:

- How reliable are the estimates of internal acceleration and attribution, and what are the biggest concerns with the evidence sources?
- How does the internal evidence studied compare to relevant public evidence about acceleration, and what might explain any differences?
- Overall, would the methods used reliably have identified much greater acceleration, if it had occurred?

## Access details

To answer these questions, the assessor requires measurements of inputs and outputs across the model development pipeline. Whenever possible, data should be provided over the maximum possible timeframe and with precise dates on observations to help assessors estimate changes versus a historical baseline. Where relevant, data should be broken down by team or domain, to help assessors connect specific changes in inputs to research outputs.

 Necessary access Additionally helpful access

- Capability measures across internal models, including benchmarks and key intermediate measures (e.g. pretraining loss)
- Algorithmic progress estimates in pretraining, posttraining, and other key domains
- Measurements of key R&D inputs (e.g. training compute of each model, experimental compute and labor over time)
- Interviews with researchers about progress and AI’s impact on their work

- High-level details of fully autonomous discoveries in AI R&D internally
- Self-reported labor productivity estimates over time or other crude productivity measures
- Forecasts of future models
- Amount of data created by AI
- AI agent inference-spend over time
- Time use logs across researchers on how AI is changing their work

Summary of access needs

For security, data could be analyzed on developer hardware (and possibly onsite at developer premises). Only minimal access to developer infrastructure is needed for this assessment.

Required data includes:

- Measurements of internal capabilities
- Algorithmic progress estimates
- Evidence of AI’s contribution
- Measurements of key R&D inputs
- Details of bottlenecks and forecasts
- Interviews with staff

### Measurements of internal capabilities

The assessor would need measurements of internal model capabilities over time to judge if they are accelerating. This includes details on:

- Benchmark data. Scores on all measured benchmarks across all frontier (including internal-only) models, to calculate ECI and other similar measures of progress. For robustness, details on each benchmark should be provided, including example questions and scoring details, and sample answers from models.
- Qualitative/quantitative info from researchers. Existing reflections from researchers (including excerpts from interviews or existing internal surveys) that help summarize how researchers perceive capabilities changing over time. This should be supplemented with assessors interviewing staff directly.
- Top-line progress measures for key domains. Detail on how progress is tracked/measured in pretraining, posttraining, and other key parts of the model development pipeline, along with historical records of progress in each. It may be useful to share details and analysis on how the developer understands key domains drive overall capabilities progress (e.g. how much progress is being driven by pretraining versus posttraining), as it will allow better estimates of how acceleration in key domains will flow through into capabilities acceleration.
- Other internal capability measures. Any other internal measures of capabilities that are tracked should be shared for robustness.

### Algorithmic progress estimates

We expect that developers currently maintain some estimates of algorithmic progress in key domains like pretraining and posttraining. While developers have not published details on these methods, they may be similar to the methodology defined in this paper, where research advances are mapped to a reduction in the compute required to reach certain performance levels.

The assessor does not require details of the specific research advances. However, an assessor would require estimates of the effect of these advances over time (dated precisely) and between models. Ideally, algorithmic progress estimates are as disaggregated as possible to allow for flexible analysis.

### Evidence of AI’s contribution

As it is challenging to determine the “No AI” counterfactual, we expect that a well-calibrated estimate of AI’s impact on AI R&D will require a number of lines of evidence. We expect that conversations between assessors and researchers could be highly informative in prioritizing specific data required to answer this question, but list a few illustrative examples of informative evidence here:

- Spend on AI agents. This ideally would be broken down by team and over time, denominated in tokens and inference cost.
- Researcher qualitative reflections. Specific stories of how research progress is made using models will provide significant insight into how AI is impacting the AI R&D process.
- Labor productivity estimates. This includes crude metrics like lines of code per researcher-day or self-reported uplift estimates over time.

### Measurements of key R&D inputs

Inputs other than AI may drive an acceleration in capabilities2 or algorithmic progress, and so it is important to understand how other key inputs are growing. Adjusting for the effect of other factors requires data on those factors:

- Labor inputs. The size of teams working on key domains, reported over time.
- Compute inputs: Training compute. For each model, how much compute was used on pretraining, midtraining, posttraining, etc. Experimental compute. Over time, broken down by team and function.
- Data inputs. This is domain specific and may include information about pretraining data or RL environments.
- Other key inputs. If there are other key inputs that are not externally known, those should be shared with assessors as well.

### Details of bottlenecks and forecasts

Assessors should be provided with information that allows them to forecast future capabilities and the plausibility of hitting dangerous capability milestones in the near term.

Assessors should ideally be given access to:

- Information on bottlenecks. For possible bottlenecks, assessors should be given detailed evidence on the plausibility of these bottlenecks.
- Existing forecasts. Where they exist, assessors should be able to collect forecasts of top-line metrics and details behind those forecasts.

Forward-looking estimates are highly uncertain and should be treated as such in the resulting report.

### Interviews with staff

To properly contextualize the information above, and to make sure they are not missing anything, assessors must be able to talk directly to researchers.

The assessor would need to interview staff involved in each important part of model training to confirm their understanding of the data, and to understand if there are other important missing sources of data. This would include researchers familiar with pretraining, RL, and infrastructure.

Additional conversations with researchers who have a more holistic view are likely also very helpful to the assessment, for example with researchers who study capability progress or acceleration internally, or with managers responsible for key domains.

- For example, a naive interpretation of benchmark scores may overestimate model capabilities because passing tests does not directly correspond to real-world usefulness, while quantitative estimates of “speedup” from researchers may overstate capabilities because of the difficulty of assessing the counterfactual. ↩
- For example, an above-trend compute scaleup might result in above-trend capabilities growth. ↩

items.title: Measuring the Inference Energy Efficiency of Open-Weight LLMs across Benchmarks, Reasoning Modes, and Hardware
items.content: arXiv:2610.14389v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Benchmark scores tell us what an LLM can do, but not how much energy is required to deliver that capability. We directly measure this trade-off for 86 open-weight model checkpoints, evaluated on seven benchmarks and six hardware platforms ranging from a consumer GPU to an eight-GPU server. We find large differences in energy efficiency even among models with similar capability. Most configurations lie away from the score--energy Pareto frontier: they use a median of 2.6--4.8$\times$ more energy than another configuration that scores at least as well, with differences reaching 27$\times$. Reasoning can improve capability, but enabling thinking increases energy by about 3.7$\times$ on average, and the benefit depends strongly on the model family and output budget. Generated-token count is also an imperfect proxy for energy, misordering 18--24\% of model pairs. In contrast, FP8 reduces energy by roughly a quarter with little change in score, while changing hardware largely rescales energy without changing the relative ranking of models. These results show that capability alone gives an incomplete picture of efficiency. We argue that benchmark scores should be reported together with measured energy consumption under a specified serving regime and output budget.

items.title: Attention Sinks in VLMs Are Borrowed, Not Seen
items.content: arXiv:2610.15855v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We study how to detect and mitigate visual attention sinks in vision-language models (VLMs). Visual attention sinks are image tokens that absorb a large share of attention over the image regardless of the query or task, and they mislead methods that treat attention maps as a record of where the model ``looked.'' Prior work has detected sinks through massive activation dimensions and proposed redistributing their attention, but none have addressed what makes a token become a sink. Comparing six candidate detectors on ten VLMs from four families, we find that only the centered cosine similarity between an image token's key and the key of the language model's text-sink detects visual sinks. Thus, a visual sink is an image token whose key aligns with the text-sink's key. Moving a sink's key component along this direction to the median of the image keys sends its attention back to the text-sink (\textbf{Are Borrowed}) while leaving model answers unchanged~(\textbf{Not Seen}). Building on this, we propose a training-free, entropy-triggered re-look that first cleans the attention map, then crops the most-attended region of the cleaned map and inserts it into the reasoning trace. Cleaning adds negligible computation to the forward pass, and the re-look improves accuracy with a mean gain of $+4.3$ points on fine-detail VQA benchmarks across model families.

items.summary: This study identifies what makes an image token become a visual attention sink in vision-language models, showing that only centered cosine similarity between an image token's key and the text-sink key detects sinks across ten VLMs from four families. items.reasoning: A mechanistic explanation of visual attention sinks with a validated detector across many VLM families is a solid interpretability contribution with implications for attention-based explainability methods. The finding is specific but well executed; broader impact depends on whether sink mitigation improves downstream VLM behavior.

items.title: GUIDE: Computationally Augmented Consensus for Trustworthy Clinical Practice Guidelines
items.content: arXiv:2610.16108v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Maintaining up-to-date clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) is essential for evidence-based medicine, but rapid evidence growth and complex expert consensus formation limit timely updates. We developed GUIDE, a multi-agent copilot system for human-AI collaborative guideline generation and updating. GUIDE delegates labor-intensive tasks to specialized AI agents while preserving expert judgment and final arbitration. In 12 NICE ophthalmology datasets, GUIDE achieved 88.85% literature recall, 86.06% alignment in certainty-of-evidence ratings, and 91.67% recommendation agreement, requiring 162.17 minutes per dataset on average (28.68% human intervention). Performance remained stable across 20 additional datasets from cardiology, endocrinology, gastroenterology, and respiratory medicine. items.title: TRAP: Tool-result Replay Attack for Probing Misbinding in LLM Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.16333v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: As AI agents increasingly act through external tools, tool results are no longer simple outputs but execution artifacts that must remain correctly associated with the context that produced them. Yet as results persist across caches, recovery mechanisms, and shared runtime state, this association can break, causing a real and unmodified result to be consumed in an incompatible execution context and lead the agent to an unsafe action. We characterize this failure as tool-result misbinding. To systematically study this failure, we introduce ReplayBench, a benchmark that uses controlled tool-result replay to evaluate misbinding across 19 representative agent scenarios, 4 failure properties, and 3 replay mechanisms. Across eight LLMs, three agent frameworks, and diverse stateful workflows, we find widespread replay-induced failures, with a mean Final-State Error Rate of 0.649 under cross-task replay. Stage-wise analysis localizes these failures to model-side action generation. Further analyses show that replay susceptibility varies with task similarity, shows little dependence on object similarity, and remains high under result staleness and implicit environment changes. These findings motivate runtime validity mechanisms that eliminate final-state errors in our evaluated settings while preserving legitimate recovery. The results call for explicit contextual binding in tool-using agent runtimes. Our work is public at https://github.com/Phitooo/Replaybench.

items.title: Same Operation, Different Permission: Evaluating Whether Guardrails Honor Authorization
items.content: arXiv:2610.16838v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: As language-model agents write code, move money and change records on behalf of users, deciding whether an action is authorized has become a central safety problem. Guardrails are often placed in front of these actions, yet few evaluations ask whether their decisions follow authorization: blocking unauthorized actions while still allowing the same actions under valid permission. We introduce \bench{}, a benchmark that contrasts authorization evidence for the same operation in its language track. It combines expert-annotated natural-language scenarios with executed and verified operations, plus externally sourced native-policy requests. \bench{} checks each decision for correctness, usability and resulting effect, and tracks each request across guardrail changes. Our experiments show that many blocked operations stem from failed reviews, not correct denials. Repairing the output format restores usable decisions but changes which authorized requests are honored, and adding a second reviewer removes some errors while rejecting valid authorization. Guardrails should therefore be evaluated on both the unauthorized actions they stop and the authorized actions they let through.

items.title: Releasing the Inner Jev: A Simple Recipe for Open Decision Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.17205v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: LLM-based decision-making systems, also called System One models, have recently gained popularity, most notably through Jev (Almeida, 2026). Given a typed input state, a question, and a set of options, they return a probability for each option in a single forward pass, without text generation. We show that existing open instruction-tuned language models can achieve comparable performance \textit{without any additional training}, by reading out answers from letters (A, B, C, etc.) in the model's output logits at the last token position. Furthermore, we show how a simple supervised fine-tuning recipe can improve their performance further. We evaluate four open instruction-tuned language models: Gemma 4 31B, Gemma 4 12B, Qwen3.6-27B, and Qwen3.5-4B. We fine-tune each using LoRA and a decision head initialized from a slice of the language model head. Furthermore, we introduce OpenDecisions, a novel 2,352-question validation dataset designed to reflect the task composition of JevBench (JevBench main- tainers, 2026) and which computes a Capability score based on accuracy and calibration metrics. Without fine-tuning, Gemma 4 31B scores 79.6 on OpenDecisions, compared to Jev's 80.1. After undergoing our fine-tuning recipe, it scores 84.4 on OpenDecisions and 81.5 on JevBench v1.7, outperforming Jev by 4.3 and 4.4 Capability points respectively and setting a new state-of-the-art on OpenDecisions. On a suite of public decision datasets, our models achieve accuracy comparable to Jev, with lower calibration error. Our results show that open language models already possess System One capabilities, and with simple fine-tuning they outperform Jev on a wide range of decision tasks. We release our models, serving code, and OpenDecisions.

This challenges the notion that specialized decision-model architectures are needed.

items.title: Coupled Harness--Model Evolution for Scientific Equation Discovery
items.content: arXiv:2610.17740v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to discover scientific equations from experimental data. Such a discovery system has two parts that must work together: a library of executable computational tools and the model's tool-use policy. The tools supply the solving capability, from diagnosing structure in the data to fitting candidate equations; the policy plans and orchestrates their use. Yet existing systems adapt only one part, keeping either the toolset or the model fixed, which leaves the corresponding failures uncorrectable. We develop a coupled evolution framework that improves both parts from the same verifiable fit-error signal. In the tool-evolution phase, an agent grows an executable tool library from a small set of generic numerical operations by diagnosing its own failures: it authors a new tool when a capability is missing and revises its selection rules when the right tool went unused. In the policy-evolution phase, a small open model (roughly 3B active parameters) is fine-tuned on successful tool-use trajectories collected with the frozen library, on training formulas screened to be disjoint from all evaluation benchmarks. Ablations show the two phases are complementary: with no tool library at all the same model solves almost nothing, the tools account for most of the gain, and trajectory training adds a further gain that is largest on the most difficult problems. The full system solves 79.1/71.3\% of LSR-Synth problems at fit tolerances $10^{-2}$/$10^{-3}$, reaches 63.8\% pooled accuracy on the distributionally different SRSD-Feynman panel, and obtains a normalized CP3-28 aggregate of $-7.27$. These results suggest a broader recipe for scientific agents: let the model and its instruments improve each other under verifiable feedback.

items.title: A dataset of formalised theorem statements from the Annals of Mathematics
items.content: arXiv:2610.18301v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recent progress in autoformalisation of mathematics using AI has been impressive. Measuring this progress requires datasets of formal statements that are both hard and trustworthy. We present AnnalsChallenge: 50 formalised theorem statements written by hand in Lean 4 using Mathlib. Each is the main result of a paper published in the Annals of Mathematics since 2020. Every formalisation was manually reviewed and then audited by AI. We release them without formalised proofs.

items.title: Loose Lips: Understanding Privacy Leakage in Agentic Dialogue
items.content: arXiv:2610.14071v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: As LLM agents are increasingly deployed in high-stakes enterprise settings, understanding how they handle sensitive information in agentic dialogue has become critical. Privacy leakage in such settings requires reasoning about whether information flows respect the contextual norms under which they originated. We extend CIMemories to CIMEMORIES DIALOGUE, a benchmark of 4,410 two-agent dialogue instances grounded in Contextual Integrity theory. Using this benchmark, we systematically evaluate 7 open-weight models from the Qwen3 and Llama 3.1 families across conversation lengths of 1 and 6 turns under three prompting conditions. We find that task capability and privacy leakage are fundamentally coupled: more capable models are systematically leakier, with no model in our evaluation able to decouple the two. Thinking models consistently leak more than their non-thinking counterparts, a pattern we attribute to the extended reasoning surface created by chain-of-thought. Leakage compounds with conversation length, rising up to 3x from 1 to 6 turns. Our results suggest that the coupling between task capability and privacy leakage is not an artifact of misconfiguration but a structural feature of current agentic systems.

items.title: Memory Without Curation: Learning Multi-Stream Latent Memory for Robot Policies
items.content: arXiv:2610.14406v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: It is widely appreciated that robotic policies require long-term memory to perform complex tasks. However, directly conditioning policies on all past observations leaves policy learning susceptible to learning spurious shortcuts, and introduces large latency at policy deployment. As such, today's memory-augmented policies curate what to remember, either by retaining only recent frames, selected keyframes, or textual summaries, or by learning latent representations of the visual stream alone. In this work, we propose an alternative approach IMPRINT, a policy-agnostic latent memory framework that augments vision-language-action (VLA) models with multi-stream memory without explicitly constraining what the policy should remember. IMPRINT compresses different streams into a latent memory that is updated incrementally at inference, enabling low latency. To avoid shortcut learning, IMPRINT adopts a two-stage training procedure, first supervising memory to reconstruct multiple streams (observations, actions, proprioception) of past information, as well as estimate current task progress, followed by end-to-end finetuning, jointly with the policy, on action prediction. Across both simulation and real-world tasks demanding memory, IMPRINT improves average success over the base VLA by at least 26%, outperforming popular alternatives, and maintaining lowest inference latency among memory-augmented VLAs. Through careful ablations, we demonstrate the utility of incorporating diverse information streams into robotic memory, validating the advantages of foregoing history curation. Project website: https://yilin-wu98.github.io/imprint_website/.

items.title: Sequent-Prover: Training Agents for Formal, Checkable SMT-based Reasoning
items.content: arXiv:2610.15258v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We introduce Sequent-Prover, a family of verifier-using language-model agents, and the post-training framework that produces them. Agents reason in an executable SMT-LIB scratchpad: they write complete SMT-LIB programs, query Z3 across turns, inspect solver feedback, repair formalizations, and terminate with an explicit answer. Our recipe, verifier-conditioned trajectory distillation, bootstraps from a noisy teacher proposal policy by sampling multi-turn trajectories, retaining the successful tail that is correct, non-trivial, grounded, and executable, then applying supervised fine-tuning and trajectory-level preference optimization. Because solver success alone does not guarantee semantic faithfulness, we evaluate task accuracy, k-sample reliability, and SMT program quality. Across 37 benchmarks and 7,254 problems per model family, post-training raises the 4B model's per-attempt accuracy from 85.6% to 97.0% and four-sample all-correct reliability (pass^4}) from 64.1% to 91.7%. It also reduces average SMT calls from 4.10 to 2.52 and tokens per attempt from 18.97k to 12.72k. Sequent-Prover agents give answers backed by executable formal artifacts.

Because solver success alone does not guarantee semantic faithfulness, we evaluate task accuracy, k-sample reliability, and SMT program quality. Across 37 benchmarks and 7,254 problems per model family, post-training raises the 4B model's per-attempt accuracy from 85.6% to 97.0% and four-sample all-correct reliability (pass^4}) from 64.1% to 91.7%. It also reduces average SMT calls from 4.10 to 2.52 and tokens per attempt from 18.97k to 12.72k. Sequent-Prover agents give answers backed by executable formal artifacts.

items.title: Variance-Optimal State Resampling for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
items.content: arXiv:2610.15888v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards spends much of its rollout budget on states that yield no learning signal. We recast this as a question about the sampling distribution itself: under a fixed rollout budget, which distribution over states minimizes the variance of the policy-gradient estimator? The answer admits a closed-form Neyman allocation, $\mu_{\mathrm{var}}^\pi(s) \propto d^\pi(s)\,\sigma_\pi(s)$, which connects naturally to GRPO's group-relative advantage and induces an emergent reverse curriculum as the policy improves, with no externally imposed schedule. Building on this principle, we propose VSR (Variance-driven State Resampling), a plug-in modification to GRPO using a prefix replay buffer and a zero-cost variance proxy. On mathematical reasoning benchmarks and long-horizon agentic tasks (Sokoban, BabyAI), VSR outperforms GRPO and GiGPO on most benchmarks with fewer generated tokens per update.

items.title: Compute-optimal data scaling for neural surrogates via multi-fidelity training
items.content: arXiv:2610.17221v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Neural surrogates for Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) are usually trained on synthetic data from numerical simulators. As models grow and scaling laws demand larger datasets, the cost of data generation often outweighs the training cost and becomes the bottleneck in the scaling quest. Unlike data in other domains, however, each PDE sample has a tunable cost that depends on its numerical fidelity, with the resulting cost-accuracy trade-off governed by known convergence rates. We exploit this property by formalizing neural surrogate training as a function of both data quantity and fidelity under a fixed data generation compute budget, treating fidelity as a fine-grained discrete spectrum rather than a binary distinction. Building on this, we show that multi-fidelity training enables Pareto-optimal error scaling against data generation compute. By using simulations at lower fidelities as an additional training signal, training on the optimal fidelity mixture matches the accuracy of high-fidelity-only training, with up to $6.3\times$ less data generation compute across our settings. We validate these findings across six PDE problems spanning structured grids and unstructured meshes, two distinct error sources (discretization and iterative-solver error), and four surrogate architectures, totaling over 7,000 training runs.

items.title: Train for Many, Update with One: Improving Multi-Sample Reasoning via Fenchel-Bregman Posterior Learning
items.content: arXiv:2610.17735v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Multi-sample reasoning measures candidate coverage, the probability that at least one of $K$ candidates is correct. However, minimizing the average loss of individual attempts does not directly optimize candidate coverage. We therefore formulate finite-$K$ posterior learning, which trains a distribution over solver parameters to reduce the probability that all $K$ independently generated candidates fail. To optimize this objective efficiently, we propose a Fenchel-Bregman (FB) approach that requires only one posterior draw per update, rather than the $K$ used by direct Monte Carlo optimization. FB first uses an exact Fenchel reformulation to separate problem-specific weights from the posterior update, enabling one-draw posterior updates. It then applies a closed-form Bregman update to track these weights through an exponential running average of observed failures, reusing the same draw. We instantiate FB with IVON, a variational optimizer for Gaussian posteriors over solver parameters, yielding Fenchel-Bregman IVON (FBI). Across diverse recursive and autoregressive reasoning tasks, FBI improves candidate coverage. In a matched comparison, it achieves comparable Pass@10 using 12.3% of the direct Monte Carlo baseline's measured training time per update.
items.author: Sungjun Lim, Adrian Robert Minut, Nico Carlsen Daheim, Mohammad Emtiyaz Khan, Kyungwoo Song, Thomas M\"ollenhoff
items.summary: The paper formulates finite-K posterior learning to directly optimize candidate coverage in multi-sample reasoning, and proposes a Fenchel-Bregman optimization approach that needs only one posterior draw per update instead of K. This makes training for pass@K-style objectives far more compute-efficient.
items.reasoning: Directly optimizing candidate coverage rather than average per-attempt loss is a meaningful conceptual contribution, and the one-draw-per-update trick offers real computational savings. Authors include established researchers (EMTIYAZ KHAN of RIKEN), supporting credibility. Score limited by the specialized nature of the multi-sample setting.

items.title: ProtoArena: Can AI Agents Discover and Exploit Real-World Cross-Component Protocol Vulnerabilities?
items.content: arXiv:2610.17837v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used for vulnerability analysis, yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of exploitation that depends on interactions among network protocol components. Such vulnerabilities arise from inconsistencies in message interpretation, timing, state, or trust assumptions across participants. We introduce ProtoArena, a black-box, multi-component, dynamic benchmark with 80 cross-component vulnerability-exploitation environments spanning 11 protocol and application domains and 7 attack categories. Tasks are primarily informed by published protocol-attack mechanisms. Agents interact with running systems through scoped interfaces to achieve security-effect objectives without target source code. Three information levels assess guided reproduction, exploitation with mechanism and topology context, and effect-directed black-box exploration. A hybrid verifier combines rule-based checks with LLM review of independently collected traffic and logs. We evaluate five LLMs. Claude Opus 4.8 achieves the highest observed success rates: 48.8% under L1 guidance and 12.5% under effect-directed black-box L3. In a separate DNSBomb optimization experiment, it achieves a peak downstream-response to average query-input byte-rate ratio exceeding 171,000 times. The results show that agents can achieve verifiable exploitation effects in some cross-component environments, but success with limited black-box information remains low and varies across domains and attack categories. All experiments use controlled, explicitly authorized targets; they do not test production systems or disclose previously unknown vulnerabilities.

items.title: GeoReader: Learning Latent Geometry for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.18694v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with metric and multi-view relationships that remain implicit in RGB observations. Geometry foundation models recover this structure from RGB, but existing methods either fuse the estimated features with visual tokens and learn to use them from question answering alone, or align VLM latents with geometry features. Capturing geometry, however, does not ensure its use: zeroing the aligned latents of a released feature-alignment model leaves its accuracy unchanged. We introduce GeoReader, a framework that learns geometric representations for the VLM that reads them. First, we train lightweight Geometric Readers to produce continuous input tokens, supervising them with geometry descriptions decoded by a frozen VLM, so that the Readers express geometry in a form the target model can already read. We then freeze the Readers to preserve this interface while fine-tuning the VLM on spatial QA, with geometry injection conditioned on the question. Geometry descriptions serve only as training targets: at inference, the VLM answers directly from the continuous geometric tokens without generating a geometry chain of thought. With geometry predicted from RGB images, our approach reaches 94.3 on MindCube-Tiny with Qwen3-VL-4B and, with a multi-source QA mixture, an average of 72.5 across six additional spatial benchmarks with Qwen3.5-9B. These results suggest that a useful geometric representation is one the receiving model can use, not merely one from which geometry can be reconstructed.

items.summary: GeoReader trains lightweight Geometric Readers that convert outputs of geometry foundation models into continuous input tokens for vision-language models, supervised by geometry descriptions, enabling VLMs to actually use latent geometric structure for metric and multi-view spatial reasoning. Notably, the paper shows that a released feature-alignment model's accuracy is unchanged when its aligned latents are zeroed, proving that fusion alone does not ensure use of geometry.
items.reasoning: Addresses a well-documented VLM weakness (spatial/metric reasoning) with a sharp diagnostic finding and a training solution validated by strong ablations. Credible author list spanning BIGAI and academic groups; impact depends on adoption of geometry-foundation-model outputs in VLM pipelines.

items.title: Verifier-Grounded Agentic RL for Provably Correct Code
items.content: arXiv:2610.19298v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reinforcement learning for code usually rewards passing tests, which a model can do while remaining wrong on the inputs the tests do not cover. A program verifier instead decides whether a program satisfies a formal specification for all inputs. Language models are almost always paired with verifiers at inference time only, and turning a verifier into a reward raises two difficulties. It reports only acceptance or rejection, which gives no gradient when every attempt fails, and a policy can cheat it, most simply by telling it to assume what the proof was supposed to establish. We build an agentic environment and reward that address both. The reward reads the verifier's diagnostics rather than its verdict, scoring a candidate by the weighted fraction of proof obligations it discharges, extended with hidden probes from a reference proof's annotations. An integrity audit outranks the verifier, rejecting any candidate that alters the specification or assumes what it was meant to prove. The model works as an agent against a live verifier over many turns, with a separately trained proof specialist as a frozen collaborator. Across Qwen3 models from 1.7B to 14B and a 35B Qwen3.6 mixture-of-experts model, held-out verification on code generation rises from 66.1% to 93.5% on DafnyBench and from 56.3% to 100% on SWE-Proof. This reward leads every other training signal we compare, including a binary pass-or-fail reward trained under otherwise identical settings, with the widest margin on code generation. When the agent must also deliver the repository patch, graded by each project's withheld tests, the fraction of held-out issues it resolves rises from 59.6% to 72.5%. Evaluated unchanged on three verification suites withheld from training, the checkpoints improve on all of them, including one whose language and verifier are absent from training.

This moves beyond test-passing rewards toward provably correct code generation.

items.title: Can LLMs Access their World Knowledge for Event Prediction?
items.content: arXiv:2610.19021v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recent work has questioned whether large language models (LLMs) can be useful for temporal event prediction. Despite vast pretrained world knowledge, LLMs often underperform simpler specialized models. We ask whether this knowledge is truly inaccessible, or whether current methods fail to present event prediction in a form LLMs can use. We argue for the latter and show that LLMs become effective event forecasters when the interface is designed around two choices. The first grounds each event in a natural-language description, and the second separates event semantics from the prediction space to prevent semantic bias from label associations. To test this, we introduce DescribeEvent, a benchmark of ~150K events across seven datasets and six domains with event-level descriptions. We find that capable LLMs substantially benefit from descriptions and symbolic labels, outperforming description-free variants and non-LLM baselines, while weaker models gain little. These results suggest that accessing LLM world knowledge for event prediction is an interface problem, and that event descriptions offer a practical way to elicit the knowledge LLMs already encode.

items.summary: This paper investigates why LLMs underperform specialized models on temporal event prediction despite rich pretrained world knowledge, arguing the problem is interface design rather than inaccessible knowledge. It shows LLMs become effective forecasters when events are grounded in natural-language descriptions and event semantics are separated from the prediction space to avoid label-association bias, introducing the DescribeEvent benchmark of roughly 150K events across seven datasets. This reframes a negative result into actionable interface guidance.

items.title: Weighted Ensemble Sampling for Rare-Event Estimation in Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.19202v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Rare but severe failures of large language models can become practically significant at deployment scale. Estimating their probabilities with direct Monte Carlo sampling is highly inefficient, while proposal-based methods typically require auxiliary learning of an additional proposal distribution. We introduce \textbf{Weighted Ensemble (WE)}, a training-free framework for rare-event estimation in language models. WE samples exclusively from the original language model and improves upon direct Monte Carlo by periodically reallocating the sampling budget toward prefixes that appear more likely to reach the target rare event. To guide this reallocation without learning a separate proposal distribution, we exploit internal LLM representations as prefix-level signals and empirically validate their effectiveness. We provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed algorithm. Experiments on safety-related tasks spanning both small-scale and modern large-scale LLMs demonstrate that WE improves the efficiency and reliability of rare-event probability estimation.

items.summary: This paper introduces Weighted Ensemble, a training-free framework for estimating the probability of rare but severe LLM failures at deployment scale. Instead of direct Monte Carlo sampling or learned proposal distributions, WE samples only from the original model and periodically reallocates sampling budget toward promising prefixes using internal LLM representations. This makes rare-event risk estimation far more statistically efficient, relevant to AI safety evaluation.

The use of internal representations for budget reallocation is clever, and the training-free property aids adoption; impact depends on empirical gains over importance-sampling baselines.

items.title: Likelihood Is Not Authorship: Can We Reliably Measure Human Contribution in AI-Assisted Writing?
items.content: arXiv:2610.19767v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: AI-text detection generally asks whether a machine wrote a text. As AI becomes an increasingly integral and accepted part of writing, the more relevant question is no longer whether AI was used, but how much of the text reflects human contribution. A prominent line of work estimates this by measuring how predictive a person's prompt is of the final text. We show that this measure can be easily manipulated. We introduce SPECIFICITY PADDING that simply asks the model to copy a few random IDs from the prompt, and that alone makes a title-only request look more human than one that supplies the article's key ideas. A context-swap audit then holds each document fixed, and only shows or hides the IDs to the evaluator. The score of the unchanged text swings by a third to half of its scale, and it rises for every document we test, on news and scientific abstracts, across varied LLMs from 3.8B to 753B parameters. The same articles can average 85\% human or 15\% human depending only on which prompt is on record, and even with no prompt at all, the output-only variant rewards the random strings themselves. An exact identity, the credit ledger, explains why. The score is a surprisal-weighted average over the text, so rare strings that the context makes copyable collect the credit, whatever they mean. A two-point bound marks a deeper limit. If the prompt could have been machine-written, every transcript-only method must, in the worst case, miss by half the contribution at stake. Likelihood-based scores alone cannot reliably establish human contribution without evidence of what the person added and how the text was produced.
items.author: Hasan Amin, Zhuoran Lu, Ming Yin
items.summary: Shows that widely used prompt-predictiveness measures of human contribution in AI-assisted writing can be trivially manipulated: a SPECIFICITY PADDING attack that asks the model to copy random IDs from the prompt makes minimal human input look highly human-authored. A context-swap audit confirms the score changes for unchanged text, undermining the measure's validity.
items.reasoning: A crisp, timely critique with a simple devastating counterexample against an emerging evaluation practice; important for anyone building AI-writing attribution or detection systems, though the contribution is fundamentally a negative result.

The score of the unchanged text swings by a third to half of its scale, and it rises for every document we test, on news and scientific abstracts, across varied LLMs from 3.8B to 753B parameters. The same articles can average 85\% human or 15\% human depending only on which prompt is on record, and even with no prompt at all, the output-only variant rewards the random strings themselves. An exact identity, the credit ledger, explains why. The score is a surprisal-weighted average over the text, so rare strings that the context makes copyable collect the credit, whatever they mean. A two-point bound marks a deeper limit. If the prompt could have been machine-written, every transcript-only method must, in the worst case, miss by half the contribution at stake. Likelihood-based scores alone cannot reliably establish human contribution without evidence of what the person added and how the text was produced.

items.title: Remember, Revisit, Revise: Scaffold Memory for Long-Horizon 3D Geometry
items.content: arXiv:2610.19674v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Geometry foundation models estimate camera poses and 3D scene structure from video sequences, but maintaining consistent reconstructions over long horizons remains challenging. Feed-forward models process long sequences as independent, fixed-length frame windows and align their predictions, causing pose and reconstruction errors to accumulate across windows. Streaming models retain information from past frames to inform future predictions, but cannot revise earlier estimates when later observations reveal errors. To address this, we introduce Scaffold MemOry for Revision (SMORE), a framework equipping frozen geometry foundation models with a revisable external memory for long-horizon inference. Inspired by hippocampal associative memory in biological brains, which links spatial context with sensory experience, SMORE associates where an observer is with what it observes, enabling past observations to be stored, retrieved, verified against new evidence, and revised when inconsistencies are detected. We evaluate SMORE with eight competitive geometry models on five datasets spanning camera pose estimation, multi-view depth estimation, 3D point-cloud reconstruction, simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), and novel view synthesis. Across all evaluated models, SMORE consistently improves long-sequence pose estimation, reduces multi-view depth error by up to 58%, reduces Chamfer distance for 3D point-cloud reconstruction by up to 43%, and achieves average trajectory error as low as 2.9 cm in long-horizon SLAM. By retaining corrected poses and observations, SMORE further improves the fidelity and spatial consistency of large-scale 3D scene reconstruction. These results establish revisable external memory as a flexible interface for extending pretrained geometry models beyond fixed-context prediction toward iterative, error-correcting inference over long visual sequences.

items.title: Active Generative Simulation: Meta-Learning What to Simulate for Sim-and-Real Policy Co-Training
items.content: arXiv:2610.19479v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Sim-and-real co-training is an effective way to scale robot learning by augmenting limited real-world demonstrations with simulation data. However, existing approaches typically treat simulators as fixed data sources, relying on uniform generation, offline retrieval, or manual parameter alignment by domain experts. We formulate \textit{Active Generative Simulation}: optimizing a simulator's data-generation distribution to maximize downstream real-world performance. To solve this problem, we propose MetaGenSim, a meta-learning framework that trains an auxiliary rater network via meta-gradients to automatically discover high-utility data-generation distributions within a user-specified simulation parameter space, without manual parameter alignment. Across simulation and real-world manipulation tasks, MetaGenSim outperforms uniform generation and retrieval baselines, achieves a 150% relative improvement in real-world full-task success over uniform generation, and matches expert manual alignment. We further show that distributions curated with a lightweight proxy policy transfer to VLA fine-tuning, and that MetaGenSim can exploit partial alignment through atomic skill stitching and object-receptacle composition when exact sim-and-real task alignment is unavailable. Project website: https://meta-gensim.github.io

This replaces uniform generation, offline retrieval, or expert tuning of simulators. A compelling step toward autonomous simulation curation for robot learning.

items.title: One-shot Human Video-Guided Adaptation for Vision-Language-Action Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.19746v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have recently achieved remarkable progress by leveraging large-scale robot datasets and foundation models for general-purpose robot manipulation. However, their ability to rapidly adapt to novel manipulation tasks beyond the training distribution remains limited. Existing approaches often require task-specific robot demonstrations and additional training, which are labor- and compute-intensive, limiting the scalability of VLA adaptation to open-world scenarios. To reduce this dependence on target-task robot data, we propose CapPro, a framework that enables a VLA policy to adapt to previously unseen manipulation tasks using only a single human demonstration video. CapPro consists of two components. First, a phase-aware human video representation module constructs a compact video representation through learned visual token selection and learns task-relevant query representations under phase-caption supervision. Second, a video-conditioned adaptation module jointly incorporates the compact video and query-derived representations into the action-conditioning context of the pretrained VLA policy. % This design introduces task-specific guidance while largely preserving the original VLA action-generation backbone. In this way, the human demonstration provides task-specific execution guidance rather than an embodiment-aligned trajectory to imitate, without requiring target-task robot demonstrations or target-task fine-tuning. Experiments across source and unseen target tasks show that CapPro improves average performance across unseen target groups while maintaining comparable performance on the source tasks. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of human-video guidance for cross-task VLA adaptation.

items.summary: CapPro enables VLA policies to adapt to unseen manipulation tasks from a single human demonstration video, removing the need for target-task robot demonstrations and retraining. It combines task extraction from the human video with a mechanism that transfers the demonstrated capability into the VLA policy at test time.

items.title: Physical Time as a Missing Dimension of Robot Policy Memory Dynamics
items.content: arXiv:2610.20524v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Existing robot policy memories typically evolve with observation sequences, implicitly treating each update as the same amount of physical time. Yet identical observation histories can span different durations and require different actions, exposing physical time as a missing dimension of policy memory. We introduce Temporal Flow Policy (TFP), which learns memory dynamics to retain past events and evolve the memory state over measured time intervals. Observations and prior memory determine the content and time scales of each transition; elapsed time determines how far the state advances. TFP conditions diffusion and flow-matching policies through this memory state and is trained with their native imitation objectives. We evaluate TFP with Diffusion Policy and $\pi_{0.5}$ through controlled comparisons of memory designs. These experiments show that successful timing depends on both measured intervals and retained history. TFP achieves higher average success than the recurrent and state-space memories we equip with the same intervals and than a variant that feeds the interval to a learned gate. Memory readouts recover the time since an event and motion information after occlusion. Changing the supplied intervals systematically delays or advances actions, linking time inputs to behavior. Real-robot tasks requiring timing or memory, together with LIBERO evaluations, demonstrate benefits in physical and general manipulation. These results suggest viewing robot memory not as stored observation history, but as a state that retains past events and evolves with physical time.
