items.title: What Is a Clarification? Estimating Model-Dependent Input Ambiguity
items.content: arXiv:2610.20052v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Ambiguous inputs can admit multiple interpretations, each potentially yielding a different answer. Existing work largely treats this ambiguity as a property of the input, yet for a particular language model, only some alternatives may be known and answerable. We therefore distinguish world ambiguity, capturing all alternatives admitted by an input, from model ambiguity, capturing those accessible to the responding model. To characterize these alternatives, we formalize natural-language clarifications through three desiderata: \emph{uniqueness}, \emph{faithfulness}, and \emph{answer equivalence}. We show that these desiderata induce a one-to-one correspondence between valid answers and equivalence classes of clarifications, implying that any interpretation can be represented either by its answer or by the clarifications that uniquely express it. We leverage this correspondence to introduce \circleclar{}, a black-box method that estimates the set of answers available to a model by checking consistency along an answer--clarification--answer cycle. Across open-domain QA and executable Text-to-SQL, \circleclar{} achieves strong recovery of these answer sets. In QA, the recovered support yields the strongest overall performance in model-dependent ambiguity detection and enables effective selection among answering, clarifying, and abstaining. Together, these results demonstrate the practical value of a model-dependent view of ambiguity and its characterization through an answer-clarification correspondence.

items.title: Learning Perception to Action Rules through Reinforcement Learning for Theory-of-Mind Reasoning
items.content: arXiv:2610.19796v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In Theory-of-Mind (ToM) reasoning, large language models may correctly infer the agent's mental state but fail to use that inference when predicting or judging the agent's subsequent actions. In this work, we investigate whether explicitly connecting perception, belief, and action with rules improves ToM reasoning. We generate concise \textit{if--then} rules that express relations between perception to action and use Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to train Qwen2.5 and Llama3 models across four ToM benchmarks. GRPO with rule generation outperforms prompting, supervised fine-tuning, and think reasoning. Moreover, rules generated by larger models ($\geq$3B) provide transferable knowledge that improves downstream performance of GPT-4o-mini. These findings suggest that explicit rules help models bridge the reasoning gap in ToM and support knowledge transfer across models.

items.title: Decoupled Drift-Diffusion World Models for Consistent Future Frame Prediction
items.content: arXiv:2610.19212v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: World models of visual information predict future image frames conditioned on given action sequences. This predicted scene evolution is driven by deterministic changes such as controlled motion on a robot platform, as well as stochastic changes such as rendering of manipulated objects or previously occluded regions. Our key insight is that the spatial location of these stochastic changes is itself learnable. We leverage this insight by jointly regressing both the deterministic next-state prediction and the spatial uncertainty map, then using the uncertainty map to guide a conditional diffusion process. We propose Decoupled Drift-Diffusion World Model (D3WM), which uses a transformer trained with a Gaussian negative-log-likelihood objective to produce both the deterministic next-state prediction and a spatial map of heteroscedastic aleatoric uncertainty. The learned uncertainty map then provides a structured spatial gate for a conditional diffusion model: deterministic regions are anchored to the predicted state, while uncertain regions, such as disocclusions or dynamic textures, are sampled by the diffusion process. We frame this decomposition under a variance-gated stochastic differential equation that separates deterministic drift from stochastic diffusion. D3WM shows improved results over competitive baselines in two distinct types of action spaces: robotic tabletop manipulation and camera motion.

items.summary: D3WM decouples deterministic and stochastic components of future frame prediction: a transformer jointly regresses the deterministic next state and a spatial uncertainty map, which then guides a conditional diffusion process for the stochastic parts. This yields more consistent world-model rollouts by learning where uncertainty lives.
items.reasoning: Conceptually clean decoupling of deterministic dynamics from learned spatial uncertainty for diffusion-based prediction; shares authors with Action Jets, suggesting a coherent research program in efficient world models.

items.title: WinARDet: Compressed Window Auto-Regression for Long-Horizon Vision-Language Grounding
items.content: arXiv:2610.19419v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: MLLM-based detectors formulate vision-language grounding as autoregressive coordinate generation, yet in dense scenes, they often collapse into a box repetition loop, repeatedly emitting identical boxes until the decoding budget is exhausted. We trace this failure to historical-answer attention takeover: Under full-history autoregression, repeated coordinate tokens in the growing answer history attract disproportionate attention, crowding out the attention sinks needed to attend to new visual evidence. % To break this loop, in this paper, we propose \textbf{Compressed Window Auto-Regression} (WinAR). This new mechanism partitions a long answer sequence into consecutive generation windows and restricts full token-level autoregression to the current window only while compressing each previous window into a fixed set of latent tokens that condition subsequent decoding. This design reduces the repeated exposure to raw historical coordinates that triggers the attention takeover, yet preserves cross-window dependencies essential for coherent multi-object generation. On RSDense, which contains 200-2,000 objects per image, our model WinARDet improves RexOmni F1-score (IoU=0.5) from 32.16 to 39.36 over the baseline, while reducing the redundancy rate from 35.48% to 13.00%. WinARDet also generalizes across decoding strategies and output formats, including parallel box decoding and polygon generation, providing a practical paradigm for long-horizon vision-language grounding across scene densities.

items.title: TextVerifier: Seeing Beyond Recognition to Verify Chinese Text Rendering
items.content: arXiv:2610.19551v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Text-to-image models increasingly generate readable Chinese text that still contains local rendering defects, such as a character with an extra or missing stroke or a malformed component. Such errors are invisible to OCR and vision-language models, which are trained for recognition and are therefore invariant to the very structural deviations that define a rendering error. We formalize text rendering verification as a target-conditioned problem: given a target character and an image crop, decide whether the crop is a correct rendering of that character. Our verifier TEXTVERIFIER feeds the text tower a character's Ideographic Description Sequence (IDS) rather than a single-character symbol, and is trained on 12.7M crop-IDS pairs plus label-free "same-character, different-quality" hard pairs sampled from the training trajectory of a text-region inpainting model. To evaluate this ability we build TEXTRENDERBENCH-ZH, the first per-character benchmark for generated Chinese text, annotating position, identity, and correctness for 7,358 characters. TEXTVERIFIER reaches an F1 of 0.844, far above OCR confidence (0.526), a general VLM (0.329), and TextPecker (0.590). Used as a per-character reward for Flow-GRPO post-training, it further reduces rendering errors, showing that its score can both detect and correct errors.

items.title: DeltaStreamer: Towards Human-Like Agentic Streaming Video Understanding
items.content: arXiv:2610.19849v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We propose DeltaStreamer, a novel agentic framework for streaming video understanding inspired by how humans observe, remember, and investigate. Streaming video understanding requires a system to retain evidence before knowing which details future queries will need. Existing approaches often obscure event transitions and omit relevant details when compressing video history, and cannot recover missing visual evidence. DeltaStreamer addresses these limitations by combining change-aware memory with query-driven planning and targeted evidence gathering with replay. Before a query arrives, it continuously observes the stream and explicitly records visual changes in structured memory, preserving how events unfold rather than only what is present. When a query arrives, a query-driven planner identifies the required evidence and guides memory retrieval and targeted replay. By revisiting historical frames, the agent can recover visual details omitted during observation and ground its answer in evidence beyond the retained descriptions. This connects continuous observation with active investigation tailored to each question. Experiments on OVO-Bench and StreamingBench demonstrate improvements over representative streaming video understanding methods, with overall scores of 66.07% and 59.53%, respectively.   Project page: https://bbbbchan.github.io/DeltaStreamer/

It records how events unfold before queries arrive, then recovers missing visual evidence on demand, addressing detail loss and unrecoverable history in prior compressive approaches.

items.title: Glance Forcing: Making Bidirectional Diffusion Autoregressive at a Glance
items.content: arXiv:2610.20220v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Autoregressive generation underlies real-time, causal video synthesis and is the backbone of video world models. Today's dominant approach distills a bidirectional diffusion model into a causal few-step student, but existing pipelines make this conversion prohibitively expensive, requiring offline Probability Flow ODE} (PF-ODE) trajectories that cost tens of thousands of GPU-hours and terabytes of storage. We show it can be made dramatically more efficient. Pushing this efficiency to its extreme, we reduce trajectory supervision to a single sample, the strictest setting possible, and find that it causes severe quality collapse. We trace this to the teacher's trajectory geometry: the high-noise regime, governing semantic layout and motion, and the low-noise regime, governing fine texture exhibit fundamentally different curvature and optimization behavior, so a single monolithic student cannot jointly fit both, causing severe representation interference. Motivated by this, we propose Glance Forcing, a lightweight distillation framework that decouples the denoising trajectory into two complementary slow and fast experts, each guided by a tailored, stage-specific objective, while keeping the pretrained teacher entirely frozen. This decoupling further reveals a general mechanism underlying few-step distillation: PF-ODE distillation mainly straightens the few-step trajectory geometry, while the subsequent distribution-matching stage independently governs distributional quality. Using only one PF-ODE trajectory, Glance Forcing already surpasses the fully-trained state-of-the-art baseline, raising the VBench Total score from 84.04 to 84.22 while cutting trajectory-collection cost from thousands of GPU-hours to about one A100-GPU-hour, with markedly larger gains in dynamic degree, VisionReward, and instruction-following, and consistent preference from human raters over strong baselines.

items.title: $\lambda_0$: Scaling Open-World Egocentric Human Data for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
items.content: arXiv:2610.18950v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated whole-body interaction with the physical world, yet collecting robot demonstrations at scale remains costly. Human demonstrations offer a scalable alternative, but existing egocentric human supervision often omits locomotion and posture, while embodiment differences and controller dynamics hinder accurate end-effector execution. We introduce HumanVerse, a 500-hour dataset of open-world human loco-manipulation pairing egocentric video with synchronized body and hand motion. Our human-to-humanoid pipeline aligns camera viewpoints and arm appearance, and refines motion references and controller inputs offline to reduce end-effector errors while preserving whole-body coordination. We validate the pipeline through zero-shot transfer to Unitree G1 on representative whole-body manipulation and long-range loco-manipulation tasks, without target-task robot demonstrations. Building on this pipeline, we develop $\lambda_0$, a humanoid foundation model for whole-body loco-manipulation, with robot-aligned human demonstrations providing supervision for mid-training. Increasing whole-body human data consistently improves downstream task progress. $\lambda_0$ achieves 90.0% success on SIMPLE and 62.5% across real-world loco-manipulation tasks. We expect this study to guide scalable whole-body human data collection toward humanoid foundation models for richer interaction with the physical world. Homepage: https://lambdahumanoid.github.io/

items.title: Back on Track: Deployment-time Policy Improvement via World Model Planning
items.content: arXiv:2610.19579v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: State-of-the-art visuomotor policies are increasingly capable of executing complex tasks, yet can fail during deployment in ways they cannot predict or recover from on their own. Improving their performance and robustness typically requires collecting more data, retraining, or modifying the policy architecture, all of which are time- and resource-intensive in practice. We instead propose an offline-trained monitoring-and-intervention framework that improves a policy during deployment using only black-box query access. From a limited set of labeled on-policy rollouts, we learn a policy-conditioned liveness value that measures the nominal policy's progress toward task completion; we additionally train a compact latent world model using these rollouts together with play data. At deployment, the liveness value continuously monitors execution. When it detects a loss of progress, a short-horizon planner searches the world model for corrective actions using the same value as its planning objective, after which control returns to the nominal policy. We evaluate our method on the LIBERO-Goal task suite and on a Franka Panda manipulator, using the vision-language-action model $\pi_{0.5}$ and a diffusion policy as nominal policies, and demonstrate significant improvements in task success rates, while supporting real-time control. Additional results and videos are available on the project website (https://policy-improvement-wm.pages.dev/).

items.title: Learning from Demonstrations meets Symbolic Control - A Supervisory Control Architecture for Formal Certification of Learned Motion
items.content: arXiv:2610.19815v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Dynamical system (DS)-based learning from demonstration generates flexible robot motions, but existing guarantees rely on certificate generation to obtain formal guarantees of safety and goal convergence. We propose a symbolic supervisory control architecture that automatically generates a fail-safe backup plan, certifying safety, reachability, and actuator feasibility directly from the robot's dynamics, independent of the learned DS. A nominal controller tracks the learned DS, while the supervisory controller monitors safety and target convergence, providing non-conservative intervention when the nominal controller violates necessary constraints. Experimental results include simulations and real robot deployment with various 2D and 3D datasets, including handwriting datasets, validating the effectiveness of our approach in providing formal guarantees with learned motion even in complex, dynamic environments.

items.title: Atomic-WAM: Execution-Grounded Atomic-Motion Reasoning for World Action Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.20157v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) typically adapt video foundation models to robotic control through joint video and action prediction. However, task-level instructions may leave the next physical interaction underspecified, requiring semantic grounding and state-dependent motion selection. To this end, we introduce Atomic-WAM, an understand-then-execute framework that connects task reasoning to action generation through atomic-motion descriptions. Specifically, a vision-language reasoner describes the next local motion from the task instruction and visual context, guiding a WAM to predict future video and an action chunk. Furthermore, an automatic annotation pipeline curates temporally aligned, contact-enriched supervision from multi-view DROID demonstrations. To make atomic-motion predictions executable by the WAM, we post-train the reasoner with Execution-Grounded GRPO (EG-GRPO). With the WAM fixed, EG-GRPO adapts the reasoner through rewards for motion appropriateness and execution success. Finally, Atomic-WAM achieves 39.6% task success under default instructions and 31.6% under vague instructions in a real-to-sim evaluation on RoboLab. Project page: https://ssj9596.github.io/Atomic-WAM-project

items.title: Towards Agentic Robots: Model, Data, Environment, and Harness
items.content: arXiv:2610.20442v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Foundation models are driving a paradigm shift in robotic intelligence, moving beyond low-level action prediction to goal-directed orchestration of data collection, model training, task planning, and real-world execution. We characterize this emerging paradigm as an agentic robots, in which agents reason over human instructions, interact with robotic environments, rectify execution errors autonomously, and dynamically adjust operational strategies. Although this field develops fast, current studies are not well connected. Researchers have no consistent view of how to combine different agentic functions into a complete robot system. This paper provides a unified overview of existing research on agentic robots. We first trace the development from robot policies to agentic systems, covering vision-language-action models, world models, and world-action models. We then clarify the definition and scope of agentic robots and organize existing research into seventeen categories across four functional domains: Model, Data, Environment, and Harness. Across these domains, we examine how agents shape model learning and robot decisions, collect and curate robot data, construct worlds, tasks, and tests for learning and evaluation, and organize capabilities for robot use. Finally, we discuss open challenges and outline directions for future research. Looking forward, we hope this work contributes to a clearer understanding of agentic robots and supports new approaches to making them more capable, reliable, and adaptive.

items.title: VLRLA: Deployment-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language-Action Models through In-Context Reinforcement Learning
items.content: arXiv:2610.19517v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual perception and language understanding with robot control, providing a foundation for instruction-conditioned manipulation. However, conventional pretrained VLA policies lack a mechanism for gradual adaptation through accumulated interaction experience during deployment. We therefore propose VLRLA, a general framework that equips existing VLA models with \textit{in-context reinforcement learning} capabilities for deployment-time adaptation. Our approach augments a VLA model with a reinforcement learning module that learns from historical observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals. During deployment, the policy gradually refines its action generation and progressively improves task success while keeping model parameters fixed. Our approach is also designed for general applicability and compatibility with diverse learning history construction strategies and model training pipelines. Finally, through extensive experiments, we systematically investigate the learning properties of VLRLA in simulation and demonstrate its ability to adapt to unseen scenarios during real-world deployment.
items.author: Diyuan Shi, Yiqi Tang, Hongyin Zhang, You Wu, Donglin Wang
items.summary: VLRLA equips pretrained vision-language-action models with in-context reinforcement learning so they can continue improving from their own interaction experience after deployment. A reinforcement learning module learns from accumulated histories of observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals, progressively refining the policy's action generation without weight retraining. This addresses the static nature of conventional VLA policies in deployment.
items.reasoning: Addresses a real limitation of VLA foundation models, namely their inability to adapt at deployment time, by connecting in-context learning with reinforcement learning for robot manipulation. The idea is timely and well-motivated, though the framing as a bolt-on module raises questions about how much genuine improvement is achievable without gradient updates.

items.title: Our approach to working with AI companies
items.content:
This blog post explains how we approach working with AI companies on projects that the public might rely on to understand risks. It was published on Oct 14, 2026, and we expect to update it over time.

At METR, we gather and publish evidence about whether humans could lose control of AI agents on a large scale. We work with AI companies to conduct evaluations, assessments, and investigations,1 and to share this evidence publicly. As we have seen increasing expectations for these kinds of voluntary engagements to provide external ‘safety assurance’, we want to explain our perspective. In this post, we clarify our overall goals for this work, our approach, and what our approach looks like in practice.

## Our motivations

Our goal is to give the public accurate, timely, and independent evidence about AI loss-of-control risk, so that they (along with policymakers and developers) can make their own informed decisions. Our primary approach is collecting high-quality, concrete evidence and publishing what we find. Beyond this, we may also work with companies or regulators to share our comments on unpublished sensitive information,2 to review risk reports, or to provide an independent judgment on claims about risk. However, many of the relevant claims involve open scientific questions so can’t be straightforwardly verified.

We see it as our role to collect evidence for the public; we do not intend to decide how companies should develop or deploy their agents. Decisions about frontier AI will likely be messy, high-stakes judgment calls relying on uncertain science, which should not be made behind closed doors, much less within any one organization. On the contrary, we think that the current situation requires open discussion about both what the risk levels are given the evidence and what risk levels are acceptable.

## Our approach

To correctly interpret our outputs, the public needs to understand the processes, constraints, and incentives that produced those outputs. For instance, if important evidence of risk was redacted by an AI developer that METR collaborates with during an assessment, the reader should be informed of that. METR currently takes the following measures for work we do with AI companies bearing directly on the public’s understanding of risks from AI development (such as pre-deployment testing, risk report reviews, and risk assessment exercises):

- Transparency about process: 3 We will clearly and publicly describe the limitations of our work with companies, in line with our process transparency policy. This information should include at least: Scope and duration: We should publicly describe the agreed-upon scope and duration of our work. Access, data, and resources: If we face access limitations, we should publicly describe whether these limitations impact our conclusions, and describe the nature of those access limitations where possible. Redactions: If a company makes redactions, we should publicly describe whether the company redacted information that was important to our conclusions, and describe the nature of those redactions where possible. Constraints: We should publicly describe other formal restrictions and informal pressures we were subject to that may have had material impact on our conclusions.
- Transparency about independence: We will clearly and publicly describe relevant staff conflicts of interest, per our COI policy.
- Financial and operational independence: Also per our COI policy, we will ensure that METR is not financially dependent on the AI companies we work with, promote a culture of impartiality, and recuse any employees with a significant conflict of interest with the company in question when selecting the team for a risk assessment project.
- Confidentiality and security: We will secure any nonpublic information and access that AI companies provide us, in accordance with our confidentiality and security practices and our agreements with them.

We also aim to meet the following principles, intended to minimize the amount the public needs to defer to us:

- Transparency about evidence and methods: We aim to publicly describe the evidence underlying our findings in enough detail that other external experts can decide for themselves whether they agree or disagree with our judgments. We aim to publish evidence we collect in a manner that allows others to conduct their own analyses. To put the evidence we share into context, we also aim to describe in detail our evidence sources and their limitations (e.g., incomplete or unreliable data), as well as our methods and their limitations (e.g., limitations due to using AI agents for analysis).
- Iteration and speed: Even when we cannot fully answer some questions in scope or arrive at confident claims, we aim to publish frequent and iterative reports to get evidence promptly out to the public.
- Consistency and fairness: We aim to take an approach that allows the public to compare reports across companies, and that makes it incentive-compatible for each company to engage with us or with similar external organizations.

In the next section, we give more detail on how this approach has worked historically.

## In practice

We arrived at the approach above after several years of working with AI companies. For example, we documented4 a similar approach this May in our pilot Frontier Risk Report, which grew out of work with Anthropic, Google, Meta and OpenAI. In addition to our own experience, we also draw on the work of other organizations in the AI evaluation ecosystem.

### Examples from past METR work

Redaction summary in our pilot Frontier Risk Report

Excerpt of discussion of informal constraints in our pilot Frontier Risk Report

In-text redaction disclosure in our OpenAI / Hugging Face incident investigation report

Discussion of agreement terms from our OpenAI GPT-5.1-Codex-Max report

Discussion of scoping for our Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 system card summary

Discussion of access and duration of work from our OpenAI o1-preview preliminary report

  1 / 6

Our typical practice is to disclose limitations, such as our agreement terms, the process our publications go through, and redactions companies make. For example, in the OpenAI / Hugging Face incident report, the investigators devoted a section of the report to explaining the scope, timeline, access, and limitations of their investigation. In the same report, the investigators used inline text and footnotes to explain where information was redacted and (in some cases) why. One arrangement that we have found works well is for METR to retain the right to unilaterally and prominently attach a “redaction summary” to our reports. This summary is meant to indicate whether a company redacted information that was important to our overall conclusions but did not permit us to adequately describe what was redacted. This enables redaction dialogue between AI developers and METR to focus on the question of whether a redaction would change our report’s overall conclusion, while retaining some flexibility in wording and allowing rephrasing. Beyond formal control over our publications, we have also tried to discuss softer, informal pressures that shape the evidence that the public receives.

Our website, our recent funding update, and our COI policy describe some of the measures we have taken to establish independence and address conflicts of interest. While we recognize that other groups can usefully make different independence tradeoffs, to date we have chosen not to accept payment or donations from frontier AI companies, and have declined offers of funding when an AI company would have influence over us, e.g. funding from an AI company executive or foundation. Though we accept a large amount of free model access, we ensure that we can afford to pay for any free tokens we receive without materially affecting our operations.

Even with these measures, it has proved challenging to ensure that we have adequate independence to collect and publish evidence under the current voluntary regime. We remain dependent on the companies we work with to voluntarily engage, provide access, and permit us to publish. In many instances, we rely on information that we cannot or do not verify, which might be filtered adversarially. Even with transparency about limitations, it is possible for a company to use its rights to withhold access or redact to exert control over what evidence the public receives from us.

## Appendix: Process transparency policy

This is an excerpt from a METR policy, current as of October 2026.

### Our communications about AI company engagements

In any new engagements with companies that could be interpreted as providing public assurance, we try to ensure:

- Right to disclose: We have the ability to unilaterally disclose: 5 (a) contractual restrictions on our ability to disclose or publish information; (b) external review, redaction, or approval processes we are subject to; (c) informal restrictions or pressures we are under; and (d) how (a)-(c) should impact the takeaways for the relevant audience. 6
- Active disclosure: We will actually disclose this information wherever it could impact the interpretation of our outputs (or the absence of outputs).

We have found this to be a tricky line to walk: companies understandably want to protect sensitive information they share with us, but this also means they want the final say on what we can and cannot publish. Moreover, the standard legal agreements that companies use can cut against process transparency. For example, sometimes non-disclosure agreements will treat the existence of the NDA itself as confidential.

We’re continuing to iterate on how to implement this in our work with companies. Not all of our previous or in-flight work meets this bar, but our current best practices include:

- Freedom for us to disclose, at minimum, the broad terms of the engagement and details of any redaction and publication terms.
- Freedom for us to make general statements (like the overall state of AI risk) that do not reveal confidential information, even if these might be informed by our work, without requiring company review or approval.
- Freedom for us to say whether we ultimately received adequate access and whether redactions were adequately disclosed.
- Time limits on steps in our process (for example, on how long companies have for redaction) so that our work is promptly shared.

items.content_html:
This blog post explains how we approach working with AI companies on projects that the public might rely on to understand risks. It was published on Oct 14, 2026, and we expect to update it over time.

At METR, we gather and publish evidence about whether humans could lose control of AI agents on a large scale. We work with AI companies to conduct evaluations, assessments, and investigations,1 and to share this evidence publicly. As we have seen increasing expectations for these kinds of voluntary engagements to provide external ‘safety assurance’, we want to explain our perspective. In this post, we clarify our overall goals for this work, our approach, and what our approach looks like in practice.

Our motivations

Our goal is to give the public accurate, timely, and independent evidence about AI loss-of-control risk, so that they (along with policymakers and developers) can make their own informed decisions. Our primary approach is collecting high-quality, concrete evidence and publishing what we find. Beyond this, we may also work with companies or regulators to share our comments on unpublished sensitive information,2 to review risk reports, or to provide an independent judgment on claims about risk. However, many of the relevant claims involve open scientific questions so can’t be straightforwardly verified.

We see it as our role to collect evidence for the public; we do not intend to decide how companies should develop or deploy their agents. Decisions about frontier AI will likely be messy, high-stakes judgment calls relying on uncertain science, which should not be made behind closed doors, much less within any one organization. On the contrary, we think that the current situation requires open discussion about both what the risk levels are given the evidence and what risk levels are acceptable.

Our approach

To correctly interpret our outputs, the public needs to understand the processes, constraints, and incentives that produced those outputs. For instance, if important evidence of risk was redacted by an AI developer that METR collaborates with during an assessment, the reader should be informed of that. METR currently takes the following measures for work we do with AI companies bearing directly on the public’s understanding of risks from AI development (such as pre-deployment testing, risk report reviews, and risk assessment exercises):

  • Transparency about process: 3 We will clearly and publicly describe the limitations of our work with companies, in line with our process transparency policy. This information should include at least: Scope and duration: We should publicly describe the agreed-upon scope and duration of our work. Access, data, and resources: If we face access limitations, we should publicly describe whether these limitations impact our conclusions, and describe the nature of those access limitations where possible. Redactions: If a company makes redactions, we should publicly describe whether the company redacted information that was important to our conclusions, and describe the nature of those redactions where possible. Constraints: We should publicly describe other formal restrictions and informal pressures we were subject to that may have had material impact on our conclusions.
  • Transparency about independence: We will clearly and publicly describe relevant staff conflicts of interest, per our COI policy.
  • Financial and operational independence: Also per our COI policy, we will ensure that METR is not financially dependent on the AI companies we work with, promote a culture of impartiality, and recuse any employees with a significant conflict of interest with the company in question when selecting the team for a risk assessment project.
  • Confidentiality and security: We will secure any nonpublic information and access that AI companies provide us, in accordance with our confidentiality and security practices and our agreements with them.

We also aim to meet the following principles, intended to minimize the amount the public needs to defer to us:

  • Transparency about evidence and methods: We aim to publicly describe the evidence underlying our findings in enough detail that other external experts can decide for themselves whether they agree or disagree with our judgments. We aim to publish evidence we collect in a manner that allows others to conduct their own analyses. To put the evidence we share into context, we also aim to describe in detail our evidence sources and their limitations (e.g., incomplete or unreliable data), as well as our methods and their limitations (e.g., limitations due to using AI agents for analysis).
  • Iteration and speed: Even when we cannot fully answer some questions in scope or arrive at confident claims, we aim to publish frequent and iterative reports to get evidence promptly out to the public.
  • Consistency and fairness: We aim to take an approach that allows the public to compare reports across companies, and that makes it incentive-compatible for each company to engage with us or with similar external organizations.

In the next section, we give more detail on how this approach has worked historically.

In practice

We arrived at the approach above after several years of working with AI companies. For example, we documented4 a similar approach this May in our pilot Frontier Risk Report, which grew out of work with Anthropic, Google, Meta and OpenAI. In addition to our own experience, we also draw on the work of other organizations in the AI evaluation ecosystem.

Examples from past METR work

Redaction summary in our pilot Frontier Risk Report

Excerpt of discussion of informal constraints in our pilot Frontier Risk Report

In-text redaction disclosure in our OpenAI / Hugging Face incident investigation report

Discussion of agreement terms from our OpenAI GPT-5.1-Codex-Max report

Discussion of scoping for our Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 system card summary

Discussion of access and duration of work from our OpenAI o1-preview preliminary report

1 / 6

Our typical practice is to disclose limitations, such as our agreement terms, the process our publications go through, and redactions companies make. For example, in the OpenAI / Hugging Face incident report, the investigators devoted a section of the report to explaining the scope, timeline, access, and limitations of their investigation. In the same report, the investigators used inline text and footnotes to explain where information was redacted and (in some cases) why. One arrangement that we have found works well is for METR to retain the right to unilaterally and prominently attach a “redaction summary” to our reports. This summary is meant to indicate whether a company redacted information that was important to our overall conclusions but did not permit us to adequately describe what was redacted. This enables redaction dialogue between AI developers and METR to focus on the question of whether a redaction would change our report’s overall conclusion, while retaining some flexibility in wording and allowing rephrasing. Beyond formal control over our publications, we have also tried to discuss softer, informal pressures that shape the evidence that the public receives.

Our website, our recent funding update, and our COI policy describe some of the measures we have taken to establish independence and address conflicts of interest. While we recognize that other groups can usefully make different independence tradeoffs, to date we have chosen not to accept payment or donations from frontier AI companies, and have declined offers of funding when an AI company would have influence over us, e.g. funding from an AI company executive or foundation. Though we accept a large amount of free model access, we ensure that we can afford to pay for any free tokens we receive without materially affecting our operations.

Even with these measures, it has proved challenging to ensure that we have adequate independence to collect and publish evidence under the current voluntary regime. We remain dependent on the companies we work with to voluntarily engage, provide access, and permit us to publish. In many instances, we rely on information that we cannot or do not verify, which might be filtered adversarially. Even with transparency about limitations, it is possible for a company to use its rights to withhold access or redact to exert control over what evidence the public receives from us.

items.title: SAT-RL: Training Language Models for Logical Reasoning with Symbolic Solvers
items.content: arXiv:2610.14402v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance in mathematical and logical reasoning, yet they still suffer from the curse of complexity and struggle as problem difficulty increases with the number of constraint interactions and the size of the search space. In contrast, satisfiability solvers such as Z3 provide scalable and verifiable reasoning through constraint solving under formal theories, but lack the flexibility to interpret natural-language problem descriptions. In this work, we propose SAT-RL, a reinforcement-learning (RL) framework that trains LLMs to interact with symbolic solvers through multi-turn tool execution. SAT-RL leverages synthetic data generation with verifiable solutions, supervised warm-up on solver-augmented traces, and solver-grounded reinforcement learning with tool-aware rewards. Experiments show that SAT-RL substantially improves symbolic reasoning with tools on both in-domain and out-of-domain logic tasks. Our code is available on https://github.com/sunjia72/SAT-RL.
items.author: Jialiang Sun, Kuldeep Meel
items.summary: SAT-RL is a reinforcement learning framework training LLMs to interact with symbolic solvers like Z3 through multi-turn tool execution, using synthetic data with verifiable solutions and a supervised warm-up phase. It targets the curse of complexity in logical reasoning as constraint interactions and search spaces grow.

items.title: MCPDisCo: Seesaw-Mitigated Tuning for MCP-Native Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.14956v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The Model Context Protocol provides a shared interaction substrate for the agentic web, allowing heterogeneous services to expose capabilities through a standardized interface. Learning to use this ecosystem entails a hierarchy of capabilities: tool-format skills, server-level transfer, and cross-server composition. We present MCPDisCo, an ecosystem-scale reinforcement learning framework for MCP-native agents. Using a Thought-Markov Decision Process (Thought-MDP), the framework explicitly represents internal reasoning alongside routing, execution, and termination and trains on real-server, long-horizon interactions spanning 70 MCP servers and 527 tools across six domains. We study the reasoning--tool seesaw, a joint-learning failure mode in which improvement in one objective can accompany deterioration in the other. To mitigate potential interference, MCPDisCo combines token-masked reward attribution with bidirectional gradient surgery: the former separates direct supervision for reasoning and action spans, while the latter removes conflicting components from both objective gradients in shared parameters. MCPDisCo achieves higher success with fewer chain-of-thought tokens. On the out-of-distribution MCP-Atlas and the GAIA benchmark, MCPDisCo maintains monotone gains, confirming that the learned behavior generalizes beyond the training server distribution and broader agentic tasks. Model weight and implementation are available.

Trained across 70 real MCP servers and 527 tools, it identifies and mitigates a reasoning-tool seesaw failure mode in joint learning.

items.title: Small but Mighty: Test Suites as Improvement Signals for Self-Evolving Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.15964v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: A self-evolving agent rewrites its own harness and must decide which rewrites to keep, so its improvement signal is the check a rewrite has to pass. Verifying a rewrite by agent rollout is expensive and subjective, while executable checks such as the repository's own tests are too sparse to catch behavior-changing rewrites, rejecting only a quarter of them. We instead take test feedback as the executable signal, and search for test suites that are both small and strong with a quality-diversity evolutionary algorithm, so that the signal is dense and informative. TeSearch treats suite size as a behavior descriptor, so that quality is pursued at every size and a small, strong suite is reachable, and learns a transition kernel during the search that denoises the LLM as an actuator on that descriptor. Across 129 real-world modules and three backbones, TeSearch delivers the highest-quality suites of any method compared, LLM-driven evolutionary search included, and the smallest of any LLM-based one. Used as the improvement signal of a self-evolving agent, it rejects 59.9% of behavior-changing rewrites against 25.3% for the repository's tests, at a 4.0% false-alarm rate and 3.5 s per decision. The code and data are available at https://github.com/ccsnow127/TeSearch.
items.author: Yutong Cheng, Wei Cheng, Wenchao Yu, Dawei Zhou, Haifeng Chen
items.summary: TeSearch improves the signal used by self-evolving agents deciding which harness rewrites to keep, finding repository tests alone too sparse (rejecting only a quarter of behavior-changing rewrites) and rollouts too costly. It uses a quality-diversity evolutionary algorithm to find small, strong test suites that provide dense, executable improvement signals.
items.reasoning: Choosing good improvement signals is a foundational question for self-evolving agents, and the quality-diversity search over test suites is an elegant, executable alternative to rollout-based verification. The overlap with the same group's SpecForge suggests a coherent research program; impact hinges on demonstrating that the small suites generalize across codebases.

items.title: Phantom Merge: When Your Large Language Model Agents Pick One but Tell You About Another
items.content: arXiv:2610.16141v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: LLM agents increasingly operate over multiple entities, where reliable response generation requires not only retrieving relevant evidence but also preserving its association with the correct entity. We identify Phantom Merge (PM), an entity-evidence binding failure in which an agent attributes unsupported claims to its committed entity, potentially even when the task is completed correctly. We formalize PM at the claim level and characterize its prevalence and error subtypes across four agent domains and four backbone families. To address this problem, we propose a two-stage framework for claim-level risk estimation and correction. First, Anchor-Grounded Risk (AGR) combines a representational readout of the agent's pre-emission hidden state with Jacobian-based functional information, providing complementary slot-level and anchor-value risk scores. Second, Fixed-Anchor Correction (FAC) audits flagged claims and selectively revises them using observed anchor evidence or removes them when no supported replacement is available. On the held-out Shopping detection cohort, AGR-slot achieves an AUROC of 96.2% and an average precision of 97.3%, outperforming the evaluated detection baselines. In the end-to-end Shopping mitigation evaluation, FAC reduces trajectory-level PM from 51.4% to 6.2%, with an output-to-original claim ratio of 80.7%. These results demonstrate the prevalence of entity-specific grounding failures and the effectiveness of combining internal risk estimation with evidence-constrained claim correction. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/LabRAI/PhantomMerge.

items.title: LIBERO-Industry: Benchmarking Robotic Manipulation under Industrial Process Constraints
items.content: arXiv:2610.16782v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Industrial manipulation in flexible manufacturing, e.g., high-mix, low-volume (HMLV) electronics assembly, requires robot policies to adapt to changing products and production conditions. Such settings impose industrial process constraints, including product variants, moving material flows, finite execution windows, and tight geometric tolerances. However, existing evaluation frameworks do not systematically capture these constraints when assessing generalist robot policies. To address this gap, we introduce LIBERO-Industry, a novel benchmark built on the widely used robot learning benchmark LIBERO, that translates the aforementioned industrial constraints into controllable task conditions and measurable success criteria. Specifically, LIBERO-Industry comprises three classic task scenarios: Static-to-Dynamic (S2D) loading, Dynamic-to-Static (D2S) unloading, and Dynamic-to-Dynamic (D2D) transfer. The suites contain 216 tasks in total that systematically vary object geometry, conveyor speed, interaction-window duration, and geometric acceptance region size. Extensive experiments across five generalist robot policies (including vision-language-action models and world-action models) show that performance progressively degrades as industrial constraints are introduced and combined. Under a shared fine-tuning and evaluation protocol, the LIBERO-Industry co-training condition achieved higher observed target-transfer completion than the original-LIBERO condition.

Such settings impose industrial process constraints, including product variants, moving material flows, finite execution windows, and tight geometric tolerances. However, existing evaluation frameworks do not systematically capture these constraints when assessing generalist robot policies. To address this gap, we introduce LIBERO-Industry, a novel benchmark built on the widely used robot learning benchmark LIBERO, that translates the aforementioned industrial constraints into controllable task conditions and measurable success criteria. Specifically, LIBERO-Industry comprises three classic task scenarios: Static-to-Dynamic (S2D) loading, Dynamic-to-Static (D2S) unloading, and Dynamic-to-Dynamic (D2D) transfer. The suites contain 216 tasks in total that systematically vary object geometry, conveyor speed, interaction-window duration, and geometric acceptance region size. Extensive experiments across five generalist robot policies (including vision-language-action models and world-action models) show that performance progressively degrades as industrial constraints are introduced and combined. Under a shared fine-tuning and evaluation protocol, the LIBERO-Industry co-training condition achieved higher observed target-transfer completion than the original-LIBERO condition.

items.title: Do Theorem Provers Need Theorem-Proving Agents? mini-Lean-agent: A Coding-Agent Baseline for Lean
items.content: arXiv:2610.17331v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: General-purpose coding agents use standard shell and file interactions, yet formal theorem-proving agents often rely on specialized, ad-hoc tooling. This makes it difficult to determine which components of theorem-proving agents provide benchmark gains: an improved base model, a specialized harness, a specific tool, or a combination of any of them. We introduce mini-Lean-agent, a deliberately minimal agent for Lean tasks whose only model-visible tool is bash. The model must use bash to inspect and edit the repository, search local libraries, invoke Lean, and manage its own intermediate work, while a separate trusted evaluator verifies the final artifact. We compare mini-Lean-agent against AxProverBase and Numina-Lean-Agent on the Putnam 2025 benchmark. Experiments with Gemini 3.8 Flash as the base model show that mini-Lean-agent solves 7/12 problems at \$2 per problem limit, compared with AxProverBase's 4/12. With Astra as the base model, mini-Lean-agent solves 12/12 problems at an average cost of \$1.28 per problem. This suggests that a generic coding agent with a minimal harness can already achieve strong performance on Lean benchmarks. Our results motivate using mini-Lean-agent as a standard baseline when evaluating theorem-proving infrastructure.

items.title: CompanionSafe: From Multi-turn Safety Evaluation to Guardrails for AI Companions
items.content: arXiv:2610.18095v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: AI companions provide users with emotional support and ongoing companionship, but their sustained relational interactions also introduce distinct safety risks. Prior work largely targets general harms or specific companion platforms and risk categories, while relying on manually collected conversations, limiting scalable and user-grounded evaluation and mitigation. To address this, we introduce CompanionSafe, a unified evaluation-to-mitigation framework for AI companion safety. Its evaluation component, CompanionEval, provides scalable multi-turn evaluation by constructing 1,300 relationally grounded settings from diverse personas, matched companion characters, and dialogue scenarios across four turn tiers. Its mitigation component, CompanionGuard, converts benchmark-exposed failures into turn-localized supervision for companion-specific risk detection. Our results show that even strong LLMs and existing guard models remain vulnerable to companion-specific relational harms, while both closed- and open-source models exhibit increasing safety risks as interactions become longer. Together, CompanionEval and CompanionGuard form a practical evaluation-to-mitigation loop for AI companion safety, turning relational safety failures exposed during multi-turn interaction into supervision for companion-specific guardrails.

This addresses a growing consumer-facing safety domain.

items.title: Reading Right, Acting Wrong: Diagnosing Decision Failures of System One Models in Agent Loops
items.content: arXiv:2610.18579v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: System One models choose an agent's next action by scoring a supplied set of options in a single pass. This makes them fast and cheap, but when they choose wrongly there is nothing to inspect: did the model misread what the agent has seen, or read it correctly and still act wrongly? We answer behaviorally. On a frozen benchmark of agent decision states from simulated environments, customer-service policies, tool use, web navigation and coding, we pair every next-action question with factual probes about the same state, each answered independently. Across seventeen fast systems and a reasoning model, the answer is consistent: most wrong actions follow correct reading, and the more accurate a system, the more of its errors take this form. These errors are not noise; they gather on the same states across systems of every kind. Where the probed facts provably determine the action, models that read every fact still fail to combine them, and their own answers, composed by code, repair the failure. On real states, what is missing is often not a fact but the next sub-goal.

Across seventeen fast systems, more accurate models make a larger share of these read-right-act-wrong errors, implying failures lie in the action-selection stage.
items.reasoning: Clean behavioral diagnostic with a counterintuitive finding that error location shifts with model quality; useful for guiding where agent improvements should be targeted, though limited to single-pass scoring models and simulated states.

items.title: GameSmith: Scaling Zero-Sum Self-Play with Synthesised Games
items.content: arXiv:2610.13995v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Post-training large language models (LLMs) on two-player zero-sum games provides a verifiable reward, and the gains have been shown to transfer to general reasoning. Existing pipelines, however, rely on a handful of hand-written games and on advantage estimators tied to them, so both the supply of games and the advantage estimate on a large corpus limit scaling. We present GameSmith, which scales both. An LLM synthesises games inside templates whose reward, observation, and hidden-information code is fixed. Each game is verified by seed-paired replay and by an independent re-implementation of its specification, then expanded into encoding, rule, and size variants, giving 26 new games in 29 families and 336 verified variants from the three SPIRAL templates. The model is distilled from the self-play of a larger teacher (Qwen3-32B) on these games and then trained by self-play reinforcement learning with CRAB, an advantage estimator that credits each decision against a shrinkage estimate of the expected return of its position and is defined on every variant. On Qwen3-4B-Base, distillation raises the 13-benchmark mean pass@1 from 45.5 to 62.5, above the three SPIRAL games at the same budget, and self-play with CRAB reaches 64.9. The ordering holds across models, and transfer grows with the number of game families.
items.author: Weixian Waylon Li, Jiaxin Zhang, Han Zhou, Chengzu Li, Ke Wang, Fengxiang He, Yiwen Guo
items.summary: GameSmith scales LLM self-play training on two-player zero-sum games by having an LLM synthesize new games within templates with fixed reward, observation, and hidden-information code, each verified via seed-paired replay and independent re-implementation of its specification. This yields 26 new games in 29 families and 336 verified variants from a small seed set, addressing the bottleneck that prior pipelines rely on a handful of hand-written games. The approach supports verifiable-reward post-training whose gains are known to transfer to general reasoning.

The connection between game self-play and general reasoning gains makes this strategically relevant, though results on downstream transfer are the key open question.

items.title: Can We Trust This Evaluation? Instance-Level Reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge
items.content: arXiv:2610.14029v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: LLM-as-a-judge evaluation commonly aggregates multiple judges' decisions into a majority vote, yet this panel decision process does not guarantee that the evaluation of an individual item is reliable. We propose Structured Cross-fitted Uncertainty Risk (SCUR), a label-free approach for estimating instance-level evaluation reliability based on the judge panel's behavior. A latent measurement model serves as the backbone for measurement system analysis, from which SCUR derives three complementary signals capturing panel uncertainty, measurement cross-entropy, and perturbation sensitivity. These three sources of evidence are combined into a risk score. We evaluate the SCUR approach on five real-world benchmarks using majority-vote error ranking, selective trust, and risk stratification. Furthermore, we show our approach to be more effective at detecting high-consensus risk items, which are the blind spots for many other LLM-as-a-judge evaluation methods.

items.title: GeoFix: Geometry Fixing for 4D Consistent Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.14293v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Video diffusion models increasingly serve as priors for 4D generation, but the generated videos often lack geometric consistency. Recent approaches address this through post-training by designing geometric rewards, yet this can degrade texture and fine detail, requiring auxiliary appearance rewards and careful reward balancing. To address this challenge, we propose GeoFix, a unified framework that improves geometric consistency and visual quality with a single geometric reward, applicable to both training and inference-time reward alignment. Our reward measures cross-view depth consistency in static scene regions, targeting structural inconsistencies without directly constraining appearance or penalizing valid object motion. Crucially, depth agreement increases with camera field-of-view overlap even in real videos and 4D datasets, allowing a smaller camera movement to be mistaken for better geometry. We account for this effect by calibrating the reward against the overlap-dependent trend. GeoFix achieves a 39% improvement in WorldScore 3D consistency and a 4% increase in VBench Quality Score.

items.summary: GeoFix improves geometric consistency of 4D generation from video diffusion models using a single cross-view depth-consistency reward applied to static scene regions, avoiding the texture degradation typical of multi-reward post-training. The method works for both training-time and inference-time reward alignment and preserves valid object motion.

items.title: CacheLink: Functional KV Transport for Zero-Prefill Cross-Model Context Handoff
items.content: arXiv:2610.15509v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: KV caches make long-context serving efficient by reusing past computation, but model switching breaks this reuse and forces the receiver to prefill the context again. We study \emph{zero-prefill cross-model context handoff}: translating a sender cache into a receiver-compatible state so that the receiver can continue directly without prefilling same context. Existing affine transport methods show that receiver KV states can be substantially reconstructed from sender caches. However, through extensive analyses, we find that reconstruction fidelity is a poor proxy for receiver utility. Similar K/V reconstruction errors can lead to substantially different attention patterns, predictive distributions, and downstream accuracy, because conventional reconstruction objectives overlook the query-dependent functional importance of K and V in receiver attention. We thus introduce CACHELINK, which learns a coupled K/V correction through the receiver behavior directly. Across four independently trained sender--receiver pairs and seven evaluation panels, CACHELINK improves the equal-weight mean over all methods for every pair. In matched diagnostics, CACHELINK changes K/V squared error by less than 0.4% while substantially changing receiver attention and next-token behavior. At 32K context, it reduces handoff latency by up to $7.27\times$ relative to receiver re-prefill. Our findings verify that reconstruction fidelity alone is insufficient and that preserving the receiver computation induced by the transported cache is important for effective cross-model KV transport.

items.summary: CacheLink addresses zero-prefill cross-model context handoff — translating a sender KV cache into a receiver-compatible state so a different model can continue without reprefilling. The key finding is that reconstruction fidelity is a poor proxy for receiver utility, since similar reconstruction errors can produce very different attention patterns and downstream accuracy, motivating a functional rather than pixel-level transport objective.
items.reasoning: The insight that functional utility, not cache-reconstruction error, should drive cross-model KV transfer is both technically interesting and practically relevant for multi-model serving pipelines. The negative result about affine transport proxies is valuable. Novelty is good but applicability is limited to models with compatible architectures.

items.title: Of Errors and Echoes: Responsibility-Aware Credit Assignment for Tool-Use Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.16027v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Reinforcement learning improves tool-use agents, yet fine-grained credit assignment remains challenging even with step-level feedback. An observed error may be inherited from an earlier decision, while multiple responsible decisions may share the same downstream consequence or participate in later recovery. We introduce Error-Chain-Aware Optimization (ECHO), a responsibility-aware credit assignment framework that separates responsibility identification from credit allocation. A frozen judge combines retrospective trajectory analysis with decision-time assessment from the policy-visible prefix to distinguish newly introduced errors, inherited consequences, missed corrections, and successful corrections. ECHO then counts shared downstream consequences once across responsible decisions and constrains rewards for repairing self-induced errors through source-funded recovery, producing bounded action-level supervision alongside terminal supervision. Experiments on six diverse tool-use benchmarks at both 4B and 8B scales show strong and consistent improvements over the compared baselines, with ECHO achieving the highest score on five of six benchmarks at each scale. These results support decision responsibility as a useful basis for fine-grained credit assignment in tool-use agents. Our code is available at https://github.com/xid32/ECHO.

items.title: VLA-GAUGE: Systematically Evaluating Generalization and Robustness in Vision-Language-Action Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.16567v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have achieved high success rates on familiar manipulation tasks, yet it remains unclear whether such scores reflect genuine zero-shot generalization and perturbation robustness. Existing evaluation frameworks provide limited capability-level diagnosis and combinatorial perturbation coverage, often without connecting diagnosis to targeted model refinement. We introduce VLA-GAUGE, a diagnostic framework that unifies both evaluations under a shared executable task representation. It combines (1) paired in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks across six capability suites, (2) single-factor sensitivity analysis with combinatorial perturbation screening and evaluation, and (3) diagnosis-driven refinement through targeted data augmentation and model fine-tuning. We evaluate 12 VLAs spanning different model sizes and action-modeling paradigms under a unified protocol. We find that (1) The mean Zero-Shot Score on VLA-GAUGE is only 22.3%, with SimpleVLA-RL scoring 8.0% and ranking second to last among the evaluated models. (2) Under three representative combinatorial perturbation configurations, the mean R-Score is 9.3. (3) Diagnosis-driven fine-tuning improves $\pi_{0.5}$'s zero-shot generalization and robustness under a selected perturbation combination on held-out scenarios by 72.4 and 31.8 scoring points, respectively; the latter exceeds the 10.9-point gain from LIBERO-Plus single-factor fine-tuning despite fewer successful training trajectories. These results show that high reported success rates on familiar manipulation tasks do not guarantee strong zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks or robustness to combinatorial perturbations, while diagnostic evaluation provides actionable signals for targeted model improvement.

It tests whether high success rates reflect genuine zero-shot generalization.

(3) Diagnosis-driven fine-tuning improves $\pi_{0.5}$'s zero-shot generalization and robustness under a selected perturbation combination on held-out scenarios by 72.4 and 31.8 scoring points, respectively; the latter exceeds the 10.9-point gain from LIBERO-Plus single-factor fine-tuning despite fewer successful training trajectories. items.title: Know-Thy-Not: Training-Free Targeted Negation in Dual-Encoder Vision-Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.17440v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Dual-encoder vision-language models systematically fail at negation, scoring ''a cat without a dog'' nearly identically to ''a cat with a dog.'' We show that this failure is inherent to the single-embedding framework. Under contrastive training, single-embedding methods can at best ignore the negated concept (dilution) but never penalize its presence (rejection). We propose Know-Thy-Not (KTN), a training-free method that introduces an image-side rejection dimension to penalize the negated concept directly in the visual representation. We also introduce COCO-Confusion, the first benchmark requiring genuine rejection to succeed. Across 9 backbones, KTN improves COCO-Confusion mAP by up to +25.6 over vanilla VLMs and +9.6 over the strongest existing method.

items.title: Explore with Memory, Learn without It: In-Context Exploration and Self-Distillation for LLM Reasoning
items.content: arXiv:2610.17734v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Exploration bounds learning efficiency in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Current methods explore mostly through independent sampling, without fully using the information gathered along the way, such as known wrong answers and environment feedback. We propose LEAF, which injects a dynamic, problem-specific memory into the context before every rollout. The memory contains the most recent response, its reward, and other environment feedback. It is updated after every verifier call. We decouple policy updates from rollouts and update the policy through self-distillation. On four benchmarks and two open models, LEAF accelerates exploration by about 4x compared with a random sampling baseline. On unseen test sets, it improves accuracy over the strongest baseline by 1.59 and 1.83 percentage points on the two models, while using less compute than any RL baseline. These results highlight the potential of LEAF in improving both exploration and learning efficiency. Code is available at: https://github.com/on1262/LEAF

items.title: SpecCloak: Probing Harmful Code Generation through Engineering Specifications
items.content: arXiv:2610.17907v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The code generation capabilities of large language models (LLMs) can equally be misused to implement harmful functionality, underscoring the need to understand their safety behavior in response to programming requests. While request phrasing is known to influence refusal, it remains unclear whether the form in which coding task requirements are stated affects the refusal process for malicious code generation. We introduce PseudoSpec, a template that organizes functional requirements as engineering specifications, and investigate its effects through controlled comparisons, representation analysis, and activation interventions. Across five open-weight models, removing explicit risk keywords only partially reduces refusal, whereas specification prompting substantially lowers refusal even when these keywords are retained. This reduction accompanies consistent shifts toward code-output-related representations, and interventions along condition-difference directions alter refusal behavior. Output analysis further distinguishes code-related responses from generation degeneration. Building on these findings, we propose SpecCloak, a black-box red-teaming framework combining PseudoSpec with discriminator-guided optimization, achieving an average execution-verified attack success rate of 28.91\% across eight target models on RedCode-Gen. We also introduce SpecReveal, a defense prototype combining natural-language intent reconstruction with dual-view detection without target-model fine-tuning. It achieves a 96.88\% attack detection rate in a separate prompt-detection evaluation, with false positives assessed on benign programming and specification-style inputs. These results connect specification-induced response differences to practical security consequences and identify intent reconstruction as a complementary detection approach.

items.title: Two Clocks: Why Larger Rollout Batches Learn Slower but Fail on Schedule in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
items.content: arXiv:2610.18853v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) relies on costly model-generated responses, motivating larger rollout batches and square-root learning-rate scaling. Reported to approximately preserve progress per sample with one optimizer step per rollout, this rule is less understood in practical multi-step training. We develop a two-clock framework that separates the samples needed to make progress from those consumed before collapse. Under a local quadratic model, the square-root rule preserves first-order drift per sample but not progress: larger batches take fewer, longer updates and lose more to curvature, yielding a learning-rate-dependent critical batch beyond which sample efficiency degrades. A drift-threshold hypothesis predicts a complementary failure clock whose sample count remains approximately invariant along the square-root rule. Controlled GRPO experiments on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B across a $16\times$ batch range support both predictions. Ratio clipping delays failure, especially for larger batches, but the progress gap persists without it. Widening the clip trades stability for a transient speed gain. The progress gap reappears on another dataset, a general-purpose checkpoint, and a 7B model. Finally, we use the two-clock framework to derive a simple multi-step RLVR schedule: start below the critical batch and switch to a larger batch before failure. Our code is available at: https://github.com/WinstonLiyt/two-clocks-rlvr.

items.title: Backpropagating Verifier Rewards Through Continuous Flow Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.19080v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has substantially improved the reasoning of autoregressive and discrete-diffusion language models. Language models that generate continuous token embeddings are emerging as a strong alternative, but RL post-training for them remains understudied. We propose \method{}, a post-training framework for continuous flow language models. Such a model denoises token embeddings over multiple steps and decodes them into discrete tokens only at the last step. To obtain pathwise gradients, which backpropagate through continuous actions and have much lower variance than REINFORCE, we introduce a critic that estimates the value of intermediate token embeddings, bypassing the non-differentiable decoding step. The critic must also keep track of the value function as the policy changes; to this end, we design a critic that predicts a value from every token representation and improves policy optimization. Across four reasoning tasks, \method{} reliably improves a continuous flow language model through RL post-training and outperforms baseline methods of the same type.

items.reasoning: Targets an emerging model class (continuous flow language models) with a concrete variance-reduction technique for RL post-training, extending the RLVR paradigm beyond autoregressive models. Novelty is good, but the model class is early-stage, limiting near-term impact.

items.title: Spectral-MoE: Heterogeneous Per-Layer Expert Utilization in Dense-to-MoE Conversion
items.content: arXiv:2610.19232v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language models impose substantial memory demands and arithmetic costs during inference. Dense-to-mixture-of-experts (MoE) conversion is a model optimization technique that aims to reduce these arithmetic costs. Dense-to-MoE conversion partitions pretrained feed-forward network (FFN) neurons into experts and selects a subset for each token. Leading methods fall into two categories: analytic methods produce a converted model quickly using heuristics, while learning methods produce a model much more slowly by optimizing via gradients. Both approaches, however, fix the same active expert count, or "utilization," at every layer. We introduce Spectral-MoE, which learns to allocate a utilization budget heterogeneously across layers. Its name draws a metaphor between separating a dense FFN into experts and separating a light beam into its spectrum. Spectral-MoE consists of two distinct approaches: a static approach that uses a single per-layer scalar which is shared across tokens, and a dynamic approach which emits a per-token schedule. We demonstrate that both allocators improve performance over uniform on both the analytic-based and learning-based SOTA dense-to-MoE methods. At 25% FFN utilization, dynamic allocation reduces WikiText-2 perplexity relative to uniform by 1.04, 2.96, and 2.71 points on the learned base for Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B, respectively. The corresponding reductions on the analytic base are 2.45, 6.26, and 2.17 points. On the learned base, dynamic allocation improves six-task mean accuracy over uniform by an average of 1.5, 4.2, and 3.6 percentage points across the three models at FFN utilizations of 12.5%, 25%, and 50%, respectively. These results establish per-layer expert utilization as a novel optimization axis in dense-to-MoE conversion.

items.summary: Introduces Spectral-MoE, a dense-to-MoE conversion method that learns heterogeneous per-layer expert utilization budgets, unlike prior analytic or gradient-based methods that fix the same active expert count at every layer. This should reduce inference arithmetic costs more effectively by matching expert allocation to layer-specific redundancy.
items.reasoning: Addresses inference efficiency for LLMs with a clear, well-motivated extension to an active optimization technique. The heterogeneity idea is intuitive and likely yields gains, though results would need to be substantial to shift practice given established competitors.

items.title: Learning to Compute Is Not Learning to Retain or Reuse in Looped Transformers
items.content: arXiv:2610.19768v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Looped transformers compute by applying one block repeatedly, so they can run for more loops than they were trained with. Recurrent reasoners are known to overthink: iterating past the trained depth can turn a correct answer into a wrong one. Such a late error can reflect failed computation, loss of retention, or a state that later computation cannot reuse. We separate these cases in in-context Mealy-machine execution, where a simulator supplies intermediate targets and exact counterfactuals for hidden-state interventions. Models trained to answer at loop 32 are fully correct there but keep only 22% of these answers at loop 64. Retention depends on what training asks for: supervising one randomly chosen position per example, instead of always the last, keeps 99.8%, and randomizing the number of training loops also helps; truncating gradients, as in progressive training against overthinking, does not. The computation itself is exact: position $k$ is computed at loop $k$, and swapping its loop-$k$ hidden vector for the one from another input redirects every later position to that input's exact continuation (237/237 pairs in each of ten models). Retention, however, is not reuse. Even in models that keep nearly all answers, holding each position $k$ fixed from loop $k$ drops accuracy to 4--6%, whereas holding it from loop $k+4$ is harmless. A released recurrent maze network trained to avoid overthinking behaves the same way. Learning to compute is thus not learning to retain, and avoiding overthinking does not make a state reusable when its answer first appears.

items.summary: Using in-context Mealy-machine execution with exact counterfactual hidden-state interventions, this paper separates overthinking failures in looped transformers into failed computation, loss of retention, and unreusable states. Models fully correct at trained loop depth 32 retain only 22 percent of answers at loop 64, and retention depends on training supervision choices. The findings clarify why looping beyond trained depth breaks recurrent reasoning.
