items.title: DSABench: Benchmarking Source Discovery, Coordination, and Execution for Multi-Database Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.14700v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Most text-to-SQL benchmarks provide the target database. In a large data catalog, however, choosing the sources is part of the problem: an agent must find every database needed for a request, determine how their results fit together, and execute the resulting workflow. We present DSABench to evaluate these capabilities jointly. Its 815 human-reviewed tasks draw on Spider, BIRD, and LiveSQLBench; 618 require several databases to contribute, and 105 allow more than one interpretation of the required sources. Executable contracts define source participation, cross-source dependencies, and source-local execution, while RouteEnv lets agents inspect public catalog evidence without revealing the gold annotations. In our routing-only study across seven model backends, the highest RA-Set score is 60.55%, compared with a highest RA-Graph score of 34.66% when coordination requirements are included. The gap becomes more pronounced when execution is required. Across four backends, median non-privileged Route+Exec-Graph success ranges from 6.69% to 7.98% without clarification and from 11.44% to 13.25% with one clarification; the best observed clarified configuration reaches 16.99%. On ambiguous tasks, clarification improves exact branch-source recovery by 39.8-43.2 percentage points. These findings illustrate why retrieving plausible databases or producing correct local SQL is not enough: an agent must carry the right information through the entire multi-database workflow.

items.title: Harmony Harness: Multi-Objective Self-Evolution of Agent Harnesses
items.content: arXiv:2610.15150v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recent work on self-evolving LLM agents treats the agent harness as an optimization target that can be iteratively improved through execution feedback. Existing approaches, however, largely optimize a single objective and evolve the harness as a monolithic artifact, limiting their ability to handle competing goals and to separate transferable design from environment-specific adaptation. We introduce Harmony Harness, a framework for multi-objective, compositional harness evolution. Harmony Harness formulates harness evolution as a multi-objective optimization problem and uses decomposition-based evolutionary search to maintain solutions across different regions of the Pareto frontier, avoiding reliance on a hand-designed structural diversity metric for repository-scale harnesses. In parallel, we introduce factorized evolution operators that separately refine general-purpose harness mechanisms and benchmark-specific adaptations, together with a dynamic composition workflow that integrates them at inference time. Across SecRepoBench and BaxBench, Harmony Harness consistently outperforms strong harness-evolution baselines, with gains exceeding 10% on both benchmarks. Our results show that explicitly modeling both objective trade-offs and harness structure yields substantially stronger and more transferable agent evolution than existing single-objective, monolithic approaches.

items.title: When Skills Remain But Access Fails: Factorized Skill Memory for Continual Skill Internalization
items.content: arXiv:2610.15492v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Skill internalization aims to convert externally specified procedural skills into persistent model capabilities, allowing language-model agents to execute them without retrieving or reinjecting skill descriptions at inference time. Yet when new skills are learned continually, whether previously internalized skills remain usable is still poorly understood. We study forgetting in continual skill internalization and uncover a clear hierarchical structure. Early in subsequent training, a model may lose the ability to invoke an old skill from the raw request, while supplying only the correct canonical skill name substantially restores the learned behavior; with further optimization, this conditional execution also degrades. We call these two stages skill-addressing forgetting and skill-execution forgetting. Guided by this finding, we introduce Factorized Skill Memory (FSM), which separates continual skill memory into a plastic Address Memory and a stable Execution Memory. At each stage, FSM trains a new LoRA executor using only current-stage data, freezes it after acquisition, and appends it to Execution Memory; in parallel, Address Memory incrementally learns to map current requests to executors without replaying historical requests or execution trajectories. At inference time, Address Memory selects one executor from the raw request, and only that frozen executor performs a single language-model generation. On a five-stage benchmark built from 100 TaskBench skills, FSM achieves 65.95% mean exact match and 93.38% addressing accuracy across two task orders, improving over the strongest replay-free parameter-isolation baseline by 14.3 percentage points while remaining within 1.9 points of Replay, which retains historical training examples.

It uncovers a two-stage hierarchical forgetting structure: a model first loses the ability to invoke an old skill from a raw request while a canonical skill name restores it, and later conditional execution also degrades. items.title: Revocation Is Not Complete at Receipt: An Executable Outcome Contract for Distributed Agent-Tool Gateways
items.content: arXiv:2610.15991v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Distributed agent workflows cache delegated authority at tool gateways. Revocation may be reported at issuer commit, transport acknowledgment, or receiver persistence, although none of these observations establishes that all gateways enforced the change or that guarded effects stopped. We define C0-C5, a bounded outcome contract spanning issuer commit through effect prevention, and implement it as a persistent monitor over a frozen gateway set, call set, and observation window. A 14-case fault matrix checks conservative classification, sticky violations, restart persistence, and evidence immutability. In a derived audit of its eight semantic cases, treating C3 or C4 as completion produces seven or five false positives, respectively; the bounded C0-C5 verdict produces none. Descriptive scaling covers 1,024 gateways and 10,000 effect vectors. The primary experiment uses the maintained Keycloak 26.7 identity server and measures the contract across two durable receivers, eight physical agent-tool gateways, Filesystem and PostgreSQL effects, and 16 AWS hosts in three availability zones. Normal delivery and recovery commit no effects. Under receiver-selective non-delivery, transport acknowledgment and receiver persistence still succeed, but 112 of 225 calls (49.78%) are admitted, and all 112 effects commit in every treatment block. A separately provisioned execution repeats the result. OPA/Toxiproxy and a live three-role LLM workflow with networked MCP tools reproduce the persisted-but-not-enforced boundary on narrower surfaces. Finally, an unmodified external MCPMark agent executes 60 closed-loop task arms. Normal C4 denies all 31 exposed post-barrier calls and commits no effect; selective C3 allows 344 calls and commits 145 effects across Filesystem and PostgreSQL. Transport success is therefore evidence of progress, not a revocation-completion verdict.

items.title: ProCARE: Real-World Study Automation via Profile-Grounded Evidence Contracts
items.content: arXiv:2610.16175v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Real-world studies (RWS) analyze routinely collected healthcare data, such as electronic health records and insurance claims, to estimate treatment effects, monitor safety, and identify risk factors outside randomized trials. Automating RWS with large language model agents is appealing but brittle: valid analyses depend on dataset-specific clinical semantics, including index dates, follow-up windows, patient/event-level units, and outcome boundaries that are often implicit in observational data. This leads to schema mismatches, temporal errors, inconsistent analytical granularity, and unsupported clinical claims. We present ProCARE, a profile-grounded framework that reformulates RWS automation as constrained compilation. ProCARE converts heterogeneous data profiles into Evidence Contracts specifying available variables, temporal attributes, distributions, and evidentiary limits, and compiles study objectives into RWS-IR, a strongly typed intermediate representation for variables, time relations, analysis units, and statistical tasks. Deterministic validation and localized repair then check and revise generated workflows across schema mapping, cohort construction, variable derivation, analysis, and interpretation. On 36 EHR-based benchmark tasks, ProCARE outperforms strong LLM-agent baselines in code executability, semantic consistency, and conclusion traceability, with automated violation diagnoses showing moderate-to-substantial agreement with blinded expert review.

items.title: Geospatial Vector Geometry as a Native Spatial Modality for Vision-Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.16769v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Geospatial reasoning links VLMs to real-world action and decision making. Reliable reasoning requires accurate spatial information and effective spatial representations. However, current VLMs obtain this information mainly from language and vision. At larger geographic scales, limited visual observations make it difficult to establish accurate spatial references and recover precise spatial relations. This leads to a bottleneck for VLM spatial perception and reasoning. This paper proposes that geospatial vector geometry can become a native spatial modality within a VLM and introduces GeoVec-VLM. First, we develop a structured geometry representation that preserves the spatial structure and arrangement of vector objects, building an explicit spatial basis. Second, we introduce a geometry interaction strategy that brings this basis into multimodal computation, where it interacts with visual content and language references according to the queried spatial relations. Together, these designs allow perception and reasoning to operate on shared geometric references. Across five spatial reasoning tasks, GeoVec-VLM improves mean accuracy by about 11\% relative to the strongest baseline, maintains its gains under geographic transfer, and shows greater geometric consistency. Our results show that geospatial vector geometry offers a promising internal spatial basis for VLM spatial reasoning. https://github.com/TXFR/GeoVector-VLM

items.title: ChemExplain: A Multimodal Benchmark for Explanatory Chemical Reasoning
items.content: arXiv:2610.17183v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Current chemistry benchmarks primarily evaluate outcome prediction or reaction pathway generation, but rarely test whether a model can explain why an observed chemical effect occurs. We introduce ChemExplain, a benchmark of 1,180 multiple-choice chemistry questions drawn from 383 peer-reviewed papers. Each question pairs a molecular or reaction image with an observed chemical effect and four candidate explanations, each associated with a different structural feature visible in the image. Answering requires the model to perceive the depicted structure, apply chemical knowledge, and identify which feature most directly explains the effect, a capability we term explanatory attribution. The correct feature-mechanism relation is derived from supporting evidence in the source paper rather than invented by the question-generation LLM. We construct the benchmark automatically with a multi-agent framework that applies progressive quality control at three stages and validate it with eight chemistry domain experts. The strongest evaluated model reaches 78.6% accuracy, leaving considerable room for improvement. On a 600-question expert-reviewed subset, reasoning-trace analysis classifies 71.4% of the strongest model's errors as attribution failures. Attribution is also the largest error category for the open-source and chemistry-specific models included in our analysis.

items.title: RAN-JEPA: An Action-Conditioned World Model for Energy-efficient Mobile Network Control
items.content: arXiv:2610.17584v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Operational mobile networks are rich in observations but poor in interventions: they continuously generate large volumes of passive telemetry, while controlled action--response trajectories remain comparatively scarce and costly to collect. This observation--intervention asymmetry is a central obstacle to building practical world models for RAN control. We address this problem with RAN-JEPA, an action-conditioned world model that separates representation learning from intervention learning. The model first learns a predictive latent representation from observation-only network data, adapts that representation to the target deployment domain, and then learns action-conditioned latent dynamics from controlled sleep/wake trajectories while keeping the encoder fixed. We evaluate RAN-JEPA using public operator performance data for pretraining and a real-equipment four-cell 5G testbed for domain adaptation, post-training, and control. Across four future 15-minute intervals, RAN-JEPA achieves lower action-conditioned prediction error than a GPT-2 world-model baseline and a mechanistic rule, while remaining close to a strong persistence reference. What-if evaluation further shows that the model produces distinct and coherent future trajectories under matched SLEEP and KEEP plans. In closed-loop control, RAN-JEPA consistently supports higher sleep ratios than the two baselines at comparable congestion cost. These results show that observation-first, action-conditioned learning can turn abundant passive telemetry and limited intervention data into a practical predictive model for energy-aware RAN control.

The model separates representation learning from intervention learning: it first learns predictive latent representations from observation-only data via a JEPA-style objective, then adapts to the deployment domain and learns action-conditioned dynamics from limited sleep/wake control data. This enables energy-efficient RAN control with a credible author list including Joseph Sifakis and Ya-Qin Zhang.

We address this problem with RAN-JEPA, an action-conditioned world model that separates representation learning from intervention learning. The model first learns a predictive latent representation from observation-only network data, adapts that representation to the target deployment domain, and then learns action-conditioned latent dynamics from controlled sleep/wake trajectories while keeping the encoder fixed. We evaluate RAN-JEPA using public operator performance data for pretraining and a real-equipment four-cell 5G testbed for domain adaptation, post-training, and control. Across four future 15-minute intervals, RAN-JEPA achieves lower action-conditioned prediction error than a GPT-2 world-model baseline and a mechanistic rule, while remaining close to a strong persistence reference. What-if evaluation further shows that the model produces distinct and coherent future trajectories under matched SLEEP and KEEP plans. In closed-loop control, RAN-JEPA consistently supports higher sleep ratios than the two baselines at comparable congestion cost. These results show that observation-first, action-conditioned learning can turn abundant passive telemetry and limited intervention data into a practical predictive model for energy-aware RAN control.

items.title: Empowering Edge Agents: A Systematic Analysis of Edge-Cloud Collaboration in LLM Agent Execution
items.content: arXiv:2610.17816v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Edge-cloud collaboration combines the lower inference overhead and greater data locality of edge-side execution with the stronger capabilities of cloud-hosted models. However, as LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon scenarios, cloud participation becomes interleaved throughout execution rather than a one-shot decision for each query. Such interleaved participation introduces trajectory-level effects that remain insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we introduce EC2-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating edge-cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution. It provides executable digital-workspace agent tasks and a unified evaluation framework covering task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure. Using this benchmark, we empirically study diverse forms of edge-cloud collaboration. Our study reveals three findings. First, collaboration achieves a favorable balance among task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure compared with edge-only and cloud-only execution. Second, as edge models become stronger, collaborative execution approaches cloud-only performance, and performance differences across strategies shrink, while privacy exposure remains strongly strategy-dependent. Third, stronger edge capability shifts preferred collaboration from externally controlled cloud participation and direct cloud execution toward more edge-controlled collaboration. Further analyses identify cloud-invocation decision-making and instruction following as important edge-side abilities for effective collaboration. These findings provide a systematic understanding of edge-cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution and insights for designing future edge agents that effectively collaborate with cloud models. Code and resources are available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/EC2-Bench.
items.author: Pengcheng Huang, Zhenghao Liu, Shixin Ren, Shi Yu, Sijia Yao, Yukun Yan, Chaojun Xiao, Maosong Sun
items.summary: Introduces EC2-Bench for evaluating edge-cloud collaboration during long-horizon LLM agent execution, where cloud model participation is interleaved throughout a trajectory rather than a one-shot routing decision, covering task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure. This matters because edge-cloud hybrid agents are a growing deployment pattern where latency, cost, and data locality tradeoffs interact in poorly understood trajectory-level ways.
items.reasoning: Addresses a practically important and underexplored deployment question with a systematic benchmark including privacy exposure metrics, which is unusual and valuable. From a group affiliated with Tsinghua's THUNLP, adding credibility, though the contribution is benchmarking and analysis rather than a new method.

items.title: Judges Follow the Reference: The Derivation Gap in Verifying Tool-Call Arguments
items.content: arXiv:2610.18497v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Tool-call judges evaluate argument values proposed by LLM agents. We find that they accept a correct value less often when their input holds no reference for it, that is, no text that says what the value should be. This happens when the value is a default value from the function schema that the user did not mention, when it has to be inferred, or when the text it comes from was cut from the judge input. We call this drop in acceptance the derivation gap. It appears across all seven judges we evaluate, including System One models CLM and Jev. The gap is not only a truncation artifact: correct default values have the largest gap on a benchmark with no truncation. A controlled source-relocation test shows that judges follow the reference in their input: they favor a visible incorrect value over a correct value whose source is hidden. We introduce DeRef (Derived Reference): a separate model reads the full history without seeing the candidate and writes a reference for the judge. Across three benchmarks, DeRef improves overall argument AUROC for all judges tested. On the controlled test, it raises AUROC from chance or below to between 98.40 and 99.59.
items.author: Linhai Ma, Yan Wang, Lingfei Qian, Yupeng Cao, Victor Gutierrez Basulto
items.summary: The paper identifies a derivation gap: LLM tool-call judges accept correct argument values far less often when no reference text stating the value is present, such as schema defaults or values that must be inferred. The effect appears across seven evaluated judges and persists even without truncation, showing judges rely on references rather than derivation.
items.reasoning: A well-designed diagnostic study with a clear named phenomenon, controlled relocation tests, and broad judge coverage; relevant to anyone building LLM-as-judge verification for agents, though scoped to tool-call argument checking.

items.title: Posterior Flow Matching
items.content: arXiv:2610.13994v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Flow matching learns how to transport noise toward data, but its mean prediction does not directly report the endpoint uncertainty remaining at an intermediate state. This paper introduces Posterior Flow Matching (PFM), a general generative modeling framework that learns conditional velocity means and componentwise variances with a Gaussian posterior model. The same model evaluation supplies both a transport prediction and endpoint uncertainty, making posterior diagnostics available throughout generation. These learned moments support a mean-driven ordinary differential equation (ODE) and a posterior-driven stochastic differential equation (SDE), whose local noise scales adapt to the predicted uncertainty. Across image, point-cloud, molecular, and action generation, PFM improves generation quality and provides endpoint-posterior readouts throughout generation.
items.author: Chenrui Ma, Xi Xiao, Lin Zhao, Xinru Jiang, Tianyang Wang, Yanning Shen, Ferdinando Fioretto
items.summary: Posterior Flow Matching (PFM) extends flow matching by learning conditional velocity means and componentwise variances through a Gaussian posterior model, so a single model evaluation yields both a transport prediction and endpoint uncertainty at any intermediate state. These learned moments support both a mean-driven ODE and a posterior-driven SDE with adaptive local noise scaling. Experiments span images, point clouds, and molecules.
items.reasoning: A clean, general extension to a foundational generative modeling method that adds principled uncertainty quantification essentially for free, with adaptive-noise SDE sampling as a bonus. Strong methodological pedigree among authors and multi-domain validation; impact depends on uptake by the flow matching community but the contribution is broadly applicable.

items.title: Pick the Mixture, Not the Samples: Combinatorial Data Selection for LLMs
items.content: arXiv:2610.14028v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Data selection for LLM fine-tuning faces two facts about real training: data pools draw from many distinct domains, and evaluation spans diverse tasks. As a result, the same sample helps different tasks differently, and samples interact during training so that a subset's value is not the sum of its parts. Current data-selection methods leave these realities largely unaddressed. We formalize them as Combinatorial Data Selection (CDS), a framework that separates attribution (how samples are scored) from selection (which subset to pick) and models the non-additive interactions among samples. On a real instruction-tuning data pool, we find substantial cross-domain complementarity (joint utility exceeds the sum of singletons), alongside redundancy within domains. Inspired by this, we propose Mixture-then-Select, a two-stage algorithm that first decides how many samples to take from each domain, then ranks samples within each domain by attribution score. Theoretically, the gap to the optimal subset is linear in the selection size and independent of data pool size. Empirically, Mixture-then-Select outperforms strong baselines by 20 to 54%, is robust across attribution methods, and works across different models and data pool sizes. The framework also extends to the data purchasing problem under a budget constraint when sample prices vary. Our findings suggest that allocating selection across domains offers a promising path toward more efficient and effective data selection for modern LLMs.

items.reasoning: Addresses a genuine and under-modeled problem: subset value in data selection is not additive across samples. The formalization and mixture-level perspective are useful for efficient training, though abstract-level empirical gains are not fully visible and similar data-mixture work exists.

items.title: Akule: Fast and Scalable Multi-Robot Motion Planning via Sparse Interaction Diffusion
items.content: arXiv:2610.14248v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Diffusion models provide expressive trajectory priors for multi-robot motion planning (MRMP), but scaling them to large teams requires coordinating individual motions without expensive joint computation. We introduce Akule, a sparse interaction diffusion framework that augments a frozen single-robot prior with three learned modules: a reusable pairwise correction model $R_{\phi}$, a contextual selector $U_{\psi}$ that determines which corrections to evaluate, and a composer $G_{\omega}$ that combines their effects through context-dependent signed weights. This decomposition separates which interactions merit computation from how their effects should be combined into coordinated denoising updates. We train $R_{\phi}$ using matched pairwise trajectory optimizations, then learn $G_{\omega}$ and $U_{\psi}$ from physically optimized joint trajectories without requiring a prescribed ground-truth interaction graph. The resulting joint proposals are passed to a downstream search-based planner for validation and repair. Across diverse MRMP benchmarks, Akule achieves competitive planning success, complete-planner speedups of up to $25\times$, zero-shot population transfer, and successful planning with up to $256$ robots. Ablations further demonstrate that learned selection and composition reduce pre-repair conflicts and downstream repair effort relative to heuristic selection and uniform summation.
items.author: Manav Vora, Gokul Puthumanaillam, Aditya Penumarti, Jane Shin, Melkior Ornik
items.summary: Akule scales diffusion-based multi-robot motion planning by augmenting a frozen single-robot prior with learned modules for pairwise interaction correction, contextual selection of which interactions to compute, and composition of their effects. This decomposition separates deciding which interactions matter from how their effects combine, avoiding expensive joint computation for large robot teams.
items.reasoning: Elegant modular design addressing a real scaling bottleneck in multi-robot planning with diffusion models; strong systems contribution though specialized to the motion-planning domain.

items.title: Target-ESS Tempered Policy Optimization (TETPO): Smooth Variance Control via Bridge Importance Sampling
items.content: arXiv:2610.14440v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement-learning post-training of large language models is computationally efficient but inherently off-policy: the learner updates on rollouts generated by a stale policy, while correcting this mismatch requires importance weights that can be extremely heavy-tailed. A small number of trajectories may then dominate an update, collapsing the effective sample size (ESS) and increasing the variance and instability of the resulting gradient estimates. Existing stabilizers apply fixed interventions regardless of the realized severity of weight concentration, either discarding selected samples or reweighting them without adapting the correction strength. We introduce \emph{Target--ESS Tempered Policy Optimization} (TETPO), which replaces each importance weight $\rho$ by $\rho^\alpha$ for a data-adaptive exponent $\alpha\in[0,1]$: $\alpha=1$ preserves the original importance weights, whereas $\alpha=0$ assigns uniform coefficients. For each prompt group, TETPO selects the largest $\alpha$ whose tempered weights satisfy a target ESS fraction $\kappa$, applying little tempering to healthy groups and stronger tempering when weight degeneracy is severe. At the population level, the tempered coefficients are exact importance weights for a geometric bridge between the sampler and learner policies. The exponent is efficiently found by one-dimensional bisection, while the resulting weights satisfy deterministic bounds on normalized-weight dispersion and weighted-gradient norm that are independent of policy drift, together with a fixed-$\alpha$ bound on bridge-target discrepancy. Power tempering also introduces no explicit zero-weight mask. On mathematical-reasoning benchmarks under high staleness, TETPO outperforms strong on- and off-policy baselines.
items.author: Shayan Mohajer Hamidi, Kayhan Behdin, Wenhui Zhu, Aida Rahmattalabi, Jincheng Cao, Jelena Markovic-Voronov, Alborz Geramifard
items.summary: TETPO addresses heavy-tailed importance weights in asynchronous off-policy RL post-training of LLMs, where a few stale-policy trajectories can collapse the effective sample size and destabilize gradient estimates. It adaptively tempers correction strength via bridge importance sampling to target a desired ESS, unlike fixed interventions that discard or reweight samples regardless of severity.
items.reasoning: Directly relevant to a practical pain point in asynchronous RLHF/RLVR pipelines at major labs; principled adaptive variance control with clear motivation, though empirical scale of validation appears moderate.

items.title: Vela: User Behavior as Supervision Sparks LLM Intelligence
items.content: arXiv:2610.14709v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in applications that act on users' long-term behavior histories, from personal assistants to recommendation and advertising systems. These applications demand the user dimension of LLM intelligence: inferring a person's preferences, intent, and likely future actions from weeks to years of behavior data. Yet current models are trained on static text or synthetic data, neither of which captures how user behavior evolves over time. Real-world behavior records, already available at scale on content platforms and in personal-assistant agents, offer a natural supervisory signal. We propose user behavior as supervision and introduce Vela, a framework that converts real user behavior data into trainable tasks and trajectories. From the anonymized behavior records of 100,000 users, Vela generates 100,000 tasks across 91 real-world task templates; difficulty-based filtering and trajectory acceptance criteria retain approximately 75,000 tasks with selected training trajectories. Fine-tuning Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on these trajectories improves performance over the base model by up to 11.5 points on user-related tasks and by an average of 4 points on general benchmarks. Training on more user behavior data further improves user-related performance, and reinforcement learning after fine-tuning outperforms reinforcement learning from the base model by up to 7.7 points. These gains suggest that real-world user behavior is a scalable source of supervision for both user-centered capabilities and the broader intelligence of LLMs.

items.title: Too Late to Prune: Generative AI, the Screen, and Team Creative Decisions
items.content: arXiv:2610.14984v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Generative AI makes options cheap and shifts the bottleneck of creative work from generating options to screening them. We argue that AI's value depends on whether its options arrive before or after the team's screen. In our model, early options compete for a place in the portfolio; late options arrive after that competition and are kept unscreened. In a preregistered experiment, we randomly assigned 148 three-person teams to five schedules of access to the same language model during a product-design task with timed search and selection stages. Moving the same 15 minutes of access from search to selection lowered expert-rated creativity by 0.62 standard deviations, although teams used the model at similar rates. Platform logs locate the difference at the screen. Early access enlarged the pool of ideas fivefold, and teams pruned it. Late-access teams reached the screen with the same small pool as teams without AI and then searched again, devoting 29% of their selection-stage queries to generating new options, compared with 11% for teams with access throughout. Late access added breadth, not quality: these teams submitted 73% more proposals than did teams without AI. Language-model judges detected the benefit of access but not the cost of late timing.
items.author: Difang Huang, Shumin Yu, Fadong Chen, Weihua Zhou
items.summary: Using a preregistered experiment with 148 three-person teams on a product-design task, the study shows that moving the same 15 minutes of LLM access from the search stage to the selection stage lowered expert-rated creativity by 0.62 standard deviations. The results support a model where AI options arriving before a team's screen add value while late options remain unscreened.
items.reasoning: Preregistered, controlled experimental design with a clear, quantified effect on human-AI creative collaboration; the timing-of-AI-access insight is actionable and methodologically stronger than most generative-AI workflow studies.

items.title: REPRO: Reflective Evolutionary Prompt Optimizer for Automated LLM Red-Teaming
items.content: arXiv:2610.15513v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to adversarial prompts that bypass their safety training. Existing automated red-teaming methods either require privileged access unavailable in production, rely on manually engineered per-model templates, or optimize a single objective without population-level diversity. We present REPRO (Reflective Evolutionary Prompt Optimization), a pure black-box framework that discovers adversarial prompts through evolutionary optimization driven entirely by a compressed open-weight 7B reflective model on a single consumer GPU. REPRO introduces two mechanisms absent from prior work, both isolated in a component ablation: semantic crossover, an LLM-guided multi-parent recombination operator, and Bayesian strategy selection via Thompson Sampling informed by structured failure analysis.   We catalog REPRO's behavior on AdvBench, JailbreakBench, and HarmBench across 36 target models from 11 families, including GPT-5-nano, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and Grok-4.1. Under our protocol REPRO reaches 100\% attack success rate (ASR) on every evaluated target in a single turn, at a median of 24 target queries per behavior. Two properties of the protocol qualify that figure. The judge scoring candidates during optimization also produces the reported ASR, and search halts when it accepts, so ASR reports whether search succeeded within the iteration budget rather than success at a fixed budget. All baseline figures are transcribed from their original papers, which use different judges, budgets, and model versions. We therefore present this as a catalog of model coverage under one protocol rather than a head-to-head ranking, and develop both qualifications in the paper.
items.author: Abrar Alotaibi, Moataz Ahmed
items.summary: REPRO is a pure black-box automated red-teaming framework that uses evolutionary optimization driven by a 7B open-weight reflective model on a single consumer GPU, introducing semantic crossover for multi-parent recombination. It targets adversarial prompt discovery against safety-aligned LLMs without privileged access or per-model templates.
items.reasoning: Practical, accessible red-teaming tooling with ablation-isolated novel components advances AI safety evaluation, and the black-box single-GPU constraint matches realistic attacker capability modeling. Dual-use concerns exist but red-teaming research is standard; novelty is moderate since evolutionary attack methods predate this, though the reflection-driven crossover is new.

Existing automated red-teaming methods either require privileged access unavailable in production, rely on manually engineered per-model templates, or optimize a single objective without population-level diversity. We present REPRO (Reflective Evolutionary Prompt Optimization), a pure black-box framework that discovers adversarial prompts through evolutionary optimization driven entirely by a compressed open-weight 7B reflective model on a single consumer GPU. REPRO introduces two mechanisms absent from prior work, both isolated in a component ablation: semantic crossover, an LLM-guided multi-parent recombination operator, and Bayesian strategy selection via Thompson Sampling informed by structured failure analysis. We catalog REPRO's behavior on AdvBench, JailbreakBench, and HarmBench across 36 target models from 11 families, including GPT-5-nano, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and Grok-4.1. Under our protocol REPRO reaches 100\% attack success rate (ASR) on every evaluated target in a single turn, at a median of 24 target queries per behavior. Two properties of the protocol qualify that figure. The judge scoring candidates during optimization also produces the reported ASR, and search halts when it accepts, so ASR reports whether search succeeded within the iteration budget rather than success at a fixed budget. All baseline figures are transcribed from their original papers, which use different judges, budgets, and model versions. We therefore present this as a catalog of model coverage under one protocol rather than a head-to-head ranking, and develop both qualifications in the paper.

items.title: Adaptive Look, Flexible Thought: Learning How and How Long to Think in Multimodal Reasoning
items.content: arXiv:2610.15810v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The introduction of long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning and external tools has substantially improved the performance of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on general and reasoning tasks. However, existing fast-slow reasoning paradigms mainly regulate textual reasoning length, while visual computation introduced by external tools or visual tokens is often treated as an auxiliary component. This separation prevents MLLMs from jointly optimizing visual perception and textual reasoning. To address this issue, we propose L2T (adaptive Look, flexible Thought), a unified reasoning framework that jointly optimizes the form and depth of computation. L2T first discretizes tool-produced visual states into visual tokens, bringing visual perception and textual reasoning into a shared autoregressive space. Based on this unified representation, L2T introduces a modality-aware routing reward to select appropriate reasoning modes and a difficulty-aware fast-slow strategy to adapt reasoning depth according to task complexity. Experiments on general perception and reasoning-intensive tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of L2T. Compared with explicit tool-calling approaches, L2T maintains competitive performance while achieving 1.7--3.6 times higher throughput.

items.title: A Scaled-Up Empirical Study of Syntactic Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.16837v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Syntactic language models (SLMs) that generate sentences along with their syntactic tree structures have shown promise in both syntactic generalization and downstream tasks. Prior studies, however, have mostly evaluated smaller models trained on less pretraining data and tested on narrower task suites. In addition, the design space of tree linearization and attention masks remains underexplored. We conduct a large-scale empirical study of 12 controlled configurations---one terminal baseline and 11 SLM variants spanning different linearizations and masks---at scales up to 1B parameters and 100B training tokens, evaluated across 11 downstream tasks and two syntactic benchmarks. The experimental results show that SLMs with standard causal attention match or exceed structural-mask variants across downstream and syntactic benchmarks. They require no architectural modifications and remain compatible with FlashAttention. We also observe that when scaling up to the 1B-parameter scale, the top-performing SLM variant no longer shows a clear advantage over a compute-matched non-structural baseline, suggesting that SLMs may become less competitive with scale. Our code is available at https://github.com/qlwpc/TG-Interpolation.
items.author: Pengcheng Wang, Zhexuan Zhang, Chao Lou, Kewei Tu
items.summary: This paper presents a large-scale controlled study of syntactic language models, comparing 12 configurations of tree linearization and attention masks at scales up to 1B parameters and 100B tokens, evaluated on 11 downstream tasks and two syntactic benchmarks. Results clarify whether the promise of SLMs on syntactic generalization holds at scale with standard causal attention.
items.reasoning: Valuable scaling study settling open questions about a research direction with claims that may not transfer to larger models; the controlled 12-configuration design and multi-task evaluation are methodologically strong. Findings inform architecture research but SLMs remain a niche direction.

items.title: D-World: An Explicit World-Language-Action Model with Recursive Self-Improvement under Dual Control
items.content: arXiv:2610.17114v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) now reason about space well enough to program robots, yet the world models behind robot policies are implicit, held in network weights or predicted video, and cannot be inspected or corrected directly. We present D-World, an explicit world-language-action model built on the Sense, Plan and Act decomposition. A perception agent writes the scene as an executable digital twin using generated vision and geometry code. A planning agent searches for actions in simulation and, after each executed action chunk, revises the twin's object states and named physical parameters against what the robot measured. A parameter revision is accepted only if replaying the latest chunk does not increase any measured residual beyond its tolerance, and every chunk is checked in the updated twin before it runs. Structural mismatches return to perception for reconstruction. We call this measurement-grounded cycle of correction and revision recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which the LLM stays frozen while the world it acts in improves. We model the choice of actions that both advance the task and expose model error as a dual control problem and show that the cost of incorporating evidence into the twin sets the threshold at which probing pays, so cheap local revision counteracts the turn-off of cautious controllers. Each episode runs a real-to-sim-to-real loop, and its recorded twins can be refitted and re-rendered offline into higher-fidelity environments for post-training. Because perception and planning communicate only through the twin and language, either can be replaced by a learned model, and since inference dominates the loop, the loop speeds up with faster models. On a dual-arm robot, towel and toaster tasks show local revisions, such as one reducing the bread's rendered-depth residual from 22.4 to 1.5 mm, that let execution continue without reconstruction.

This makes the robot's world model inspectable and correctable, unlike implicit weight-based or video-predicted models.

items.title: Agentic-MatriBO: Capability-Compiled Agentic Bayesian Optimization for Materials and Chemical Design
items.content: arXiv:2610.17832v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Materials and chemical optimization must choose the next synthesis, characterization, or high-fidelity simulation from sequential observations under a limited budget. Large language models can use task knowledge to propose adjustments, but composing surrogates, acquisition functions, and search strategies is constrained by compatibility, parameter dependencies, and evidence requirements. We present Agentic-MatriBO, a capability-compiled agentic Bayesian optimization (BO) framework that represents BO components and selection conditions as composable capabilities. A language policy proposes BO recipes and candidate plans; a compiler checks proposals against the registered capability catalog; and a deterministic execution layer validates and commits candidates. Oracle observations are stored in research memory and inform later rounds. We compare Agentic-MatriBO with eight baselines on four offline finite candidate pools---COF, PCE10, Buchwald--Hartwig (BH), and Suzuki--Miyaura---using five seeds per condition; results are reported descriptively. Across the four tasks, Agentic-MatriBO has the best mean endpoint quality after orienting each objective so that higher is better. On COF, it reaches the tabulated optimum in all five seeds both in the end-to-end comparison and after shared initialization, where it also retains an advantage in cumulative quality. Its normalized area under the best-so-far quality curve during the BO stage (nAUC-BO) is substantially higher on COF, near parity with the best baseline on PCE10 and BH, and lower on Suzuki. COF ablations show that removing the capability compiler or evidence gate coincides with lower cumulative quality and fewer exact-optimum hits. The framework provides an inspectable interface for evidence-conditioned BO adaptation.

items.summary: Agentic-MatriBO composes Bayesian optimization components (surrogates, acquisition functions, search strategies) as registered capabilities that an LLM policy proposes and a compiler validates against the catalog, with deterministic execution. This enables reliable agentic orchestration of materials and chemical design under experiment budgets.
items.reasoning: The capability-compilation idea directly addresses the reliability gap in LLM-agent-driven scientific workflows by separating LLM proposal from validated execution. Score reflects a promising architecture for AI-for-science with moderate novelty over prior agentic-BO combinations.

items.title: Does self-distillation improve reasoning?
items.content: arXiv:2610.18613v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Self-distillation is an emerging approach that trains a model to imitate its own predictions when conditioned on privileged information, such as correct answers or environmental feedback. Recent methods have reported better sample efficiency and generalization than reinforcement learning (RL), but it remains unclear whether these gains extend beyond in-distribution evaluations and whether they stem from privileged distillation. In this paper, we revisit two representative methods, Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) and On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), across code, science, tool use, and math reasoning tasks. We find that their reported gains do not consistently generalize to unseen problems and are largely explained by overfitting or transferring existing reasoning behavior, rather than effectively using privileged information. Moreover, self-distillation gradients show weak alignment with policy gradients that directly optimize expected reward, questioning whether they provide an effective direction for policy improvement. Our experiments across Qwen3 models (1.7B-14B) and OLMo-3-7B suggest that effectively leveraging privileged information to improve reasoning remains an open challenge. Our code is available at https://github.com/sleepypandu/does-sd-improve-reasoning
items.author: Jason Ken Adhinarta, Raina Wu, Ashutosh Sharma, Avinash Balakrishnan, Rameswar Panda, Polina Golland, Yoon Kim, Zhang-Wei Hong
items.summary: The authors revisit self-distillation methods (SDPO and OPSD) for reasoning, finding that reported gains over RL do not consistently generalize to unseen problems and are largely explained by overfitting to privileged-conditioning artifacts. This is a careful reproducibility-style audit across code, science, tool use, and math tasks. It tempers enthusiasm for self-distillation as an RL alternative.

items.title: Loss Curvature as a Sampling-Free Proxy for Memorization in Diffusion Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.19042v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Understanding the mechanism behind why diffusion models memorize their training data remains an open question in generative modeling. In this paper, we examine this question from two perspectives: (a) the model-level perspective concerning the onset of memorization in a model during training, and (b) the sample-level perspective concerning the proclivity of an individual sample to be memorized by a given model. We show that the so-called input loss curvature, or the Frobenius norm of the Hessian of the diffusion model's training loss, is an effective metric for quantifying both perspectives on memorization. In particular, we empirically demonstrate that input curvatures averaged across training and validation samples can identify when a model is likely to start regurgitating its training data when tracked over training time. However, this metric is not sufficient for measuring an individual sample's likelihood of being memorized. To address this perspective, we introduce a counterfactual definition of memorization in diffusion models, extending the analogous notion from supervised learning proposed by [Feldman, 2019]. We prove that this counterfactual memorization is controlled by the input curvature of the leave-one-out model, thus establishing a direct theoretical link between a sample's local loss landscape and its generation likelihood. We validate our derived bounds through several empirical experiments and show that input-dependent curvature provides a proxy for memorization.

items.summary: This paper shows that the Frobenius norm of the Hessian of a diffusion model's training loss quantifies memorization at both model level (onset during training) and sample level (per-sample proclivity). Empirically, input loss curvatures can identify memorization onset without sampling, providing a practical diagnostic for a key generative-model risk.
items.reasoning: Addresses the important problem of training-data memorization in diffusion models with an actionable, sampling-free metric spanning two levels of analysis. The finding is empirically grounded and relevant to both generative modeling science and privacy/safety, though theoretical grounding is primarily empirical.

items.title: DTDD: Divergence-Triggered Dynamic Distillation for Reliable On-Policy Supervision
items.content: arXiv:2610.19302v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision on student rollouts, but this supervision can become unreliable when the student and teacher diverge, either because of a large initial policy gap or compounding errors in long-horizon reasoning and tool use. We introduce Divergence-Triggered Dynamic Distillation (DTDD), an adaptive OPD framework that uses segment-level student-teacher divergence to trigger teacher takeover during training. When divergence triggers an intervention during reasoning, the student prefix continues to receive standard OPD supervision. The teacher then generates a recovery suffix, which the student learns through behavior cloning, using cross-entropy on the teacher-generated tokens. We evaluate DTDD in three regimes: long-horizon reasoning, distillation from a base initialization without offline supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and multi-turn agents. We also compare alternative trigger designs and teacher-intervention rates. DTDD reduces the post-warmup peak gradient norm by $8.6\times$ and, from a base initialization, reaches $21.3\%$ held-out math accuracy in $2.6\times$ fewer optimizer updates than OPD; both methods finish near $22\%$. It improves best-observed performance by $4.8$ and $4.1$ percentage points on ALFWorld with LoRA and agentic code, respectively. Ablations show that segment-averaged triggers outperform token-spike triggers. Behavior cloning is also more effective than the tested OPD surrogate for training teacher-generated recoveries. Across 23 experimental arms, takeover tends to help when the teacher substantially outperforms the OPD-trained student, provided that the teacher can recover from student-visited states, the student can learn those recoveries, and teacher intervention is neither excessive nor insufficient.

items.title: RA$^2$: Retain-Anchored Attraction Preserves Forget-Adjacent Utility in LLM Unlearning
items.content: arXiv:2610.19385v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) unlearning is often evaluated primarily by target suppression and clean retain utility. These metrics can miss a local failure mode: a model may perform well on standard retain prompts, yet degrade on benign reasoning when prompts lie near the forgotten domain. This phenomenon is termed forget-adjacent utility loss. A fundamental question is: where should forget representations go after they leave the removed behavior? Successful unlearning depends not only on whether forget-conditioned representations depart from the harmful computation, but also on the direction in which they are redirected afterward. We propose RA$^2$ (Retain-Anchored Attraction), a latent-space unlearning method that redirects forget-token states toward nearby retain-supported representations while preserving higher-layer behavior on retain data. On WMDP and MUSE, RA$^2$ yields higher forget-adjacent utility than strong unlearning baselines at similar broad-utility levels. These results show that the migration direction of forget representations materially affects benign behavior near the forget boundary. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZacLing/retain_anchored_attraction.

items.summary: The paper identifies forget-adjacent utility loss in LLM unlearning, where models degrade on benign prompts near the forgotten domain despite good standard retain metrics, and argues that the redirection direction of forget representations matters. RA2 redirects forget-token states toward retain anchors in latent space, preserving utility in forget-adjacent regions. This addresses a genuine blind spot in unlearning evaluation and methods.

items.title: From Global to Tail Convergence: Dynamics of $\alpha$-Stable Score-Based Generative Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.19773v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Score-based generative models driven by $\alpha$-stable L{\'e}vy processes have been proposed as an alternative to Brownian diffusion models, with empirical evidence suggesting improved sampling and better modeling of heavy-tailed data. Yet theoretical guarantees for these models remain limited. We develop a non-asymptotic convergence analysis for scale-preserving $\alpha$-stable generative dynamics, covering both compactly supported and power-law targets. In p-Wasserstein distance, we quantify the effects of early stopping, initialization, score approximation, and time discretization, and show exponential decay of the initialization error. A comparison with Brownian dynamics reveals that global Wasserstein convergence alone does not fundamentally distinguish the two models: both initialization errors decay exponentially with the forward horizon on the common class of heavy-tailed targets. A sharp separation emerges instead in the tails. At any positive generation time, stable dynamics produces power-law tails with index $\alpha$, whereas Brownian dynamics remains light-tailed. For a target with tail index $\nu$, asymptotically correct extreme-quantile scaling is possible precisely when $\alpha$=$\nu$. These results identify tail-index matching as a principled mechanism behind the ability of stable generative models to capture extreme events.

items.title: MorphingNet: Symbolic Regression Where the Network Is the Formula
items.content: arXiv:2610.19942v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We introduce MorphingNet, a network for symbolic regression (SR) whose units change their function continuously. Instead of searching over expressions built from a fixed operator library, MorphingNet trains the form of each function as a parameter, so SR becomes one continuous optimization problem. Its units are either pole-free rational functions or complex exponential--logarithm functions, which move between exponentials, sinusoids, damped oscillations, power laws and logarithms as their parameters change. The network is a readable formula at every step of training, and no operator library is needed to train it; a structure-recovery step afterwards rewrites the trained formula into short elementary expressions. Training is dense linear algebra, so it is GPU-friendly and scales to large data. MorphingNet achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on SRBench, recovers most generating formulas on synthetic benchmarks, and on large data is up to two orders of magnitude faster than the strongest search method. By turning the search for a formula into the training of a network, MorphingNet offers a new paradigm for SR and for scientific discovery from data.

items.title: Decoupled Marginal Sharpening for Training-Free Inference-Time Scaling
items.content: arXiv:2610.20483v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We study how to improve LLM reasoning at inference time without updating model weights or using external reward models. Recent reward-free power-sampling methods define the sequence-level power target $\pi_\alpha(y\mid x)\propto p_0(y\mid x)^\alpha$, where $\alpha>1$, which increases the relative probability of completions that are already likely under the base model. Existing methods use Metropolis--Hastings or Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) to approximately sample from this target. However, two challenges arise at different levels. At the target level, full-sequence sharpening can concentrate probability on a few exact reasoning--answer trajectories, suppressing alternative paths that support the same answer. At the sampler level, finite-particle SMC can suffer from path collapse when resampling repeatedly duplicates a few high-weight prefixes. To address these challenges, we propose Decoupled Marginal Sharpening (DMS), which separately controls how strongly the model favors particular reasoning paths and how strongly it favors final answers after aggregating support across those paths. At the target level, DMS first samples from a sharpened reasoning distribution, then marginalizes the model's answer probabilities over the resulting weighted reasoning population and sharpens the induced answer marginal. Separate exponents allow mild reasoning sharpening to encourage exploration of diverse paths, followed by stronger answer-marginal sharpening to concentrate probability on answers with greater aggregate support across those paths. At the sampler level, we develop Fully Adapted Annealed SMC, which combines an annealed sequence of power targets with locally fully adapted proposals and predictive ancestor resampling. Experiments on MATH500, GPQA-Diamond, HumanEval, and AIME24/25 across three base models show that DMS achieves the highest mean pass@1 among the compared methods in all tasks.

items.summary: The paper improves training-free LLM inference-time scaling by fixing two failure modes of reward-free power-sampling: full-sequence sharpening over-concentrates on exact reasoning trajectories suppressing alternative valid paths, and finite-parallelism samplers underperform. Decoupled marginal sharpening targets marginals rather than full sequences to preserve answer-diverse reasoning paths. This matters because inference-time compute scaling without reward models or weight updates is a fast-growing deployment strategy.

items.title: Beyond Equation Search: Conjecture-Guided Discovery with SCOPE and ClosureBench
items.content: arXiv:2610.18938v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Most symbolic regression methods optimize candidate equations, but improving an equation's fit does not establish whether its underlying scientific conjecture should be retained, revised, or rejected. A conjecture may admit multiple mathematical realizations, and similarly accurate equations may imply different explanations. This motivates a shift from refining individual expressions to developing and testing the conjectures that guide them. We introduce SCOPE, a framework that sustains multiple conjecture-driven research trajectories. Multiple scientist agents independently pursue conjectures through equation modeling, question formulation, and active experimentation, then exchange evidence to revise their conjectures and research directions. Their findings are consolidated into a scientific report linking models, conclusions, and evidence. Existing equation-discovery benchmarks primarily assess recovered expressions, leaving the evidence and scientific conclusions established through the investigation underexamined. We therefore introduce ClosureBench, an interactive benchmark of 60 closure-discovery tasks across five scientific domains. ClosureBench focuses on closure-discovery tasks to give equation discovery a concrete scientific purpose. Each task embeds an unknown algebraic relation in a known PDE system, where agents control experimental conditions in OpenFOAM to acquire new data for equation discovery. Beyond equation accuracy, ClosureBench proposes three metrics to evaluate the discovery process: evidence faithfulness, mechanism insight, and experimental effectiveness. Compared with diverse baselines, SCOPE achieves higher equation accuracy on both ClosureBench and a real-world scientific discovery case, while producing more accurate, reliable, and effective scientific discoveries.

Positions AI-driven discovery at the level of scientific hypotheses rather than curve fits.

items.title: ReproBAIT: Can coding agents build their own biological AI tools?
items.content: arXiv:2610.19810v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large language models are increasingly competent at leveraging scientific knowledge and existing computational tools to execute complex workflows. At present, little information exists on their ability to reconstruct tools when given limited descriptions of such tools. We introduce an evaluation titled ReproBAIT (Reproducing Biological AI Tools), which measures the ability of coding agents to design, implement, and train biological AI tools taken from published research across a range of information access conditions. The coding agent is securely sandboxed without internet access and receives training data, a fixed time and compute budget, and limited information about the tool to replicate. We then score the reproduced biological AI tool based on its performance (tool-specific metrics) on held-out data. We evaluated a set of biological AI tools of varying complexities: ProteinMPNN, an inverse protein folding tool, RFdiffusion3, an all-atom generative diffusion tool, and a closed-source molecular design tool. We institute a methodology to check for memorisation, as the open source tools are likely to be included in models' pretraining corpus. Across a range of leading closed- and open-source coding agents, we find substantial reproduction capability for some selected tools, though limited capability for a highly complex tool. We find moderate evidence consistent with memorisation, varying across coding agents. These results suggest that tool developers need to be increasingly cautious when releasing information about the tools publicly; re-creation of the tool based on such information could undermine a tool's commercial value or invalidate dual-use managed access strategies.

items.title: DUALVIEW: Leveraging Broad and Output-Specific Evidence for LLM-based Multi-Output Text Regression
items.content: arXiv:2610.19206v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: While work on LLM-based regression has largely focused on scalar prediction, multi-output text regression remains less explored. We present DualView, a parameter-efficient approach to leverage LLMs for multi-output text regression. \method{} first extracts broad and output-specific representations from a frozen LLM, then uses a dual-branch architecture to produce the full score vector. Across five heterogeneous regression tasks and eight LLMs (up to 122B), DualView outperforms seven supervised regression baselines while requiring 82--1842 times fewer fitted parameters than the three strongest baselines. These improvements extend across individual output dimensions and persist even with limited training data. Notably, DualView using a smaller open-weight LLM can outperform unsupervised prediction with Gemini 3.1 Pro. Controlled ablations show that broad and output-specific evidence provide complementary predictive benefits, while lightweight shared predictors achieve strong performance with fewer trainable parameters.

It opens up an underexplored regression setting for LLMs.

items.title: Model vs. User: Whose Values Prevail? Inference-Time Value Alignment in Multi-Turn Conversations
items.content: arXiv:2610.19817v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Human values shape how we expect language models to behave. Dominant alignment approaches treat values as global objectives, although the appropriate value orientation is personal and contextual. Training-free alignment can steer models toward target values at inference time, yet has been largely evaluated in single-turn settings and with a single steering direction (e.g., toward safety). We evaluate four prompt- and activation-based steering methods in multi-turn conversations, where user and assistant models push toward the same or opposing, equally desirable values. We track alignment with a linear probe across three models and two value trade-offs. When assistant and user pull in opposite directions, the side matching the assistant's baseline bias often prevails, and effects that look successful early often fade or reverse after a few turns. Steering should therefore be evaluated over full conversations and in both directions of a value trade-off.

When values conflict, the side matching the assistant's baseline orientation tends to prevail, revealing limits of inference-time value steering.

items.title: Why Generate a Click? Plug-in Decision Heads for Web Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.20107v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Web agents built on vision language models decide every action by generating text such as click(12), although most of that text encodes a choice among a few action types and a few dozen marked elements. We read these choices directly from the hidden states that the generator computes while it reads the goal and the screenshot. Plug-in decision heads on a frozen generator predict the action type, pool the visual tokens inside each numbered box to pick the target, and point at a listed text option or at a WRITE slot that leaves the writing of new text to the generator. A confidence cascade executes the heads' action when they are sure and otherwise lets the generator decode from the KV cache of the same forward pass. With Qwen3-VL 4B and 8B generators trained on 213k web steps, a strict threshold keeps the cascade between 0.3 points below and 1.4 points above the generator on seven offline test sets while the heads decide 12 to 64% of the steps. A looser threshold raises step success on unseen Mind2Web websites by 3.1 and 1.8 points, costs up to 2 points on GUIAct and MiniWoB++, and lifts WebArena task success from 12.5 to 13.8% (4B) and from 13.6 to 14.6% (8B) with less than half of the generated tokens. Training the heads jointly with the generator lowers the generator's own step success by up to 4.9 points; heads on a frozen generator avoid this cost.

Tested with Qwen3-VL 4B and 8B generators, the approach reuses a single forward pass and its KV cache.

items.title: What Does LALM Post-training Learn? Rethinking Audio Understanding and Reasoning Capabilities
items.content: arXiv:2610.19476v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Post-training often improves the performance of large audio-language models on audio understanding and reasoning benchmarks. However, these improvements may reflect adaptation to specific question formats, such as multiple-choice questions, rather than genuine advances in audio understanding and reasoning capabilities. To investigate what LALMs actually learn from post-training, we conduct controlled experiments that disentangle improvements in audio understanding from adaptation to specific question formats. Across different models and post-training methods, we find that much of the reported improvement persists even without informative audio, but largely disappears when the question format changes. These findings suggest that post-training often teaches models to exploit task-specific textual cues and answer patterns rather than developing generalizable audio understanding and reasoning capabilities.

This suggests post-training gains often reflect multiple-choice format fitting rather than real capability advances.

items.title: Kandinsky S2V 1.0: Audio-Driven Avatar Video Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.19290v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We present Kandinsky S2V 1.0, an open family of speech-to-video models for controllable audio-driven human animation, comprising Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Lite (2B parameters) and Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro (21B parameters). From a single reference image, a speech waveform, and a text prompt, the models generate long-form 25 FPS video in which lip motion, expression, pose, and gesture follow the speech. The architecture draws text and audio conditioning from one Qwen2.5-Omni model and adds a reference-aware three-scale visual memory. Training starts from the Kandinsky 5.0 Video foundation models [1] and combines mixed reference-memory layouts with an area-adaptive face loss. The training corpus contains 1.17M single-speaker clips selected by active-speaker detection, with captions generated directly in English and Russian. A side-by-side human evaluation against the strongest open-source baseline and two proprietary commercial models shows that Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro performs comparably to or better than these models on average and is also preferred for lip synchronization. On common speech to video benchmarks, Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Lite and Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro rank among the top performing models according to mean rank over five reported metrics. Beyond the base models, we provide {\pi}-Flow distilled variants of both Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Lite and Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro. The distilled Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro model generates video in 16 sampling steps without classifier-free guidance, achieving a 5.4 times end-to-end speedup over the base model, while matching or exceeding it on nearly all reported benchmark metrics. items.title: GeoCloak: An Agentic Framework for Semantics-Preserving Geolocation Privacy via Peripheral Clue Manipulation
items.content: arXiv:2610.20055v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The rapid advancement of large vision language models (LVLMs) has made geolocation inference from images highly accurate and accessible. This poses serious privacy risks: a passive adversary with black-box LVLM access can infer a user's location from a single photo with no metadata. Existing protection methods rely almost exclusively on adversarial perturbation, which introduces perceptible visual artifacts and utility degradation. We identify the visual-geolocation asymmetry: geolocation-decisive clues, such as street signs, tend to be visually peripheral but dominate location inference. Exploiting this asymmetry, we propose GeoCloak, an agentic framework for semantics-preserving geolocation privacy protection. It acts as a clue-aware planner that analyzes each image to identify geolocation-relevant clues, dispatches targeted semantic edits to directly suppress peripheral clues, and autonomously configures adversarial perturbation to further suppress residual geolocation features, all under iterative utility-aware feedback. We evaluate GeoCloak on four diverse datasets spanning 108 countries and 576 cities against five LVLMs and three inference methods. GeoCloak reduces overall city-level accuracy from 41.2% to 9.9%, approximately half of the best-performing baseline, while achieving substantially superior utility preservation both qualitatively and quantitatively. We hope this work takes a meaningful step toward practical, semantics-preserving geolocation privacy protection, giving users greater control over the location information inadvertently embedded in their shared images.

items.title: Quantifying privacy risks in foundation model representations of brain MRI
items.content: arXiv:2610.20494v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Pretrained representations are increasingly used to share and reuse information from medical images without exposing the original scans, but it is unclear how much patient-specific information these representations retain. We investigate this question for brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) by evaluating five frozen pretrained encoders spanning different architectures, pretraining objectives, and training domains on two longitudinal T1-weighted datasets, OASIS-2 and MIRIAD. Under an attacker model with access to released embeddings, the corresponding public encoder, and auxiliary MRI scans, we evaluate patient linkage and sensitive-attribute inference. Across the evaluated representations, we observe substantial subject-specific information: rank-1 patient linkage reaches up to 99\% on MIRIAD and exceeds 90\% on OASIS-2 for the highest-risk representation, despite the absence of an identification objective during encoder training. We further show that the released embeddings retain information about a demographic attribute, with recorded-sex prediction reaching balanced accuracy of 90.9\% on OASIS-2 and 95.5\% on MIRIAD. Overall, our results demonstrate that replacing raw brain MRI with learned embeddings does not, by itself, eliminate patient-linkage or attribute-inference risk, and is therefore insufficient on its own to establish anonymity.

items.title: ForceBench: Benchmarking Force Integration for Robotic Manipulation
items.content: arXiv:2610.19604v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Force feedback provides vision-language-action (VLA) policies with physical observations that can guide action selection and execution. However, differences in tasks, demonstrations, and control settings across existing systems hinder reliable comparisons of force integration designs. We introduce ForceBench, a simulation benchmark for evaluating six-axis wrist-force integration under a unified protocol. ForceBench combines eight tasks spanning physical-property inference, resistance-dependent interaction, and contact-rich assembly with 1,600 synchronized demonstrations and task-specific success criteria. We compare one no-force baseline and six force integration designs on a shared $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone. Prompt Fusion achieves the highest observed mean simulation success of 35.31%, compared with 23.25% for the baseline, and improves success rates across all three task categories. Predictive and temporal gains in simulation concentrate on physical-property inference, while both temporal designs underperform the baseline on assembly. Real-world evaluation of eight systems across five tasks supports the main qualitative trends: Prompt Fusion and Dual-Path Fusion achieve 63.00% mean success, compared with 40.00% for the baseline, but only Prompt Fusion improves every task. These findings support ForceBench's practical value for identifying the benefits and limitations of force integration across manipulation demands. The project page is available at https://forcebench-platform.github.io/.

items.title: KinoGen: Customizable Humanoid Loco-Manipulation References via Kinematically Grounded Video Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.20552v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We present KinoGen, a framework that synthesizes customizable humanoid loco-manipulation references through kinematically grounded video generation. KinoGen conditions a pretrained video generator on calibrated renders of the target robot and object in a simulated task instance and recovers the reference by fitting the same models to the generated two-view video, so that the reference lies in the robot configuration space by construction without a human body proxy or retargeting. Body, hand, and object priors initialize the reconstruction, and direct optimization against cross-view evidence refines it. Since an edited keyframe is simply another rendered state, a user can prescribe a goal object pose, regenerate the video around the edited keyframe, and obtain a reference that satisfies the pose exactly. Across eight loco-manipulation tasks, KinoGen yields lower penetration and foot skating than video-based baselines and preserves over 90% of annotated contacts, and its customized references satisfy every prescribed target with substantially less penetration than direct interpolation. Tracking policies trained on the synthesized references are deployed on a Unitree G1 humanoid with dexterous hands. Project webpage: https://kinogen-humanoid.github.io/.

items.title: Should SLMs be in the Driver's Seat? A Study of Local Models as Interpreters in Cloud-Written Agent Programs
items.content: arXiv:2610.14209v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The most accurate agents executing user-provided tasks are driven by large, cloud-hosted models, which solve them by reading the private data of the user. Agents powered by models small enough to run on edge devices keep that data local, but yield far worse results. A third option is to have cloud models write a program that devices execute: the data stays local, but as the program is written before any data is seen, it fails whenever a step depends on interpreting content that appears only at run time. We explore an intermediate architecture, in which the cloud-written program defers bounded questions over user data to a small local model through an ordinary function call. On AppWorld this improves the success rate of a code-only agent in all six combinations of backbone model and test partition we evaluate, by up to 14.9pp, recovering a substantial part of the gap to a cloud-hosted ReAct loop while keeping user data on the device.

items.summary: The paper explores a hybrid agent architecture where a cloud model writes a program that defers bounded runtime questions about private user data to a small local model via function calls. This keeps data local while improving success rates of code-only agents on AppWorld compared to pure program execution.
items.reasoning: Practical privacy-preserving architecture with empirical gains on a recognized benchmark; the idea is a sensible intermediate point rather than a breakthrough, but it addresses a real deployment trade-off between capability and privacy.
