items.title: MAGNET: Manifold-Aware Graph Diffusion Network for Connectome Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.17014v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Functional brain connectome represents neural connectivity as a matrix of pairwise interactions between brain regions. Generation of functional connectomes is not only a question of validity; rather, having satisfied the constraints on the correlation matrix, the next step is to recover the class-conditional geometry buried under coarse labels. We propose MAGNET, a Manifold-Aware Graph Diffusion Network which uses a normalized-Cholesky representation of the manifold of correlation matrices that guarantees validity. MAGNET lifts noisy latent states into ROI-level region tokens and performs denoising with a relational inductive bias over brain atlas regions. To deal with structural problems induced by coarse labels, MAGNET employs class-anchored conditioning, amortized structural bridge, and relevance-preserving corruption. Across ABIDE, ADNI, and OASIS-3, MAGNET consistently achieves favorable results compared to previous manifold-aware approaches, demonstrating improvements of 7-21% in class-conditional fidelity ($\alpha,\beta$-F1) across three cohorts and better sampling efficiency. Moreover, while training only with strict binary labels, MAGNET is capable of maintaining clinical heterogeneity through fine substructure of the connectomes in a zero-shot setting, improving subclass covariance alignment ($\lambda$-MSE) by over 30%. These results suggest that geometric validity is a necessary but insufficient condition for clinical utility in connectome synthesis. Moreover, efforts in making the diffusion denoising class-conditional manifold aware finds utility beyond the highly curved brain connectome generation as this is a critical problem in various general settings. The code repository can be found at https://github.com/protyayofficial/MAGNET.

items.title: Dissociating Answerability from Extraction in LLM Question Answering over Radiology Reports
items.content: arXiv:2610.17576v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Answering questions from radiology reports involves two decisions: whether the report contains an answer and which span gives it. A false answer presents an unsupported claim as fact; an over-abstention hides what the report says. Yet RadQA results are reported as a single F1 that merges both. We propose an evaluation method that separates them, reporting false-answer and over-abstention rates beside F1 and splitting F1 changes into extraction and answerability terms. We apply it to 13 LLMs on the RadQA test set, zero-shot and with three cumulative demonstration sets, the last adding an unanswerable example. Models with similar F1 differed more than twofold in false-answer rate. The unanswerable example changed when models answered, not how well they extracted: 12 of 13 models abstained more often, and three-quarters of the answers they withdrew had F1 $\geq$ 0.5. Within models, false answers showed no clear association with extraction quality, but acting on the decision itself helped: keeping an answer only when enough other models also answered lowered the zero-shot false-answer rate by 4 points without a detectable F1 change. Because the two decisions can change independently, we suggest radiology QA evaluations report them separately, not through F1 alone.

Applying it to 13 LLMs shows that models with similar F1 differ more than twofold in false-answer rates, and that adding an unanswerable demonstration changes when models answer rather than how well they extract.
items.reasoning: The evaluation-methodology contribution is clean and clinically important, since conflating unsupported claims with extraction errors obscures safety-relevant failure modes. The finding that demonstrations shift answerability thresholds rather than extraction quality is useful, though the scope is one benchmark and task type.

items.title: Dynamic K-Head: Difficulty-Supervised Budget Selection for Continuous Latent Reasoning
items.content: arXiv:2610.17679v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) improves reasoning but incurs substantial autoregressive rationale cost. Continuous CoT moves intermediate computation into recurrent hidden states, yet typically uses a fixed number of updates even though the best budget varies across questions and accuracy need not improve monotonically with $K$. We introduce Dynamic K-Head, a question-conditioned, pre-rollout budget selector. It is jointly trained with the reasoner under selected budgets, using difficulty supervision based on scores assigned from the question alone. We also show that latent-update count can misrepresent end-to-end cost because a short latent rollout can shift computation into a longer explicit continuation. We therefore count latent updates, implementation-specific special tokens, and all decoded text. Instantiated with CoDI on Llama 3.2 1B and GSM8K, Dynamic K-Head reaches 54.44% exact-match accuracy at 12.03 average reasoning/output tokens, compared with 52.31% at 15.21 tokens for fixed-$K=6$ CoDI---a 2.12-point gain with 20.9% lower token cost. Across three out-of-distribution arithmetic datasets, it reduces cost by 19.3--25.7% while improving accuracy by 0.30--2.22 points. These results demonstrate that difficulty-supervised budget selection can improve both accuracy and efficiency, while stable budget selection remains a central challenge.
items.author: Ying Li, Yuqi Chen, Sixuan Li, Yunfeng Cai
items.summary: Dynamic K-Head introduces a question-conditioned, pre-rollout selector for the number of latent reasoning updates in continuous chain-of-thought, jointly trained with the reasoner using difficulty supervision from question-only scores. It also highlights that latent-update counts can misrepresent end-to-end cost when short latent rollouts shift computation into longer explicit continuations.
items.reasoning: Adaptive compute allocation for latent reasoning is a current and relevant direction, and the observation about misleading end-to-end cost accounting adds analytical depth. The setting (continuous CoT) is still niche, and the approach is a targeted efficiency mechanism rather than a broad advance.

items.title: LoOPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation with Looped Teachers
items.content: arXiv:2610.18162v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: On-policy self-distillation improves a model using guidance from the model itself, but it still requires a teacher that provides more useful predictions than the student. Existing approaches obtain such guidance by giving the teacher additional context or instructions. We ask whether it can instead come from changing how the same model uses its own layers. To address this, we introduce LoOPSD, which searches over a model's layer execution order to construct a stronger teacher and distills its advantage into the student. Specifically, we keep the model weights unchanged while searching for layers to repeat, and use the resulting teacher's predictions on student-generated prefixes to guide learning. We then alternate search and distillation, rebuilding the teacher from the updated student in each round so that the student progressively absorbs the gains from alternative layer execution. Experiments on mathematical and logical reasoning tasks show improvements across models. On GSM8K with a 400-token thinking budget, LoOPSD raises Qwen3-1.7B accuracy from 42.30% to 79.61%; subsequent distillation rounds yield further gains beyond the first round. Together, these findings show that by searching layer execution to construct teachers, we can turn a model's additional computation into improved student capabilities, opening a new avenue for self-distillation to derive supervision from the model's own computation.
items.author: Wei Fan, Qingyue Yang, Chao-Hong Tan, Qian Chen, Wen Wang, Xiangang Li, Kejiang Chen, Weiming Zhang, Nenghai Yu
items.summary: LoOPSD explores whether self-distillation guidance can come from changing how a model uses its own layers rather than from extra context: it searches over layer execution orders (repeating layers with weights frozen) to construct a stronger teacher, then distills its predictions on student-generated prefixes. Search and distillation alternate iteratively. This is a novel take on self-improvement exploiting looped/adaptive computation.
items.reasoning: Creative mechanism combining layer-looping with on-policy self-distillation, offering a fresh angle on self-improvement without external teachers. Novelty is real but the approach is computationally indirect and results in the abstract are limited to initial evidence.

items.title: Graph-free Retrieval with Graph-Modified Embeddings
items.content: arXiv:2610.18410v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Dense vector retrieval can miss evidence connected through intermediate entities, while direct graph retrieval requires access to the graph at query time. We compare five offline graph-based embedding transformations and strategies for using the resulting graph-modified embeddings alongside the originals, without query-time graph access. On a synthetic professional-network benchmark with complete supporting-evidence sets, direct replacement of the original embeddings reduces evidence recovery. Multi-stage strategies improve recovery by using graph-modified embeddings to guide the search while retaining the originals for semantic relevance. On questions requiring linked facts or comparisons among candidates, the strongest configuration improves recovery by up to 25.9% relative to plain vector retrieval. It also matches baseline recovery with 40% fewer returned nodes. Controls confirm that graph information contributes beyond multi-stage retrieval alone. Across the tested methods, retrieval performance depends more on how graph-modified embeddings are used than on how they are produced.

A multi-stage strategy that uses graph-modified embeddings to guide search while retaining originals improves evidence recovery, notably on linked-fact and comparison questions.
items.reasoning: Practical contribution to the hot RAG area, offering a middle ground between pure dense retrieval and query-time graph traversal, with a careful comparative design. Synthetic benchmark limits ecological validity and gains are configuration-dependent.

items.title: Knowledge Graphs as Files: An Agent Harness Where Tool Creation and Tool Use Co-Evolve
items.content: arXiv:2610.18616v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Searching text-rich knowledge graphs requires following relations while examining textual evidence. Predefined graph interfaces constrain what evidence agents can access, even when they write code to combine tool calls or process retrieved subgraphs. We propose direct knowledge graph interaction (DKGI), a harness in which language model agents create graph access tools directly over complete node and edge files. The agent writes Python code to follow relations, combine node sets, and select textual evidence, interleaving execution with shell search and file inspection. This lets agents process large node sets in bulk while returning selected text for the model to assess. Execution feedback guides tool creation and revision, while the evolving tools determine what evidence the agent gathers next. On benchmark datasets spanning three domains, training-free DKGI exceeds the strongest published baseline by at least 6.7 Hit@1 points on every graph, even with a minimal harness. Controlled ablations show the benefits of multi-turn programming over shell-only access and predefined graph tools, while trajectories show agents revising code to extend searches or address errors. These findings highlight the value of allowing tool creation and tool use to co-evolve during graph search. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/leopoldwhite/DKGI.

This bypasses restrictive predefined graph interfaces and enables bulk processing of large node sets. It improves how agents access text-rich knowledge graphs.

items.title: IR-PRM+ with Previous-Utility Prediction: Constant Regret and Best-Iterate Convergence
items.content: arXiv:2610.19016v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Regret matching (and its variants) and counterfactual regret minimization are central algorithms in practice for normal-form and extensive-form game solving. Yet these have historically lacked the stronger theoretical convergence guarantees available to optimistic and extra-gradient methods. Recent work introduced IREG-PRM+, a regret matching variant which does have strong theoretical convergence guarantees. However, it relies on a simultaneous, extra-gradient update. IREG-PRM+ is an instance of the more general IR-PRM framework, where empirically optimistic and alternating updates often have better performance. However, the prior extra-gradient analysis does not extend to these cases. We introduce a new approach that covers both settings. For simultaneous and alternating IR-PRM+ in finite two-player zero-sum matrix games, previous-utility prediction recovers the constant-regret and convergence-rate guarantees previously obtained with extra-gradient prediction: external regret bounded independently of T, an O(T^{-1}) average duality gap, and an O(T^{-1/2}) best-current-iterate gap. Moreover, the current duality gap vanishes and the current profile converges to the Nash equilibrium set. The key step bounds the component of consecutive strategy movement not controlled by the existing IR-PRM+ regret inequality using the relative growth of the nondecreasing regret-vector norm rho_t. items.title: TEX-MEX: Similarity-Guided Temporal Contrastive Learning for Time Series
items.content: arXiv:2610.19557v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Contrastive learning for time series depends on deciding which pairs of inputs should be treated as similar and dissimilar. Because few augmentations reliably preserve meaning in time series, prior methods have relied on two disjoint notions of similarity between windows: structural similarity, which relates windows with similar morphology, and temporal similarity, which relates windows that occur close together in time. We introduce TEX-MEX, to our knowledge the first approach to unify the two into a single relationship. Given a random batch of windows drawn across the dataset, TEX-MEX uses the encoder to identify which windows are structurally similar or dissimilar to each other. It then pulls each window toward the temporally shifted versions of similar windows and pushes it away from those of dissimilar ones, learning what typically accompanies similar windows in time. Across PPG, EEG, ECG, accelerometry, and continuous glucose monitoring, TEX-MEX broadly achieves state-of-the-art performance against contrastive, reconstructive, JEPA-based, and modality-specific approaches, establishing it as a strong general SSL objective. We further train a 560K-parameter PPG foundation model that achieves state-of-the-art performance across a broad range of downstream benchmarks while being roughly 50x smaller than the next-best unimodally pretrained PPG foundation model in our evaluation. We will release this foundation model open-source and open-weight to the community to support future work and practical applications.

items.summary: TEX-MEX unifies structural and temporal notions of similarity in time-series contrastive learning by using the encoder to identify structurally similar windows and pulling each window toward temporally shifted versions of structurally similar samples while pushing away dissimilar ones. items.title: One Size Does Not Fit All: Curvature-Aware Adaptive Perturbation for SAM
items.content: arXiv:2610.20415v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Poor generalisation in deep neural networks is frequently associated with convergence to sharp minima. Sharpness-Aware Minimisation (SAM) improves generalisation of deep neural networks by minimising a combination of the training loss and the local sharpness of the loss landscape, biasing convergence towards flat minima. However, SAM relies on a fixed perturbation radius $\rho$ that ignores local curvature, leading to inefficient behaviour: the perturbation may be too small to escape poor basins defined by sharp local minima, or too large to allow convergence to solutions with good loss-sharpness tradeoff. We reinterpret $\rho$ as the intensity of the perturbation signal and propose Curvature-Aware Adaptive Perturbation for SAM (CAP-SAM), a geometry-aware method that modulates the perturbation radius based on a sharpness ratio, enabling a more effective search for robust minima on the loss landscape. We prove that CAP-SAM preserves the same convergence rate as standard SAM in non-convex stochastic settings. Extensive experiments indicate that our approach consistently outperforms SAM and its most prominent variants across diverse network architectures on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet.
items.author: Alessia Rossi, Felipe Campelo, Gabriel L. Oliveira
items.summary: CAP-SAM replaces Sharpness-Aware Minimization's fixed perturbation radius with a curvature-aware adaptive scheme, reinterpreting the radius as perturbation signal intensity that should vary with local geometry. This avoids the failure modes of too-small perturbations failing to escape sharp basins and too-large perturbations hurting convergence. Improving SAM's efficiency and generalization has broad relevance across deep learning.
items.reasoning: Addresses a recognized weakness of a widely used optimizer with a natural adaptive fix; useful but fairly incremental within the growing SAM-variant literature.

items.title: Learnable Hodge-Laplacian Driven Mixture of Experts for Steady-PDE Surrogates on Coarse Unstructured Meshes
items.content: arXiv:2610.20585v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Current approaches for steady partial differential equations surrogate models on unstructured meshes apply a single mixing mechanism to the whole solution. This paper proposes an architecture that partitions the solution among vanilla transformer experts, each focused on a different spectral scale. The partition is built from a discrete Hodge Laplacian $L_0=\star_0^{-1} d_0^{\top}\star_1 d_0$, that serves as a fitting layer measuring high-frequency content. A gating mechanism takes the mesh as input and produces the per-vertex weights that recombine the expert outputs. AirFRANS is a steady Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) airfoil benchmark. We evaluate our approach in a reduced remeshed version of the benchmark with each unstructured mesh counting 9.6K faces and 4.9K vertices. We compare our approach with the Transolver on the same dataset and dataset slit. Our approach reduces relative $L_2$ error by 31\% and interior mean squared error by 47\%.

items.summary: Proposes a mixture-of-experts architecture for steady PDE surrogates in which a discrete Hodge Laplacian partitions the solution among transformer experts specializing in different spectral scales, with a mesh-conditioned gate recombining per-vertex outputs. Evaluated on a RANS airfoil benchmark (AirFRANS) on coarse unstructured meshes. Combines discrete differential geometry with MoE scaling for engineering surrogate modeling.

items.title: Structure-aware Bayesian full waveform inversion via diffusion-regularized Stein variational gradient descent
items.content: arXiv:2610.19187v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Full waveform inversion (FWI) is a powerful tool for high-resolution subsurface model reconstruction, but it remains highly nonlinear and ill-posed, especially when the initial model is inaccurate or the acquired data are noisy and incomplete. Annealed Stein variational gradient descent (ASVGD) provides a particle-based Bayesian framework for FWI by approximating the posterior distribution with an ensemble of velocity models, thereby enabling uncertainty quantification beyond a single deterministic solution. However, conventional ASVGD-FWI commonly relies on simple handcrafted priors, such as Gaussian or smoothing assumptions, which are often insufficient to represent complex geological structures. To address this limitation, we introduce a learned diffusion model (DM) as an implicit regularization mechanism within the ASVGD-FWI framework. Instead of explicitly evaluating the diffusion prior density, the trained diffusion model acts as a learned geological projection operator that guides updated particles toward the distribution of plausible velocity models. In this way, the proposed method combines data consistency from FWI, posterior diversity from ASVGD, and structural realism from the diffusion prior. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the diffusion-regularized ASVGD-FWI produces more geologically consistent mean models, suppresses nonphysical artifacts, and yields uncertainty estimates that are more concentrated around structurally complex and poorly constrained regions. These results suggest that learned diffusion priors can effectively enhance Bayesian FWI by improving both inversion stability and the interpretability of posterior uncertainty.
items.author: Chao Li, Mrinal K. Sen, Sergey Fomel, Yangkang Chen
items.summary: This work enhances annealed Stein variational gradient descent for Bayesian full waveform inversion by replacing handcrafted Gaussian/smoothing priors with diffusion-model priors that capture complex geological structures, approximating the posterior with an ensemble of velocity models for uncertainty quantification. This improves robustness to inaccurate initial models and noisy, incomplete seismic data. Relevant to geophysics and as a case study in learned priors for Bayesian inverse problems.
items.reasoning: Solid integration of diffusion priors with particle-based variational inference for an important inverse problem, with established authors in seismic imaging. The technique is a domain instantiation of increasingly standard diffusion-prior methods.

items.title: Typed Decision Models on Tabular Data
items.content: arXiv:2610.19536v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Typed decision models are language models that answer a question with a fixed set of possible answers by returning a probability for each answer instead of generating text. We study them on tabular data and compare four decision models with three large language models (LLMs) on row classification, fact verification and anomaly detection. Every request is sent in its original form and under 21 types of rewrite that keep its content, such as renaming the options or writing the table in another format. The decision models perform as well as the LLMs at a lower cost. Three of them are also far more robust to how the question is formulated. No model we test is robust to how the table is organized. For every model, at least a third of the row decisions change under some rewrite of the table or the question. The decisions to which a decision model gives low probability are the ones most likely to change. Decision models are a practical choice for tabular decisions, but their robustness remains an open problem.
items.author: Baowen Zhang, Hangting Ye, Hongyuan Zha
items.summary: This paper studies typed decision models, language models that return probabilities over a fixed answer set instead of generating text, on tabular tasks including row classification, fact verification, and anomaly detection. Under 21 content-preserving rewrite types, decision models match LLM accuracy at lower cost and are substantially more robust to question reformulation, though no tested model is robust to table reorganization. The robustness findings are notable for anyone deploying models on tabular data.
items.reasoning: A well-designed robustness study with a useful contrast between decision-head and generative LLM paradigms on tabular data. The finding that table formatting breaks all models is practically important, but the evaluation scope is limited to a few models and tasks.

items.title: HRTF Upsampling and Personalization via Neural Operators
items.content: arXiv:2610.20400v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Head-related transfer function (HRTF) spatial upsampling from sparse measurements is a fundamental challenge in personalized binaural audio. We formulate HRTF upsampling as an operator learning problem and introduce SPARO, a neural operator that maps sparse measurements at a set of spatial directions to the HRTF field, a continuous representation that can be queried at arbitrary positions. SPARO projects the measurements onto a learned set of spherical latent modes, processes the latent modes with Transformer blocks, and decodes the resulting representations at query directions. On SONICOM, using the LAP24 measurement configuration, SPARO attains the best log-spectral distortion (LSD) and interaural level difference (ILD) error at every sparsity level from 3 to 100 measurements (18% lower LSD and 43% lower ILD error than the strongest baseline at 100 measurements) while remaining competitive in interaural time difference (ITD) error. It reconstructs a dense HRTF 15 to 373 times faster than the leading neural-field method RANF. We further validate the approach on HUTUBS, demonstrating its effectiveness across HRTF datasets.

It achieves the best log-spectral distortion and interaural level difference error across sparsity levels on the SONICOM dataset.
items.reasoning: A well-executed application of neural operators to personalized binaural audio with strong benchmark results on a standard dataset; the domain is specialized, but the operator-learning formulation generalizes naturally and has practical value for spatial audio.

items.title: Evaluating Compressed Memory: Dependence, Utility, and Content Benefit
items.content: arXiv:2610.19373v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Does a language model answer better because its compressed memory contains useful document information? Replacing memory vectors with zeros can lower a trained model's score without showing that it outperforms a model trained without memory. We combine zeroing with separately trained models that cannot access stored text or receive the same constant input for every document. Across nine systems, some models rely on memory yet perform worse than the trained alternative. For example, in experiments that predict states in generated stories, zeroing memory worsens a model's prediction loss, yet a model trained without memory achieves lower loss than the original model with intact memory. On TriviaQA, giving xRAG memory from another question's passage raises F1, which measures word overlap with accepted answers, from 19.38 without a document to 24.78. Its effect on how often outputs contain an accepted answer is statistically uncertain. The question's retrieved passage scores higher still (29.88 F1). Thus a gain over no document alone does not establish that the gain requires the question's passage. Evaluations must therefore specify the comparison model, absolute performance, and generation and scoring conditions.

items.summary: The paper critiques standard evaluation of compressed-memory language models, showing that zeroing memory vectors can lower scores without proving the memory actually beats a memory-free alternative. Across nine systems, some memory-dependent models perform worse than models trained without memory, with evidence from story-state prediction and TriviaQA/xRAG experiments.

items.title: Beyond Reachability: A Relation-Semantic Reasoning Framework for Biomedical Multi-hop QA
items.content: arXiv:2610.19754v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Biomedical multi-hop reasoning over knowledge graphs requires identifying a semantically valid relation sequence that supports the answer. Existing methods can retrieve correct answers, yet often rank them poorly within a large pool of seemingly relevant candidates. Even when a correct answer is retrieved, its associated evidence and reasoning path may fail to support the relation composition required by the question. We term this disconnect between answer reachability and evidential validity the reachable-but-invalid problem. We present ReSemReason, which shares a question-induced distribution over typed, directed relation schemas between candidate discovery and evidence selection. Schema compatibility guides graph search; ReSemAttn then uses relation-conditioned key/value projections and an uncertainty-weighted path prior to attend to candidate-specific evidence. A separate absolute-support score complements normalized attention when all retrieved paths are weak. The reported experiments on BioHopR, PrimeKGQA, and MedReason show improvements in answer ranking and answer-set quality. Path-discrimination analyses examine the distinction between endpoint correctness and evidential support. We also specify matched controls for search, attention, and schema uncertainty.

items.summary: Identifies the reachable-but-invalid problem in biomedical knowledge-graph multi-hop QA, where retrieved answers lack evidentially valid relation paths. ReSemReason shares a question-induced distribution over typed relation schemas between candidate discovery and evidence selection, using schema compatibility to guide search and a ReSemAttn attention mechanism.
items.reasoning: A thoughtful diagnosis of a real flaw in KGQA evaluation and retrieval with a coherent technical fix; impact is confined to the biomedical multi-hop QA niche.

items.title: Not All Criteria Matter: Importance-Aware Criteria Weighting for Rubric-Based LLM Evaluation
items.content: arXiv:2610.19915v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Rubric-based evaluation assesses the responses of large language models (LLMs) by aggregating the verification results of explicit criteria, yet not all criteria matter equally. However, existing methods commonly aggregate the verification results with uniform weighting, which assigns minor and overlapping criteria the same weight as essential ones and thus produces misleading evaluation scores. Although some methods prompt an LLM to directly assign weights, direct weighting requires a holistic judgment over all criteria that LLMs struggle to make reliably. To address these limitations, we propose Importance-Aware Criteria Weighting (ICW), which derives the weights of criteria from pairwise importance comparisons made by an LLM. Specifically, ICW transforms the holistic judgment over all criteria into a series of pairwise importance comparisons, checks and revises inconsistent comparisons, and derives the weights from the principal eigenvector of the comparison matrix. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ICW consistently outperforms uniform weighting and competitive weighting methods, and translates into better policy models in downstream reinforcement learning.
items.author: Haocheng Yang, Licheng Pan, Yiming Dong, Xiaoxi Li, Yuan Lu, Zhenhao Chen, Jiajun Fan, Shuai Shao, Chunyuan Zheng, Hao Wang
items.summary: Proposes Importance-Aware Criteria Weighting (ICW), which derives criterion weights for rubric-based LLM evaluation from pairwise importance comparisons rather than uniform weighting or unreliable holistic LLM-assigned weights. This prevents minor overlapping criteria from masking essential ones in evaluation scores.
items.reasoning: Addresses a real weakness in rubric-based evaluation with a sensible pairwise-comparison mechanism; a solid incremental contribution to a growing evaluation-methods area without headline results.

items.title: PerSo: Investigating Facets of LLMs' Social Intelligence in Real-World Persuasion Scenarios
items.content: arXiv:2610.20548v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Understanding the social intelligence of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly important for applications involving human-AI interaction and multi-agent environments. Social intelligence comprises two aspects: cognitive intelligence, the ability to infer others' mental states, and behavioral intelligence, the ability to select appropriate social actions based on these inferences to achieve social goals. Persuasion provides a natural testbed in which both aspects are simultaneously at play, yet prior benchmarks typically evaluate them in isolation using synthetic scenarios. We introduce PerSo, a benchmark that evaluates both aspects on real-world persuasion dialogues from Reddit's ChangeMyView community, using an LLM-in-the-loop pipeline to construct the evaluation tasks, validated through human annotation. Our evaluation of diverse LLMs shows that performance generally scales with model size but varies across dimensions. The strongest LLM slightly surpasses the best observed human performance on the behavioral task, while the best human participant remains ahead on the cognitive task.
items.author: Ali Zamani, Soroush Esfahanian, Erfan Shahabi, Mohammad Taher Pilehvar, Azadeh Shakery, Yadollah Yaghoobzadeh
items.summary: PerSo is a benchmark that jointly evaluates cognitive and behavioral social intelligence of LLMs on real-world persuasion dialogues from Reddit's ChangeMyView, using an LLM-in-the-loop pipeline rather than synthetic scenarios. It moves beyond prior work that assessed mental-state inference and social action selection in isolation.
items.reasoning: Grounding social intelligence evaluation in authentic persuasion data is a meaningful improvement over synthetic benchmarks; the LLM-in-the-loop methodology raises some circularity questions, and persuasion benchmarks carry dual-use considerations.

items.title: Adaptive Observation Control for Active Visual Recognition
items.content: arXiv:2610.19624v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Visual recognition models usually process a fixed view under a fixed computation budget, although images often benefit from different scales and amounts of spatial evidence. Active vision can adapt by observing a coarse scene and then selecting informative fixations, but the public AdaptiveNN-DeiT-S pipeline still fixes both field of view and observation count. We extend this fixed-step recognizer with a controllable observation interface that adapts both the field of view and the number of fixations to the input. Specifically, the model predicts a per-fixation scale that sets its field of view, refines each selected crop with optional scale-gated foveation and a residual high-resolution detail-token branch, and uses label-grounded stop heads for input-dependent early termination. Experiments across fine-grained benchmarks, full ImageNet-1K, and ImageNet-A/R-derived classification splits show that the interface remains competitive with fixed-step references while exposing a controllable observation budget. The same checkpoint enables threshold-controlled accuracy-compute trade-offs without per-threshold retraining. On sequential ImageNet-1K, the learned stop rule outperforms fixed-step truncation of the same checkpoint, sustaining 81.9% top-1 using 2.45 of the four focus steps and exceeding three-step truncation at lower cost. On each benchmark, a variant combining scale control and detail-token fusion achieves the highest accuracy among the tested component-added non-exit variants. Our code is available at https://github.com/GZHU-DVL/LI-Dikai.
items.author: Dikai Li, Weijia Wang, Yuan-Gen Wang
items.summary: The paper extends a fixed-step active recognition pipeline (AdaptiveNN-DeiT-S) with a controllable observation interface that adapts both field of view and number of fixations per input, using per-fixation scale prediction, scale-gated foveation, a residual detail-token branch, and a label-grounded stop head. This lets recognition models allocate spatial evidence and computation adaptively.
items.reasoning: Adaptive computation and active vision remain relevant for efficiency, and adapting both view scale and fixation count is a sensible extension. The work builds directly on an existing public pipeline, making it an incremental contribution.

items.title: LiFi: LiDAR Generation from Multi-View Images via Geometric and Semantic Collaborative Guidance
items.content: arXiv:2610.19786v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Generating LiDAR point clouds from multi-view camera images is a valuable task with applications in controllable data synthesis, cross-modal simulation and various perception tasks. However, most existing methods are not specifically designed for this task, and the quality of their generated LiDAR remains limited. Moreover, these methods typically focus only on semantic cues in images or generate LiDAR from a monocular camera image. In this work, we introduce LiFi (LiDAR From images), a dedicated framework for generating visually and geometrically aligned LiDAR scenes from multi-view camera images. LiFi guides the latent diffusion process through two complementary branches: geometry and semantics. The geometry branch constructs scene features from images through a reverse sampling algorithm and an uncertainty-aware geometric encoder combined with DepthAnything3, whereas the semantic branch provides high-level semantic representations via a cross-view interaction module. We further introduce a dual-branch balanced classifier-free guidance (CFG) strategy, which enhances the model's conditional generation capability while preserving the independent learning and collaborative controllability of the two branches. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LiFi outperforms state-of-the-art methods in generating high-fidelity LiDAR scenes. The code will be publicly available at: https://github.com/szzhou88/LiFi.
items.author: Sizhuo Zhou, Xiaosong Jia, Fanrui Zhang, Qifeng Li, Junjie Li, Zirui Wang, Yukang Feng, Yu Hong, Shaofeng Zhang, Wenlong Liao, Tao He, Juyong Zhang, Junchi Yan
items.summary: LiFi is a dedicated latent diffusion framework for generating geometrically and semantically aligned LiDAR point clouds from multi-view camera images, guided by complementary geometry and semantics branches. It targets controllable data synthesis, cross-modal simulation, and perception applications where existing monocular or semantics-only methods fall short.
items.reasoning: A well-motivated task with clear applications in autonomous driving simulation and data augmentation. The dual-branch guidance design is sensible but follows established diffusion conditioning patterns; impact hinges on demonstrated quality gains over adapted baselines.

items.title: Dataset-Level Regularization for Joint-Embedding Self-Supervised Learning
items.content: arXiv:2610.20158v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Self-supervised joint embedding learning aligns representations of augmented views while regularizing their distribution to prevent collapse. Regularization aims to shape the overall representation distribution, but most joint embedding methods restrict its computation to the active minibatch. We propose out-of-batch regularization, which maintains a dataset-level state in CPU memory and uses globally constructed per-instance targets during minibatch training. Evaluated on natural images and biomedical datasets, these anchors approximate the full-dataset regularization gradient more faithfully than conventional minibatch estimation at small batch sizes. Applications to contrastive (SimCLR) and non-contrastive (SIGReg) approaches show consistent improvement over the corresponding in-batch objectives for image classification, minority-class performance under controlled imbalance, instance retrieval, and continued self-supervised pretraining, with the largest gains at small batch sizes. These results suggest that dataset-level regularization can be decoupled from minibatch optimization, making batch size an optimization choice that does not affect the geometry of the regularizer.
items.author: Konstantinos Almpanakis, Anna Kreshuk

On natural image and biomedical datasets, this approximates full-dataset regularization more faithfully than minibatch estimation at small batch sizes, with consistent gains for SimCLR and SIGReg-style methods.
items.reasoning: A simple, broadly applicable idea targeting a real limitation (minibatch-restricted regularization) of widely used SSL methods, validated across contrastive and non-contrastive families; impact is moderated because gains are concentrated in small-batch regimes and engineering overhead matters.

items.title: InfiniSplat v2: Analyzing and Improving Feed-Forward 3DGS from Any Views
items.content: arXiv:2610.20341v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction builds 3D scenes directly from input images for novel view rendering, but learning Gaussian attributes from predicted geometry for high-quality rendering under large viewpoint changes remains challenging. We analyze limitations in Gaussian attribute learning and introduce InfiniSplat v2, which improves rendering quality through architectural and training changes. Our method decouples geometry and attribute prediction with a frozen geometry branch, aligns predicted Gaussians using ground-truth camera poses during training, and adopts large-angle target view supervision. Across six datasets, the feed-forward outputs of the same trained model achieve state-of-the-art mean LPIPS and DISTS among the evaluated methods in both pose-conditioned and pose-free settings. In the pose-conditioned setting, mean LPIPS and DISTS decrease by 25.8% and 32.9%, respectively, compared with the strongest evaluated baselines. We further find that opacity learned with only image reconstruction supervision suppresses geometrically inconsistent points. Project page: https://zju3dv.github.io/InfiniSplat2/
items.author: Yongzhen Hu, Hao Yu, Jiawei Wang, Xianming Zeng, Jianyun Xu, Xingliang Liu, Ruizhen Hu, Xiaowei Zhou, Hujun Bao, Sida Peng
items.summary: InfiniSplat v2 improves feed-forward Gaussian splatting reconstruction under large viewpoint changes by decoupling geometry and attribute prediction with a frozen geometry branch, aligning predicted Gaussians with ground-truth poses during training, and using large-angle target view supervision. It achieves state-of-the-art mean LPIPS and DISTS across six datasets.
items.reasoning: Solid empirical advances with a clean analysis of why Gaussian attribute learning fails under large view changes; strong breadth of evaluation, but it is an iterative improvement within a very active and crowded subfield.

items.title: $S^3$-Nav: Structured Spatial-Semantic Decision Making for Language-Guided Robot Navigation
items.content: arXiv:2610.19431v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper presents $S^3$-Nav, a structured spatial-semantic decision-making framework for language-guided robot navigation under partial observability. Rather than assuming a complete environment representation in advance, $S^3$-Nav incrementally constructs persistent spatial-semantic state while exposing only a capacity-controlled, task-conditioned view to the high-level policy. This separation decouples what the robot must retain from what the policy needs to inspect, allowing decision complexity to be controlled without discarding grounded evidence required for subsequent reasoning and validation. High-level navigation outputs remain provisional and are independently grounded and validated against persistent semantic evidence and current geometric observations before physical execution or task termination. Evaluations across multiple environments and object- and relation-goal tasks demonstrate that separating persistent state, decision-facing evidence, and execution authority improves closed-loop navigation reliability while reducing policy reasoning cost.
items.author: Chaemin Lee, Hae Min Cho

High-level decisions are provisional and validated against grounded semantic evidence, decoupling what the robot retains from what the policy inspects. This structured separation addresses reliability in language-guided navigation.
items.reasoning: A thoughtful architecture for language-guided navigation with a clear principle (separate persistent grounding from policy-facing state), though the two-author scope and likely simulation-only evaluation limit demonstrated impact in a crowded language-navigation field.

items.title: Relational Semantic Grounding for Test-Time Discovery
items.content: arXiv:2610.14721v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Test-Time Discovery (TTD) aims to recognize known classes and detect novel ones from a continuous unlabeled test stream after deployment. Existing TTD methods mainly rely on visual clustering or prototype comparison, and can only assign anonymous labels to discovered classes, leaving them difficult to interpret in open-world applications. In this paper, we propose SEGA, a Semantic Grounding with Attributes framework for TTD. SEGA leverages large language models to generate attribute-rich descriptions for known classes and constructs an attribute-anchored visual-semantic space during training. At test time, we introduce Relational Semantic Grounding (RSG), which grounds unknown samples with similar and dissimilar known-class anchors, prompts the LLM to generate candidate concepts, and reranks them in the learned semantic space. The selected concept is further used for confidence-guided test-time semantic stabilization. By coupling attribute-level semantic alignment with relational concept grounding, SEGA transforms anonymous test-time clusters into interpretable semantic concepts. Experiments show that SEGA improves TTD baselines with the promise of semantic grounding for open-world.
items.author: Tianle Liu, Gongbo Cheng, Chenggong Ni, Minming Gu, Tao Zhou, Fuyuan Hu, Fan Lyu
items.summary: SEGA adds interpretability to test-time discovery by using LLMs to generate attribute-rich descriptions of known classes and building an attribute-anchored visual-semantic space during training. At test time, relational semantic grounding places unknown samples relative to similar and dissimilar known-class anchors, enabling interpretable labels rather than anonymous cluster IDs.
items.reasoning: A companion work to Energy Ring by overlapping authors, tackling a complementary weakness of TTD (uninterpretable discovered classes) by coupling open-world discovery with language-model-derived semantics. Solid idea; overlap with the authors' parallel paper suggests a broader program rather than independent breakthrough.

items.title: AlphaRLM: Aligning Language Models for Literature-Grounded Symbolic Factor Discovery
items.content: arXiv:2610.14959v2 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Formulaic alpha mining seeks to discover executable expressions that capture predictive market signals in a vast, noisy search space. Recent LLM-based approaches use prompting, iterative search, or seed-factor evolution, leaving direct factor construction through policy learning less explored. To address this, we introduce AlphaRLM, a reinforcement-learning framework that trains LLMs to construct executable symbolic factors from financial literature without input factor expressions. AlphaRLM incorporates Literature-Guided Operator Assembly (LEGO), which conditions factor construction on literature-derived ideas and executable operators, providing semantic priors for exploration. It further aligns the generation policy with market feedback through executable-validity and grouped-return-separation rewards that capture non-monotonic structures across factor quantiles. Extensive experiments on CSI 300, CSI 1000, and S&P 500 show that AlphaRLM outperforms strong factor-mining and LLM-based baselines in annualized excess return. Notably, the 8B model achieves strong cross-market performance, highlighting the promise of literature-conditioned, market-aligned factor generation.
items.author: Jie Huang, Yuecheng Hong, Yao Chen, Hao Zhong, Linfeng Xiao, Xudong Liu, Hao Xia, Jianxuan Xin
items.summary: AlphaRLM trains LLMs with reinforcement learning to construct executable symbolic alpha factors for quantitative finance from financial literature, via Literature-Guided Operator Assembly and alignment of the generation policy with market feedback. It moves beyond prompting and seed-evolution approaches to direct policy learning for factor construction.
items.reasoning: An interesting combination of RL-trained LLMs with symbolic discovery in a high-value domain, but the contribution is domain-specific, and backtest-overfitting and market-impact concerns typical of alpha-mining work temper general significance.
items.summary_html: AlphaRLM trains LLMs with reinforcement learning to construct executable symbolic alpha factors for quantitative finance from financial literature, via Literature-Guided Operator Assembly and alignment of the generation policy with market feedback. items.title: MoMaTune: Model, Match, Then Tune Language Models for Numerical Records
items.content: arXiv:2610.15235v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Despite remarkable progress in language understanding and generation, decoder language models continue to exhibit striking failures on numerical data. Numerical examples are typically serialized as text by concatenating feature names with their values (e.g., fat:3.4), while conventional task adaptation applies loss only to the downstream prediction target. This leaves two structures weakly supervised: within-value sensitivity, where digit position determines numerical magnitude, because token cross-entropy contains no explicit numerical metric; and across-field structure, where measurements in the same record are statistically dependent, because target-only tuning provides no direct loss on the measurements or their dependencies. We introduce MoMaTune (Model, Match, then Tune), a two-stage post-training strategy organized around these supervision gaps. Stage 1 applies Model, ordinary next-token prediction densely over label-free serialized records, and optionally adds Match, a same-record consistency objective that aligns representations of different partial views of the same example. Stage 2 applies Tune, supervised fine-tuning for downstream target prediction. We evaluate MoMaTune on 169,285 records from eight public datasets, with 339 of 340 input fields numerical. At 1.5B parameters, Model raises the eight-dataset masked-value imputation aggregate from 0.106 to 0.401, while the three-dataset correct-context gain rises from 0.058 to 0.167. On diagnostics, Model also increases sensitivity to numerically consequential digit changes, while Match improves robustness to informative partial views. Adding Tune yields higher target-supervised embedding aggregates for each tested Stage-1 parent, and the two-stage recipes obtain higher aggregate scores than Tune alone. The same pattern is observed at 4B, 9.6B, and 27B parameters when model embeddings are used for downstream prediction.
items.author: Weimin Lyu, Jingfen Zhang, Lingdao Sha, Peng sun, Xiaowei Chen, Vincent Gao, Rui Song
items.summary: Addresses decoder LLM failures on tabular numerical data by identifying two weakly supervised structures: within-value digit-position sensitivity and across-field statistical dependence. MoMaTune introduces a model-match-tune pipeline adding auxiliary losses over the serialized measurements and their dependencies beyond target-only tuning.
items.reasoning: Diagnoses a real, well-documented weakness (numerical reasoning in serialized records) with a clean structural analysis and targeted auxiliary supervision. The approach is engineering-heavy and incremental, but the digit-position and cross-field loss formulations are practical contributions.

items.title: CondMSP: Condition-Informed and Resource-Aware Inorganic Materials Synthesis Planning
items.content: arXiv:2610.15603v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Materials synthesis planning (MSP) connects AI-driven materials discovery to experimental realization by proposing precursors, synthesis operations, and processing conditions for a target material. Existing approaches predict these components separately or in pairs and treat conditions only as a prediction target. Consequently, MSP remains centered on recipe prediction: it leaves unexplored how conditions can serve as process context for constructing synthesis routes, and it does not address which candidate routes should be executed under limited experimental resources. We propose CondMSP, which extends MSP from recipe prediction to execution-aware planning. CondMSP predicts temperature, time, and atmosphere by combining a joint predictor with variable-specific experts, and then uses these predictions both as process context, grounding the generation and retrieval of operation sequences, and as execution requirements, specifying which thermal stages can share a furnace run and at what cost. This specification is held fixed across all compared methods; within it, CondMSP ranks routes across precursor sets by a common utility and, under furnace budgets, jointly selects routes and allocates their thermal stages by constrained optimization. CondMSP improves condition and operation prediction and, under this shared constraint, raises reference-recipe recovery from 27.9% to 32.9% at three simulated furnace runs per target and from 34.7% to 40.0% at 30 trials, while a new evaluation set of 2,344 targets supports generalization beyond oxide-dominated training chemistry.
items.author: Heewoong Noh, Gyoung S. Na, Elton Pan, Namkyeong Lee, Chanyoung Park
items.summary: Proposes CondMSP, extending materials synthesis planning from recipe prediction to execution-aware planning that jointly predicts temperature, time, and atmosphere as process context for constructing synthesis routes. It also addresses which candidate routes should be executed under limited experimental resources. Bridges AI-driven materials discovery and experimental realization.

items.content_html: arXiv:2610.15603v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Materials synthesis planning (MSP) connects AI-driven materials discovery to experimental realization by proposing precursors, synthesis operations, and processing conditions for a target material. Existing approaches predict these components separately or in pairs and treat conditions only as a prediction target. Consequently, MSP remains centered on recipe prediction: it leaves unexplored how conditions can serve as process context for constructing synthesis routes, and it does not address which candidate routes should be executed under limited experimental resources. We propose CondMSP, which extends MSP from recipe prediction to execution-aware planning. CondMSP predicts temperature, time, and atmosphere by combining a joint predictor with variable-specific experts, and then uses these predictions both as process context, grounding the generation and retrieval of operation sequences, and as execution requirements, specifying which thermal stages can share a furnace run and at what cost. This specification is held fixed across all compared methods; within it, CondMSP ranks routes across precursor sets by a common utility and, under furnace budgets, jointly selects routes and allocates their thermal stages by constrained optimization. CondMSP improves condition and operation prediction and, under this shared constraint, raises reference-recipe recovery from 27.9% to 32.9% at three simulated furnace runs per target and from 34.7% to 40.0% at 30 trials, while a new evaluation set of 2,344 targets supports generalization beyond oxide-dominated training chemistry.

items.title: Beyond Single-Pathogen Forecasts: Predicting Shared Respiratory Hospital Burden from Influenza, COVID-19, and RSV
items.content: arXiv:2610.16074v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Co-circulating influenza, COVID-19, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) create a shared hospital-admission burden, because beds, staff, testing capacity, and respiratory support are allocated to total demand rather than to one pathogen at a time. This makes respiratory forecasting a target-construction problem as well as a modeling problem: disease-specific forecasts preserve attribution, whereas hospitals also need a single planning signal for combined burden. We developed a supervised 1- to 4-week-ahead framework for weekly admissions and compared two total-burden strategies: summing independently generated pathogen-specific forecasts and forecasting the combined admission target directly. Evaluation included retrospective held-out testing and prospective operational forecasts issued before the corresponding admission weeks were observed, with performance summarized using MAE and Percent Agreement (PA; the smaller of model-generated and observed counts divided by the larger). In retrospective total-burden evaluation, the combined-burden model had PA values of 0.85, 0.78, 0.74, and 0.76 and MAE values of 80.63, 200.09, 183.97, and 156.13 from week 1 to week 4 ahead, compared with summed-forecast PA values of 0.85, 0.80, 0.69, and 0.69 and MAE values of 100.14, 200.06, 205.65, and 217.57. Prospectively, the combined-burden model had higher PA and lower MAE at all four horizons, with the largest separations at weeks 3 and 4 ahead. These results support layered respiratory forecasting: pathogen-specific forecasts remain necessary for etiologic interpretation, while combined-burden forecasts better align with hospital preparedness and shared-capacity planning.

items.title: Constructed regional photovoltaic generation fields improve ultra-short-term distributed solar forecasting
items.content: arXiv:2610.16110v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Ultra-short-term forecasting of densely distributed photovoltaic (PV) systems remains challenging because external meteorological and satellite products may not adequately resolve rapid local variations, while heterogeneous PV systems exhibit different generation responses under similar atmospheric conditions. Meanwhile, dense PV fleets provide spatially distributed measurements that reveal regional generation dynamics. Here, we reformulate fleet-level PV forecasting from modeling discrete station time series to predicting explicit, spatially structured regional PV generation fields. We develop SatPV-Field, a regional-to-local forecasting framework that transforms distributed PV measurements into image-like generation fields and models their spatiotemporal evolution. By combining historical PV fields with satellite-derived future shortwave radiation guidance and meteorological forecasts, the framework predicts future regional generation states, which subsequently provide location-specific guidance for individual-station forecasting. Experiments involving 496 distributed PV systems, including 446 source stations and 50 held-out target stations, demonstrate that these regional fields can be effectively forecast and used to improve station-level predictions. The proposed approach reduces station-level MAE by approximately 10.0% relative to the best-performing single-station temporal baseline and by 2.5% relative to a graph-based regional forecasting approach using the same source fleet. These findings establish an explicit spatial-field modeling paradigm that connects regional generation dynamics with individual-site forecasting.

items.title: Encounter-Driven City-Scale Human Mobility Generation with Large Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.17672v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for human mobility generation by modeling individual routines, activities, and mobility preferences. However, existing approaches remain largely resident-centric: generating realistic individual trajectories does not necessarily recover the encounters that emerge when multiple residents co-occur at the same place and time. To this end, we study encounter-aware human mobility generation, which jointly preserves individual mobility and population-level interaction structure. We propose EncounterMob, an encounter-driven LLM framework consisting of a coarse-to-fine Encounter Generator and an Iterative Coupling Framework. The Encounter Generator first captures city-level encounter rhythms and then instantiates participant-time-venue encounters, while the Iterative Coupling Framework coordinates these encounters with personal mobility behavior through successive refinement. We further introduce an encounter recovery protocol covering encounter marginal and joint distributions over residents, times, and venues. Experiments on the Japan and NYC datasets show that EncounterMob outperforms all external baselines on all seven encounter metrics and all six personal mobility metrics. Compared with ELLMob, it reduces the participant-time-venue joint error by 40.4%/41.7% and the mean personal mobility error by 58.8%/32.7% on Japan/NYC, respectively.
items.author: Chao Li, Renhe Jiang, Chuan Xiao, Jiawei Wang
items.summary: EncounterMob extends LLM-based human mobility generation beyond individual trajectories to jointly preserve population-level encounter structure, via a coarse-to-fine Encounter Generator capturing city-level encounter rhythms and an iterative coupling framework. This matters for urban planning and epidemiological modeling where co-occurrence patterns, not just individual paths, are key. It addresses a real blind spot in prior resident-centric generation work.

items.title: Output Discipline Sets the Floor: A Falsification-Guided, Model-Agnostic Agent Protocol for Auditable Hypothesis-Driven Decision Making
items.content: arXiv:2610.18298v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: What binds large language models on auditable, hypothesis-driven decision tasks, where every candidate can be checked against the evidence? On the public TCMEval-SDT benchmark for Traditional Chinese Medicine syndrome differentiation (200 cases), the binding constraint is output discipline and reasoning structure, not model capability alone: two years of model scaling move zero-shot scores by only -0.03 to +0.08, while output-discipline failures (non-terminating reasoning, format non-compliance, large run-to-run spread) persist even in frontier models. We test this with a model-agnostic agent framework formalizing decision making as a five-stage closed loop, enforced by a candidate x evidence matrix falsification protocol: every candidate is judged against every evidence item, at least half of the candidates must be falsified before a conclusion is licensed, and survivors are emitted in a machine-verifiable single-line format. Across five base models, the effect is sign-conditional on zero-shot output discipline: it rescues models whose discipline fails (DeepSeek-V4-Flash: +0.267/+0.271, entirely termination rescue), reduces a high-variance model's run-to-run standard deviation from 0.218 to 0.007 (Kimi K3), and significantly costs already-disciplined models (-0.087 to -0.120 on budget-matched Qwen3-4B/32B). Ablations attribute the cost to the candidate-bounded format layer and show the effect is independent of injected knowledge content (protocol-knowledge decoupling). The protocol also transfers to misinformation-robust mathematical reasoning, detecting injected false premises at 89.8% recall with a 6.8% false-positive rate (MCC 0.54; a flag-everything baseline scores 0) and restoring accuracy to the no-misinformation ceiling. Where zero-shot output discipline is weak, the reasoning protocol sets the floor; base-model capability always sets the ceiling.
items.author: Jing Liu, Yongxing Qi, Ping Yao, Ting Wu
items.summary: Using the TCMEval-SDT benchmark for Traditional Chinese Medicine syndrome differentiation, the authors show that output discipline and reasoning structure — not model scale — bind performance on auditable decision tasks, since two years of model scaling moved scores negligibly while discipline failures persisted in frontier models. They propose a model-agnostic five-stage agent loop enforced by a candidate-by-evidence falsification protocol. The finding that protocol structure dominates capability is broadly instructive for agent design.
items.reasoning: The central empirical claim (output discipline as binding constraint across model generations) is interesting and somewhat surprising, and the falsification protocol is reusable. But the evidence comes from a single narrow domain benchmark with modest case counts, limiting generalizability claims.

items.title: SemTree: Judge-Aware Semantic Decision Trees for Inspectable and Repairable Rule Decisions
items.content: arXiv:2610.13999v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Rule decisions such as content moderation, advertising compliance, and eligibility checks combine several conditions, exemptions, and missing-information cases, and an error can be fixed only once the failing condition is known. We introduce SemTree, a framework that represents a rule decision as a semantic decision tree: each node is a natural-language question with explicit Yes/No/Unknown criteria, a pluggable semantic judge answers it, and the branching structure is compiled on the answers that this judge actually gives. The executed path is the reasoning behind every decision, so errors are repaired where they occur: a reviewer corrects a single node and replays the rule, corrected nodes become training labels for the judge, and a tool-using LLM editor revises questions and subtrees while observing execution results. On all 8,276 ShARC test cases, a tree executed by a hosted judge reaches 67.70% accuracy with 2.99 questions per case, on par with asking the same judge for the final label (68.23%); an earlier tree compiled for a different judge scores 47.87% when executed by this judge, while a new tree compiled on this judge's answers to a 12-question initial pool already scores 64.39%. Node-level repair raises BANKING77 accuracy from 82.04% to 86.16%, an explicit exemption node cuts the false positives of a Chinese e-commerce moderation clause from 24 to 5, and a trained editor raises the development accuracy of edited trees from 64.47% to 73.35%.
items.author: Jincheng Gao, Wei Ding, Shuo Sun
items.summary: SemTree represents rule decisions (content moderation, compliance, eligibility) as semantic decision trees where each node is a natural-language question with explicit Yes/No/Unknown criteria answered by a pluggable semantic judge. The executed path constitutes the reasoning behind each decision, enabling local repair of single nodes, replay of the rule, and conversion of corrections into judge training labels. This makes LLM-based rule application auditable and correctable.
items.reasoning: Practical and well-motivated framework for auditable, repairable LLM decision-making in high-stakes rule-based settings; the node-level correction and label-recycling design is thoughtfully engineered. Governance and compliance relevance is significant, though the core idea of decomposing decisions into questions is not entirely new.

items.title: LabInstruct: Benchmarking Situated Instructional Video Generation for Lab Procedures
items.content: arXiv:2610.14020v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) aim to automate the full experimental loop, from scientific decision-making to physical execution. Ideally, AI-generated plans could be carried out directly by robotic systems, but reliable automation remains difficult in complex, open-world laboratory environments, where experiments often involve fine-grained manipulation, long-horizon procedures, and substantial variation across tasks and setups. Humans therefore remain an important execution interface between AI-generated plans and physical experiments, creating a need for clear and effective human-facing experimental guidance. Because laboratory procedures are inherently visual, spatial, and dynamic, video is particularly well suited to communicating apparatus configurations, manipulation actions, temporal dependencies, and state changes. Recent advances in video generation now make it possible to synthesize experimental demonstrations directly from an initial workspace image and a natural-language instruction. However, whether such models can reliably communicate real laboratory procedures has not been systematically studied. We introduce LabInstruct, a benchmark for situated instructional video generation in real laboratories. LabInstruct contains 204 tasks across 5 scientific disciplines, with real reference executions and structured annotations of objects, actions, contacts, and state transitions. Evaluating 8 frontier image-to-video models, we find that visually plausible generations frequently remain procedurally incorrect, revealing a substantial gap between visual realism and the reliability required for experimental instruction.
items.author: Yuming Fu, Weijia Wu, Jing Chen, Jiahao Tang, Feifei Chen, Hongyu Zhu, Xin Jin, Alex Jinpeng Wang
items.summary: LabInstruct is a benchmark for evaluating AI-generated instructional videos that guide humans executing lab procedures, positioned as a human-facing interface for self-driving laboratories. It targets fine-grained, long-horizon, visually grounded laboratory tasks where reliable full robotic automation is not yet possible.
items.reasoning: Novel application niche combining video generation evaluation with scientific automation, addressing the underexplored human-in-the-loop gap between AI planning and lab execution. Value depends on benchmark adoption; video generation benchmarks are rapidly proliferating, which tempers novelty.

items.title: Coarse-Graining Recursive Expert Computation: Continuation-Relative Interfaces and Failure Modes
items.content: arXiv:2610.14413v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Computational coarse-graining aims to replace a sequence of updates with a cheaper module while preserving task performance. We present a continuation-relative evaluation framework that assesses replacements through the computation that follows them, using downstream task quality and total execution cost as joint criteria. The framework distinguishes boundary representations, summaries of skipped computation, executed operations, and downstream loss. It makes interfaces and permitted deployment information explicit, combines fine-path references with directly trained controls using the same shortened architecture, and accounts for selection overhead. An exact loss decomposition separates replacement effects at a fixed downstream action from effects of changing that action. A finite construction shows how retained information can reduce the stipulated cost of zero-error prediction under fixed information and controller restrictions. Experiments in two frozen pretrained language models show that representation fidelity and task loss can favor different fitting objectives. In a prespecified comparison on a 1.7-billion-parameter model, next-token-loss training lowers in-distribution negative log-likelihood by 0.1901 nats per scored token compared with reconstructing the skipped blocks' output, using the same optimizer and update count. This ranking reverses in all nine paired comparisons under distribution shift. In a recursive expert prototype, the jointly adapted candidate lowers task error relative to frozen-bank and router-only baselines, but trails directly trained controls, and the tested input-only selectors fail the joint quality-cost criteria. Together, the protocol and studies provide explicit criteria and diagnostics for distinguishing useful computational replacement from local approximation gains within specified interfaces and evaluation settings.

items.summary: The paper presents a continuation-relative evaluation framework for computational coarse-graining, where a sequence of expensive updates is replaced by a cheaper module judged by downstream task quality and execution cost. It offers an exact loss decomposition separating replacement effects and explicitly catalogs failure modes of such substitutions.
items.reasoning: Conceptually interesting framework for evaluating learned computation substitutions (relevant to speculative decoding, draft models, cascades), but abstract framing and unclear empirical grounding reduce immediate impact.

items.title: InCLAD: A Continual Learning Benchmark for Industrial Visual Anomaly Detection
items.content: arXiv:2610.15032v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Industrial anomaly detection benchmarks have advanced rapidly, yet they remain largely static and therefore underrepresent deployment settings in which inspection systems must be extended from one industrial component to another over time. In our setting, continual industrial anomaly detection is framed as a task-incremental problem: each component defines a task, while the learning objective remains semi-supervised. The goal extends beyond conventional anomaly detection, since models should preserve their performance on all components as they are sequentially exposed to new components. This framing is especially relevant because many existing industrial pipelines either assume fully supervised defect labels or study only isolated datasets, leaving open the question of how semi-supervised anomaly detectors behave across a sequence of heterogeneous components. We address this gap by organizing the benchmark as a sequence of related component-level tasks and by defining multiple scenarios, including random, easy-to-hard, and hard-to-easy. In addition to single-dataset continual scenarios, we propose challenging scenarios spanning across multiple datasets. We further evaluate continual performance from two complementary perspectives: image-level anomaly detection and pixel-level anomaly localization. By recasting industrial anomaly detection as a continual benchmark rather than a static train/test problem, our work establishes a concrete path toward studying knowledge retention, adaptation, and generalization in evolving industrial environments.
items.author: {\L}ukasz Marcjan, Dorota Wilk-Ko{\l}odziejczyk, Roberto Corizzo
items.summary: InCLAD frames continual industrial anomaly detection as a task-incremental, semi-supervised problem where each industrial component defines a task and models must preserve performance on prior components while learning new ones. The benchmark addresses a gap left by static anomaly detection datasets that assume full supervision or isolated settings.
items.reasoning: A useful benchmark filling a real gap between continual learning and industrial anomaly detection with a realistic semi-supervised framing; impact bounded by the industrial niche and adoption of the dataset.

items.title: GeoBridge: Evolving Transferable Decoder Topologies for Geometric Vision
items.content: arXiv:2610.15280v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Depth estimation and Gaussian reconstruction share a need for multi-scale feature processing, yet use different prediction interfaces and training objectives. Whether a decoder's internal computation can be optimized once and reused across these systems remains a structural design question. Search over primitive configurations alone leaves the organization of transformations fixed. To address this gap, we propose GeoBridge, an evolutionary framework for transferable decoder topologies. First, GeoBridge makes stage-internal topology searchable through residual, sequential, and parallel composition of configurable primitives. Shape-preserving composition retains the stage interfaces of a fixed multi-scale scaffold. Second, a functional-tree encoding supports stage-aware crossover and hierarchical mutation, while a gradient sensitivity-alignment proxy evaluates candidates without training. Multi-objective evolution balances this proxy with computation and parameter cost. Third, selected topologies are instantiated and trained in target systems with task-specific prediction interfaces. A single source search takes approximately 12 GPU hours. GeoBridgeNet-A3 achieves the best depth accuracy among four adapted decoder baselines under a common encoder and training protocol on NYU Depth V2 and KITTI. The same topology reaches 27.11 dB PSNR in Gaussian novel-view synthesis on RealEstate10K, and its refined representations support open-vocabulary segmentation on LERF. These results support decoder topology as a reusable design object across the evaluated geometric vision systems. Code and pretrained weights are available at https://github.com/EMI-Group/GeoBridge-NAS.

items.title: Improving the Bounds on Approximating Weighted Maximin Share for Chores
items.content: arXiv:2610.15520v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We investigate the problem of allocating indivisible chores among agents with arbitrary positive weights and additive nonnegative cost functions. An allocation is said to be $\alpha$-weighted-maximin-share (WMMS) fair if the cost incurred by each agent is at most $\alpha$ times her weighted maximin share. We establish that every instance admits a $4.124234528$-WMMS allocation. Moreover, for instances in which all weights and costs are rational numbers represented in binary, we give an algorithm that computes a $4.12424$-WMMS allocation in time polynomial in the number of agents, the number of chores, and the total binary encoding length of the input. Complementing these upper bounds, we construct a family of instances with strictly positive, identically ordered costs for which the optimal WMMS approximation factors converge to $e$. Together, our results substantially narrow the previously best-known gap of $[2,12]$ established by Li et al.~\cite{LWX26} to $[e,4.12424]$.

It advances the fair division frontier for weighted chores.
items.reasoning: Rigorous improvement of known bounds in a well-studied fair division problem, with both existential and algorithmic results plus complementary lower bounds. items.title: PatTransBench: an ipc-stratified, multi-dimensional benchmark for patent machine translation evaluation
items.content: arXiv:2610.16538v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We present PatTransBench, a 12,000-item Chinese-English/Japanese/Korean patent machine translation (PatMT) benchmark with a four-dimensional evaluation protocol. The benchmark comprises 6,000 short-text (sentence/claim) and 6,000 long-text (paragraph) pairs, evenly split across three language pairs and both translation directions, built via IPC-section-stratified sampling and dualthreshold quality gating from upstream patent-family parallel corpora. The evaluation protocol spans literal n-gram overlap (BLEU, ROUGE-L, chrF), cross-lingual semantic textual similarity (CLSTS), 38-probe-language consistency testing, and serving performance under concurrency. A case study on PatMT2-7B and its fp8/AWQ4/AutoRound-4bit variants reveals direction-dependent quantization effects masked by aggregate scores and non-monotonic language-failure patterns across quantization schemes that are invisible to single-metric evaluation. We plan to release the benchmark, protocol, and case-study results upon publication to support reproducible PatMT evaluation.
