items.title: Tracing Morphology, Semantics, and Divergence in Language Acquisition
items.content: arXiv:2610.19041v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Understanding the dynamics of language acquisition in Large Language Models (LLMs) is crucial for uncovering how statistical representations evolve into structured linguistic capabilities. However, most existing studies focus primarily on fully trained models, leaving the developmental trajectory across intermediate training stages largely underexplored. In this work, we leverage intermediate checkpoints from open-source models (e.g., Pythia and OLMo) under teacher-forcing evaluation to systematically investigate language acquisition across training steps and model scales. We focus on four core characteristics: morphological structure acquisition, embedding drift, repetition dominance, and co-occurrence effects. Our findings reveal that models acquire morphological structures well before semantic embeddings stabilize. Furthermore, we show that training dataset size has a positive impact on divergence recognition, while co-occurrence during pre-training and repetition during inference have a negative impact on divergence recognition and associative link generation.

items.title: Beyond Time Induction: Structured Conditional Neural Solvers for Parametric Stochastic-Volatility Pricing
items.content: arXiv:2610.19254v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Physics-informed neural networks provide a flexible framework for learning parametric PDE solution families without labeled data, yet preserving accurate derivatives across heterogeneous regimes remains challenging. Structured neural solvers offer compact representations, but restrictive conditional parameterizations can limit adaptation across the solution family. We introduce BeTINN, a structured conditional architecture extending time-induced modulation through multi-directional time-parameter conditioning and a joint residual pathway. We evaluate BeTINN on the Heston stochastic-volatility PDE, a demanding parametric problem with mixed derivatives and economically relevant first- and second-order sensitivities. items.title: CktHGVAE: A Symmetric Design/State Heterogeneous Graph Variational Autoencoder for Transistor-level Analog/Mixed-signal Circuit Design and Analysis
items.content: arXiv:2610.19508v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We propose CktHGVAE, a heterogeneous graph variational autoencoder for transistor-level analog/mixedsignal CMOS circuits that takes not only design variables but also state variables as its inputs and outputs. With a single hyperparameter configuration without topology-specific tuning, comparison between model-generated and SPICE-simulated circuit operational states gives median R2 values above 0.9 for typical single-ended voltage amplifiers and the CMOS inverter, and 0.81-0.96 for differential amplifiers with larger datasets. Latent-space optimization in the PCA-reduced latent space with Bayesian optimization, evolutionary search, random search, and quasi-exhaustive search is demonstrated for a common-source voltage amplifier with NMOS input and resistive load, where the objective function is defined as a penalty for deviation from required circuit specifications. For each search strategy, 93.3 - 100% of all design candidates suggested by the model satisfy the required circuit specifications at the decoder output, and SPICE simulations verify that 90 - 100% of them indeed satisfy the requirements. The model pretrained on a batch of topologies can be transferred to unseen topologies without retraining at all, with zero-shot reconstruction median R2 values of 0.72-0.90 in three of four scenarios, including transfer from single-ended to differential topologies, although the transfer fidelity depends on the choice of pretraining topologies. Our demonstrations suggest that the proposed model can potentially serve as a basis for AMS CMOS circuit design automation.

items.title: NeuroDETR: Multiscale Discrete Spatiotemporal Tokenization for Asynchronous EEG Event Detection
items.content: arXiv:2610.20349v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Asynchronous EEG event detection supports practical brain-computer interfaces by identifying event classes and temporal boundaries directly from continuous recordings without predefined event boundaries at inference time. The primary challenge lies in extracting event-related patterns embedded in ongoing background activity. To address this, we propose \textbf{NeuroDETR}, a discrete spatiotemporal multiscale framework that combines structured tokenization with event-aware feature refinement. Multiscale temporal codebooks capture brief responses and sustained dynamics, while Spatial-Pyramid VQ hierarchically encodes spatial structure across EEG channels. These complementary representations form a compact event memory for jointly classifying events and estimating their onsets and offsets. Before tokenization, we apply FOCAL, an event-aware sparse attention module that uses predicted event presence to guide temporal feature refinement and spatial aggregation, emphasizing likely event periods while preserving context across the recording. Experiments on eight EEG datasets that span diverse paradigms demonstrate state-of-the-art performance. These findings provide a basis for the development of BCI systems that recognize meaningful neural activity during continuous interaction and monitoring.

items.title: An Initial Study of Physiological Markers for Deepfake Speech Detection
items.content: arXiv:2610.18934v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Conventional deepfake speech detectors primarily target synthesis artifacts and often degrade under unseen attacks or recording conditions. Human speech, however, contains physiological markers associated with respiration, phonation, and temporal coordination arising from the speech-production system that synthesizers may not reproduce faithfully. This motivates the hypothesis that deepfake speech can be detected by identifying inconsistencies in these patterns, which we test using 36 handcrafted physiological markers organized into respiratory, vocal, and temporal categories. We evaluate the marker vectors with logistic regression and SVM classifiers on pooled English recordings. The best in-domain system achieves a 21.40% equal error rate (EER), while logistic regression achieves 32.77% on the out-of-domain dataset pair. Since the markers describe specific speech-production properties, the logistic-regression coefficients indicate whether higher marker values push the classifier toward bona fide or deepfake speech. These results provide initial evidence that physiological markers offer a useful, interpretable signal for deepfake speech detection.

items.title: Noisy-Label Calibration with Multiple Unreliable Labels
items.content: arXiv:2610.19543v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In medical annotation and crowdsourcing, multiple annotators assign labels to each example, but these labels may be incorrect. Treating such noisy labels as ground truth can bias calibration evaluation. To address this problem, we propose methods for evaluating and recalibrating a fixed binary predictor under the underlying clean-label distribution, using only noisy annotations. First, given annotator-specific noise probabilities, we propose Noise Corrected ECE (NC-ECE), a binned estimator of expected calibration error (ECE) under class-conditional noise. We derive non-asymptotic bounds on the estimator's bias. Then, we propose practical algorithms for estimating unknown noise probabilities under conditional independence and label-orientation assumptions. We also develop loss-based and histogram post-hoc recalibration with clean-risk and calibration guarantees, respectively. Experiments on semi-synthetic benchmarks show that the proposed ECE estimator closely tracks its clean-label oracle counterpart and that the recalibration methods substantially improve latent-label calibration, whereas uncorrected recalibration against noisy annotations can degrade it.

It addresses a real gap in trustworthy model evaluation under label noise.

items.title: Multimodal Medical Image Parsing with Task-Specific Low-Rank Adapters
items.content: arXiv:2610.19901v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Adapting a single vision-language model to medical image parsing requires training choices that reflect the demands of each task. We study task-specific adaptation with Qwen3.5-9B for FLARE 2026 Task 3, covering six task families and seven imaging modalities. Our system couples a shared, frozen 4-bit backbone with LoRA adapters selected from the input question. We customize adapter ranks and prompts, rebalance rare classification targets, and supplement regression training with dermatology classification examples. On the fixed internal holdout, the task-specific adapters achieve a dataset-macro balanced accuracy of 0.7791 for classification, a dataset-macro micro-F1 of 0.6286 for multi-label classification, a counting mean absolute error (MAE) of 11.73, a dataset-macro detection F1 of 0.8914, a dataset-macro regression MAE of 9.78, and a report-generation CRIMSON score of 0.8204. On the organizer's 1,703-example hidden-validation set, the submitted system achieves 0.8496 classification balanced accuracy, 0.5338 sample-averaged multi-label F1, and 14.5950 regression MAE. The final 30.1 GB container averages 3.1 seconds per case, including model loading, and produces identical outputs across repeated verification runs. The benefits vary across tasks, supporting the use of task-specific adapter configurations and image budgets within a shared medical vision-language model. Code is available at https://github.com/TahaSabir0/FLARE26-Hexapus.

items.title: Extreme-Scale Super-Resolution of Homogeneous Turbulence from a Single Realization
items.content: arXiv:2610.20305v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Homogeneous turbulent flows exhibit recurring multiscale structures across spatially separated regions, suggesting that a single flow realization may contain sufficient information to learn representations of unresolved scales. We investigate this hypothesis through an extreme super-resolution framework in which a wide-activation deep super-resolution (WDSR) network is trained exclusively on overlapping patches extracted from a single high-resolution turbulent realization. Previously unseen flow fields are reconstructed through patchwise prediction followed by Hann-window-weighted overlap-add assembly. The framework is evaluated for two-dimensional homogeneous isotropic turbulence at super-resolution factors of x32 and x64, representing severe spatial under-resolution. Despite the limited training data, the proposed approach reconstructs coherent vortical structures and recovers fine-scale features more accurately than conventional interpolation. Spectral and statistical analyses further demonstrate improved recovery of high-wavenumber energy content and multiscale flow characteristics. To assess the effectiveness of exploiting internal spatial information, we compare the proposed framework against WDSR models trained on 1, 25, 50, and 100 complete high-resolution snapshots without patch extraction. This comparison distinguishes the benefits of localized learning from those associated with increasing the number of training realizations. The results demonstrate that exploiting spatial redundancy within a single turbulent realization enables accurate reconstruction of previously unseen flow fields, even under extreme spatial under-resolution. These findings establish single-realization patch-based learning as a promising data-efficient approach for turbulent super-resolution when high-resolution training data are scarce.

items.title: Learning What to Keep: Transfer-Aware Personal Skill Learning from User Feedback
items.content: arXiv:2610.19380v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: User feedback enables LLMs to refine reusable personalized skills, but often mixes persistent preferences with request-specific corrections. Indiscriminately retaining both risks negative transfer, motivating selective retention at the level of individual requirements. We frame this challenge as selective transfer over atomic rules and propose SkillGrain, a framework for learning reusable personalized skills from user feedback. SkillGrain decomposes feedback into independently actionable rules, predicts their transferability, and retains only those suitable for future requests. To learn these decisions, we combine rubric-guided skill rewards with fine-grained credit assignment that separately evaluates rule content and retention decisions. We further jointly optimize skill induction and skill-conditioned generation through reinforcement learning, ensuring that learned skills support downstream personalization. We construct a benchmark spanning five personalized writing tasks to evaluate cross-request generalization. Experiments across three base models in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings show that SkillGrain achieves the best overall average performance among competing methods.

items.title: RCCM: Diagnosing Gains and Harms in Reasoning-Prompt Transfer
items.content: arXiv:2610.19872v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: A reasoning prompt can improve one deployment and degrade another. RCCM (Reasoning-Control Capability Mismatch) examines these reversals by pairing answers to the same questions with records of how generation ends. Across five open-weight deployments and nine strategies, aggregate accuracy hides substantial question-level gains and harms; a common-budget MATH500 evaluation examines transfer on a separate sample. On 60 additional questions, concise reasoning improves Phi's automatic answer matching at a 2,048-token cap across three collections, but sharply reduces Qwen's. Author-reviewed final-answer commitments give a smaller, statistically unresolved Phi gain. Reserving an answer stage also improves matching, with additional input and call costs. These results show why a prompt benefit must be interpreted alongside its execution and evaluation: matching a reference answer need not mean delivering it, and an apparent compression benefit may admit another explanation. RCCM records this evidence for reproducible transfer comparisons.

items.title: VLX-Go: Robust Embodied Tracking through Multi-Stage Learning and On-Policy Refinement
items.content: arXiv:2610.19361v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Embodied visual tracking requires a robot to identify a designated target from visual observations and control its own motion to follow that target through an environment. Following an isolated person is a comparatively simple demonstration of embodied visual tracking, but following the intended person among distractors remains challenging. Existing methods exhibit a substantial drop in success from single-target to distractor tracking, motivating a focus on the shared spaces that person-following robots must navigate. We present \method{}, a vision--language waypoint policy built around the hypothesis that visual and language representations should be aligned before tracking-specific motion is learned. The policy combines complementary frozen visual encoders, multiscale temporal context, a transformer backbone, and a lightweight head for robot-centric waypoint prediction. Its training progresses through vision--language alignment, multimodal reasoning mid-training, and tracking specialization on 19,532 oracle episodes. Compared with 41.54\% distractor-tracking success for our earlier OmTrackVLA model, the complete multi-stage recipe achieves 55.80\%. We then explore on-policy refinement using filtered oracle labels for states visited by the policy. This preliminary study adds 2.42 percentage points of distractor-tracking success, reaching 58.22\%, while reducing collision rate by 1.99 pts. The final policy records the highest distractor- and ambiguous-tracking success rates among the compared methods. These results support staged multimodal learning as a promising direction for tracking among distractors and motivate further study of on-policy refinement for person following in shared spaces.

It targets the large performance drop from single-target to distractor tracking in person-following.

This preliminary study adds 2.42 percentage points of distractor-tracking success, reaching 58.22\%, while reducing collision rate by 1.99 pts. The final policy records the highest distractor- and ambiguous-tracking success rates among the compared methods. These results support staged multimodal learning as a promising direction for tracking among distractors and motivate further study of on-policy refinement for person following in shared spaces.

items.title: Quantifying Annotation Agreement in Object Detection with Optimal Transport
items.content: arXiv:2610.19912v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reliable validation of machine learning models is a crucial step in designing robust and trustworthy systems. Yet validation relies on annotated test sets treated as ground truth, even though annotations can be noisy or ambiguous. In object detection, sources may disagree on object presence, box location, or class label. Standard agreement metrics usually binarize box overlap before computing a summary score, obscuring the degree and structure of disagreement between annotation sets. Here, we study an Optimal Transport (OT)-based metric for measuring agreement between object detection annotations. Instead of binarizing bounding box overlap, this metric assigns graded costs to matched and unmatched labeled boxes. Through theoretical analysis and experiments on real and synthetically perturbed annotations, we show that OT captures graded changes in agreement and distinguishes annotation pairs that thresholded metrics score identically. Our results suggest that OT provides a richer measure of annotation agreement in object detection, especially for domains with many small or ambiguous objects. Such agreement estimates can support more reliable validation when labels are noisy or conflicting.

items.reasoning: A principled, theoretically grounded improvement to annotation quality assessment, an underrated reliability issue in ML validation. Optimal transport for matching is well-trodden, but applying it with graded costs to annotation disagreement analysis is a nice, useful contribution with modest scope.

items.title: F2A-ObjectNav: An Adaptive Agentic Architecture for Object-Goal Navigation
items.content: arXiv:2610.19618v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Object-goal navigation requires an embodied agent to explore an unfamiliar environment, identify a target object, navigate toward candidate instances, and reliably determine whether the observed object satisfies the mission goal. This work investigates this problem through a two-stage development process. In Stage I, a fixed modular framework is used to examine combinations of exploration, object detection, and target validation methods. The results reveal clear trade-offs among navigation performance, validation reliability, execution time, and model-related cost, with no single fixed configuration remaining preferable across all evaluated conditions. These observations motivate F2A-ObjectNav (Fixed-to-Adaptive Object-Goal Navigation), an adaptive agentic architecture in which a rule-based Supervisor coordinates specialized components for navigation and exploration, object detection, target validation, semantic guidance, and Mission Memory. The architecture uses event-driven recovery, strategy revision, candidate management, and conditional semantic guidance while retaining lightweight execution during normal operation. F2A-ObjectNav is evaluated over 25 episodes in each of AI2-THOR, RoboTHOR, and ProcTHOR, achieving success rate (SR) / success-weighted path length (SPL) values of 0.84/0.52, 0.40/0.22, and 0.44/0.37, respectively. In addition to task-level metrics, architecture-specific behavioral metrics are used to characterize semantic-guidance usage, strategy switching, recovery activation, memory-supported behavior, and decision stability. The results show different patterns of adaptive intervention across the three environments, with higher intervention frequencies observed in RoboTHOR and ProcTHOR than in AI2-THOR.

items.reasoning: The empirical finding that no single configuration dominates across conditions is useful, and adaptive composition is a sensible response, but the overall approach builds on established modular navigation pipelines and LLM-based agent patterns without a clearly novel mechanism.

items.title: RASSG: Repair-Aware Semantic Survival Gating for Streaming Tool Execution
items.content: arXiv:2610.14659v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Streaming speech assistants can launch tools before users finish speaking, overlapping execution with incoming speech to reduce user waiting time. However, subsequent self-corrections can invalidate apparently stable arguments, causing stale execution whose irreversible effects persist even after the final call is corrected. We propose Repair-Aware Semantic Survival Gating (RASSG) to jointly control tool launch and cancellation during streaming speech. RASSG launches a tool when three consecutive speech recognition results arrive with identical nonempty arguments, then combines calibrated argument invalidity risk with execution costs to decide cancellation at the last feasible opportunity before effects become irreversible. Evaluation on ReCAST, FDB-v3, and Audio2Tool uses a controlled execution clock with fixed tool runtimes and cancellation parameters. On ReCAST's prospective-repair subset, RASSG reduces the stale execution rate from LocalAgreement-2's 50.00% to 3.15%, with a mean delay of 3.676s across successful trajectories. The stale reduction also holds against every early-execution baseline on both public speech datasets. Ablations with identical initial launches support active cancellation, showing the value of controlling ongoing calls before their effects become irreversible. Code and data are available at https://github.com/daijinhu/RASSG.

items.reasoning: A focused, practical solution to a real safety/timing problem in voice agents as tool-calling becomes mainstream. The risk-cost gating is sensible; the niche scenario limits breadth but the problem framing is valuable as agents become proactive.

items.title: Theoretical and Practical Advances in Hierarchical Bayesian Deep Learning Methodology
items.content: arXiv:2610.19074v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reliable uncertainty quantification remains an important challenge in AI. Hierarchical Bayesian methods provide a principled framework for this by representing unknown quantities through posterior distributions. Joint inference of neural-network parameters and prior hyperparameters is challenging for conventional Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods due to strong dependencies. In this work, we introduce the multilevel particle marginal Metropolis-Hastings (MLPMMH) method, which combines pseudo-marginal inference for the hyperparameters with coupled sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) across hierarchy of network-width truncations for conditional parameter inference. The hierarchy is induced by a trace-class neural network (TNN) prior with width-dependent decay, motivated empirically by the compressible structure observed in trained neural-network parameters. Under standard multilevel coupling assumptions, we establish that MLPMMH achieves mean-square error (MSE) $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^2)$ at expected computational cost $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$, and verify the predicted rate on a Bayesian regression problem. To address larger-scale applications, we further introduce S-MLPMMH, a practical approximation that replaces the exact sampling components with a PCA-based hierarchy and scalable Bayesian Monte Carlo. Experiments on MNIST demonstrate competitive predictive performance and uncertainty quantification while exploiting the parallel structure of the approximation. Software has been made publicly available at https://github.com/submission-code-anon/mlpmmh-anon.

This targets reliable uncertainty quantification where conventional MCMC struggles with strong dependencies.
items.reasoning: Rigorous Bayesian methodology with a genuine sampling-algorithm contribution, but the audience is specialized (Bayesian deep learning methodology), and practical scalability of such methods to modern-scale networks remains questionable.

items.title: KoAGE: Do Large Language Models Know, Learn, and Coin Korean Neologisms?
items.content: arXiv:2610.19399v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Korean neologisms arise through diverse mechanisms, a demanding test of language models beyond lexical memorization. To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce NeoTrace, an automated, rerunnable framework that collects and dates neologisms across genres. Its 4,271 entries support KoAGE, a cutoff-aware benchmark with three acquisition and two generation tasks---the latter, to our knowledge, the first to compare model coinages with attested neologisms under their original materials and community context. Across 21 models, lexical recall diverges from contextual inference: in a five-model temporal analysis, models define only 13-30% of cutoff-year words, yet can infer meaning from one usage. However, structural understanding remains limited: even correct definitions barely improve formation analysis of pre-cutoff neologisms. Given word-building materials, single models often follow human formation mechanisms, whereas multi-agent coinage favors abbreviation and depends on interaction framing. KoAGE thus separates what models know, learn from use, and coin.

items.title: CB-Agent: Concept-Based In-Context Learning for Sequential Action Selection
items.content: arXiv:2610.14574v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) allows large language models to use demonstrations without updating their parameters. For interactive agents, demonstrations are trajectories of reasoning, actions, and observations that illustrate how to complete a task. Reusing demonstrations in new situations is challenging: directly inputting full trajectories consumes limited prompt space and constrains the overall effectiveness, while natural-language summaries require the agent to translate general guidance into specific action choices. Therefore, we study whether expert action choices can directly supervise a reusable scoring rule. We propose CB-Agent, which extends concept-based ICL to sequential action selection. We extract environment-action decisions from expert trajectories and fit a concept vector by maximum likelihood to model the conditional distribution over candidate actions given the context. This model combines the concept with frozen language-model features and priors. During ReAct interaction, the agent uses this distribution to select environment actions without including demonstrations in the action-scoring context. Across TextWorld, ALFWorld, and ScienceWorld, CB-Agent achieves the highest cross-benchmark average among the evaluated methods at all three tested model sizes and ranks first on TextWorld and ScienceWorld at each size. ALFWorld experiments support the learned concept's contribution beyond prior-only scoring and show further gains when combined with Reflexion. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CB-Agent-DFF9/.
items.author: Qingyue Zhang, Huaze Tang, Minyu Zhang, Yuxiang Yan, Wenbo Ding, Shao-Lun Huang
items.summary: CB-Agent extends concept-based in-context learning to sequential action selection for LLM agents, extracting environment-action decisions from expert trajectories into reusable concepts rather than feeding full demonstrations or vague natural-language summaries. This lets expert action choices directly supervise a reusable scoring rule while conserving prompt space.
items.reasoning: A practical answer to a real bottleneck in in-context learning for agents (prompt limits and summary-to-action translation). The approach is sensible but incremental relative to existing concept-based ICL work.

items.title: GREAT-ESDD: Graph Edge Attention Network for Effectively Steered Delivery Decisions
items.content: arXiv:2610.14792v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Online, same-day delivery requires operators to constantly update their routes, and the routing cost for deliveries increases with the number of customers. Out-of-home (OOH) delivery options can help companies handle increasing customer numbers while keeping delivery costs low. We develop a dynamic pricing-and-routing framework for this online ordering scenario with home and OOH delivery options. First, we develop a neural solver for the capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) based on the Graph-Edge-Attention-Network (GREAT). We train it to solve CVRP with varying instance sizes and starting conditions, allowing it to reoptimize partially executed routes under changing conditions. It is fast while achieving solution quality competitive with traditional baselines. Our solver processes several CVRP instances in parallel in batches and we use it to solve the candidate routing problems that arise from an incoming customer's choice of home or OOH delivery. This provides an estimate of the delivery cost increase per option, which we use to set dynamic prices. Further, it directly provides the updated route once the customer decides. We trade off delivery fees against routing costs and steer customers toward OOH delivery when home delivery would be costly. However, effective steering requires us to know the customer preferences. To learn those online, we use Thompson sampling with a Laplace-approximated posterior. We call the resulting framework GREAT-ESDD (GREAT for Effectively Steered Delivery Decisions). Compared to a traditional routing solver, it increases profit by around 11% under a similar pricing decision time budget. Moreover, we show that we can estimate customer preferences successfully, outperforming a static pricing strategy after only 5 days of simulated operations.

items.title: Continuous Risk-Based Scheduling for Food Safety Inspection: Integrating Historical Decay with Event-Driven Consumer Review Signals
items.content: arXiv:2610.15191v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Batch risk-based inspection scheduling struggles to detect a critical failure class: food facilities with recent clean inspections that subsequently develop severe violations. Traditional systems recompute risk on fixed planning cycles using static historical data, leaving blind spots between inspection cycles. To address this, we introduce the Continuous Inspection Risk (CIR) system, an event-driven scheduling pipeline that re-ranks the inspection queue dynamically as new data arrives. CIR combines a decay-weighted historical score with a stream of real-time consumer reviews triaged by a language-model classifier. A key structural contribution is our temporal partition rule, which strictly excludes reviews predating the most recent inspection to prevent superseded signals from skewing current risk. Evaluating CIR on 9,505 routine inspections in Santa Clara County, California (2024-2026), we show that history-based scoring alone reduces mean time-to-detection of major violations by 69 days (20.9%) under a 30% inspection budget, but fails to anticipate severe vermin-related closures (0/8 detected). Incorporating post-inspection review signals drastically improves performance, predicting 7 of 8 vermin closures with an average lead time of 117 days-firing on the exact day of review publication in four instances. Introducing a review corroboration rule improves precision from 0.70 to 0.78 without loss of recall. Finally, we analyze critical implementation challenges, documenting a data-hygiene pitfall (stale review leakage across inspection boundaries) and an evaluation limitation involving unobserved facility self-remediation. This work provides the first case-level evaluation of event-driven inspection triggering using open data and provides a reproducible benchmark for review-augmented public health systems

A temporal partition rule excludes reviews predating the latest inspection to prevent data leakage, targeting facilities that deteriorate between clean inspections.

items.title: OntoAR-HAR: Ontology-Guided Agentic RAG with Personalized Memory for Human Activity Recognition
items.content: arXiv:2610.15292v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: LLMs increasingly support sensor-based human activity recognition (HAR) by linking motion signals with activity semantics and physical knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds decisions in sensor examples and domain features, enabling training-free target-user inference with less dependence on raw numerical arrays. However, existing LLM/RAG-based HAR typically searches single-level activity spaces using static population knowledge. Consequently, they compare many unrelated candidates using the same static population evidence and overlook personalized motion patterns. We propose OntoAR-HAR, an ontology-guided agentic RAG framework combining static population and personalized knowledge. Its tree-structured activity ontology decomposes classification into local decisions among semantically related activities. The static store supplies node-constrained examples, while offline-discovered executable signal features provide numerical evidence for local distinctions. During inference, the personalized store collects selected user observations, which the LLM integrates with static knowledge and signal features while traversing the ontology to an activity label. Cross-subject and heterogeneous-sensing experiments show complementary gains from hierarchical retrieval and personalized memory across multiple LLM backbones, achieving state-of-the-art performance. By explicitly modeling hierarchical relations across activity granularities, OntoAR-HAR also addresses the long-overlooked semantic inclusion problem and avoids treating related labels as independent categories.

A tree-structured activity ontology decomposes the activity space to avoid comparing unrelated candidates using uniform population evidence. Enables training-free, target-user inference.
items.reasoning: A competent applied contribution combining several known techniques (ontology, RAG, personalization) in a niche domain. Novelty is incremental and impact is likely confined to HAR and ubiquitous computing communities.

Cross-subject and heterogeneous-sensing experiments show complementary gains from hierarchical retrieval and personalized memory across multiple LLM backbones, achieving state-of-the-art performance. By explicitly modeling hierarchical relations across activity granularities, OntoAR-HAR also addresses the long-overlooked semantic inclusion problem and avoids treating related labels as independent categories.

items.title: Comparative Study of Canvas- and Coordinate-Based Geometry-Conditioned Neural Networks for Real-Time Prediction of Indoor Environments with Varying Room Dimensions
items.content: arXiv:2610.15885v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) is computationally expensive for iterative building design. Deep learning surrogates offer faster predictions, but generalization across varying room dimensions remains challenging. This study compares two geometry-conditioned neural network surrogate models for rapid indoor airflow and temperature field prediction under varying room sizes. During the architectural design stage, this method is relevant for real-time assessment of whether conditioned supply air will effectively provide fresh and cool air throughout rooms with varying heights and lengths. The canvas-based neural network (CaNN) explicitly encodes room size by preserving different occupied regions within a fixed canvas, whereas the coordinate-based neural network (CoNN) uses normalized coordinate channels. Both employ U-Net autoencoders to separately predict airflow and temperature fields. Evaluation uses simplified rooms with varying heights and lengths as a controlled benchmark. The results show that CaNN achieves higher agreement with CFD results than CoNN, demonstrating its potential to support performance-driven building design.

The comparison targets real-time assessment of whether conditioned supply air effectively covers rooms of different sizes.

items.title: When a Conceptor Complement Becomes Gain: Operator Geometry and Behavioral Attribution in Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.16325v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: When a steering intervention changes a language model's behavior, which part of the intervention deserves the credit? We test this question for a target-centered, scaled conceptor complement by removing its fitted covariance filter while preserving the same target-specific center and gain. At the original aperture $\alpha=.05$ and gain $\beta=2$, all 21 fitted maps across three models and seven targets expand every direction at the generation intervention layers. The matrix correction is $0.093\%$--$7.815\%$ of the matched-control displacement on held-out extraction activations. In 480 paired comparisons within a 1,920-response study, retaining the matrix changes many individual texts but does not establish a consistent additional target-suppression benefit on the four-target panel. A geometric aperture sweep shows that the operating regime changes with the filter setting. Separately, an invertible soft filter preserves what an unrestricted affine readout can recover, whereas dedicated erasure methods reduce prediction by newly fitted probes. Together, the results show why a whole-intervention comparison cannot by itself attribute generated behavior to the fitted matrix: analyze the complete transformation, hold shared components fixed, and test its output consequences directly.

items.summary: This work examines which component of a conceptor-based steering intervention causes behavioral change in language models, by removing its fitted covariance filter while preserving target-specific center and gain. items.reasoning: A careful mechanistic-attribution study with a reasonably large paired comparison (480 comparisons, 1,920 responses), providing useful negative results for activation-steering methodology. items.title: Does the Explanation Drift Before the Guarantee? Label-Free Early Warning on Evolving Graphs
items.content: arXiv:2610.16534v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Deployed models can fail silently as the world they describe evolves. Attribution drift has served as an early warning in tabular data; we ask whether, in graph streams, a model's own explanations can forewarn the loss of nominal conformal coverage. Doing so requires repairing the naive drift statistic twice. A vanishing edge loses mask mass regardless of whether the model relied on it, so we condition the importance on edge presence. Evolving graphs also break edge identity: a relabelling that changes nothing shifts the identity-based statistic by 0.69 on synthetic graphs and 0.83 on real ego-networks, whereas aggregating over structural roles brings both to 0.0 and stays well-defined when the support changes. We test six pre-registered regimes on thirty seeds each. A two-channel monitor, tracking conditional mask mass and its distribution over roles, precedes coverage collapse by 8 to 14.5 steps across four gradual regimes (node addition, removal, replacement, and edge thinning), all surviving Holm correction. A sudden knockout yields the expected zero lead, and a harmless change triggers no alarm. Leads track the length of the transitional phase (Spearman 0.79 over 150 runs). On real transaction ego-networks, the untuned mass channel forewarns staged drift by 27 steps and is the only channel, attributional or structural, that never alarms on a stationary stream. The main limitation is that the mass channel is blind to covariate drift, which breaks the guarantee in every run; the distributional channel detects it and also rescues the rewiring regime, so we report the two channels separately rather than as a union.

items.summary: The paper studies whether attribution drift on graph streams can serve as a label-free early warning for the loss of conformal prediction coverage. items.reasoning: A careful, statistically disciplined contribution connecting explainability and conformal guarantees in the underexplored evolving-graph setting; pre-registration of configurations is a methodological plus. Niche topic with specialized audience and moderate empirical scope.

items.title: PRAISE: A Reproducible Workflow for Non-Programmer Scientists to Implement Published AI Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.16980v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) models are increasingly developed, published and used across scientific fields. Researchers, students and industry professionals who want to apply these models to their own research questions often lack the programming and data science expertise to do so. Existing guidelines cover single steps, but not the route from a published model to working predictions on one's own data. Here we present the hands-on workflow PRAISE, a Practical, Reproducible AI-model Implementation for Science and Education, that helps non-programmers implement published AI models step by step. Because implementations rarely work the first time, PRAISE anticipates common failures and provides a fallback route for each. As a proof of principle, three BSc chemistry students and their tutor applied PRAISE without prior programming or data science knowledge. They reproduced, validated and extended a state-of-the-art model that predicts enzyme-substrate interactions. This shows that with PRAISE, implementing an AI model from the literature becomes a learnable skill, one that turns non-programmer scientists from users into evaluators and improvers of AI models.

items.summary: PRAISE is a hands-on, step-by-step workflow helping non-programmer scientists and students implement published AI models on their own data, anticipating common implementation failures and providing a fallback route for each. It bridges the gap between single-step guidelines and the full route from a published model to working predictions, demonstrated as a proof of principle.
items.reasoning: Addresses a real accessibility problem in science and education with practical documentation value, but it is a workflow/educational contribution rather than novel technical research. Its impact is limited to adoption within target communities rather than advancing AI methodology.

items.title: Reliable Text-to-SQL in Resource-Constrained Settings with Small LLMs via Iterative Retry Workflows
items.content: arXiv:2610.17305v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently improved Text-to-SQL generation, but their computational cost can hinder deployment in resource-constrained settings. This paper evaluates the Text-to-SQL capabilities of small and medium open-source LLMs (1B-8B parameters) under a controlled inference budget, focusing on how model specialization and prompt formulation affect performance. Using the Spider benchmark, we compare multiple prompt representations and assess the accuracy of generated queries. Our results show that SQL-specialized models are consistently more reliable than general-purpose and chat-oriented models at small scales, and that performance can vary substantially depending on the prompt used. To reduce this variability without resorting to larger models, we introduce three lightweight inference workflows that automatically retry with alternative prompts and/or models when failures occur, including an optional syntax-correction step. These workflows significantly improve end-to-end success rates, with a trade-off in additional inference calls. These results demonstrate a practical path to stronger Text-to-SQL performance with small LLMs, by trading modest additional inference cost for higher reliability.

items.summary: The paper evaluates small and medium open-source LLMs (1B-8B) for text-to-SQL under controlled inference budgets on Spider, finding SQL-specialized models consistently more reliable than general-purpose ones and high prompt sensitivity. An iterative retry workflow reduces this variability without retraining.
items.reasoning: Useful practical guidance for deploying text-to-SQL on modest hardware, with a sensible lightweight mitigation. The contribution is mostly empirical and engineering-oriented with limited methodological novelty, and it relies on a single well-worn benchmark.

items.title: AgentStripes: An Evidence-Graded Maturity Model for AI Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.18603v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Benchmarks report what an Artificial Intelligence (AI) agent can do on a task suite, but not whether one released version has been engineered with the controls that make it reliable, safe and observable, or how strongly that is shown. This paper proposes AgentStripes, an evidence-graded maturity model for AI agents. It defines levels (0 to 7 stripes), process areas (12 areas holding 40 capabilities), three gates (basic, safety, proof) that hold an agent at a level however high its score, and evidence grades E0 to E5. Each applicable capability receives a rating from 0 to 3 and a separate evidence level; these are combined into a credit, aggregated into a severity-weighted score and converted into stripes that the gates limit. Instruments gather evidence, language-model judges interpret it under explicit criteria, and the arithmetic is deterministic. The model is compared with standards at topic level without a claim of conformance, and an unexecuted validation protocol is specified. An empirical evaluation (exploratory, non-confirmatory) of 30 public Python agent repositories, with static evidence only, is a demonstration and not a validation: static evidence caps every final stripe at 2, 26 repositories end at one stripe and 4 at two, and this distinction is unreliable, since re-judging changed the final stripe of 4 of 22 repositories (engine, dossier and panel changed), whereas none of 8 panel-only repeats, all at stripe 1, changed. The parameters are expert conventions without outcome based calibration, and the stripes have not been shown to predict reliability or safety.

Capabilities receive ratings and evidence levels combined into severity-weighted scores, providing a framework for assessing whether released agent versions have reliable, safe, and observable engineering controls.
items.reasoning: Addresses a real gap in assessing agent engineering maturity beyond benchmark scores, and the gate/evidence structure is thoughtful; however, it is a proposal-style framework whose adoption and empirical validation remain unproven.

items.title: AesCode: Aesthetic Code Generation with Decoupled Cross-Modal Rewards
items.content: arXiv:2610.18860v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Generating information-rich visual artifacts such as slides, posters, and dashboards as code is appealing because the outputs are structured, editable, and verifiable. Yet code models cannot see how their choices of layout and color come together on the canvas, often limiting spatial planning and aesthetic quality. Image generators excel at visual design but can misrender requested content, making their outputs unreliable targets for direct reproduction. We therefore introduce AesCode, which generates code grounded in the content prompt while using an image generated from the same prompt as an aesthetic guidance. To do so, AesCode represents the target as a design graph that describes the whole canvas and makes each property attributable. From this graph, we derive complementary cross-modal rewards: deterministic verifiers score properties parsable from code and rendering, while a VLM judge assesses the non-parsable ones with a sample-specific Visual Graph Rubric (VGR) tied to graph elements and relations. We optimize these decoupled rewards through reinforcement learning with per-channel normalization to jointly improve spatial planning, aesthetic quality, and verifiable correctness. To evaluate this setting, we build a benchmark that scores verifiable correctness and visual quality separately, with visual scores highly consistent with human judgments. We find that reference images substantially improve the visual quality of code generated by existing models, and ablations show that AesCode benefits from references both as model input and as a source of visual rewards. Relative to same-scale Qwen3-VL baselines given the same references, AesCode-8B and AesCode-32B improve visual quality by 31.1 and 22.4 percentage points, reaching scores comparable to those of closed-source frontier models such as GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8.
items.author: Xin Gao, Yifan Yang, Xin Li, Pan Wang, Yan Li, Muzhao Tian, Mingxi Cheng, Bei Liu, Kai Qiu, Qi Dai, Dong Chen, Yue Dong, Leandros Tassiulas, Rex Ying, Ji Li, Chong Luo

It represents the target canvas as a design graph so that layout and color properties are individually attributable, enabling decoupled cross-modal rewards for training. This targets the gap where code models cannot see the visual result of their choices.
items.reasoning: Interesting combination of image generators and code generation for verifiable visual artifacts, with a structured design-graph representation enabling attribution and reward decomposition. The Microsoft-affiliated author list adds credibility, but the application niche is specific and evaluation of aesthetics is inherently subjective.

items.title: Jevolution: A Framework for Studying Communication and Collective Dynamics in AI Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.14449v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Experiments with remote decision-making agents depend on more than the policy: the world may change during inference, the simulator determines which actions are available, and births and immigration alter who can act. We present Jevolution, an instrumented spatial predator-prey framework that makes these dependencies explicit. Its reference implementation separates the evolving world, asynchronous request scheduling, controller adapters, and experiment records. The model combines local observations, energy and resource constraints, predefined signals, and inherited scalar traits. We describe these mechanisms using the ODD protocol and distinguish implemented controls from research questions requiring additional interventions. Free synthetic fixtures exercise scheduling, signaling, and inheritance against the pinned implementation; they validate specified software behavior rather than model intelligence or ecological realism. A completed communication case study illustrates the end-to-end workflow using Jev to control both species. Across 6 complete habitat-seed pairs, the mean signals-on minus signals-off difference in normalized rabbit abundance was -0.0095 (nominal 95% pair-bootstrap interval [-0.0772, 0.0602]). This small study does not resolve the direction of the signal-system effect. The contribution is an inspectable experimental system and its evidence boundaries, not a new policy-learning algorithm or a demonstration of emergent language, adaptive selection, or biological predictive validity.

items.title: Depth-progressive 3D seismic velocity model building via 2D generative diffusion models
items.content: arXiv:2610.14812v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) velocity model building (VMB) remains computationally challenging with conventional approaches and native 3D neural networks, largely due to the prohibitive memory and training cost of full 3D formulations. Therefore, we introduce a depth-progressive framework that achieves 3D VMB using 2D generative diffusion models through a depth-as-channel formulation, in which the depth dimension of each 3D velocity patch is mapped to the channel dimension of a 2D U-Net. This allows the model to synthesize overlapping depth patches sequentially from shallow to deep while conditioning the prediction of the deeper patch on the shallower one, as well as on any available geophysical constraints, including well logs and structural attributes. During training, paired shallow-deep patch pairs with randomized overlaps are used to teach the network how deeper velocity structures relate to shallower information, and a classifier-free guidance strategy enables the model to handle missing constraints gracefully. At inference, starting from a shallow velocity prior, the model recursively generates deeper patches in a top-down manner, and a depth-attenuated Gaussian blending scheme merges overlapping predictions into spatially coherent 3D volumes while accounting for the progressive accumulation of uncertainty at greater depths. Numerical experiments on both in-distribution benchmark models, including Overthrust, SEAM Arid, and SEG/EAGE, and the out-of-distribution Marmousi model demonstrate that the method effectively propagates shallow velocity priors downward and produces high-quality 3D velocity volumes across a range of geological settings and conditioning scenarios. Compared to a 3D benchmark of equivalent architecture, the proposed method significantly reduces parameter count, training cost, and inference cost, while maintaining superior VMB accuracy.

The depth-progressive framework synthesizes patches from shallow to deep, conditioning deeper predictions on shallower ones and on geophysical constraints like well logs.
items.reasoning: A clever memory-efficient formulation for a computationally hard geophysics problem; solid methodological contribution within a domain-specific application, but limited crossover impact on mainstream AI research.

Numerical experiments on both in-distribution benchmark models, including Overthrust, SEAM Arid, and SEG/EAGE, and the out-of-distribution Marmousi model demonstrate that the method effectively propagates shallow velocity priors downward and produces high-quality 3D velocity volumes across a range of geological settings and conditioning scenarios. Compared to a 3D benchmark of equivalent architecture, the proposed method significantly reduces parameter count, training cost, and inference cost, while maintaining superior VMB accuracy.

items.title: Dynamic Conflict Clustering with Lightweight Learning and Strategic Repair for Distributed Constraint Satisfaction
items.content: arXiv:2610.15658v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Distributed Constraint Satisfaction Problems (DCSPs) model distributed decision-making in multi-agent systems, where agents assign values to local variables while satisfying shared constraints. However, many DCSP solvers still rely on broad, repeated peer-to-peer communication and are largely reactive, with limited support for strategic coordination or learning. This increases communication overhead, can lead to stagnation, and reduces the success of hard instances. Hence, we propose Dynamic Conflict Clustering-Incomplete (DCC-Incomplete), a repair-based solver that combines conflict-centred decomposition, structured coordination, strategic repair, and lightweight learning for stagnation recovery. DCC-Incomplete groups the unsolved part of the problem into conflict clusters and restricts communication via a coordination layer to agents within the same conflict region. It also introduces memory-guided restart, enabling agents and clusters to pause, revise, and adapt repairs based on neighbouring conflict states. A thorough evaluation of DCC-Incomplete on distributed graph-colouring benchmarks with planted satisfying assignments shows that its memory-guided restart improves the success rate from 37.50% to 61.11%, reduces median runtime from 0.565s to 0.367s, and cuts median communication from 12.493 to 6.503 messages per constraint. These results suggest that dynamic conflict clustering, combined with lightweight strategic and learning-guided repair, improves both communication efficiency and robustness in incomplete DCSP solving.

items.title: Learning Multimodal Sensor Fusion with JEPA Representations for Breathing Activity and Pose Recognition
items.content: arXiv:2610.15891v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Predictive video representations do not by themselves specify how a multimodal system should handle missing sensors. We transfer frozen V-JEPA2 features to a set of heterogeneous sensors comprised by RGB video, depth video, and radar time series. A shared fusion model uses modality queries, fixed sensor slots, and explicit availability to classify breathing activity and pose from all seven non-empty sensor subsets. The contribution is a controlled evaluation of subset supervision, pooling capacity, and representation transfer on 39 OMuSense-23 subjects with five subject-group folds and three seeds. With matched downstream parameter counts, the final model reaches recording-level activity macro-F1 of $75.23%\pm0.60$ averaged across seven subsets. Supervising all subsets in each batch improves the matched query-pooling control by 1.923 percentage points (conditional 95% subject-bootstrap interval [0.647, 3.209]), while query pooling shows no clear advantage over matched mean pooling under balanced supervision. Radar probes support transfer beyond pooled wavelet pixels, 64-token inference approximately preserves mean activity performance, and the tested Consensus-JEPA loss adds no measured benefit against its exact control.

items.title: OT-FlowRec: Optimal Transport-Guided Multi-Bridge Flow for Multimodal Sequential Recommendation
items.content: arXiv:2610.16038v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: E-commerce user preferences evolve dynamically within sessions, exhibiting concurrent and multi-centric interest distributions. While existing multimodal sequential recommendation methods leverage global attention to compress historical interactions, they inadequately capture the concurrent nature of multi-interest behaviors and fail to model the underlying multi-centric distribution of user intent. To tackle this issue, we propose OT-FlowRec, an optimal transport-guided multi-bridge flow matching framework that explicitly models multi-interest distributions to facilitate multimodal sequential recommendation. Unlike single-path generative models, OT-FlowRec constructs a mixture of parallel, interest-specific transport flows to model the multi-centric distribution characteristics, where each flow preserves a distinct user interest cluster via an optimal transport plan. Then, a geometric transport mechanism is designed to establish minimum-cost paths from the latent multi-interest distribution to target preference prototypes to provide multi-interest awareness. Moreover, a progressive time-sampling warmup strategy dynamically biases optimization weights toward the final states of the generation process, bridging the gap between continuous global distribution fitting and practical top-$k$ ranking metrics. This approach achieves explicit interest disentanglement, ensuring the preservation of a multi-peaked preference representation instead of collapsing it into a unimodal average. Extensive experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that OT-FlowRec outperforms existing state-of-the-art baselines.

items.title: KNN Implementation Details Can Dramatically Change Performance: An Example from Cover Trees
items.content: arXiv:2610.16940v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Nearest neighbor search algorithms are widely used and have a long history, but we find that key implementation details are seldom reviewed in articles about them. These details can materially impact performance, and thus change the conclusions one makes about a given algorithm's superiority. In this article, we highlight these impacts by reviewing the Cover Tree as an example, producing RustKNN, a unified Rust implementation of three construction variants of the Cover Tree with three query modes. Our analysis reveals: (1) the optimal query strategy depends on $k$ and on the dataset (single-tree search is fastest at $k{=}1$ on three of our four largest datasets, while dual-tree search is fastest at $k{\ge}5$ on the three largest), and choosing the wrong query mode can cost up to a $7.5\times$ factor in runtime; (2) the cover tree base parameter, set to 2 in theory and 1.3 in practice, is not a safe default for dual-tree search: 1.3 is optimal on only one of seven datasets, and on covtype it is $1.6\times$ slower than the optimum; (3) among five micro-optimizations, only early-exit distance computation has a consistent effect, and that effect grows with dimension (none at $d{=}32$, $1.31\times$ at $d{=}54$, and $1.49\times$ at $d{=}784$); and (4) all-nearest-neighbor and held-out benchmarks yield different implementation rankings. All main timing tables report medians over 20 independent allocations with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. RustKNN is open source at https://github.com/CrowdStrike/RustKNN.

items.summary: The paper shows that seldom-reviewed implementation details materially change nearest neighbor search performance, using the Cover Tree as a case study and releasing RustKNN, a unified Rust implementation of three construction variants and three query modes. items.title: AIPOCH Open-Science: An Open-Source AI Research Workbench with Reproducible .science Packages
items.content: arXiv:2610.17110v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: AI-assisted research leaves instructions, computations, artifact revisions and checks whose relationships matter when another researcher receives the work. We present AIPOCH Open-Science, an open-source research workbench with portable .science session packages, and specify an exchange contract for these recorded relationships. Version and assessment targets remain attributable while receiving-workspace identifiers can be remapped, eligible contents can be omitted explicitly, and imported history remains separate from a writable fork. A controlled session tested an incorrect first version, a reviewed correction, an unreviewed revision and a planned but unexecuted step. We compared complete and partial exports with source records extracted independently of the exporter, then inspected imports into separate projects within the same installation. Both conditions retained the tested version and review associations, kept the unreviewed revision distinct from earlier assessments and represented excluded content as unavailable. A documentation-rich ordinary directory also supplied evidence for all seven static inspection questions. A separate registry case connected a table to its recorded task, execution and review; offline execution of its retained script and fixed input reproduced two saved CSV tables byte for byte. The study contributes an implemented exchange contract and a controlled examination of its preservation rules, content-selection constraints and interpretation boundaries.

items.title: Convex-Analytic View of Query Selection for Safety Verification of Markov Decision Processes
items.content: arXiv:2610.17541v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Safety verification of a Markov decision process (MDP) asks whether the probabilities of reaching several failure states jointly lie in a convex safe region under every scheduler. Watanabe and Unno (2026) prove safety by refining an outer approximation of the failure probabilities, where each query bounds a nonnegative weighted sum of the probabilities. Their rule selects weights by the largest Euclidean violation. We present a unified framework to measure violation in an explicitly chosen error unit: directions are scored by the support-function gap between the outer approximation and the safe region, normalized by the support function of the unit. We show that the maximal score, when positive, equals the smallest enlargement of the safe region in multiples of that unit that contains the outer approximation. The Euclidean unit recovers the earlier rule; two new rules are generated by the unit cube and the safe region itself. We experimentally evaluate how the choice of measurement rule affects the performance of safety verification for MDPs.

The contribution is mathematically solid but specialized, with impact mostly confined to the formal-methods-for-RL community.

items.title: Uncertainty Evaluation: Bridging Machine Learning and Measurement Science
items.content: arXiv:2610.18066v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Reliable uncertainty evaluation is essential for assessing the trustworthiness of machine learning (ML) predictions, particularly in safety-critical applications. This paper explores conceptual analogies between uncertainty evaluation in ML and measurement science, drawing on the evolution of metrology from error-based approaches to the framework established by the Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement (GUM). Particular attention is devoted to the distinction between process-level and result-level quality and to the limitations of the conventional classification of ML uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic components. It is argued that this dichotomy, similarly to the traditional distinction between random and systematic measurement errors, is inherently model-dependent and provides an insufficient basis for a unified uncertainty evaluation framework. Further analogies between machine learning and measurement field of knowledge are identified concerning distribution shifts, anomalous operating conditions, and the validity of uncertainty evaluation. Building on the proposed considerations, the paper advocates a metrology-inspired approach based on the systematic identification, quantification, and propagation of uncertainty contributions. By extending the methodology already established in measurement science to ML, this approach could offer a potentially rigorous, consistent, and transferable framework for evaluating the trustworthiness of individual predictions.

The goal is to ground ML trustworthiness, especially in safety-critical applications, in established measurement science.

items.title: Looped Reasoning Finishes Earlier Than You Think
items.content: arXiv:2610.18174v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Looped reasoning with dynamic depth can be viewed as relaxation toward solution attractors in a learned dynamical landscape. In practice, however, latent trajectories often oscillate, cycle, or drift rather than cleanly converge to stable fixed points. How these non-stationary dynamics contribute to reasoning and constrain convergence remains unclear. We show that slowly decaying oscillatory modes can impose their convergence rate on coupled latent dynamics, creating a bottleneck. Yet damping these modes indiscriminately can disrupt the reasoning computation they support. This tension motivates an architectural approach: introducing rotational degrees of freedom along which symmetry-generated rotational motion leaves the reasoning-relevant quotient dynamics unchanged by construction. We propose QRR (Quotient Recurrent Reasoner), a gauge-equivariant recurrent architecture with an exact per-token phase-rotation symmetry. Motion along these symmetry directions leaves the quotient representation unchanged and is dynamically decoupled from reasoning-relevant dynamics. Empirically, QRR achieves stable and faster convergence to solution roots in quotient space, without forming a dominant slow oscillatory bottleneck, while matching or surpassing recent recurrent reasoning models on Sudoku, Maze, and Mini-ARC.

items.summary: The paper analyzes looped reasoning models with dynamic depth through the lens of learned dynamical systems, showing that slowly decaying oscillatory modes can bottleneck convergence of latent trajectories that oscillate or drift rather than settle. It proposes adding rotational degrees of freedom so symmetry-generated rotational motion separates from reasoning-relevant computation, enabling earlier, cleaner stopping. This connects recurrence dynamics to adaptive-compute efficiency.

items.title: A Controlled Evaluation of Curvature Inspired Scalar Feature Scaling for Domain Generalization
items.content: arXiv:2610.18227v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Domain-specific curvature is an appealing idea for domain generalization (DG), but curvature learning can denote substantially different computations. This paper evaluates one deliberately narrow implementation: the code calls it HyperDG, but it rescales Euclidean encoder features during training by learned positive scalars and uses an ordinary linear classifier on unscaled Euclidean features at inference. It does not implement a Lorentz or Poincar\'e representation, geodesic prediction, or a Sharpness-Aware Minimization inner loop. We audit the executed objective and evaluate six conditions on PACS, VLCS, Office Home, and TerraIncognita. The completed design contains 384 runs: six conditions, four held-out targets, and four run seeds per dataset. Checkpoints are selected using only the three source-validation environments. Inference first averages paired seed differences within each held-out target; targets, rather than 16 seed-by-target observations, are the per-dataset clusters. The full implementation's equal-dataset macro point estimate is 1.61 percentage points below native DomainBed ERM (95% clustered CI [-3.17, -0.04]). All four dataset point estimates favor ERM, but an exact four-dataset sign-flip test gives p = .125 and Holm-adjusted p = .250; we therefore claim no adjusted evidence of a difference. The cleaner domain-specificity contrast, separate learned source scales without their variance penalty versus one shared learned source scale, is -0.13 pp (95% CI [-0.53, 0.27]). Its 90% CI lies within a revision-stage $\pm 1$ pp smallest effect of practical interest (TOST p = .003), supporting equivalence only for the source-selected suite macro, not every dataset, target, or final-step endpoint. The study thus supplies a bounded negative result for this scalar training package; it does not test or refute genuine hyperbolic representation learning.
items.author: Sunny Gupta, Amit Sethi
items.summary: This paper audits HyperDG, a domain generalization method described as curvature-inspired, and finds that its actual implementation merely rescales Euclidean encoder features with learned positive scalars during training rather than using hyperbolic (Lorentz or Poincare) representations, geodesic prediction, or a SAM inner loop. The authors run a controlled evaluation of six conditions across PACS, VLCS, Office Home, and TerraIncognita with 384 total runs to isolate what the technique actually contributes. The work matters because it provides a reproducibility-style reality check on a fashionable geometric learning idea, clarifying whether gains come from curvature itself or from simple feature scaling.
items.reasoning: The paper is methodologically careful, with a large controlled experiment (384 runs, multiple benchmarks and seeds), but it is an evaluation/audit of an existing narrow technique rather than a novel method or major scientific advance. Its contribution is rigor and transparency in a subfield (domain generalization) with a history of overstated claims, which is valuable but niche. Authors are from academia and the scope is limited to four standard DG benchmarks, so impact is likely confined to the DG community.

items.content_html: arXiv:2610.18227v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Domain-specific curvature is an appealing idea for domain generalization (DG), but curvature learning can denote substantially different computations. This paper evaluates one deliberately narrow implementation: the code calls it HyperDG, but it rescales Euclidean encoder features during training by learned positive scalars and uses an ordinary linear classifier on unscaled Euclidean features at inference. It does not implement a Lorentz or Poincar\'e representation, geodesic prediction, or a Sharpness-Aware Minimization inner loop. We audit the executed objective and evaluate six conditions on PACS, VLCS, Office Home, and TerraIncognita. The completed design contains 384 runs: six conditions, four held-out targets, and four run seeds per dataset. Checkpoints are selected using only the three source-validation environments. Inference first averages paired seed differences within each held-out target; targets, rather than 16 seed-by-target observations, are the per-dataset clusters. The full implementation's equal-dataset macro point estimate is 1.61 percentage points below native DomainBed ERM (95% clustered CI [-3.17, -0.04]). All four dataset point estimates favor ERM, but an exact four-dataset sign-flip test gives p = .125 and Holm-adjusted p = .250; we therefore claim no adjusted evidence of a difference. The cleaner domain-specificity contrast, separate learned source scales without their variance penalty versus one shared learned source scale, is -0.13 pp (95% CI [-0.53, 0.27]). Its 90% CI lies within a revision-stage $\pm 1$ pp smallest effect of practical interest (TOST p = .003), supporting equivalence only for the source-selected suite macro, not every dataset, target, or final-step endpoint. The study thus supplies a bounded negative result for this scalar training package; it does not test or refute genuine hyperbolic representation learning.

items.title: FALLNEST: Dual-Domain Dataset Condensation of Imbalanced IMU Data for Wearable Fall Detection
items.content: arXiv:2610.18260v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Wearable fall detection is hampered by rare fall events, scarce labeled IMU data, and the cost of training deep models on large, imbalanced corpora. Existing methods either rely on hand-crafted features with shallow classifiers, which limits learning from raw signals, or train deep networks on full datasets that require re-sampling to counter class skew and demand substantial data and compute. To address this, we propose a novel Fall detection framework via Normalized-gradient and Embedding matched Synthetic Time-frequency condensation, dubbed FALLNEST, a data-centric approach that distills large, imbalanced IMU datasets into tiny, class-balanced synthetic training sets. Building on dual-domain time-series condensation (CondTSC), FALLNEST introduces a fall-specific 7-channel input with accelerometer vector magnitude, class-balanced K-Means initialization, and normalized gradient matching with gradient clipping, combined with MMD-based embedding alignment and multi-view Fourier-domain augmentation, so that class balance arises from the condensed set itself rather than from re-sampling. We evaluate on SisFall, KFall, and MobiFall using strict subject-wise splits and naturally imbalanced test sets, reporting accuracy, Macro-F1, and PR-AUC over five seeds. A 102K-parameter TinyCNN trained on only 32 to 146 synthetic windows (about only 1% of the training windows) reaches 93.5-95.8% mean accuracy and 0.89-0.98 PR-AUC, with standard deviations of 1.0-1.7% in accuracy, demonstrating the efficacy of our approach.

items.title: Bytes to Threats: Byte-Sequence Transformer For Malware Detection
items.content: arXiv:2610.18787v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Existing malware detection approaches heavily rely on handcrafted features derived from static or dynamic analysis of the executable files. These methods require specialized domain expertise, dedicated analysis tools, and time-consuming analysis, which limits their scalability and robustness in the face of the increasing complexity and diversity of modern malware. Consequently, there is a growing interest in approaches that operate directly on raw bytes, which contain rich semantic and structural information. However, capturing long-range dependencies within executable files remains challenging for conventional static and CNN-based methods. This paper presents MalwareFormer, a transformer-based, byte-level malware detection framework that operates directly on raw bytes, without requiring domain knowledge or feature extraction. MalwareFormer achieves an accuracy of 98.35%, a balanced accuracy of 98.32%, a macro-F1 of 98.32%, and a false positive rate of 1.94%, outperforming both baselines across all threshold-dependent classification metrics and demonstrating that transformers provide a powerful and scalable approach for byte-level malware detection.
items.author: Abdelrahman Yassin Eljamal, Abdeltawab Hendawi
items.summary: MalwareFormer is a transformer-based, byte-level malware detection framework that operates directly on raw executable bytes, avoiding handcrafted static or dynamic analysis features, and captures long-range dependencies that CNN-based methods miss. This improves scalability and robustness against increasingly complex and diverse modern malware.
items.reasoning: Solid applied security work applying a well-known architecture (byte-level transformers, echoing ByteNet-style approaches) to malware detection. The direction is sensible but conceptually incremental; two-author academic team and no indication of comparisons to the strongest recent baselines limit impact.

items.title: Graph Coarsening Enables Escaping Local Optima in Compute-Constrained Nonconvex MAX-CUT
items.content: arXiv:2610.19043v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Because its binary optimization landscape contains exponentially many local optima, MAX-CUT is highly sensitive to initialization. We study Particle Polynomial Relaxation (PPR), a moment-based nonconvex continuous reformulation possessing an advantageous optimization landscape. We warm-start PPR with Combinatorial Multigrid (CMG), a spectral graph-coarsening method that produces structure-aware initial solutions in near-linear time without training data. On \texttt{t2g20} ($n=400$), benchmark instance with known exact optimum, the combined CMG+PPR pipeline reaches $97.5\%$ of optimum on average and $98.4\%$ on the best run. An extended variant with discrete local-search refinement reaches the published optimum on all sixty Biq Mac instances evaluated by a recent neural branch-and-bound method. Using a sparse CSR representation, the same approach scales to G-set instances with up to $20{,}000$ vertices reducing memory requirements by up to $3333\times$ while maintaining a consistent improvement over the CMG warm start. Gains are largest on sparse weighted graphs; on dense graphs we complement the pipeline with spectral sparsification.

The combined pipeline reaches 97.5% of optimum on a benchmark instance with known exact optimum and matches published optima across sixty Biq Mac instances with local-search refinement.
items.reasoning: Solid algorithmic engineering with strong empirical results, and the author list includes NVIDIA researchers, but the topic (combinatorial optimization for MAX-CUT) is peripheral to core AI research and the contribution is a pipeline combination.
