items.title: AgriJev: Efficient Agricultural Candidate Scoring with Multi-Scale Adapted Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.19478v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Agricultural systems make decisions over heterogeneous entity types, textual judgments, and knowledge-question options. Generating a textual answer adds decoding and extraction steps to decisions that ultimately require a candidate choice. We introduce AgriJev, a family of adapted Qwen3.5 models at 0.8B, 2B, 4B, and 9B. A shared interface conditions on agricultural text, a judgment question, and candidate definitions, returning scores and relative probabilities in one forward call. We prepare source-aware training records and frozen evaluations from existing agricultural resources, retaining original groups and annotation provenance. Comparisons include original Qwen3.5 models and matched agricultural SFT models, both evaluated through native answer generation. Across 17 external test views, AgriJev-9B reaches 75.44% mean accuracy, exceeding the original and SFT generators by 5.89 and 3.79 percentage points. It outperforms the original generator on 13 views and narrows the mean gap to hosted Jev 1.13.0. On a fixed A100 workload, its median scoring latency is approximately half that of same-scale answer generation. Task-dependent gains and failures characterize a practical choice among agricultural model weights and inference contracts.

items.title: Does Machine Translation Retain Media Bias?
items.content: arXiv:2610.19945v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Within the most recent two decades, machine translation (MT) has been advanced from a research area to a mature, deployed technology for prose text and most language pairs. However, language has different dimensions of meaning, and the alluded progress has primarily been demonstrated for propositional meaning.   In this small exploratory study, we investigate whether one type of affective meaning, namely different types of linguistically expressed media bias, are retained under automatic translation for two language pairs, English and German as the source languages, and Bulgarian as the target language. We evaluate four state-of-the-art translation methods to answer the question whether and to what degree a loss of non-neutral language (specifically, 27 types of media bias) can occur as a result of applying MT.   Our empirical findings are consistent with the claim that MT does not fully retain existing news bias of its input source text, but also may add extra bias of its own. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first experimental study of MT media bias retention.

items.title: Analyzing performance of Retrieval Augmented Generation models for Question Answering Tasks
items.content: arXiv:2610.20419v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models have become almost a cornerstone of open-domain question answering tasks; in which the quality of answers generated in the process, greatly relies on the effectiveness of retrieval mechanisms. In the realm of LLM, the last two years have seen tremendous progress in RAG architectures, with many models reporting to have improved performance through various design innovations. The cultural question and answering systems of South Asia, in particular, present a specific challenge since the region is home to the vast number of languages and traditions, which are closely interrelated. Along with these deeply intertwined historical narratives increase the need for culturally grounded and context-aware interpretation. Despite major architectural advances in LLMs, claiming significant improvements, challenges remain when answering these region specific questions in native languages. In this study, we aim to extract high-performing factors to guide the development of optimized hybrid RAG systems. We further explore whether the integration of RAG changes performance differently for culturally grounded and non-cultural questions in a South Asian multilingual setup, and whether RAG produces a higher overall percentage of correct answers than contexted answering. We also examine how LLM performance changes when RAG methods are integrated into the question-answering pipeline in comparison with non-contexted and contexted answering and, evaluate whether the introduction of RAG benefits popular or non-popular culturally grounded questions more. Not only does our work evaluate the current methods but also carves a path for future designs of more accurate and efficient question-answering pipelines.

items.title: Reliability-Aware Multimodal Sentiment Prediction Under Local Modality Missingness
items.content: arXiv:2610.20543v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multimodal sentiment models are usually evaluated on complete utterances, yet streams often lose a contiguous span of text, audio, or video. We study local missingness on aligned CMU-MOSEI features. Our reliability-aware network (RM-Net) keeps the original temporal positions, represents unobserved positions with a learned token, outputs bounded per-modality intensity contributions gated by observation quality, and is trained with dual-view masking of contiguous segments. We fuse five RM-Net seeds with a LoRA-adapted BERT text expert, using a fusion weight that depends only on the visible fraction of content tokens. Architecture, checkpoint, and fusion choices were made on the validation split. On the held-out split, the fused model reaches a macro-F1 of 0.655 on clean inputs and 0.634 under 40\% mixed missingness; its two-view average exceeds the auxiliary-head baseline by 0.024 (95\% video-cluster bootstrap interval [0.003, 0.045]). Because this split was inspected during development, these numbers are not a blind test. For explanations, exact Shapley attributions over the eight modality subsets and position-level occlusion show that top-ranked positions reduce the predicted-class probability faster than random positions (AUC gap 0.113 on validation). We also describe an auditable word-level alignment pipeline for raw clips; its outputs do not feed the predictive models.

items.title: A$^3$PreCore: Robust Rigid Registration for Native FLAIR-Space Brain-Mask Transfer
items.content: arXiv:2610.20561v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reliable brain-mask transfer into native fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) space can fail when T1-to-FLAIR rigid registration is unstable. We developed A$^3$PreCore, a six-degree-of-freedom rigid-registration strategy that aligns the full bias-corrected T1-weighted image to native FLAIR using normalized mutual information while preserving the established T1-space anatomical mask. We also introduced extended quantitative quality control (E-QC), which characterizes mask extent, field-of-view-relative position, FLAIR intensity support, boundary support, inferior morphology, and pairwise geometric disagreement. In 78 participants with paired T1-weighted and FLAIR imaging, A$^3$PreCore was compared with fsl_anat and the Brain Extraction Tool (BET). Gross rigid-body misregistration occurred in 21/78 fsl_anat outputs (26.9%) and 0/78 A$^3$PreCore outputs (exact two-sided McNemar p=9.54 x 10^-7). Among 57 participants without gross fsl_anat misregistration, A$^3$PreCore preserved close agreement (median Dice=0.993; median paired Delta NMI=-0.00007, p=0.429). A$^3$PreCore remained broadly concordant with BET (median Dice=0.955), with less inferior and extracranial extension in representative comparisons. Method-blinded neuroscientists ranked A$^3$PreCore first in 35/40 participants (87.5%). E-QC additionally exposed severe orientation-related disagreement not evident from global descriptors or centroid displacement alone. These findings support A$^3$PreCore as a robust native-FLAIR brain-mask transfer strategy and E-QC as a complementary framework for multidimensional mask characterization and participant-specific geometric quality control.

items.title: PPA 3: A Brief Defense of Indexical Reasoning
items.content:
[This is the third piece in my series on the Parametric Process Assumption (PPA), a new model of anthropics. You should start here if you are just seeing this for the first time.

The previous piece is "Mosaic Plots for Visualizing Anthropic Distributions."

TLDR:

- Non-indexical reasoning (what we're calling the "Updateless Double Halfer" method, or UDH) states that you should not assign explicit probability to the statement "I am a particular observer"
- Unlike the SSA or SIA, this approach is not robust to observations of randomness independent of all other variables.
- Radford Neal's Full Nonindexical Conditioning (FNC) states that as you observe more randomness, the UDH converges to the SIA

The next piece is "Parametric Modeling and Types of Uncertainty."]

As we discussed in the last piece, this series will be primarily focused on indexical models of anthropics, where “who you are” is modeled explicitly with a variable, and the existence of this variable causes a distortion in the probabilities you assign to world states. These distortions, applied unilaterally, inevitably seem to cause all sorts of paradoxes. The appeal of non-indexical models is that, by virtue of not adding these variables, they produce no distortions to the prior.

There was a point where I found this sort of non-indexical reasoning very tempting, mostly because it really did seem, at first, to resolve many problems of anthropics. In particular, Ape in the Coat’s series on the topic did a lot to convince me that no indexical model could be truly self-consistent....

items.summary: Defends indexical models of anthropics (SSA, SIA) against non-indexical alternatives like the Updateless Double Halfer and Radford Neal's Full Nonindexical Conditioning, noting that UDH converges to SIA as randomness observations accumulate.
items.reasoning: Engages seriously with published work (Neal's FNC) and clarifies trade-offs between indexical and non-indexical approaches; solid philosophical analysis but limited novelty and reach.

items.title: ScienceBuddy-PV: A Verifier-Governed Recursive Improvement Protocol for Panvascular Intervention Research
items.content: arXiv:2610.14523v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: ScienceBuddy-PV adapts the ScienceBuddy recursive-in-recursive design to panvascular intervention research through a structured evidence ledger, device-vessel ontology, abstention contract and retained failure bank. Recursive harness optimization and outer-loop model learning, including reinforcement learning, are specified but not executed. We audit a fixed component, rather than the complete agent system, using separate ARCADE syntax and stenosis tasks (1,000 training, 200 validation and 300 test images per task). A shared task-masked convolutional model was trained once per representation setting; its parameters and the heuristic support gate were then held fixed, with the stenosis threshold selected on validation data. On the locked test sets, syntax Dice was 0.475 (95% CI 0.459-0.490) and stenosis Dice was 0.231 (95% CI 0.214-0.249). Stenosis pixel AUROC was 0.957 and AUPRC was 0.180 at prevalence 0.00975. The gate accepted 76.7% of stenosis-frame outputs versus 100% for a score-only comparator. In a constructed mask audit, it accepted 44.3% of reference candidates and rejected 55.7%, exposing the cost of abstention. Acceptance does not establish correctness or clinical safety. This public-data component audit makes support and abstention measurable and provides a reproducible protocol for future collaborative agent studies. It does not demonstrate recursive improvement, patient-level validity or clinical device recommendations.

items.title: Active Neural Matter: A Finite-Window Response Framework for Physical Systems and Distributed AI Workflows
items.content: arXiv:2610.14549v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Physical systems and distributed AI workflows can retain past information, receive delayed feedback and combine conflicting signals. These features pose a common modeling problem: determining what information about past interactions a state must retain to account for future responses. Active Neural Matter (ANM) addresses this problem through a finite-window response framework. Forward analysis uses each system's dynamics to predict state and output responses to perturbations, separating propagation from output sensitivity. Inverse analysis tests whether a candidate state retains enough information for these responses. With the system and future inputs or interaction rules fixed, distinguishable responses from histories assigned the same state identify distinctions the representation must preserve. Their distributional separation gives a lower bound on the worst-case error of approximating behavior from that state. Uncertainty bounds distinguish rejection, support within a fixed tolerance on tested comparisons, and unresolved cases. Delayed-consensus simulations check analytical predictions of response amplitude and phase over a narrow range of delays; flocking illustrates dependence on the chosen observable. An exact delayed-return construction establishes a sufficient state for a specified program. The AI studies identify distinctions in interaction history and evidence order that a representation must preserve to reproduce observed response distributions. Tests on new histories in a controlled feedback task provide bounded support for a state specified by the task instructions; the instructed rule predicts every observed action. ANM connects response prediction to measurable information requirements, separating behavioral fidelity from task correctness and initial-state adequacy from a closed evolution law for that state.

items.title: AI-Native Product Management: A Vision
items.content: arXiv:2610.14823v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to support product management tasks. At the same time, AI-native research and development (R&D) may increase software realization capacity. Organizations may realize software faster than they can identify, qualify, and reconsider what should be realized. This paper asks how product management should be re-envisioned under these conditions. We synthesize research on software product management, product learning, human-AI collaboration, and the Product Management and R&D boundary. We propose a vision in which AI becomes a persistent participant in product work. The vision covers sensing, exploration, decision-making, realization, and learning. We propose six principles and make the vision tangible through an operating model grounded in human professionals, AI personas, agents, skills, and a shared product context. We further argue that AI-native Product Management and AI-native R&D can form a continuous product-learning process. Finally, we identify four AI-specific research directions that require empirical investigation.

items.title: Protein Crystallization Segmentation and Classification Using Subordinate Color Channel in Fluorescence Microscopy Images
items.content: arXiv:2610.15286v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The accuracy of detecting protein crystals for fluorescence microscopy images is very critical for high throughput and automated systems. Although the trace fluorescent labeling method could highlight protein crystals, reflection and emission from the fluorescence dye is not always due to crystal regions. Therefore, the analysis of the peak wavelength in the emission spectra of a fluorophore may not always yield effective results. In this paper, we show that using the subordinate color intensity corresponding to longer wavelengths than the peak wavelength of the emission spectra could improve the accuracy of protein crystal detection. Hence, we have built a segmentation method based on the percentile intensity of the subordinate color for trace fluorescently labeled (TFL'd) protein crystallization trial images. Compared to using the dominant color channel, our segmentation method on subordinate color channel was able to reduce the misclassification rate of likely-leads or crystals as non-crystals by the percentage of from 9.71% to 2.02% depending on the classifier. Similarly, the accuracy of classifiers were increased by the percentage of from 1.77% to 5.53%. Our method reached around 94% accuracy while keeping misclassification of likely-leads and crystals as non-crystals below 1%. Although the trace fluorescent labeling method could highlight protein crystals, reflection and emission from the fluorescence dye is not always due to crystal regions. In this paper, we show that using the subordinate color intensity corresponding to longer wavelengths than the peak wavelength of the emission spectra could improve the accuracy of protein crystal detection. Similarly, the accuracy of classifiers were increased by the percentage of from 1.77% to 5.53%. Our method reached around 94% accuracy while keeping misclassification of likely-leads and crystals as non-crystals below 1%. Moreover, to evaluate the generalizability of our method, we have conducted new wet lab experiments on two proteins, Concanavalin A (Con A) and Ab inorganic pyrophosphate (AbIPPase), and the misclassification rate was below 1%. Our experiments show that using the subordinate channel may be more helpful for TFL'd protein trial image classification.

items.title: Resolution Allocation with Learnable Resizing and Spectral Filter Parameterization
items.content: arXiv:2610.20274v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Learnable downsampling and spectral-domain filter parameterizations have each made convolutional networks more flexible, but their interaction has not been systematically examined. We bridge this gap by examining convolutional kernels learned in the spatial and spectral domains, together with learned downsampling ratios under a cropped resizing implementation. We find that spectral and spatial kernels respond differently to learned resolution allocation, with larger gains for the spectral kernel. We observe this consistently on three datasets (EuroSAT, CIFAR-10 and STL-10) and at two model sizes (differences in accuracy gain of +0.013 to +0.028 on held-out test sets). Part of this difference reflects the greater gain of the spectral kernel from retaining more spatial area, but the difference remains positive when total retained area is matched. This pattern is observed across datasets and model sizes, although its magnitude and dependence on the complexity budget vary with model size and the resizing implementation.

items.summary: The paper systematically studies the interaction between learnable downsampling ratios and spatial versus spectral kernel parameterizations in convolutional networks under a cropped resizing implementation. items.reasoning: A careful but modest empirical study of a narrow architectural interaction; effect sizes are small (+0.013 to +0.028 accuracy) and the relevance to modern transformer-dominated architectures is limited.

items.title: Knowledge Distillation from Large Reasoning Models to Compact Student Models: A Case Study on the John O Bryan Mathematics Competition
items.content: arXiv:2606.31048v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This paper investigates knowledge distillation from a large reasoning model (DeepSeek-R1) to a compact student model (Qwen2.5-7B). Using historical problems from the John O'Bryan Mathematics Competition at Northern Kentucky University (2011-2025), we build a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) training corpus through a dual-agent framework. The dataset is used to fine-tune the student model with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on Apple Silicon hardware using the MLX framework. The base Qwen2.5-7B model achieves 64.67% accuracy on competition problems, while the DeepSeek-R1 teacher achieves 91.40%. An initial 1,000-iteration training run revealed severe overfitting, with validation loss reaching a minimum at iteration 200 before rising steadily. Based on this finding, we ran five independent training runs each limited to 200 iterations with varied random seeds to assess result stability. Across these five runs, the fine-tuned student model achieves a mean accuracy of 69.43% (std dev 0.17%) on the competition dataset, a 4.76 percentage-point improvement over the base model, and generalizes to 73.1% (std dev 0.18%) on the MATH-500 benchmark. We further study how response length affects answer quality across six reasoning levels (R1-R6): accuracy declines consistently from 69.43% at R1 (mean 220 words) to 41.9% at R6 (mean 31.2 words), with the two-person speed section most sensitive to token reduction. These results demonstrate that CoT distillation improves compact student models and that response length is a critical factor in mathematical reasoning quality.

The paper documents overfitting behavior in an initial run and its mitigation, improving student accuracy from 64.67% toward the teacher's 91.40%.

items.title: Deep Learning for Atmospheric Turbulence Mitigation: A Comparison Between GANs and Transformers
items.content: arXiv:2610.19274v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Atmospheric turbulence creates complex spatial and temporal distortions that significantly reduce image quality. This work compares two deep learning methods for turbulence reduction: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Transformer-based models. Both methods are trained and tested on the SOTIS dataset, which includes multi-frame sequences under different turbulence conditions with ground truth references. Our results show an important finding: GAN-based models perform better in severely degraded, low-quality situations, while Transformer-based models achieve better results in moderate to high-quality settings, especially in correcting geometric distortions. We also enhance the Turbulence Mitigation Transformer (TMT) by introducing a refined training strategy, an augmented input design that includes a temporally averaged frame as prior structural information, and a modified loss function that incorporates the Structural Similarity Index (SSIM). These improvements lead to consistent performance gains across various turbulence conditions. Overall, this study provides an in-depth evaluation of deep learning methods for turbulence reduction and offers practical guidance for selecting models in different imaging environments.

items.title: A VR Training System for Robot-Assisted Vascular Intervention with Dual-Mode Control and Model-Based Interaction Response
items.content: arXiv:2610.19413v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Virtual reality training for robot-assisted vascular intervention requires accurate robotic control and effective feedback on guidewire--vessel interactions. This paper presents a VR training system combining asynchronous dual-mode command mapping with sensorless interaction estimation. The system supports velocity-controlled navigation and position-driven incremental manipulation. Guidewire deformation and a Hunt--Crossley-type contact response are combined and temporally filtered to estimate interaction intensity, while trajectory-based visualization supports post-procedure review. Tests confirmed distinct command-dispatch patterns across three velocity gears and the position mode. During hybrid-scene navigation, the estimated response remained low during straight insertion and increased as the guidewire bent within the vascular model. Trajectory analysis yielded a model-derived cumulative trauma work (CTW) value of 15.166 in normalized units and localized regions of elevated interaction. In a preliminary study with 15 novices, physical-phantom task success increased from 53.3% to 93.3% after VR training, while mean completion time decreased from 132.4 s to 96.7 s. These results demonstrate the system's dual-mode operation, deformation-sensitive feedback, and potential to improve subsequent physical-phantom task performance.

A practical surgical-training simulation tool rather than a research advance.

items.title: PPA 6: Indexical Models Don't Have Diversity Biases
items.content:
[This is the sixth piece in my series on the Parametric Process Assumption (PPA), a new model of anthropics. You should start here if you are just seeing this for the first time.

The previous piece is "Improper Priors and the Infinite SIA."

TLDR:

- Neither the SSA nor SIA have any bias towards observer attributes which aren't directly correlated with the number of observers in the universe
- For the Basic Model, which we discuss more at the end of the series, this will apply to any properties of various species (physiology, local universe observations, etc.) which don't a priori tell us something about how long our species will survive.

The next piece is "Temporal Consistency and Texas Sharpshooting."]

Another misconception I had at one point was that the SIA produced a great bias for diversity than the SSA.

By diversity, I mean basically any measure of observers having different experiences from my own. That could mean the existence of a person having a different childhood from mine, or it could mean four-armed green-skinned aliens from the Andromeda Galaxy. Literally anything that isn’t directly correlated with the number of observers in the universe counts.[1]

Both the SIA and SSA update on this type of information identically. To see why, let's start with a simple example where, with 50% probability, only humans exist, and with 50% probability we have a more diverse universe where in addition to the humans we also have an equal number of aliens. Unconditionally, the SIA does say the alien universe is more likely, but once we learn we are human, we revert to the universe prior and the bias disappears:

After learning you are human, the "Human + Alien" universe has the same mass as the "Human Only" universe

So, in practice, the conditional SIA is agnostic about observers different from us in ways we can observe, which includes all of our experiences up to this point....
items.author: Onid
items.summary: Argues that neither SSA nor SIA inherently bias conclusions toward observer attributes (like alien physiology or different life histories) unless those attributes correlate with the total number of observers. This clarifies a common misconception about anthropic diversity effects.
items.reasoning: A useful conceptual correction in anthropic reasoning, but it is a series installment with narrow scope and no empirical or AI-specific content.

items.title: Reference Wording Shapes Retrieval of Robot Task Instructions
items.content: arXiv:2610.17549v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Identifying a robot task from a short instruction is sensitive to which descriptions are available for retrieval. We investigate this effect in the natural-language instructions included with the RLBench manipulation benchmark. We extract 296 fixed descriptions from 62 publicly available task files and compare five training-free lexical rankers over 80 random choices of one indexed description per task. Exact strings assigned to conflicting task labels are excluded from the primary score. Character n-gram TF-IDF achieves 61.3% mean top-1 accuracy on the resulting held-out instructions, compared with 55.6% for BM25 and 54.9% for word TF-IDF. Across gallery choices, character TF-IDF ranges from 55.2% to 66.8%; its 5th-95th percentile range is 56.9%-64.8%. Adding a second indexed description improves character TF-IDF by 7.0 percentage points on matched queries. These results quantify the influence of reference wording and representation choice on instruction-to-task retrieval under a consistent evaluation protocol.

items.summary: This single-author study examines how the choice of indexed reference descriptions affects training-free retrieval of robot task instructions in RLBench, comparing five lexical rankers over many random gallery choices. Character n-gram TF-IDF achieves 61.3% mean top-1 accuracy versus 55.6% for BM25, with notable variance across gallery choices. The work is a modest empirical note on a sensitivity usually ignored in robot instruction retrieval.

items.title: Beyond Black Boxes: Visual Grounding for Text Embeddings
items.content: arXiv:2610.18047v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In this paper, our goal is to represent text embeddings as sketches for three main reasons. First, to visualize text representation and to explore their potential their potential for AI explainability. Second, to investigate the potential benefits of the sketch-based representation for information retrieval. Third, to explore their potential for reasoning, drawing inspiration from the concept of mental imagery. We propose a sketch-based visual grounding framework that transforms text representations into visual topographic sketches. Our approach aims to emphasis the semantics content encoded in the text embeddings through the corresponding sketch.   Evaluations are conducted on the MS-COCO dataset to examine the utility of these sketches for text retrieval. The comparative study of SBERT and Sketch-based method reveals that SBERT retains an advantage in strict top-1 retrieval accuracy while achieving comparable performance to the sketch-based method in top-5 retrieval. A cascaded approach combining SBERT and the sketch-based method outperforms SBERT alone, suggesting that the Sketch-based representation could offer significant potential for information retrieval if trained directly on text.

items.title: ST-GRU PredRNN-V2: A GRU-Based Reformulation of PredRNN-V2 for Video Prediction
items.content: arXiv:2610.18645v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Video prediction requires models to capture complex spatiotemporal dependencies and to retain relevant information over long sequences. PredRNN and its successor PredRNN-V2 address this challenge with spatiotemporal Long Short-Term Memory (ST-LSTM) units that maintain two separate memory states, at the cost of a relatively complex recurrent building block. In this work, we investigate whether the simpler gating of Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) can be transferred to spatiotemporal predictive learning. To this end, we develop a spatiotemporal GRU (ST-GRU) unit as a GRU-based alternative to the ST-LSTM. The ST-GRU replaces the ST-LSTM's three gates per memory state with two GRU-style gates (update and reset), and merges the temporal memory state into the hidden state, which reduces the number of parameters by about 5%. We incorporate the ST-GRU into PredRNN-V2 and evaluate the resulting model on the Moving MNIST video prediction benchmark, following the original experimental protocol. Averaged over ten predicted frames, the ST-GRU-based PredRNN-V2 achieves an MSE of 55.1, an SSIM of 0.883, an LPIPS of 0.065 and a PSNR of 19.53dB. It does not surpass the original ST-LSTM-based PredRNN-V2 on MSE, SSIM or PSNR, but it achieves a lower LPIPS and performs on par with the earlier ST-LSTM-based PredRNN, while using a simpler recurrent cell. These results suggest that ST-GRUs are a promising building block for spatiotemporal predictive learning and motivate further work on their design and integration.

items.summary: The authors replace PredRNN-V2's complex ST-LSTM units with a simpler spatiotemporal GRU having two gates per merged memory state, investigating whether simpler gating suffices for video prediction. This is an architectural simplification study for spatiotemporal predictive learning. Simpler recurrent units could reduce cost while retaining prediction quality.

items.title: Continual Learning for Reliable In-Sequence Molecular Communication
items.content: arXiv:2610.20426v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper considers reliable in-sequence molecular communication, where bio-nanomachines exchange molecule-encoded information in a specified order, and investigates a new simulation-based method to incrementally evaluate communication protocols by gradually increasing the complexity of experimental settings. The proposed method, called Affine Memory Replay (AMR), builds a continual learning (CL) model to estimate communication performance between bio-nanomachines. AMR stores past simulation samples and synthesizes additional replay samples through interpolation and extrapolation between past samples. Through incremental performance estimation tasks, it replays both past and synthetic samples to regularize model updates, helping the model adapt to new experimental settings while retaining knowledge from earlier ones. Experimental results show that AMR significantly outperforms existing CL methods in maintaining overall estimation accuracy across sequentially learned estimation tasks. It effectively balances memory stability and learning plasticity under moderate training cost.

items.summary: The paper proposes Affine Memory Replay, a continual learning method that stores past simulation samples and synthesizes replay samples via interpolation and extrapolation to estimate communication performance between bio-nanomachines as experimental complexity grows incrementally. It targets reliable in-sequence molecular communication, an emerging nanoscale networking domain. The contribution is primarily a simulation-based evaluation methodology with an attached CL technique.
items.reasoning: Novel application area but narrow audience; the continual learning component (memory replay with synthetic samples) is fairly standard, limiting broader significance.

items.content_html: arXiv:2610.20426v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper considers reliable in-sequence molecular communication, where bio-nanomachines exchange molecule-encoded information in a specified order, and investigates a new simulation-based method to incrementally evaluate communication protocols by gradually increasing the complexity of experimental settings. The proposed method, called Affine Memory Replay (AMR), builds a continual learning (CL) model to estimate communication performance between bio-nanomachines. AMR stores past simulation samples and synthesizes additional replay samples through interpolation and extrapolation between past samples. Through incremental performance estimation tasks, it replays both past and synthetic samples to regularize model updates, helping the model adapt to new experimental settings while retaining knowledge from earlier ones. Experimental results show that AMR significantly outperforms existing CL methods in maintaining overall estimation accuracy across sequentially learned estimation tasks. It effectively balances memory stability and learning plasticity under moderate training cost.

items.title: Digital Self-Interference Cancellation for In-Band Full-Duplex Systems Based on Transformer Neural Operators
items.content: arXiv:2610.19490v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Digital-domain self-interference cancellation is essential in in-band full-duplex radios after passive suppression and analog cancellation. It is particularly challenging when the desired signal is strong relative to the residual self-interference. In this regime, conventional iterative digital cancellers update their coefficients from desired-signal-contaminated received samples and may suffer substantial performance degradation. This paper reformulates digital-domain self-interference cancellation as an operator-learning problem. The proposed framework learns the temporal evolution of the residual self-interference channel from historical observations and uses the learned operator together with the known local transmit signal to reconstruct the current residual self-interference. A Transformer neural operator is used to realize this framework. The resulting method is trained in a desired-signal-free setting and then applied in the presence of a desired signal. A continuity-based analysis characterizes the sensitivity of the learned operator to the resulting input perturbation. Numerical experiments in static and time-varying channels, including time-varying SIR conditions, demonstrate stable cancellation performance over a wide range of interference levels. At 30 dB SIR, the proposed method improves the cancellation performance by 5--15 dB over the considered conventional methods.

items.title: Neural POS Tagging for the Low-Resource Saraiki
items.content: arXiv:2610.20279v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Part-of-speech tagging is a fundamental sequence labeling task and an important component for many downstream natural language processing applications. However, Saraiki, written from right to left in a Perso-Arabic script, remains an under-resourced Indo-Aryan language, despite being spoken as a mother tongue by 28,849,579 people (approximately 28.9 million) according to Pakistan 7th Population and Housing Census 2023. This paper presents a manually annotated Saraiki Universal POS tagging dataset developed from plain-text. We annotated the text with 17 POS categories. We evaluate three pretrained transformer encoders under the same fine-tuning setup: XLM-RoBERTa base, Urdu RoBERTa small, and multilingual DistilBERT. Experimental results over five random seeds show that XLM-RoBERTa base achieves the best performance, with 87.29% +/- 0.21% development accuracy and 88.60% +/- 0.21% test accuracy. Urdu RoBERTa small and multilingual DistilBERT also provide competitive results, suggesting that multilingual and related-script pretrained encoders are effective for Saraiki UPOS tagging. The dataset, evaluation setup, and baseline results introduced in this work provide a benchmark for future research on Saraiki NLP and low-resource sequence labeling.

items.title: From Efficiency to Sufficiency: The Cost-Aware Measurement Design Framework for Automated Essay Scoring
items.content: arXiv:2610.19287v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Compute cost in automated essay scoring (AES) is usually treated as a technical efficiency issue rather than a measurement design concern. Yet deployment decisions require more than reporting latency, model size, or inference expense. In high-stakes settings, total burden includes validation, monitoring, adjudication, compliance, and governance; in instructional settings, pricing, licensing, and integration may dominate cost. This paper reframes AES as a cost-constrained measurement system and introduces the Cost-Aware Measurement Design (CAMD) Framework, a four-layer structure consisting of metering, allocation, unit economics, and decision, for translating computational and workflow resource records into decision-relevant cost constructs. Direct cost is specified as monetary outlay plus attributable labor and time, and two criteria, design attribution and auditability, determine what the cost boundary excludes. Burdens that satisfy neither criterion, such as institutional capability and governance posture, are represented as constraints on which designs are admissible rather than priced. The paper defines cost per defensible score (CPDS) and argues that AES systems should be compared by quality-cost sufficiency: minimizing cost among defensible scoring designs that satisfy measurement requirements. Scoring volume conditions all four layers, so cost per defensible score is treated as a function of scale rather than as a single transferable number. CAMD provides a portable basis for representing, comparing, and evaluating cost across AES studies and deployment contexts.

items.title: LLM-Based Policy Compliance Verification of Loan Applications
items.content: arXiv:2610.20155v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Banks rely on extensive internal policy frameworks to ensure that corporate lending decisions comply with regulatory requirements and internal risk standards. Reviewing loan applications against these policies is a largely manual and knowledge-intensive process, which can lead to overlooked policy violations or exceptions. This report presents a prototype of an LLM-based policy checker that automatically verifies loan applications against internal lending policies.   The proposed approach follows a two-step architecture. First, compliance-relevant rules are automatically extracted from policy documents and converted into structured, machine-readable representations. Second, loan applications are evaluated against the extracted rules to identify policy exceptions, non-compliant findings, missing information, and cases requiring manual review.   Evaluation results demonstrate that the rule extraction process is highly stable across multiple runs and consistently captures rules identified as critical by a domain expert. When evaluated on 11 real loan applications with known policy exceptions, the system successfully detected the majority of these exceptions and identified additional compliance issues that had previously been overlooked during manual reviews. While the approach produces false positives and cannot fully replace human judgement, the results indicate that LLM-based policy compliance verification can provide valuable support in the loan application verification process by highlighting potential compliance risks.

items.title: Instruction Mining From Images: Constructing a Synthetic Dataset for Multimodal Learning ILSP DCVLR Competition Submission
items.content: arXiv:2610.19932v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This work presents a compact and reproducible pipeline for synthesizing and curating image-based instruction-response pairs for DCVLR. We draw from the Cauldron collection and use Magpie-style instruction and response synthesis with Qwen2.5-VL-7B Instruct to create concise, image-conditioned instruction pairs. The pipeline consists of instruction synthesis, conditioned on input images and controlled via a system prompt, sanitization, tagging, and filtering of the instructions based on the score obtained by a reward model (DeBERTa-v3). We retain samples with positive scores to maximize the quality of the generated instructions. We observe that score distributions have a median and mean reward score of ~ 1.53 and ~ 1.75 respectively, indicating that most generated instructions are of good quality. The resulting dataset contains diverse instructions in the math, spatial, and social reasoning domains.

items.title: Attention-Based Spatio-Temporal Approach for Fire and Smoke Detection
items.content: arXiv:2610.20141v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In various industries, smoke and fire are two of the most important threats in the workplace. One of the common methods for detecting smoke and fire is the use of infrared thermal and smoke sensors, which cannot be used in outdoor applications. Therefore, the use of vision-based methods seems necessary. The problem of smoke and fire detection is spatiotemporal and requires spatiotemporal solutions. This paper presents a method that uses spatial features along with temporal-based features to detect smoke and fire in the scene. It consists of three main parts; the task of each part is to reduce the error of the previous part so that the final model has a robust performance. This method also uses transformer modules to increase the accuracy of the model. The results of our model show the proper performance of the proposed approach in solving the problem of smoke and fire detection and can be used to increase workplace safety.

items.summary: This paper presents a three-stage vision-based pipeline combining spatial and temporal features, with transformer modules, for detecting smoke and fire in scenes where thermal sensors are impractical, such as outdoors. Each stage is designed to reduce the errors of the previous stage for robust performance.
items.reasoning: An applied detection system using well-established components; useful for safety-relevant industrial deployment but methodologically incremental with limited novelty or evaluation evidence visible in the abstract.

items.title: Topology-Preserving Multi-Usage Pipe Centerline Refinement under Permanent Tubular Occupancy
items.content: arXiv:2610.19403v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Discrete multi-group pipe routers place channels on a grid or coarse graph. The resulting centerlines are topologically feasible but typically contain many axis-aligned corners. For permanently occupied fluid tubes---as in additively manufactured hydraulic manifolds---those corners are undesirable: they degrade geometric fairness and, in practice, flow quality. This technical report studies the downstream geometric stage that starts from a fixed routing topology and a feasible coarse layout, and refines tubular centerlines under permanent clearance.   Unlike classical robotic path smoothing, which usually fair one temporary open trajectory, our setting is a branched manifold with declared terminal usages, finite tube radii, and static cross-group occupancy. We formalize the refinement problem, highlight the multi-usage junction conflict that a single shared branch point cannot resolve, and outline a hybrid trunk-share / junction-split parameterization with soft geometric costs and hard clearance acceptance. On a multi-group suite ($8$ groups $\times$ $8$ terminals, $r{=}2$) with capsule clearance, the refine reaches full hard-accept success, $\kappa r\lesssim 1$, and about a $95\%$ relative drop in the soft objective. Physics-based pressure-drop optimization is intentionally deferred to a later PDE stage; here the objective remains geometric.

items.title: Rogue AI developers as hostis humani generis: under an international AI treaty, should they be subject to international concurrent jurisdiction?
items.content:
An international treaty banning superhuman AI will, necessarily, require the arrest of rogue AI developers who violate the treaty. But who should be authorized to conduct these arrests? Should there be some sort of international concurrent jurisdiction, allowing at least some countries to conduct arrests of defectors within other countries’ territory?

The default approach - allowing countries to make such arrests only within their own borders - may quickly cause the treaty to fall apart. If national governments operate under the thesis that anyone who achieves superhuman AI (artificial superintelligence, or ASI) will immediately have dominion over the rest of the world, any government has reason to defect and begin racing to build ASI if they even suspect any other country is also defecting (for instance, by choosing not to arrest their own citizens who are defecting and racing to ASI). As a result, bad intelligence collection by a single country could lead to the collapse of the treaty, even with nobody actually defecting beforehand.

Another approach is inspired by the hostis humani generis doctrine applied to pirates during the Age of Sail, in which any seagoing country had the right to interdict pirates and try the pirates in their own admiralty courts, regardless of the pirates’ nationality. Under this system, any country would be permitted to conduct arrests of rogue AI developers within any other such country, even though this would mean operating unilaterally within another country’s territory. This solves the previous approach’s core problem, but introduces many new problems of its own. One country might decide to fabricate evidence, or use spurious evidence, as justification to arrest all of another leading country’s known AI researchers. Forces of one country operating on another country’s territory unannounced, or with short notice, could easily lead to a completely unnecessary shooting war that a better-structured treaty would avoid entirely. items.title: Boosting the Learning for Ranking Patterns
items.content: arXiv:2610.16511v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Pattern mining is a valuable tool for exploratory data analysis, but identifying relevant patterns for a specific user is challenging. Various interestingness mea- sures have been developed to evaluate patterns, but they may not efficiently estimate user-specific functions. Learning user-specific functions by ranking patterns has been proposed, but this requires significant time and training samples. In this paper, we present a solution that formulates the problem of learning pattern ranking functions as a multicriteria decision making problem. Our approach uses Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) to elicit weights for different interestingness measures based on user preference. We also propose an active learning mode with a sensitivity-based heuristic to minimize user ranking queries while still providing high-quality results. Experiments show that our approach significantly reduces running time and returns precise pattern ranking while being robust to user error, compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

items.title: Enhanced Trading Systems with Intelligent Market Analysis
items.content: arXiv:2610.13998v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This paper proposes a hybrid reinforcement learning trading framework integrating intraday market data with transformer-based financial sentiment signals. The system extracts sentiment dynamics and semantic event clusters from financial news and incorporates them into a PPO-based trading agent. Experiments on intraday NSE data demonstrate improved risk-adjusted returns compared to price-only baselines.

items.title: Seamless Deployment of Machine Learning Inference at the Far Edge: An Empirical AWS IoT Greengrass Architecture for Industrial Predictive Maintenance
items.content: arXiv:2610.14815v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Industrial IoT sensors produce continuous, high-volume data streams that predictive maintenance needs to analyse in real time. Cloud-centric architectures send all raw telemetry to central servers, which costs latency, bandwidth and resilience. This paper presents a hybrid cloud-edge architecture for manufacturing predictive maintenance built on AWS IoT Core and AWS IoT Greengrass v2, with local machine learning inference at the edge and selective cloud synchronization. We deploy two configurations on real AWS infrastructure and compare them: a cloud-only baseline (Configuration A) and the proposed hybrid edge architecture (Configuration B). We measure end-to-end inference latency, bandwidth consumption and inference accuracy. Configuration B cuts cloud-bound bandwidth by 86.8% (63.6 KB to 7.2 KB per 200-reading window) and decision latency by 256x (23.1 ms cloud round trip to 0.09 ms local inference). At the edge, with no cloud involvement, it keeps an anomaly-class F1 score of 0.84 and 91% recall. The evaluation also instruments system uptime and Stream Manager queuing under cloud disconnection; the quantitative disconnection experiment is left as planned work. Our review of the literature points to four gaps that this work addresses: the lack of empirically validated Greengrass v2 deployments for predictive maintenance, unquantified bandwidth savings from selective edge synchronization, unmeasured resilience under cloud disconnection, and the open MLOps feedback loop at the edge.

items.title: DTScribe: Generating Models for Digital Twin Reporting using Local Large Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.18635v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The development of a digital twin brings together many stakeholders and technical components. We have previously investigated the reporting of the conceptual architecture for these digital twins as an artifact for discussion. However, we find that the activity of modeling the digital twin for visualization and consensus-building can be quite tedious and time-consuming.   In this article, we explore the automation of model generation using large language models, targeting the model required for digital twin reporting. Our approach is designed to ingest digital twin documents and output both the conceptual architecture visualization and a reporting page for that digital twin. We first extract from the input the key details aligning with our twenty-one-characteristic Digital Twin Description Framework described in previous work. Then, we generate a description model in the Ontological Modeling Language, representing the digital twin as a constellation of models, data, enablers, and services. We utilize refinement loops with large language models acting as judges and ontological reasoning to increase artifact quality as measured by our metrics.   We investigate how architectural and parameter choices affect artifact quality, such as how refinement loops enable local large language models to produce sufficiently high-quality results comparable to larger models. We also detail insights and lessons learned useful for practitioners, such that they can integrate our techniques to accelerate their digital twin reporting or for other model generation tasks. These insights include the use of medium-sized local models (around 20 billion parameters), the avoidance of large language models as judges and clustering for characteristic extraction, and the recommendation of at least two reasoner loops for Ontological Modeling Language refinement.

items.summary: DTScribe automates the tedious modeling required for digital twin reporting by using local LLMs to ingest digital twin documents and produce conceptual architecture visualizations and reporting pages. It targets stakeholder consensus-building in digital twin development. A practical workflow-automation contribution using privacy-preserving local models.

items.title: KANLab: TensorFlow Playground for Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
items.content: arXiv:2610.20117v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: KANLab is a browser-based visualization tool designed to interactively teach the core concepts of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN), forked from the widely successful TensorFlow Playground. To maximize educational clarity, KANLab omits residual connections and learnable scaling parameters found in modern KAN implementations, ensuring that displayed B-spline activation curves directly correspond to their underlying trainable control points. Users can inspect and modify activation functions, initialization schemes and observe gradient descent correcting manual disruptions. Furthermore, user can explore phenomena such as activation variance, interactive pruning, and re\-/training within a compact 2D machine learning setting. KANLab is open-source and available at https://kanlab.app/

items.title: A Gradient-Regularized Deep Learning Method for Restoring Image in Myopic Vision
items.content: arXiv:2610.19218v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Myopic vision degrades the quality of human vision due to spherical eye defocus aberrations that impair the perception of fine spatial details. To address this limitation, this work proposes a deep learning-based approach to computationally design transformed images that allow individuals with myopia in fixed distance to perceive scenes with enhanced clarity. The method trains a neural network to counteract defocus aberrations modeled using the second-order Zernike polynomial $Z_2^0$. The approach employs a U-Net architecture trained with a loss function combining reconstruction error minimization with spatial difference structural preservation through $\ell_1$ regularization. Training is carried out exclusively on the KITTI dataset, while testing is performed on DIV2K and ImageNet datasets, demonstrating generalization across diverse image distributions. Under myopic conditions modeled by $Z_2^0$, baseline performance shows visual degradation with PSNR values ranging from 19.47 to 27.42 dB across datasets and severity levels. The proposed gradient-regularized method achieves consistent improvements, delivering PSNR gains ranging from 1.48 to 7.34 dB and significantly lower perceptual compared to classical baselines.

items.title: AI Marketplaces Can Contribute to, and Profit From, the AI 2040 Plan: Research Directions and Strategy
items.content:
Epistemic status: Draft-Quality. Partially motivated reasoning.

After my “Not Pinning Your OpenRouter Provider Might Invalidate Your Research” post, a representative of an AI marketplace reached out to me about providers and reproducibility. I unofficially chatted with a representative there[1] about this essay, but they do not endorse this document.[2]

This document is entirely human written. Particular research investigations that can be taken by researchers in AI Marketplaces are in bold. I do not currently plan to work more on this project myself, but I wanted to get the idea out so that others might consider it and build on it.

# Introduction

AI developers are racing towards recursive self-improvement and artificial superintelligence. If this happens, most likely all of humanity loses control to the AIs or the frontier lab irreversibly concentrates their power.

One faction which currently has not-insignificant power over the AI ecosystem are AI Marketplaces. These are organizations like OpenRouter which do not produce frontier models but generate hundreds of millions in revenue (OpenRouter brings in $140 million in annualized revenue, an estimated $50 million / 5% = $1 billion flows through their marketplace, and they just sold to Stripe for $7 billion) as they connect users to the models and providers best suited to their use cases.

If an AI pause or slowdown were to occur, these AI Marketplaces could continue being profitable and influential for years or decades. If no pause or slowdown occurs, then they will quickly become irrelevant, as superintelligence outcompetes their would-be customers and has no need for AI Marketplaces since it can handle its own compute.[3]

This implies that it is in the personal, commercial, and altruistic interests of AI Marketplaces to facilitate and push for an AI slowdown or pause and to prepare to capitalize on one if one occurs. These are the futures in which most of the value exists for AI Marketplaces....

The post sketches how marketplaces' revenue and position could be leveraged for beneficial outcomes amid recursive self-improvement concerns. It is intended as a seed for others to build on.
items.reasoning: Raises a genuinely underexplored governance angle regarding AI marketplaces and includes actionable research directions, but the post is explicitly draft-quality, speculative, and partially motivated by the author's prior interactions. Its contribution is agenda-setting rather than analysis or evidence.

items.title: PPA 4: Parametric Modeling and Types of Uncertainty
items.content:
[This is the fourth piece in my series on the Parametric Process Assumption (PPA), a new model of anthropics. You should start here if you are just seeing this for the first time.

The previous piece is "A Brief Defense of Indexical Reasoning."

TLDR:

- There are two different kinds of uncertainty aleatoric uncertainty pertains to random events like coin flips. It is true randomness and cannot be reduced epistemic uncertainty pertains to things that are fixed but unknown, like the digits of pi. It can be reduced by learning more about the world
- Bayesianism handles epistemic uncertainty by assigning it subjective subjective probabilities, this is known as constructing a prior. Frequentism refuses to assign probabilities to epistemic unknowns, and must use alternative methods When a Bayesian assigns a probability to an epistemic unknown, it is often called a parameter.
- Not everything can be an aleatoric unknown, at some point we must say that certain facts are merely epistemicly unknown, not aleatoric.

The next piece is "Improper Priors and the Infinite SIA."]

## Ways of not knowing

Before diving into the PPA and its implications, let’s take a moment to motivate it philosophically: what do we mean when we say that we are uncertain about something? 

One idea I really like, but which hasn’t really made its way into the LessWrong water supply as much as I might expect, is that there are really at least two different types of uncertainty. The first kind, known as aleatoric uncertainty, is what we conventionally think of as randomness. The roll of a die, the flip of a coin, the configuration of a deck of cards dropped to the floor - that kind of thing....

items.title: (Why) we’re launching the next cohort of Generator
items.content:
TL;DR: The first round of the Generator Residency went very well.

Our residents created and ran several large-scale fieldbuilding, talent infrastructure, and operational projects that have already had important impacts on the ecosystem.  

Six weeks after the program ended, 12 of our 27 residents have been hired to full-time roles at core AI safety orgs, and most have received several offers. 

Kairos and Constellation are running a second round from January to April 2027. Apply to the next round of the Generator Residency by November 1st. 

## Introduction

In April, we wrote AI Safety's Biggest Talent Gap Isn't Researchers. It's Generalists. 

We wrote this because we noticed that organizations across the ecosystem were struggling to hire for key non-research roles. While these roles were often getting many applicants, candidates didn’t meet basic requirements.

The original memo we wrote (that became the post above) inspired us to create the Generator Residency as an intervention to support more generalists trying to break into AI safety.

The program concluded six weeks ago, and this post details the successes we’ve seen from the first round of Generator, which have inspired us to launch a second round of the program.

items.title: Deep Learning-based Semantic Segmentation of Dental Radiographs: Comparative Evaluation of PSPNet, DeepLabv3, UNet, and UNet++
items.content: arXiv:2610.15061v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Accurate and efficient analysis of dental radiographs has become increasingly important for disease diagnosis and clinical decision making. In particular, dental radiographs segmentation plays a critical role as it is challenging due to several reasons, such as low contrast, noise in the images, variations in the image quality, etc. Previous studies have primarily addressed these challenges using convolutional neural networks (CNN)-based models. However, direct comparison of these segmentation models is still challenging due to the variations among the experimental settings. Therefore, we mainly compared four segmentation models, including Pyramid Scene Parsing Network (PSPNet), DeepLabV3, UNet, and UNet++, through a fair, controlled experimentation setting under varying conditions such as image sizes and batch sizes. For this, we used 1269 dental radiography images, and prior to training, we implemented a series of preprocessing techniques. To assess the models, we used several metrics, including Dice coefficient (DICE), Intersection over Union (IoU), accuracy, precision, training and validation losses. According to our results, UNet++ demonstrated the highest IoU score of 0.6719, and a DICE value of 0.7869, showing superior results in terms of segmentation, specifically when configured with an image size of 300x300 and a batch size of 16. In addition, we also explored the effect of image resolutions and batch sizes on model performance and accuracy under different architectures. Therefore, this study provides insights into the strengths of different segmentation models and the potential of deep learning-based semantic segmentation methods for improving automated dental radiograph analysis.

The work supports disease diagnosis and clinical decision making in dentistry.

items.title: Should We Edit the Human Genome?
items.content:
Crossposted from my substack.

## Procreative Beneficence and Genetic Enhancement

## 1. Introduction

Imagine a world where everyone is healthy, intelligent, long living and happy. Intuitively this seems wonderful albeit unrealistic. However, recent scientific developments in genetic engineering, namely CRISPR/Cas bring the question into public discourse, how the genetic enhancement of humans should be evaluated morally. In 2001, when preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) and in vitro fertilisation (IVF), enabled parents to select between multiple embryos, Julian Savulescu introduced the principle of procreative beneficence (PPB), arguing that parents have the obligations to choose the child that is expected to have the best life [11].

In this essay I argue that accepting the PPB and the consequentialist principle (CP) that two acts with the same consequences are morally on par, commits one to accepting the parental obligation to genetically enhance their prospective children, i.e. embryos, a position Savulescu doesn’t explicitly endorse but I argue is committed too. As the argument I provide may seem like a slippery slope, the largest part of this essay is tasked with responding to a multitude of possible objections. I will argue that even though there are differences between the application of PPB and genetic enhancement of embryos, they do not demarcate a relevant moral difference between the two in respect to their obligatoriness....
items.author: Walter Veit
items.summary: A philosophy essay arguing that accepting Julian Savulescu's principle of procreative beneficence, together with the consequentialist principle that acts with identical consequences are morally equivalent, commits one to an obligation of genetic enhancement of embryos via technologies like CRISPR. The bulk of the essay defends this argument against objections.
items.reasoning: Careful, structured bioethical argument building on established literature, but it is philosophy rather than AI research, largely republishes substack content, and breaks little new ground beyond extending an existing position.
items.summary_html: A philosophy essay arguing that accepting Julian Savulescu's principle of procreative beneficence, together with the consequentialist principle that acts with identical consequences are morally equivalent, commits one to an obligation of genetic enhancement of embryos via technologies like CRISPR. The bulk of the essay defends this argument against objections.

In this essay I argue that accepting the PPB and the consequentialist principle (CP) that two acts with the same consequences are morally on par, commits one to accepting the parental obligation to genetically enhance their prospective children, i.e. embryos, a position Savulescu doesn’t explicitly endorse but I argue is committed too. As the argument I provide may seem like a slippery slope, the largest part of this essay is tasked with responding to a multitude of possible objections. I will argue that even though there are differences between the application of PPB and genetic enhancement of embryos, they do not demarcate a relevant moral difference between the two in respect to their obligatoriness....

items.title: PPA 2: Mosaic Plots for Visualizing Anthropic Distributions
items.content:
[This is the second piece in my series on the Parametric Process Assumption (PPA), a new model of anthropics. You should start here if you are just seeing this for the first time.

TLDR:

- This series will use a visualization called " mosaic plots "
- Mosaic plots represent outcomes in a probability distribution as boxes, with relative sizes representing the probabilities of different outcomes
- Mosaic plots can be conditioned by throwing out all boxes that don't meet some condition
- We show Mosaic plots for the SSA, SIA, and explain that they are "indexical" because they assign probability to being a particular observer
- A non-indexical distribution we call "Updateless Double Halfer," all in the Sleeping Beauty Problem

The next piece is "A Brief Defense of Indexical Reasoning."]

A tool we will be using a lot in this series is what is known as a mosaic plot. A mosaic plot is just an illustration of a probability distribution with a bunch of boxes, where each box corresponds to some outcome and the size of each box is proportional to the probability of that outcome. The roll of a six sided die, for instance, would look like this:

Here, you can see that each outcome (1 through 6) is equally likely, as all boxes are the same size.

The main value of mosaic plots for us is that they make conditioning very easy. For instance, if the only thing you knew was that the die had come up even, then you could remove all odd boxes and get a new mosaic plot that shows only the even ones as options.

In this new chart, we have three equally likely outcomes: 2, 4, and 6. From these two charts we could conclude that, for example, P(4) = 1/6 and P(4 | even) = 1/3.

In terms of anthropics, if we were to apply the SSA to the Sleeping Beauty problem, it would look like this:...

items.title: EmoXpt: Analyzing Emotional Variances in Human Comments and LLM-Generated Responses
items.content: arXiv:2501.06597v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The widespread adoption of generative AI has generated diverse opinions, with individuals expressing both support and criticism of its applications. This study investigates the emotional dynamics surrounding generative AI by analyzing human tweets referencing terms such as ChatGPT, OpenAI, Copilot, and LLMs. To further understand the emotional intelligence of ChatGPT, we examine its responses to selected tweets, highlighting differences in sentiment between human comments and LLM-generated responses. We introduce EmoXpt, a sentiment analysis framework designed to assess both human perspectives on generative AI and the sentiment embedded in ChatGPT's responses. Unlike prior studies that focus exclusively on human sentiment, EmoXpt uniquely evaluates the emotional expression of ChatGPT. Experimental results demonstrate that LLM-generated responses are notably more efficient, cohesive, and consistently positive than human responses.
items.author: Shireesh Reddy Pyreddy, Tarannum Shaila Zaman
items.summary: EmoXpt is a sentiment analysis framework that examines emotional dynamics in human tweets about generative AI (ChatGPT, OpenAI, Copilot, LLMs) and compares them with the sentiment of ChatGPT's own responses. It uniquely compares human sentiment toward generative AI against the emotional tone of an LLM's replies. The study offers descriptive insight into public perception and LLM emotional presentation.
items.reasoning: A modest empirical study with limited methodological novelty; sentiment analysis of tweets about AI plus response comparison is largely descriptive and dated (January 2025 arXiv, referencing earlier models). Useful as a snapshot of public opinion but unlikely to influence the field materially.

items.title: Object Pose from 2-D to 3-D Point and Line Correspondences
items.content: arXiv:2610.19734v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In this paper we present a method for optimally estimating the rotation and translation between a camera and a 3-D object from point and/or line correspondences. First we devise an error function and second we show how to minimize this error function. The quadratic nature of this function is made possible by representing rotation and translation with a dual number quaternion. We provide a detailed account of the computational aspects of a trust-region optimization method. This method compares favourably with Newton's method which has extensively been used to solve the problem at hand, with Faugeras-Toscani linear method [6] for calibrating a camera, and with the Levenberg-Marquardt non-linear optimization method. Finally we present some experimental results which demonstrate the robustness of our method with respect to image noise and matching errors.
items.author: Thai Quynh Phong, Radu Horaud, Adnan Yassine, Pham Dinh Tao
items.summary: A classical computer vision method for optimally estimating camera-object rotation and translation from point and/or line correspondences, using dual number quaternions to obtain a quadratic error function minimized via trust-region optimization. It is compared favorably against Newton's method, Faugeras-Toscani calibration, and Levenberg-Marquardt.
items.reasoning: Solid but essentially classical geometry work in the long-established pose estimation literature; dual number quaternions and trust-region methods are well-known tools. Limited novelty for the modern AI research agenda, likely a revival or extension of older techniques.

items.title: Where Polanyi Meets Galois: Tacit Knowing as an Algebro-Deterministic Operation, Toward Re-rooting AI-Generated Science
items.content: arXiv:2610.16102v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We argue that tacit knowing is better modelled as an operating regime of one memory substrate than as a kind of content. The substrate is VaCoAl, an algebro-deterministic XOR-and-shift hyperdimensional memory over GF(2), realized as CASRAM (commercial SRAM-CAM) and PyVaCoAl (DRAM-CAM).In VaCoAl/PyVaCoAl a directed acyclic graph (DAG) reads two ways. Repairing every collision (Rescue mode) makes the trace exactly auditable but ranks no path higher; tolerating collisions (Don't Care mode) yields a path-integrated confidence, CR$_2$, that silently favours direct routes. This audit-valuation complementarity is a formal counterpart of Polanyi's claim that tacit and explicit knowledge are not sharply divided. It separates contingent tacitness, which a new query brings out (AlphaGo's game tree), from regime-bound tacitness, statable only in a regime where it is gone (AlphaGo's hunches). (1) Polanyi's from-to structure reads as non-commutative binding, the Identikit as role-filler composition, recognition as majority-vote coincidence. (2) Explicating the valuation destroys it, as attending to his fingers can make Polanyi's pianist falter, yet a closed-form law states it. Polanyi, Nonaka, Tsoukas and Collins each capture part of this but narrowly; even Nonaka and von Krogh's continuum cannot tell contingent from regime-bound tacitness. (3) Collins's three tacit knowledges become strata, one outside the substrate. (4) Our mentor-student DAG is a tacit-transmission graph. (5) Terence Tao's remark that AI-solved problems spawn few follow-ups is diagnosed as rootless explicit knowledge: checkable results whose route no one can follow and that no one yet understands well enough to extend, teach or judge. To re-root them, LLMs generate, VaCoAl/PyVaCoAl keeps an auditable trace with its confidence, and people value, a role virtue epistemology shows cannot be offloaded. Testable predictions follow.

It maps auditability versus confidence-tolerant path ranking in a DAG onto the tacit-explicit knowledge distinction, with implications for AI-generated science.

items.title: Agronomic Characterization and Time-Series UAV Phenotyping to Support Field Pea Breeding in Iowa
items.content: arXiv:2610.19154v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Field pea has gained interest in the Midwest U.S. and has the potential to benefit Iowa cropping systems. This study evaluated 17 accessions and 7 Canadian varieties for agronomic and seed yield performance. This study found that PI accession trials exhibit genetic diversity in phenology and canopy traits, whereas the Canadian elite varieties demonstrated great yield potential under Iowa conditions. The accession genotypes matured between 75 DAP (late June) and 95 DAP (late July) across six site-years. The top-yielding Canadian varieties averaged 1961 kg/ha across two site-years. To comprehensively assess field pea performance, this study extracted time-series Unmanned Aerial Vehicle(UAV)-derived traits, assessed UAV-derived traits, and evaluated their correlations with multiple agronomic traits and yield. The results found that UAV-derived time-series canopy area was the most yield-relevant trait (r = 0.63) among all UAV-derived canopy features, vegetation indices, and manually collected measurements. Compared with yield, UAV-derived canopy area showed higher selection reliability (H2 = 0.87, CV = 13.46%), making it suitable for phenotypic selection and accelerating Midwest field pea breeding programs. This study identifies useful UAV-derived features for pea breeding and demonstrates the value of integrating diverse germplasm, elite commercial varieties, and time-series UAV phenotyping. Combining genetic variation from the accession trial with the yield potential of high-performing commercial varieties provides valuable breeding materials and phenotyping strategies for developing locally adapted, high-yielding field pea varieties for future production in the Midwest.

items.summary: A field study evaluating 17 accessions and 7 Canadian field pea varieties in Iowa, combining agronomic yield data with time-series UAV-derived phenotypic traits across six site-years to support Midwest crop breeding decisions. Top Canadian varieties averaged 1961 kg/ha across two site-years.

items.title: Why are some explanations bad?
items.content:
I like understanding things. Many explanations strike me as insufficient, and I wanted to know what features characterize the explanations that frustrate me. I looked through answers to why questions on Quora, found ones I didn’t like, and tried to find patterns in them. So far, I've come up with the following ways that explanations can go wrong:

## Insufficient specificity

Often, when I'm asking a why question, a general answer will not satisfy my confusion or curiosity. It’s common, though, to not answer specifically enough, ranking as my top complaint with explanations I looked at on Quora.

Here are some examples of cases where an explanation lacks contrast:

Question

Insufficient explanation

Problem

Why do people believe in the supernatural?

Because they have confirmation bias

Any belief can be related to confirmation bias. What about supernatural beliefs make it more related to confirmation bias than others?

Why do people scroll social media?

Because they get dopamine from doing that

Any behavior could be explained in these terms. What is special about social media?

Why are plants green?

Because they emit wavelengths in the range of 495–570 nm

All green things emit those wavelengths!

Why do shot-for-shot remakes exist?

Profit (based on this)

Any movie could be made with profit in mind. A more complete answer could be:

Shot-for-shot remakes are especially profitable because they walk the line of peoples’ preferences for familiarity and nostalgia with novelty. Most people wouldn’t watch the exact same movie twice in theaters, but they are more interested in a new movie if it’s something they’re already familiar with. 

Interestingly, not all questions should be answered with the specificity that the question asker is looking for. Here are some examples:

Question

Explanation

Why does Bill have four legs?

Because he’s a cat and cats have four legs.

Why do men commit more murders than women?

Because men commit more violence in general....
items.author: Elijah
items.summary: The author analyzed answers to why-questions on Quora to identify characteristic failure modes of bad explanations, with insufficient specificity emerging as the top complaint. Examples illustrate how generic answers like confirmation bias or dopamine fail to provide contrastive content that actually resolves the question. The post is an informal epistemics analysis relevant to explanation quality, including for AI-generated explanations.
items.reasoning: A thoughtful informal analysis of explanation quality with taxonomy-building value and indirect relevance to evaluating LLM explanations, but it lacks rigor, systematic methodology, or empirical depth beyond curated Quora examples.
