items.title: PPA 11: The Basic Model
items.content:
[This is the eleventh piece in my series on the Parametric Process Assumption (PPA), a new model of anthropics. You should start here if you are just seeing this for the first time.

The previous piece is "Deriving the PPA."

This piece is part of the technical portion of this series.

TLDR:

- Most of this piece contains proofs for the statements in this piece
- We prove the PPA is negligibly presumptuous, in the sense that, when modeling life emergence as a Poisson point process, we have a presumptuousness of exactly one additional species
- We define anthropic temporally consistency in terms of random processes and show that the PPA, liked the SIA, is temporally consistent

The next piece will be on the using the PPA with infinite universes, and is coming soon.]

At the start of this series, we introduced the “Basic Model” of anthropics. In the Basic Model, the universe is a large random process, and as this process progresses it sometimes spawns subprocesses that generate observers. The parameter of our model, which we call the “propensity for life,” is the average number of times one of these sub-processes emerges.  “Propensity” is a stand-in for the size of everything that exists across any potential multiverse, and it is epistemic - fixed but otherwise unknown, like the digits of pi.

Each species emerges somewhere in the universe, exists and grows for some time, and then goes extinct. Each color represents the different physiology/conditions under which the species exist, controlled by the diversity variable....

items.summary: This is the eleventh technical installment in a series developing the Parametric Process Assumption (PPA), a proposed new model of anthropic reasoning. The piece proves formal properties of the Basic Model, showing the PPA is negligibly presumptuous when life emergence is modeled as a Poisson point process, and defines temporal consistency in terms of random processes, showing PPA is temporally consistent like SIA. It is heavily proof-based.
items.reasoning: Technically serious work within its own framework, but anthropic reasoning is a speculative philosophical area with no established empirical anchor, and this series is self-published without external validation. Its significance depends entirely on whether the PPA framework gains philosophical acceptance.

items.title: (Why) we’re launching the next cohort of Generator
items.content:
TL;DR: The first round of the Generator Residency went very well.

Our residents created and ran several large-scale fieldbuilding, talent infrastructure, and operational projects that have already had important impacts on the ecosystem.  

Six weeks after the program ended, 12 of our 27 residents have been hired to full-time roles at core AI safety orgs, and most have received several offers. 

Kairos and Constellation are running a second round from January to April 2027. Apply to the next round of the Generator Residency by November 1st. 

## Introduction

In April, we wrote AI Safety's Biggest Talent Gap Isn't Researchers. It's Generalists. 

We wrote this because we noticed that organizations across the ecosystem were struggling to hire for key non-research roles. While these roles were often getting many applicants, candidates didn’t meet basic requirements.

The original memo we wrote (that became the post above) inspired us to create the Generator Residency as an intervention to support more generalists trying to break into AI safety.

The program concluded six weeks ago, and this post details the successes we’ve seen from the first round of Generator, which have inspired us to launch a second round of the program.

items.title: Hindsight: a trivia + calibration game
items.content:
I made a betting game called Hindsight (AI slop rulebook at https://hindsight.markets/rules). At last year’s Metagame conference I playtested a face-to-face version but ultimately we gave up trying to come up with methods to trade the chips around conveniently.

The online version is a “TV party game” like JackBox where players view public info on a common screen and private info and decisions on their phones.

Each player starts with 100 chips. The game progresses in a series of rounds until all players but one are bankrupted. In each round there’s a hidden target year between 1900 and 1999. The round has three stages and during each stage:

- A clue is revealed about the year—a birth, death, or event (“Grand Rapids, Michigan becomes the first city in the world to add fluoride to its public drinking water”).
- There’s an auction in which the players bid down how wide a market they’re willing to make (“I’ll quote a market six years wide”… “I’ll do four”…).
- Then the market maker presents a bid and ask price and everyone else must buy or sell N contracts with the market maker where N is the round number. (The escalating stakes prevent the game from going on forever.)

After all three stages, the year is revealed and the contracts settle at one chip per year of distance. The slop rulebook includes other details like who eats the losses when someone goes bankrupt.

I'm trying to test out the game some more: https://signal.group/#CjQKIKhbem4Stz_jiIo8-ZPADFh03t8836fSNFEcMxu_iVYNEhD_NvYQw2RkzfPonZaPvhYZ

items.title: When bureaucracy gives you something it shouldn't
items.content:
Epistemic status: two cases and the statute behind them. The first case rests on one side's account in a lawyer's call-in video; I have not seen her file. I am not a lawyer. I could not find a base rate.

AI use: a Codex session did the research: pulled the video captions, found the Policy Manual section and the Turfah opinion plus related cases, and summed the fiscal year 2025 totals from USCIS's spreadsheet. Claude then fact-checked every claim against the primary sources, proofread, and wrote the footnotes. The text and the opinions are mine.

Bureaucracy is a complex and well-oiled machine. But the individual parts of it are still humans, who make mistakes. I stumbled upon this video, which I found an interesting example of this.[1]It is a conversation between an immigration attorney and a Canadian woman. She married an American citizen and applied for a green card because of that. However, for religious reasons she didn't want to get a tetanus shot. This was already surprising to me - I didn't know there was a religious exception to vaccination when immigrating to the US.[2]Her adviser at the time (not the attorney in the call, and not an attorney at all) told her that in order to achieve this she should apply as normal, without proof of vaccination. USCIS would then send her an RFE (request for evidence) for the vaccination proof, and she would submit a special form requesting the religious exception. It is unclear whether this would have worked at all, because USCIS only grants the religious exception if you refuse all vaccines, i.e. you cannot pick and choose, and in the call it sounded like she didn't want the tetanus one specifically.[3]It is also not explained why it was done this way; apparently one can just include this form in the original application.[4]According to the story, USCIS just approved the application without the RFE, the vaccination or the religious waiver. The adviser told the lady that this was the discretion of the immigration officer,...

It is primarily an anecdotal case study of bureaucratic error and AI-assisted research.

items.title: Too Many Yellow Flags
items.content:
Okay, let's do this thing...

Premise: If a concept can be easily conveyed in an academic setting then the labor required to write it is too boring, too undignified, for a human to perform merely to ensure its conveyance. Instead, to expect a human to write it, the concept itself can no longer be the only thing being conveyed. What must also be conveyed is the sharpness of the concept, exposed through the literary talent and humanity of the writer.

I have a stupid fucking problem. Right now I am floating in the middle of the ocean on a big boat. This is my first vacation in years and it is going poorly. The food is bad, the port stops are being cancelled due to apocalyptic weather phenomena, and it seems there are more mobility scooters and walkers on board than passengers under forty. But none of these are my stupid fucking problem. Rather, my problem is that I must spend part of my miserable time on this earth endeavoring to be accepted on LessWrong as a full writer because the CEO of my company wants me to be able to publish the groundbreaking alignment research that we work on in our internal alignment lab in a place where it will be publicly accessible to thousands of researchers. It is a completely instrumental problem subject to completely instrumental reason. How boring.

However, because of the pace of development I don’t really have the time to write documents myself. The development of complex scientific concepts does deserve some care but it’s increasingly difficult for me to believe that the care they deserve lies in the human provenance of the writing of the academic paper itself --- if it ever did. Most papers are skimmed by most readers most of the time, and while the details can absolutely matter, and some rarefied academic writing is knock-your-socks-off beautiful, most of the work of the university is a university discourse: a very dry thing indeed....
items.author: Dr. Diction
items.summary: A personal essay by a researcher on vacation, reflecting on the awkward process of seeking LessWrong publication approval for their company's internal alignment research, framed around the premise that purely conveyable concepts are too tedious for humans to write without added literary value.
items.reasoning: Colorful meta-commentary on publishing norms and incentives in the alignment community, but contains no substantive research content and is largely anecdotal.

items.title: Did Homo Sapiens scale its Brain by eating Brains?
items.content:
Epistemic status: uncertain, but plausible

I'm going to make the claim that eating meat, and specifically DHA-rich meat, fish and most importantly the brains of land animals, is core to who and what we are as human beings. And because we have mostly stopped doing this in the amounts that are necessary, we are now, long-term, totally screwed.

I think we've all seen this chart:

At some point in evolution the brain to body ratio of some primate species diverged.

My claim is that. Although there will be genetic interrelated reasons for this, the tissue to scale our brains like this came, simply put, from eating the brains of other animals. It could not have come from any other places. There's simply not enough nuts with ALA to get enough DHA to sustainably make brains this big, and too many human tribes lived too far away from coastal areas to get their DHA from fish.

The human primate is quite special, whereas other primates eat mostly fruits and nuts and the like. The human primate was once the apex predator among apex predators.

The Apex Predator.

How high on top of the food chain did we once stand?

all the way at the very top

To figure out what animals eat scientists do this thing called nitrogen isotope analysis.

Scientists say that nitrogen isotopes give us a rough way of reconstructing trophic position and that as you move upward through a food chain, the heavier isotope nitrogen-15 becomes progressively enriched. Plants sit low. Herbivores eating those plants sit higher. Carnivores eating those herbivores sit higher still....
items.author: noma
items.summary: A speculative evolutionary hypothesis claiming that human brain expansion was fueled by consumption of DHA-rich animal brains and meat, arguing plant and coastal fish sources could not have sufficed, and warning that modern diets low in these foods have negative long-term consequences. Self-labeled as uncertain but plausible.
items.reasoning: Interesting armchair speculation with some anthropological grounding, but the author admits high uncertainty, the reasoning is largely informal, and there is no original data or AI relevance.

items.title: South Korea, ACX Meetups Everywhere Fall 2026
items.content:
Hello! Join us if you're broadly interested in ratsphere (LW/ACX/AI safety/EA/etc) stuff and also at Korea around the date of this meetup. I don't have any formal structure or discussion topics in mind, mostly intending it to be just a casual come-and-chat social event.

For language, Korean or English, whichever you’re comfortable with. I’m bilingual, so if it’s a small group I’m happy to bridge between the two (or if everyone happens to share a language, we’ll just use that), and if it’s bigger we’ll probably split into conversations by language anyway.

RSVP here, or email me at dalcy.mail@gmail.com or DM me at @dalcy_me in Discord so that I can get a sense of how many people will be here.

Look for the ACX meetup sign at Terarosa Coffee, POSCO Center (Samseong stn exit 4).
